papers.abstract: Video foundation models have advanced rapidly in understanding and generating visual sequences, while video world models seek to capture the underlying dynamics of the world they depict. Despite their different objectives, both concern the relationship between video observations and an evolving world. This survey adopts world modeling as a unifying lens for examining these developments. Viewing an observed video as a partial, lossy, and temporally ordered projection of a latent temporal world, we organize the literature around four complementary operations: reading infers world properties from observed video; writing synthesizes video from specified or learned world conditions; sharing integrates understanding and generation through common modeling mechanisms; and interacting predicts and updates world states under actions and evolving observations. This perspective distinguishes temporal coherence in observed or generated sequences from consistency in the underlying world state. Across tasks, representations, models, datasets, and benchmarks, we trace a shift in emphasis from clip-level recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and evaluation grounded in interaction and downstream decisions, and we distill the open challenges that follow.
authors: Shengqiong Wu, Meng Luo, Bobo Li, Ziwei Liu, Shuicheng Yan, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Philip Torr, Hao Fei
bullets: Frames video as a partial, lossy, time-ordered projection of a latent temporal world.
Organizes research into reading world properties, writing videos, sharing understanding and generation, and interacting through actions and observations.
Distinguishes sequence-level temporal coherence from consistency of the underlying world state.
Highlights a shift from clip recognition and perceptual fidelity toward persistent state, controllable evolution, physical and causal validity, and decision-oriented evaluation.
Identifies open challenges in representations, models, datasets, benchmarks, and interaction-based assessment.

papers.selection_reason: Survey unifying video foundation models and world models directly fits world modeling and video understanding.
papers.title: Reading, Writing, Sharing, and Interacting with the World through Video
papers.tldr: This survey unifies video foundation and world models through four operations—reading, writing, sharing, and interacting—to study how videos represent and support reasoning about evolving worlds.

papers.abstract: Video object removal and injection are reciprocal editing operations between object-present and object-absent video states, yet they differ substantially in training difficulty. Removal can be effectively bootstrapped from video inpainting and further adapted to erase object-related interaction effects. Injection, however, requires large-scale paired supervision to model object appearance, dynamics, and scene-dependent effects, while perfectly aligned real-world pairs are difficult to collect and synthetic data lacks sufficient realism and diversity. To address this challenge, we present UniVOE, a removal-driven framework for training both video object removal and injection models. We first train an effect-aware remover by transferring video inpainting priors and finetuning on object-present/object-absent pairs. The trained remover converts real object-present videos into object-absent counterparts, creating large-scale paired supervision for injection. An injection model is trained on these pairs in the reverse direction to recover objects together with their dynamics and interaction effects. Moreover, since pixel-level reconstruction alone cannot adequately capture perceptual realism, we introduce a reward-based post-training method that aligns injection results with human preferences using a proprietary reward model. Experiments against strong open-source and commercial systems demonstrate that UniVOE achieves state-of-the-art performance on both object removal and injection, particularly in challenging interaction-effect cases.
authors: Shuzhou Yang, Lanqing Guo, Lingen Li, Weiqi Li, Zhao Zhong, Liefeng Bo, Jian Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training object injection models without large, aligned real-world video pairs.
Transfers video-inpainting priors to train an effect-aware object remover, then adapts it using object-present/object-absent pairs.
Uses the remover to convert real object-present videos into paired object-absent videos for reverse-direction injection training.
Adds reward-based post-training to improve perceptual realism and align injection outputs with human preferences.
Reports state-of-the-art performance against open-source and commercial systems, especially for challenging interaction effects.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models have learned rich 3D/4D priors, making them promising for scene generation and video re-rendering. However, their use in spatial tasks is limited by imprecise camera control, spatial and temporal inconsistencies, and entangled camera motion with scene dynamics. Existing approaches, such as task-specific fine-tuning and post-process warping, often introduce visual artifacts, generalize poorly, or incur high computational costs. We propose WorldForge V2 to achieve accurate camera control while preserving the generative capabilities of pretrained video models. We first develop a training-free guidance framework using warped references to iteratively refine generation along a target camera path. Optical-flow analysis identifies motion-related latent channels for selective guidance, helping separate motion control from appearance. A dual-path strategy further compares guided and unguided predictions to correct artifacts from imperfect references. Together, these components guide viewpoint changes while preserving scene appearance and object motion. To reduce refinement costs, v-cache approximates the correction using the preceding denoising prediction, avoiding an additional model evaluation. We further extend motion localization from latent channels to network blocks and introduce Trajectory LoRA, which concentrates adaptation on blocks most responsive to trajectory guidance. A two-stage training strategy teaches these adapters to denoise the states encountered during guided generation, using limited supervision effectively. This enables reliable camera control with very little training data, with a single training scene already supporting generalization to unseen scenes. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations across multiple datasets show that our method achieves state-of-the-art generation quality and trajectory accuracy in camera-controlled video generation.
authors: Chenxi Song, Yanming Yang, Tong Zhao, Ruibo Li, Joey Tianyi Zhou, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses imprecise camera control, temporal/spatial inconsistencies, and entanglement between camera motion and scene dynamics.
Uses warped-reference guidance, optical-flow-based motion localization, and dual-path prediction to refine generation along target camera paths.
Introduces v-cache to reduce refinement cost and Trajectory LoRA to adapt only trajectory-responsive network blocks.
A two-stage training strategy enables reliable control with limited supervision; one training scene can generalize to unseen scenes.
Experiments across multiple datasets report state-of-the-art camera trajectory accuracy and generation quality.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of WorldForge V2. Given a single image or video frame and a target camera trajectory, the scene geometry is reconstructed and rendered into trajectory-aligned warped frames. WorldForge V2 first performs training-free trajectory guidance in the predicted clean latent space using IRR, FLF, and DSG. Building on this framework, we further introduce an efficient route that directly fuses trajectory information in the noisy latent space with V-Cache, together with a trajectory-sensitive lightweight LoRA scheme for camera trajectory control using only limited training data. The resulting video follows the specified camera path while preserving the generative capability of the pretrained video diffusion model.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of camera-controlled scene generation. Our LongCat and H3 models recover coherent object shapes and material detail from incomplete warped references, including thin structures and partially revealed objects. Compared with the baselines, they produce fewer rendering remnants and more continuous geometry, preserving scene appearance as the camera reveals new content.

Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison for 3D novel-view synthesis and 4D trajectory-controlled re-rendering. For single-image 3D generation (left), our method produces more coherent geometry and plausible newly revealed content. For dynamic re-rendering (right), it preserves human appearance and object motion while reducing floating structures and flattened faces. The training-free guidance yields more realistic results in both static and dynamic scenes.

Fig. 9. Qualitative comparison of Trajectory LoRA training strategies. For LongCat (a) and H3 (b), two examples per backbone place the input and warped reference beside No LoRA, Standard FM, and the full method. The full strategy reduces fragmented geometry and residual rendering artifacts, producing more continuous surfaces and finer scene detail than No LoRA and Standard FM. Red boxes and enlarged crops compare corresponding regions.

Fig. 6. Qualitative transfer of Trajectory LoRA across camera-control methods. Without additional fine-tuning, the same trained LongCat adapter improves surface continuity and object detail in WAH [18] and GWF [16], demonstrating transferable trajectory control.

Fig. 4. Noise-state consistency under different reference-insertion strategies. Direct Insertion leaves gaps in the inferred-noise mean and log-variance between visible and model-generated regions, accompanied by noisy patches and broken structure. IRR reduces these gaps, and V-Cache approximates its correction while retaining continuous surfaces and clear geometric detail.

papers.title: WorldForge V2: Eliciting Camera-Trajectory Alignment in Video Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: WorldForge V2 improves camera-trajectory control in video diffusion models while preserving scene appearance and object motion, using training-free guidance plus targeted lightweight adaptation.

papers.abstract: Large language models have shown outstanding performance on text-first tasks such as coding, math, and writing. Recent efforts are shifting models' training to include scientific problems that often live in highly specialized domains beyond text, such as protein structure and biological images. However, in these scenarios, their general-purpose accuracy compared with specialized algorithms remains in question. One such domain is cell tracking, which requires spatiotemporal awareness of cell dynamics. To evaluate this, we created a new benchmark, CellTrack-Bench, which assesses Vision-Language Models' (VLMs) cell-tracking-related performance against specialized trackers. The full benchmark draws from 15 standard cell-tracking datasets across four imaging modalities and comprises 1,537 problems corresponding to 9,041 cell-linking decisions. We selected a hard subset requiring greater reasoning effort by identifying failures shared across distinct algorithmic trackers. With this proposed dataset, we: (i) evaluated different environment harnesses for VLMs; (ii) benchmarked 9 frontier closed-source models and 13 open-weight models; and (iii) provided a detailed analysis of their failure modes. Code, the stored model outputs, and a pipeline that regenerates the benchmark from the source datasets are available at https://github.com/royerlab/celltrack-bench.
authors: Ilan Theodoro, Jord\~ao Bragantini, Lo\"ic A. Royer
bullets: Covers 15 standard cell-tracking datasets, four imaging modalities, 1,537 problems, and 9,041 cell-linking decisions.
Includes a harder subset built from failures shared by different tracking algorithms.
Evaluates environment harnesses, 9 closed-source frontier models, and 13 open-weight models.
Analyzes VLM failure modes and releases code, model outputs, and benchmark-generation tools.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong potential for video anomaly detection, but dense frame-level inference makes them impractical for real-time deployment. Existing acceleration commonly relies on uniform sampling, which ignores content dynamics and can either waste computation on static segments or miss localized anomalies. We propose MoG-VLM a motion-adaptive anomaly detection framework that leverages motion purely as a lightweight control signal to decide when VLM inference is necessary. To this end, we introduce Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) which performs content-aware sampling to concentrate computation on informative regions while avoiding redundant processing. We further introduce a hierarchical dual-stream design in which dense multi-frame VLM reasoning is activated only around frames with elevated anomaly likelihood, via anchor-triggered context-window expansion with early termination. A fusion module then reconciles these instantaneous semantic cues with temporal action dynamics. Across four benchmarks, our method achieves 91.91%, 84.30%, 87.88%, and 78.96% AUC-ROC on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, MSAD, and ShanghaiTech, respectively, establishing new state of the art on three benchmarks under the zero-shot, training-free setting. On XD-Violence, we improve over the previous best result by +0.57% while delivering a 1.31x inference speedup. These results demonstrate that content-aware allocation of VLM capacity, processing fewer frames more intelligently rather than all frames uniformly, is a more effective axis of progress than uniformly densifying VLM inference across frames. Code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kdawoud91/MoG-VLM.
authors: Khaled Waleed Dawoud, Muhammad Zaigham Zaheer, Khan Muhammad, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of dense frame-level VLM inference and the limitations of uniform sampling.
Uses Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) for motion-adaptive, content-aware frame selection.
Employs hierarchical dual-stream reasoning with anchor-triggered context expansion and early termination.
Fuses instantaneous semantic cues from the VLM with temporal action dynamics.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on three of four benchmarks and a 1.31× speedup on XD-Violence.

papers.abstract: Many questions about a video concern one physical object. Where does the ball end up after the cups are shuffled? Which card is the queen? How often was the mug covered? Video-language models (Video-LMs) recognise such objects in single frames but do not keep them apart over time. On real shell-game videos, open models from 8B to 235B parameters, their thinking variants, a reinforcement-learned tool agent and three training-free tool agents all stay within ten points of chance. We separate semantic identity binding from temporal identity maintenance. An object's identity should be fixed at a moment when the evidence for it is visible, and carried afterwards by a tracker. \emph{Track, Then Bind} implements this principle without training. A promptable video tracker follows every candidate object and draws it with a track number. A frozen vision-language model answers a static question about the identifying evidence, which binds the target to a track. The answer is then derived from the tracked state in text, without asking the model to reinterpret the original video during read-out. A single configuration covers all benchmarks. With Qwen3-VL-32B it solves both VET-Bench tasks, where a fine-tuned trajectory model reaches 92\% and 90\% and the same VLM voting over 16 samples stays at 30--32\%. It answers 55.4\% of the hardest Perception Test cup games, where the best published model answers 41.5\%, and, using track-derived timelines, 48.6\% of TOC-Bench questions, against 37.1\% for the same model answering directly. Drawing the same tracks on the video and asking the question directly falls 12--19 points short of the agent on real cup games.
authors: Di Yang, Xiaochang Li, Muyang Liu, Yufei Wang, Yanhai Xiong
bullets: Video-LMs often recognize objects in individual frames but lose identity across time, especially in shell-game-style videos.
Track, Then Bind uses a promptable tracker to follow candidates and a frozen VLM to identify the target from visible evidence.
The system derives answers from track-based state and timelines rather than making the VLM reinterpret the full video during read-out.
With Qwen3-VL-32B, it reaches 55.4% on the hardest Perception Test cup games and 48.6% on TOC-Bench, outperforming the cited direct-answer baselines.
A single training-free configuration handles multiple benchmarks, though performance remains far from perfect on difficult cup games.

papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity's position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses $\sim$10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games exported from GEAR, an AI game-creation tool; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9\% to 62.9\%, missed count changes fall from 34.7\% to 21.3\%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.
authors: Ruicong Liu, Liangyang Ouyang, Fengbo Lan, Zhixiang Wang, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses programmer-art visuals produced by AI-built games.
Uses video-to-video generation from plain footage, without G-buffers, object labels, or 3D proxies.
LoRA-fine-tunes a reference-video-conditioned video model on paired game-rendering clips and gameplay recordings.
Introduces an entity-level benchmark with 59 held-out cases and 753 entities.
Improves temporal entity matching from 50.9% to 62.9% and reduces missed count changes from 34.7% to 21.3% versus the base model.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of AnyGameRenderer. (a) Paired data from three sources. GEAR games use multi-stream rendering, which pairs each game render with several aligned crude streams such as blockouts and semantic maps. Unreal Engine scenes use two-stream rendering, which pairs a full render with blockouts. Real gameplay recordings are converted into blockouts by detecting 3D bounding boxes. (b) One training sample: the crude clip is the input video <Video 1>, the target’s first frame serves as an optional anchor, and a six-segment caption defines which real entity each crude shape represents and what must be preserved. (c) Text, <Video 1>, anchor, and noisy target tokens form one sequence for the frozen MiniMax-H3 DiT. Only the LoRA adapters on self-attention and feed-forward layers are trained, and the model renders the input gameplay in the prompted style.

The zero-shot model leaves crude shapes unrendered (rows 1–4), drops the input viewpoint for out-of-domain styles (rows 5–6: a top-down blockout becomes a frontal anime scene or a first-person voxel scene), and adds captionnamed characters although the input has only two blocks (row 7). AnyGameRenderer fixes all three. For rows 5–6, the “GT” column is the original in-domain render and serves only as a layout reference.

papers.abstract: World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible-impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.
authors: Taekoan Yoo, Wonkyung Jung, Kyunghun Kim, Kyeongbo Kong
bullets: Addresses the lack of evaluations that identify which physical expectations conflict with video observations.
Uses MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations aligned with video windows to detect and describe violations without task-specific probes or classifiers.
Introduces IntPhys2-Timing, an extension of IntPhys2 with annotated violation intervals.
Achieves up to 70.7% hit rate across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and improves overall possible–impossible discrimination accuracy over compared methods on IntPhys2.
Reveals attribute- and noise-dependent violation-localization patterns across timesteps in reconstructed diffusion- and flow-based video trajectories.

papers.abstract: Real-time polyp segmentation in computer-assisted colonoscopy is hampered by the difficulty of deploying high-accuracy models under strict latency budgets. Frame skipping, which performs inference every K frames and reuses or interpolates the rest, improves throughput but introduces motion blur and lesion misalignment that degrade temporal consistency. To close this gap, we propose the Lightweight Frame Compensator (LFC), a 77K-parameter plug-and-play module inserted before a frozen segmentation backbone. Operating on a three-frame window, LFC fuses consecutive frames via spatio-temporal attention into a single compensated frame, and is trained only on pseudo-labels generated by a differently seeded model, without any expert annotation. Experiments on three polyp video benchmarks show that LFC recovers most of the accuracy degraded by direct frame skipping and, in several settings, reaches the accuracy of frame-by-frame inference, while retaining a 2.05X--2.55X throughput gain. We further evaluate the temporal stability of three backbones spanning CNN, pyramid Transformer, and global-attention Transformer architectures, revealing a spectrum of sensitivity to frame skipping that arises from how locally or globally each architecture aggregates misaligned input. The compensation gain of LFC follows this spectrum: it is largest for high-capacity Transformer backbones, which achieve the best static accuracy but suffer the most under skip-frame inference. LFC thus offers a lightweight, pluggable, and deployment-friendly route to real-time polyp segmentation.
bullets: Addresses motion blur and lesion misalignment caused by skipping frames during real-time colonoscopy segmentation.
Uses a 77K-parameter, plug-and-play module before a frozen backbone to fuse a three-frame window with spatio-temporal attention.
Trains solely on pseudo-labels from a differently seeded model, requiring no expert annotations.
Across three polyp-video benchmarks, often matches frame-by-frame accuracy and recovers most skipping-related degradation.
Benefits high-capacity Transformer backbones most, as they are more sensitive to misaligned skipped-frame inputs.

papers.abstract: Moving object segmentation is conventionally formulated at the sequence and object level, marking an entire instance as moving once it moves anywhere in a video. Recent instantaneous formulations distinguish moving from stationary intervals, but still generate masks at the object level through frozen segmentation foundation models. Because the mask is derived from an instance-level proposal, motion is typically attributed to the entire instance rather than localized to the regions that actually move. Moreover, such instance-level predictions can produce masks even when no part of the instance is actually moving, revealing a more fundamental issue: motion is not an intrinsic property of an instance; it can only be determined by comparing at least two frames. Building on this premise, we introduce MoRSe, which jointly interprets two frames to predict a moving-region mask, distinguishing actual scene motion from apparent motion induced by the camera. A single RGB encoder replaces multi-stage foundation stacks, so no optical flow, point tracks, or separate mask generator is needed at inference. We release MoRSe-5K, a benchmark of 42 sequences with Static, Dynamic-Static, and Dynamic settings designed to evaluate the model's ability to distinguish and localize moving and stationary regions under different camera and scene motion conditions. MoRSe outperforms both specialized moving object segmentation methods and dense 4D reconstruction methods with motion-thresholded predictions, while producing the fewest false positives on sequences where nothing moves.
authors: Wenhua Jin, Tiancheng Chen, Sheng Tang, Jiahao Li, Yupeng Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Juntong Fang, Zesong Li
bullets: Existing instance-level methods label an entire object as moving even when only part moves—or when nothing moves.
MoRSe treats motion as a relational property requiring comparison between frames.
A single RGB encoder predicts moving-region masks without optical flow, point tracks, or separate mask-generation stages.
MoRSe-5K contains 42 sequences spanning Static, Dynamic-Static, and Dynamic motion settings.
It outperforms specialized and motion-thresholded reconstruction baselines, with the fewest false positives on static sequences.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MoRSe architecture. Both frames pass jointly through a UniQuery4R-initialized ViT and a shallow convolutional branch; the two are fused and split into source and target feature pyramids. A camera head reads the ViT camera tokens and predicts per-view pose and field of view as auxiliary outputs that never enter the mask path. Sampled source coordinates form the decoder queries; target features provide keys and values, and four cross-attention blocks refine each query before a shared MLP predicts the motion logit.

Figure 4: Moving regions under a moving camera. Top (Static): the camera moves while the person stands still; every baseline paints the whole person, while MoRSe leaves the frame empty. Bottom (Dynamic-Static): only the child’s hand moves; MoRSe marks that hand alone, whereas the baselines cover the whole child.

Figure 1: Motion is a pair relation, not an object property. Motion needs two observations, so we condition on an ordered source–target pair. Holding the source fixed and advancing the target through the sequence, MoRSe returns an empty mask while the person stands still, then the moving region alone when only an arm lifts, then the whole body once it walks. GMOS marks the same person in every frame, whatever the target.

papers.abstract: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. This task has direct practical value because it helps users locate relevant moments, verify claims, reproduce demonstrated procedures, and make informed decisions from video content. We present a skill-based workflow and OmniDR-Bench for this task. For evaluation, we propose Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs). Each tree contains three dimensions, 23 shared directions, and task-specific atomic binary criteria. The directions test audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation. Audited Rubric Construction (ARC) builds these trees through independent evidence collection, automated checks, behavioral calibration, and iterative human review. OmniDR-Bench contains 50 Chinese and English tasks across 19 realworld subcategories. It includes 6,414 criteria. Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3 out of 100. Current agents still need broader content coverage, stronger causal and logical analysis across modalities, and more accurate citation support. We further analyze models, harnesses, skill configurations, video categories, and research trajectories. The code and data are released at https://github.com/marinero4972/OmniDR-Bench.
authors: Jiahao Meng, Qize Yang, Yuxuan Wang, Yunfei Chu, Wensi Dai, Jin Xu, Yunhai Tong
bullets: Targets video-centered research, where agents must identify questions, retrieve multimodal web evidence, and link report claims to relevant video moments.
Proposes a skill-based workflow, OmniDR-Bench, and Omni Atomic Rubric Trees (Omni-ARTs) covering audiovisual grounding, multimodal evidence use, and interactive presentation.
Uses Audited Rubric Construction to create reliable, task-specific evaluation criteria across 50 Chinese and English tasks in 19 real-world categories.
Across 18 agent configurations, the best system scores 63.3/100, indicating substantial room for improvement.
Remaining weaknesses include limited content coverage, weak cross-modal causal and logical analysis, and inaccurate citation support.

papers.abstract: Generated robot videos can look convincing while depicting the wrong interac- tion: a different object is moved, a grasp disappears, or a placement ends out- side its destination. We introduce RGraph-Eval, a reference-based framework that makes these discrepancies explicit through task-grounded temporal scene graphs. Unlike approaches that construct separate evidence representations for different evaluation dimensions, we organize task entities, interactions, and motion within a unified, interpretable scene graph representation. A foundation-model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, grounds persistent object masks, infers and verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs manipulated- object motion in three dimensions. Applying this representation to a generated video and a reference demonstration supports an interpretable RGraph-Eval score with visible-object, relation-change, and 3D path-shape components. We also introduce ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources annotated with the multimodal representation. Our eval- uation separates graph-generation quality from agreement with human video judgments, and includes comparisons with adapted SVG2 and SG-Ego, a bench- mark of three video generators. The framework connects robot-video assessment to the observable entities and interactions underlying a task, while making the graph annotations reusable beyond evaluation. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/SashaDance/rgraph-eval.
authors: Aleksandr Lazarev, Sofia Zimina, Roman Kuznetsov, Tatiana Zemskova, Iaroslav Koshelev, Dmitry Yudin

Introduces ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 annotated manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources.
Separately evaluates graph-generation quality and alignment with human judgments, and benchmarks three video generators.

papers.abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.
authors: Songlin Yang, Zhe Wang, Xiaotong Zhao, Xi Wang, Ran Zhang, Shuai Li, Taiyi Wu, Songlian Li, Eric Liu, Alan Zhao, Anyi Rao
bullets: Addresses the gap between useful MLLM representations and their reliable use by video diffusion transformers.
Uses latent-only generator grounding to make the DiT depend on frozen MLLM latents.
Learns factor-aware editing through paired videos with target-factor changes and non-target preservation.
Trains temporal inference from text or incomplete video by optimizing the MLLM and connector through a frozen DiT.
Reports consistently better performance than baselines across sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL). Stage I freezes the MLLM and its original connector and trains the DiT using MLLM latents. Stage II retains this configuration and swaps factor-specific output spans between paired examples to supervise factor-aware changes. Stage III freezes the trained DiT and jointly updates the MLLM and connector through video reconstruction, and text-only and text-plus-complete-video inputs share the same generation target.

Figure 2: MLLM latents are easily bypassed in existing MLLM–DiT models. (i) Under MLLMonly conditioning, Omni-Video 2 (1.3B DiT) produces noise, while Omni-Video 2 (14B DiT) and UniVideo produce artifacts and depict one person’s successive actions as two people acting differently. MLLM latents alone therefore fail to provide reliable generation guidance in these examples. (ii) Under conflicting conditions, VAE references dominate the output.

Figure 4: Under limited inputs, baseline models fail to predict temporal visual details. With only text and no visual references, we compare UniVideo with FAPL (Ours), highlighting representative baseline limitations across four cinematic factors. (i) Character. Long hair is generated as short hair, failing appearance details specified only by text. (ii) Scene. The background is not preserved and incorrect content appears. (iii) Action. The requested sequence, e.g., gesturing outward with the left hand and extended fingers, is missing. (iv) Camera. UniVideo ignores the instruction and keeps the camera static, while Ours orbits around the character. FAPL better realizes promptspecified appearance, scene, and motion from text alone.

Figure 5: FAPL improves factor-aware control. For each factor, we modify only the corresponding description in the structured prompt and generate twice, comparing UniVideo with FAPL (Ours). UniVideo does not confine the change to the requested factor and alters unrelated content, whereas Ours modifies the selected factor while preserving the others. This indicates that factor-level latent augmentation enables selective control.

Figure 1: Cinematic video generation requires inference from limited inputs and factor-aware control. (i) The man turns toward the box, places his right hand on top, and steadies the bundle with his left hand. Text-only conditioning misses this sequence, while observing the complete video enables the same model to reproduce it. (ii) Keeping the descriptions of all other factors fixed and replacing only the character-related prompt, the non-character factors change as well. These cases illustrate failures in temporal inference and factor control, with editing providing a probe of what the generator changes and preserves.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, placing greater demands on reliable AI-generated video detection. Existing artifact-based detectors typically identify generation artifacts as evidence for source prediction, yet they may either fail to recognize subtle artifacts or reach the correct source decision without faithfully identifying the evidence underlying it. In this work, we systematically investigate how to design and train effective artifact detectors and formulate artifact detection as a structured process comprising three complementary capabilities: Inspection Planning, which determines what should be examined; Evidence Verification, which verifies whether the inspected content exhibits genuine generation artifacts; and Evidence Aggregation, which integrates the verified evidence into the final source decision. Building on this formulation, we introduce Verus-Insight, trained with human-anchored full-process supervision and progressive capability training to strengthen both fine-grained artifact detection and video-level detection. We further introduce Verus-Bench, a benchmark with fine-grained human annotations of perceptible artifacts for evaluating artifact detection. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that Verus-Insight achieves strong performance in both fine-grained artifact analysis and AI-generated video detection, with substantial gains in recovering human-perceived artifacts. Further analyses reveal that the three capabilities are complementary yet distinct, and that Verus-Insight more reliably converts relevant inspection targets into supported artifact evidence without increasing spurious artifact claims.
authors: Zhuoran Zhang, Yang Shi, Qixun Wang, Tengfei Liu, Yuqi Tang, Xuanyu Zhu, Yizhuo Jia, Jingyun Hua, Shixuan Liu, Xianghua Ying, Haotian Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Wenjing Yang

Verus-Insight uses human-anchored full-process supervision and progressive capability training.
Verus-Bench provides fine-grained human annotations of perceptible video artifacts for evaluation.
Experiments show strong fine-grained artifact analysis and video-level detection, with better recovery of human-perceived artifacts without more spurious claims.

papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generation enables low-latency streaming, yet prevailing training pipelines separate causal adaptation from distribution matching. Recent representation-based text-to-video methods retain this separation by starting from ODE-initialized checkpoints, even when the target distribution is defined directly by reference videos. We introduce Direct Forcing, a single-stage framework that uses reference videos both as paired examples of how a history continues and as a target population for self-generated rollouts. Causal Continuation Alignment learns paired spatiotemporal correspondence under reference histories, while Rollout Distribution Matching uses maximum mean discrepancy to align the representation distributions of self-generated and reference videos. Together, these complementary signals allow a pretrained video model to learn causal continuation and the target video distribution in a single training stage. Dynamic Gradient Balancing adapts the relative gradient contributions of continuation alignment and distribution matching during training. Starting from bidirectional Wan2.1-1.3B, Direct Forcing learns a four-step autoregressive generator in 250 updates without a separate initialization stage or online diffusion-score supervision, achieving 84.63 VBench Total and 86.01 Quality. Ablation studies further demonstrate the benefits of dynamic gradient balancing and reveal distinct representation preferences: deeper features benefit continuation alignment, whereas intermediate features yield better performance for rollout distribution matching.
authors: Haojun Xu, Jie Huang, Xin Lu, Mingchen Zhong, Zihao Fan, Linjiang Huang, Si Liu

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based audio-visual generation methods typically perform joint denoising of audio and video latents throughout the entire sampling trajectory, repeatedly executing modality-specific denoising branches and cross-modal attention at every timestep. However, we observe that such uniform joint computation is not always necessary. The key is a modality-asymmetric recoverability: audio-side drift introduced by mid-stage caching can be substantially reduced by only a few terminal joint denoising steps, whereas video-side degradation caused by caching leads to persistent loss of motion and temporal details. This asymmetry suggests that inference acceleration should selectively cache recoverable audio-side computation while preserving full video refinement. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Convergence-Adaptive Audio-Visual Cache (CAVC)}, a training-free modality-asymmetric caching framework. CAVC adopts a sandwich-structured computation allocation: after detecting that audio denoiser outputs enter a cache-tolerant regime, it caches and reuses the audio denoiser output to bypass audio denoising and cross-modal attention in the middle stage, while the video branch continues independent spatio-temporal refinement; a few joint steps are then restored at the end to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and improve synchronization. Experiments across multiple public benchmarks demonstrate that CAVC achieves 1.10--1.35x wall-clock acceleration, improves several visual dynamics and temporal statistics, and maintains competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment.
authors: Lifan Jiang, Yibo Zhao, Senlin cheng, Bolei Xu, Xiaobo Li, Can Ye, Dehai Zhao, Deng Cai, Boxi Wu
bullets: Addresses unnecessary joint audio-video denoising and cross-modal attention at every sampling step.
Uses a training-free, convergence-adaptive cache with sandwich-structured computation allocation.
Caches audio denoiser outputs in a cache-tolerant middle regime while video undergoes full spatio-temporal refinement.
Restores a few terminal joint denoising steps to reduce cross-modal drift and improve synchronization.

Across public benchmarks, achieves 1.10–1.35× wall-clock acceleration while maintaining competitive audio fidelity and audio-visual alignment and improving several visual dynamics and temporal statistics.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the CAVC framework. The denoising trajectory (t = T → 0) is dynamically partitioned based on modality convergence. (1A) Full AV Warm-up: During early high-noise stages, audio/video branches and AV cross-attention fully execute to establish semantic binding. (Trigger τ): An online monitor tracks audio prediction changes; once stabilized, the audio cache activates. (1B) Cached Continuation: Cached audio predictions are reused. Bypassing the expensive audio branch and AV attention frees the video branch for independent spatio-temporal refinement without being over-constrained by static audio. (2) Final Joint Refinement: Full joint computation is terminally restored for a few steps to reduce accumulated cross-modal drift and refine audio-visual synchronization before decoding.

For this 121-frame 1K example, their cache-state estimation and update operations also introduce net overhead (see Table 1). In contrast, CAVC achieves a 1.15× inference speedup while preserving stronger visual quality, spatio-temporal consistency, and dynamics.

papers.abstract: Video provides a natural source of supervision: what happens next serves as a learning signal for visual world modeling. Yet masked video pretraining focuses on recovering missing content from surrounding context rather than predicting the future from the past. Autoregressive methods instead predict forward one token at a time, but have yet to match joint-embedding methods in representation quality. This gap motivates us to revisit the granularity and space of future prediction. In this work, we introduce VANE, a self-supervised visual pretraining framework built on next-frame prediction in embedding space. A causal encoder summarizes past observations for a state predictor that infers the representation of the entire next frame, making temporal evolution the primary learning signal. This prediction is carried out in a fixed embedding space provided by a frozen semantic tokenizer, emphasizing scene content and structure. To retain fine-grained spatial detail alongside semantic content, a lightweight auxiliary generative decoder reconstructs future-frame patches conditioned on the predicted representations. To unify visual modeling across images and videos, we construct a local-to-global crop sequence for still images, allowing the same encoder to predict newly revealed regions from earlier crops under the same objective. Experiments show that VANE improves with model and data scaling, achieving SOTA on most anticipation, recognition, and dense perception benchmarks among unified encoders. Especially on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation, it surpasses V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 points in mean-class recall@5. These results demonstrate that next-frame prediction in embedding space is effective and scalable for visual world modeling.
authors: Yifeng Yao, Jinghan Li, Zhihao Zhang, Yajiao Xiong, Yang Jin, Kun Xu, Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao
bullets: Motivation: Existing masked and autoregressive video methods do not fully capture future dynamics or match joint-embedding representation quality.
Method: A causal encoder summarizes past observations, while a state predictor infers the next frame in a fixed space from a frozen semantic tokenizer.
Detail: An auxiliary lightweight decoder reconstructs future-frame patches to preserve spatial detail alongside semantic content.
Unification: Still images are converted into local-to-global crop sequences so the same prediction objective applies to images and videos.

Results: VANE improves with model and data scaling, reaches state-of-the-art on most evaluated unified-encoder benchmarks, and exceeds V-JEPA 2.1 by 7.1 mean-class recall@5 points on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 action anticipation.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | Overview of VANE. VANE predicts the embedding of the next frame from the frames observed so far. Top: the causal encoder maps the observed frames 𝑥1, . . . , 𝑥𝑡 to context states ℎ1, . . . , ℎ𝑡, which are concatenated with prediction tokens 𝑝𝑡+1; the state predictor uses the context states only as keys and values and outputs the predicted state 𝑠𝑡+1. Middle: a projector maps 𝑠𝑡+1 to the embedding space of the frozen semantic tokenizer, where it is supervised by the embedding of the next frame 𝑥𝑡+1 with an 𝐿1 loss; the generative decoder, conditioned on 𝑠𝑡+1, predicts the flow velocity 𝑣𝑡+1 from the noisy next frame 𝑥𝑡+1. Bottom: images are presented as local-to-global crops and videos as frame sequences, so both share the same objective.

Figure 1 | From masked completion to next-frame prediction in embedding space. (a) V-JEPA masks part of a clip, encodes the visible patches with bidirectional attention, and predicts the embeddings of the masked regions, supervised by an EMA encoder of the full video. (b) VANE encodes previous frames with frame-causal attention and predicts the embedding of the entire next frame from them, with targets from a frozen semantic tokenizer. An auxiliary generative decoder, used only during pretraining, regularizes the predicted embedding to retain fine-grained spatial detail.

Figure 6 | Attention masks. Left: frame-causal attention in the causal encoder, bidirectional within each frame and unidirectional across frames. Right: context-isolated causal attention in the state predictor. Prediction tokens for frame 𝑡 + 1 read the context states of frames up to 𝑡, which supply only keys and values, and attend to each other only within the same target frame.

Figure 9 | Qualitative short-term anticipation results on Ego4D STA v2. Each example pairs the top-scoring predictions of VANE (left) with the ground truth (right). Each box marks a next-active object and is labeled with the interaction verb, the object noun, and the time to contact (TTC). Predictions are produced by a probe trained on frozen VANE features.
Figure 4 | Qualitative comparison on ADE20K. V-JEPA 2.1 and VANE with the same dense linear probe on frozen features.
Figure 5 | Cumulative training recipe.
Figure 3 | State predictor attention. Context states supply only keys and values; prediction tokens attend within their own target frame.

Figure 7 | Visualization of local-to-global next-crop prediction. Each row shows the spatial layout of three sampled crops and the corresponding prediction sequence Crop1 → Crop2 → Crop3. The first two observations are local crops and the last provides broader scene context. At each step, supervision is restricted to spatial regions newly revealed by the next crop. Crops are resized to a common display size for visualization only; their original spatial coordinates are used during training.

Figure 8 | Additional examples of local-to-global next-crop prediction. We show additional sampled crop sequences following the same local-to-global sampling strategy as in Fig. 7. Supervision is applied only to regions newly revealed by each subsequent crop. Crops are resized to a common display size for visualization only; their original spatial coordinates are used during training.
Figure 12 | Qualitative monocular depth estimation on NYUv2. The error column shows Δ𝑒 = 𝑑𝑉𝐴𝑁𝐸 − 𝑑gt − 𝑑V-JEPA 2.1 − 𝑑gt ; blue favors VANE, while red favors V-JEPA 2.1.

Figure 13 | Qualitative monocular depth estimation results on KITTI. Predicted depth maps are obtained from dense readouts trained on frozen visual features using the same protocol as the quantitative evaluation.

Figure 10 | Qualitative semantic segmentation results on ADE20K. Each example shows the input image, ground truth, and predictions from dense probes trained on frozen features. All compared encoders use the same downstream protocol.
Figure 11 | Qualitative semantic segmentation results on Cityscapes. Each example shows the input image, ground truth, and the prediction from a dense linear probe trained on frozen VANE features.

Table 6 | Model architectures. The main model uses a ViT-g causal encoder, a 12-layer context-isolated state predictor, a frozen DINOv2 ViT-L semantic tokenizer, and a six-layer patch-isolated DiffMLP decoder.

Table 3 | Global classification. Top-1 accuracy (%) of attentive probes on frozen features, covering appearance understanding (IN1K, K400) and motion understanding (SSv2, Diving-48). Avg. is reported for models evaluated on all four tasks. Bold denotes the best result in image–video encoders.

Table 2 | Short-term object-interaction anticipation on Ego4D STA v2. The model localizes the next-active object and predicts its noun, the interaction verb, and the time to contact. Each column reports Top-5 AP or mAP counting a prediction as correct only if all listed components are correct: box (𝑏), noun (𝑁), verb (𝑉), and time to contact (𝛿). Bold denotes the best results.
Table 7 | Multi-stage training strategy. The base model is first trained with 16-frame clips at 256 × 256, followed by long-video post-training with 64-frame clips and a final high-resolution stage.

Table 4 | Dense perception. Semantic segmentation (mIoU, %) and monocular depth estimation (RMSE, lower is better) with a linear probe on frozen final-layer patch features. Param./patch denotes encoder size/patch size. Bold denotes the best result among image–video encoders.

Table 5 | Ablation studies. Top-1 accuracy on IN1K/SSv2 and mIoU on ADE20K with a ViT-L encoder trained for 50K iterations. (a) Prediction space and granularity; next-frame and next-token variants share the frozen DINOv2 ViT-L target space. (b) Image objectives, with the video objective, tokenizer, and generative decoder fixed. (c) Auxiliary generative decoder.
Table 1 | Action anticipation on EPIC-KITCHENS-100. Mean-class recall@5 (%) for verb, noun, and action on the validation set, with a one-second anticipation gap. Bold denotes the best result.

Table 8 | Masked versus next-frame prediction under matched pretraining. All models use ViT-L encoders trained on VISTA for 50K iterations. The frozen-target V-JEPA 2.1 variant uses the same DINOv2 ViT-L semantic tokenizer as VANE. We report top-1 accuracy (%) on IN1K and SSv2 and mIoU (%) on ADE20K.
Table 9 | Ablation of the number of image crops. We vary the number of local-to-global views 𝐾 while keeping the remaining training configuration fixed.

Table 10 | Ablation of state-predictor attention. Context-isolated prediction treats historical encoder states as read-only context rather than jointly updating them with prediction tokens inside the predictor.

papers.selection_reason: Next-frame prediction in embedding space for scalable visual world modeling and video representation learning.
papers.title: Learning from Next-Frame Prediction: Towards Unified and Scalable Visual Representation Learning
papers.tldr: VANE learns scalable visual representations by predicting entire future-frame embeddings, combining semantic next-frame prediction with fine-grained spatial reconstruction across images and videos.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have substantially improved visual fidelity, yet existing models still struggle to understand the physical evolution implicit in user prompts, making it difficult to generate videos with continuous physical state evolution. Here, we propose PhyEvolve, a multi-agent framework that enhances natural-language prompts through structured state-evolution planning. PhyEvolve consists of three agents: a Director, a Physical Evolver, and a Composer. Given a user prompt and an optional first frame, the Director grounds the scene and disentangles physical events from observation changes. The Physical Evolver uses scene evidence to identify physical mechanisms then constructs causally linked state transitions that unfold throughout the video, whether visible or not. The Composer utilizes these transitions to enhance the original prompts. Without retraining or model modification, PhyEvolve works directly with existing generators through prompt replacement. Extensive experiments on four major benchmarks show that PhyEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the cutting-edge prior agentic baseline by 7.9 percentage points on average. These results demonstrate that explicit causal state-evolution planning improves physical consistency and state continuity in generated videos through natural-language prompt enhancement.
authors: Yang-Hao Zhou, Lixing Tan, Zhiqi Li, Guang Yang, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses poor modeling of continuous physical evolution in text-to-video generation.
Uses three agents: Director, Physical Evolver, and Composer.
Plans causally linked physical state transitions, including changes that may not be directly visible.
Works with existing video generators through prompt replacement and optional first-frame input.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results and a 7.9-point average gain over a prior agentic baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PhyEvolve. The Director separates actions from observations, the Physical Evolver models causal state evolution under occlusion, and the Composer refines prompts for physically consistent video generation.

Figure 5: Role-level prompt template for the Director. Scene grounding establishes the initial conditions, while action–observation disentanglement separates physical drivers from visibility changes. A separate reviewer guides bounded local revisions of the structured plan.

Figure 6: Role-level prompt template for the Physical Evolver. Physical Mechanisms Analysis establishes evidence, prerequisites, and responses; causal state rollout propagates them into continuous physical evolution. Both steps share one generation call, followed by a joint review of their outputs and local revisions when needed.

Figure 7: Role-level prompt template for the Composer. Prompt construction integrates the source requirements and upstream physical records. Physical-fidelity refinement uses evidence-grounded sentence-level feedback to correct omissions and contradictions while locking unrelated text.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on state-evolution prompts. We compare Minimax-H3, NEWTON, Co-Director, and PhyEvolve (ours) on four cases from StEvo-Bench (Top) and other in-sight physical benchmark (Bottom). Frames are uniformly sampled along time from left to right; dark marks the light-off interval. green boxes mark physically consistent state changes, and red boxes locate failures.

Figure 1: PhyEvolve plans physical state evolution before video generation. Compared with single-pass Minimax-H3, PhyEvolve produces physically consistent videos, including when processes continue out of sight.

Figure 8: Additional qualitative comparisons. Top: a burning candle thrown onto dry grass . Bottom: a vertical rocket launch . Seven frames are sampled uniformly over time; green and red boxes mark correct and failed state evolution. Minimax-H3 and NEWTON fail to ignite the grass, and NEWTON and Co-Director fail to show a rocket leaving the ground, while PhyEvolve completes both processes.

Figure 9: Additional qualitative results on StEvo-Bench. Each case contains an interval where the scene is unobserved (Lights off, curtain drop, cardboard occlusion). PhyEvolve carries the underlying state change through this interval, so the scene reappears in a physically consistent, updated state.
Figure 10: Additional qualitative results on PhyGenBench.
Figure 3: Component ablation on a scene where a falling glass is occluded by a curtain.

Table 1: Unified evaluation of video generators and agentic frameworks across physical-video benchmarks. All scores are reported as percentages; higher is better. Average denotes the unweighted arithmetic mean across the four benchmarks.
Table 4: PhyWorldBench: physics-category results. All scores are reported for the Both metric.
Table 3: PhyGenBench: physical commonsense accuracy.
Table 5: VideoPhy-2: automatic evaluation under the NEWTON reporting protocol.
Table 8: User preference for PhyEvolve over each baseline (%). Each entry reports the percentage of votes favoring PhyEvolve.
Table 6: Component ablation on StEvo-Bench.

Table 9: Efficiency comparison with Minimax-H3.

papers.selection_reason: Agentic prompt planning for physics-aware text-to-video generation improves video diffusion outputs.
papers.title: PhyEvolve: Multi-Agent State-Evolution Planning for Physics-Aware Video Generation
papers.tldr: PhyEvolve improves physics-aware video generation by using multi-agent causal state-evolution planning to enhance prompts without modifying or retraining the video generator.

papers.abstract: Adding control to video generation often requires training, which demands additional computational resources, data, or architectural changes. We propose a training-free approach that utilizes pretrained video diffusion models to control object layout and motion using coarse layouts. Our method operates in two passes: first, it steers spatiotemporal placement through prompt-guided cross-attention to produce a coarse visual guide; second, this guide conditions the same model to generate a high-quality, layoutconsistent video. The approach enables coordinated motion with strong temporal consistency, supporting diverse trajectories and object interactions without additional training. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms prior work in overlap and trajectory accuracy, as well as visual quality across static, dynamic, and multi-object scene settings.
authors: Asaf Joseph, Moshe Mandel, Ohad Fried
bullets: Addresses the computational and architectural costs of training-based video-generation control.
Uses prompt-guided cross-attention to create a coarse spatiotemporal visual guide.
Conditions the same pretrained model on this guide to generate layout-consistent videos.
Supports diverse trajectories, coordinated motion, and multi-object interactions without additional training.
Experiments report improved overlap, trajectory accuracy, and visual quality across static and dynamic scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our training-free layout-guided video synthesis pipeline. Given a text prompt and spatiotemporal layout constraints, we first perform Layout Generation, where the latents of a frozen text-to-video diffusion model are optimized using a cross-attention-based layout loss. This latent refinement process aligns token-specific attention with the target layout and produces a coarse spatiotemporal guiding video in latent space. Next, after the guide is optionally spatially and/or temporally upsampled, we render the final video: the guiding video is injected at an early timestep into the video diffusion pipeline. This second stage refines appearance and details while preserving the imposed layout and motion, yielding the final high-quality video.

Fig. 4. Outputs of Text-to-Video (T2V) and our method (Ours) across different backbone models (LTX-2, WAN 2.2), together with the corresponding attention maps extracted from an intermediate timestep. Attempting to control layout via textual prompt (underlined) fails, whereas controlling the attention map results in a video that corresponds to the desired layouts (orange/blue bounding boxes).

Fig. 7. Comparison of our refined video (Ours) against competing methods. Left: dynamic object layout. While T2V produces high-quality visuals, it does not follow the layout. Trailblazer (TB) and FreeTraj (FT) introduce bicycle artifacts, and Peekaboo (Peek.) shows weaker alignment. Right: multiple-object layout; empty frames indicate unsupported methods. Remaining methods fail to maintain spatial and temporal consistency: the explosion occurs prematurely, and the person does not follow the left-to-right trajectory specified by the blue box.

Fig. 8. Additional applications of our method. Left: video editing, where the input video is transformed according to the text prompt. Right: stylization, where only selected semantic elements retain color while the rest of the scene remains monochrome.

Fig. 6. Comparison between the video guide generated using an ensemble of Text-to-Image methods (left) and the refined video produced by a pre-trained video model (right). The guide fails to capture the interaction between the boy and the scarf: the hands remain static instead of grasping and moving the scarf, resulting in motion that lacks coordination between the objects.

Fig. 5. Comparison of different learning rates during optimization. In each section, guide (top) and refined (bottom) videos are shown. The left column (low learning rate) produces guide videos with weaker adherence to the intended layout (indicated by orange squares). In contrast, the right column (high learning rate) achieves stronger layout adherence, but at the cost of reduced visual quality.

Table 1. Quantitative comparison with prior training-free layout-guided methods across datasets. IoU and AP50 measure overlap accuracy. CD, I., and I-AP50 measure trajectory accuracy. FVD and ClipSim measure visual quality. Our framework achieves superior spatial alignment and trajectory consistency on all metrics. Notably, Wan 2.2 excels in guide-stage performance, while LTX-2 provides comparable or stronger refined results.
Fig. 3. The guide (left) is of low visual quality but adheres to layout, the refined video (right) improves the visual quality and maintains layout adherence.

Table 2. User study results (mean score ± confidence interval with 95% confidence level) across prompt adherence (Prompt), layout adherence (Layout), and visual quality (VQ). T2V excels in visual quality and prompt adherence but shows poor layout adherence. Our method achieves the strongest layout adherence while remaining competitive in prompt alignment and visual quality.
Table 3. Ablation study on the contribution of different layers to layout adherence. Tested on Wan 2.2. The results indicate that earlier layers perform better.

Table 4. Ablation study of resolution contributions to layout adherence. Resolution is denoted as 𝑠𝑝𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑎𝑙 ℎ𝑒𝑖𝑔ℎ𝑡 × 𝑡𝑒𝑚𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑎𝑙 resolution. Inference time of guide and refinement stages are compared to that of the backbone model. Focusing on the refined block (right) of the Wan model (top), the results indicate that it is generally better to generate the refined video at a higher resolution. At the highest resolution (480 × 81) it is preferable in terms of trajectory accuracy (CD, I, I-AP50) to generate the respective guide at the lowest resolution (row 6), with negligible decrease in overlap accuracy (IoU, AP50).

papers.selection_reason: Training-free layout-guided control of pretrained video diffusion models for temporally consistent video synthesis; fits video generation interests.
papers.title: Latent Space Jam: Layout Guided Video Synthesis
papers.tldr: A training-free two-pass method controls object layouts and motion in pretrained video diffusion models while preserving temporal consistency and visual quality.

papers.abstract: We study mountain-bike action quality assessment (AQA) with weak labels and candidate feedback. The training corpus comprises 95 field-recorded jump clips with binary labels denoting good or poor technique. These are coarse categorical labels, not continuous expert quality scores; phase-boundary and aspect-level annotations are unavailable. Our pipeline summarizes four heuristic phases using frozen V-JEPA 2 video features and two-dimensional pose and motion measurements. A small transformer predicts a binary-label score. A separate reference layer compares phase-specific measurements with those of clips labelled as good technique to propose phase, body-parameter, and direction cues. We detail the measurements, network, and evaluation so that the limits of each output are explicit. In five-fold clip-level cross-validation, the full scorer obtained pooled out-of-fold AUROC 0.768 and average precision 0.812. These are exploratory figures because the reporting fold also selected the neural training epoch and riders were not separated between folds. Removing biomechanical scoring inputs raised AUROC to 0.809. A separate inner-selection run obtained AUROC 0.678, but used about 57 rather than 76 training clips per outer fold, so its difference from the test-selected run does not quantify selection bias. The unsupervised aspect head did not learn distinct factors. On a 17-clip external probe, an earlier checkpoint obtained binary accuracy 0.412 and Spearman association -0.135 with expert scores. Candidate cues had precision 0.118 and recall 1.0 against each of two coaches, with substantial disagreement about direction. These findings do not establish rider-independent scoring or reliable corrective feedback; they identify the empirical work needed to evaluate either use.
bullets: Uses 95 field-recorded jump clips with coarse good/poor technique labels, rather than continuous expert scores or phase/aspect annotations.
Summarizes four heuristic phases with frozen V-JEPA 2 features and 2D pose/motion measurements; a small transformer predicts binary quality.
A separate reference layer compares phase-specific measurements with good-technique clips to generate body-parameter and directional feedback cues.
Five-fold clip-level cross-validation yielded pooled AUROC 0.768 and average precision 0.812, but epoch selection used the reporting folds and riders were not separated.

The external probe showed weak performance and feedback agreement: binary accuracy 0.412, Spearman association −0.135, and cue precision 0.118 with recall 1.0; the aspect head found no distinct factors.
