The labels describe the system’s partition, not expert-verified event boundaries. Table 8 gives the full set of eight cue measurements. Images are reproduced with permission.

Figure 4: Candidate-cue dataflow. The scorer supplies aspect and deficiency outputs to the OR gate, although the deficiency head has no cue-level training target; measurements and positive-class reference statistics supply the deviation. The optional vision–language step can alter direction and wording for cues with a keypoint-linked parameter, but does not change the score, chosen parameter, or schema phase. Dashed arrows denote an optional path with no established benefit.

Figure 7: High-score display case, paired at frame 24. The overlay rounds the overall score to 0.88 and shows the assigned take-off phase. The knee and elbow labels round phase summaries to 101 and 126 degrees; they are not independent measurements of this single frame. The orange and yellow cue markers denote medium and low severity, not the green overall band. The text panel partly covers the rider, an interface limitation preserved from the recorded output. Images are reproduced with permission.

Figure 6: Actual full-frame input and recorded output, paired at zero-based frame 160 (5.33 s at 30 frames/s) of one 181-frame external example. The green lines are detected pose; the colored elbow marker and text are automatically generated cues. The displayed phase is “landing” although the rider is visibly airborne. The local annotation says “open,” while the sentence says “Bend the elbow more.” These retained inconsistencies illustrate why the heuristic phase and wording are not ground truth or validated advice. The 115-degree value is a phase summary from the report, not a measurement of the single displayed frame. Images are reproduced with permission.

Figure 8: Middle-score display case, paired at frame 60. The overall display rounds to 0.43, while the hip label rounds the flight summary to 74 degrees. The visible motion blur and partially obscured body make the pose overlay especially important to treat as an estimate. The source has a good-technique label: orange is an output band, not a medium-quality ground-truth class. The phase and cue text are generated outputs. Images are reproduced with permission.

Figure 9: Low-score display case, paired at frame 40. The overlay rounds the overall score to 0.26 and the landing-elbow summary to 168 degrees. Both displayed landing cues have high severity. The local “close” label and the sentence about over-compression are reproduced as generated; their presence is not evidence of an appropriate corrective action. Images are reproduced with permission.

Figure 1: Schematic information flow. The full score consumes video and biomechanical features. Candidate cues also use the scorer’s aspect outputs and a separate parameter comparison. The cue phase is assigned by the aspect schema, rather than localized by learned attention. No branch in this diagram is claimed to provide validated interpretation of the score.

Figure 3: Trainable head for one clip (batch dimension suppressed). The mixture uses only scorehead outputs. Only the clip-level mixture score has an observed training target here. Aspect scores, deficiency outputs, and phase-attention weights have no matching supervision and are not validated explanations.

Figure 2: Operational phase partition. The three interior boundaries come from image-plane hip motion and are constrained to occur in order. The widths are schematic. The assigned flight window begins at the estimated apex; the labels have no independently measured temporal accuracy.

Figure 5: One outer-fold comparison, with colors denoting training (green), epoch selection (orange or red), and outer reporting (red). The diagnostic arms differ in both data access and fitting-set size. The widths illustrate counts, not a statistical confidence interval.
Table 3: What is observed and what is only generated by the pipeline. The coach-annotated probe evaluates an earlier checkpoint, not the main comparison model.

Table 2: Seven pose or motion parameters and six flight descriptors. Quoted names are the system’s feature labels; all measurements are image-relative proxies. The final descriptor is smaller when observed rotation is more uniform.

Table 9: Pooled out-of-fold binary metrics on 95 clips, one seed, five clip-level folds. “Full” means video and measured features; “video” means frozen V-JEPA 2 features; “pooled” means an average over four phases. The full, MLP, GRU, and transformer heads use the held-out fold for epoch selection; adapted CoRe, USDL, and pairwise heads fit for 120 fixed epochs. Classical estimators have no epoch selection. Adapted prior methods use binary technique labels, not their original expert-score tasks.

Table 1: The eight aspect-to-phase and aspect-to-parameter assignments used for jumps. The phase column is a predetermined association in the cue generator. It must not be interpreted as a learned phase prediction.
Table 5: Main corpus description. The two target values are encodings of technique categories. They do not represent expert-rated scores or a 0.55-unit difference in technique quality.

Table 4: Trainable parameter count for the jump head. The pose, bike, and V-JEPA 2 backbones were frozen. The deficiency-output head is included in the count despite having no cue-level training target.

Table 12: Mean ± standard deviation of association with binary technique labels across three subsampling seeds. The probe uses a separate training schedule and is not numerically identical to Table 9. No method equivalence or saturation is inferred.

Table 6: Selected actual cue records for the input/output example in Figure 6. Values are phase summaries, rounded for display; z is the stored deviation before rounding. The fore/aft offset is dimensionless and camera-relative. Severity is the generator’s rule-based category, not a clinician’s or coach’s risk rating.
Table 11: Single-seed ablations with the same clip-level folds and test-epoch-selected reporting protocol as Table 9. Values are pooled out-of-fold binary metrics.

Table 7: The three added demonstration cases. Frame indices are zero-based; the denominator is the total number of decoded frames. Technique labels are not independent expert judgments. Case O falls below the binary threshold despite its good-technique label. These selected examples are not a new test set.
Table 10: Full scorer’s pooled out-of-fold decisions at threshold 0.5. Epochs were selected using their reporting folds; the entries are not an independent test-set confusion matrix.

papers.selection_reason: Action quality assessment from video using temporal representations and pose/motion measurements; fits video understanding.
papers.title: V-JEPA 2 Meets AQA: Phase-Based Scoring and Reference-Based Feedback for Mountain Biking
papers.tldr: An exploratory mountain-bike AQA pipeline using frozen video features, pose/motion measurements, and reference-based cues shows moderate binary-label discrimination but does not yet support reliable rider-independent scoring or feedback.

papers.abstract: Cinematic multi-shot video generation requires both narrative planning and iterative refinement. Existing methods either lack narrative reasoning or rely on feed-forward workflows without policy updates. In this paper, we propose CineEvolve, an agentic self-evolution framework for cinematic multi-shot video generation that unifies a Director and a Critic within a single vision-language policy. Emulating real-world filmmaking that couples iterative direction with critical feedback, we train CineEvolve via alternating reinforcement learning, where the Director surfaces flaws to sharpen the Critic, and the updated Critic guides the Director's targeted revisions. To stabilize co-evolution, we introduce Evolutionary GRPO (E-GRPO), leveraging historical anchoring and revision safeguarding to mitigate advantage inflation. Additionally, we contribute CineTraj, a 40K cinematic trajectory dataset spanning creation, critique, and revision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CineEvolve outperforms existing approaches. Our code will be available at https://github.com/JingZhe-8/CineEvolve.
bullets: Addresses the need for both narrative planning and iterative refinement in multi-shot video generation.
Unifies a Director and Critic in one vision-language policy trained through alternating reinforcement learning.
Introduces Evolutionary GRPO (E-GRPO) with historical anchoring and revision safeguarding to stabilize co-evolution.
Provides CineTraj, a 40K trajectory dataset covering video creation, critique, and revision.
Experiments report improved performance over existing approaches, though specific metrics are not given.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of our proposed CineEvolve framework. (a) The Critic optimizes its diagnostic accuracy against reference defect annotations on an evolving pool of Director-generated storyboards. (b) The Director learns to draft and revise storyboards guided by self-evaluation rewards from the updated Critic, alongside narrative and visual feedback. (c) Revision safeguarding and historical anchoring are integrated to stabilize policy updates and prevent performance collapse during co-evolution.

Figure 2. Overview of the CineTraj construction pipeline. (a) Movie scenes are curated through deduplication, shot segmentation and grouping, and quality filtering. (b) The teacher Director converts annotated stories and shot descriptions into production plans and initial storyboards. (c) Teacher-guided critique, revision, and re-evaluation produce closed-loop trajectories.
Figure 5. Ablation study results with different variants of our CineEvolve framework.
Figure 4. Qualitative comparisons with existing multi-shot video generation methods.
Table 1. Quantitative comparisons and ablation results. ↑ (↓) means higher (lower) is better. The best performances are highlighted in bold.
Table 2. Human preference shares (%) across four evaluation dimensions. Higher is better.

papers.selection_reason: Agentic self-evolution framework for cinematic multi-shot video generation directly targets video generation research.
papers.title: CineEvolve: An Agentic Self-Evolution Framework for Cinematic Multi-Shot Video Generation
papers.tldr: CineEvolve uses an evolving Director–Critic agent pair to iteratively plan, critique, and refine cinematic multi-shot videos.

papers.abstract: Today's multimodal assistants are typically prompted to interpret the visual evidence presented to them. To offload the cognitive burden of remembering across long horizons, wearable assistants should instead proactively acquire and maintain useful memory as the user's surroundings evolve. Doing so on the user's behalf requires identifying what matters, understanding the scene in real time, and initiating memory maintenance in the background while the user stays focused on their activities. We introduce ProactEgoMem, a benchmark that evaluates proactive memory in streaming egocentric video. Three tasks ground the evaluation in ambient environmental needs: Information Capture (IC) preserves transient yet dense visual information, State Tracking (ST) follows changing object states, and Location Tracking (LT) records object movements. The benchmark defines its protocol at two levels of proactiveness: the Notification Level asks for a single timely notification that satisfies the user's intent, while the deeper Intervention Level asks the agent to maintain memory on the user's behalf through an active start-to-stop tool lifecycle. Parallel ProactEgoMem-Daily and ProactEgoMem-Sci tracks contain 300/100 clips covering daily and scientific use cases, paired with 1000/500 questions in ProactEgoMem-QA, which measures the quality of the proactively acquired memory. Across proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines, even the strongest models fail to capture memory both timely and accurately. ProactEgoMem provides a rigorous evaluation foundation for proactive multimodal assistance and for video agents that co-exist with their users.
authors: Ruotong Liao, Meikel Kokowski, Xiaoxiao Sun, Yongqin Xian, Laura Bravo S\'anchez, Shiye Su, Federico Tombari, Serena Yeung-Levy, Volker Tresp
bullets: Evaluates Information Capture, State Tracking, and Location Tracking for ambient memory needs.
Tests two levels of proactiveness: timely notifications and active start-to-stop memory-maintenance interventions.
Includes Daily and Scientific tracks with associated question-answering evaluations.
Finds that even strong proprietary, open-source, video-language, and streaming baselines struggle to be both timely and accurate.
Supports evaluation of proactive multimodal assistants and video agents operating alongside users.

figures.caption: Figure 11: ProactEgoMem construction pipeline. Native labels are greedily paired into candidate events; for Daily, a VLM densely captions every clip in addition to the greedy pairing. Annotators then watch each clip and modify, delete, or add events (Ego4D clips in Sci are annotated from scratch because native labels are missing). papers.abstract: Increasing the attention context length significantly improves streaming video generation quality, while incurring prohibitive memory and computational costs as the context grows. Existing methods attempt to capture this contextual information through attention selection or compression, but remain limited by bounded representations and lack explicit attention-level supervision to retain historical contributions to current queries. To address this, we introduce Attn-Forcing, a novel framework that preserves full-context attention contributions for streaming video generation under bounded memory and computation. We achieve this by introducing attention proxies that continuously approximate the attention responses induced by the historical context. Specifically, we implement the proxies as learnable visual latents and employ a Proxy Update Module to incorporate visual context from historical latents. Moreover, we propose an Attention Matching Loss to explicitly constrain the attention behavior of the learned proxies using full-context attention supervision. Extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that Attn-Forcing consistently improves streaming video generation quality and achieves state-of-the-art performance over existing baseline methods.
authors: Junyao Gao, Sibo Liu, Jiaxing Li, Yanan Sun, Hanxin Zhu, Weidong Zhang, Jun Zhang, Cairong Zhao
bullets: Longer attention contexts improve quality but create prohibitive memory and computational costs.
The method uses learnable visual latents as attention proxies for historical context.
A Proxy Update Module continuously incorporates context from historical latents.
An Attention Matching Loss provides explicit supervision from full-context attention behavior.
Experiments report consistent quality improvements and state-of-the-art performance over existing baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The framework of Attn-Forcing. papers.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of creating immersive volumetric videos from sparse and low-resolution capture resources. Conventional dense multi-view reconstruction methods can produce high-quality volumetric videos, but their reliance on costly capture setups makes them impractical in real-world scenarios. Recent approaches use generative models to relax capture requirements, but still suffer from limited resolution and 4D inconsistency. To overcome these constraints, we propose RealMe, a unified framework built around a high-resolution video diffusion model that enhances limited captures into high-resolution (2K), 4D-consistent videos for volumetric video reconstruction. Specifically, RealMe constructs auxiliary data from capture videos and encodes them into latents along with layout-aware positional embeddings. The video diffusion model adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to the multi-view capture layout, denoises these latents across viewpoints and time, and decodes them into enhanced videos to refine the 4D representation. This adaptation helps the model capture temporal dynamics and multi-view relationships, leading to more 4D-consistent generation. To reduce the data gap between generated videos and real captures, we apply a latent frequency loss that provides frequency-domain supervision in latent space. Extensive experiments on the public DNA-Rendering benchmark and our self-captured RealVV dataset demonstrate that RealMe is able to create immersive volumetric videos and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in visual fidelity and 4D consistency.
authors: Chenxu Zhou, Zhiyuan Yu, Yudong Jin, Yinji Shentu, Yu Zhang, Jiaming Sun, Xiaowei Zhou
bullets: Targets costly dense multi-view capture requirements and the limited resolution and 4D consistency of prior generative methods.
Builds auxiliary data from capture videos and combines latent representations with layout-aware positional embeddings.
Adapts factorized spatio-temporal attention to model relationships across viewpoints and time.
Uses latent frequency-domain supervision to reduce the gap between generated videos and real captures.
Experiments on DNA-Rendering and the self-captured RealVV dataset show improved visual fidelity and 4D consistency over existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our framework. These auxiliary videos are fed into a high-resolution video diffusion model to produce enhanced videos, which are then used together with the input captures to optimize the 4DGS representation for volumetric video reconstruction. The detailed model architecture is illustrated in Fig. 3.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve. Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution. We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context. Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged. Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution. Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.
authors: Ruopeng Gao, Yukun Huang, Jiarui Hu, Shuai Wang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Limin Wang
bullets: Teacher forcing can exploit temporal redundancy, favoring local continuity over genuine modeling of visual evolution.
FCP adds an auxiliary future-chunk prediction objective alongside teacher-forced denoising.
The method uses training videos directly, requires no pretrained visual encoder, and does not alter inference.
It improves physical plausibility while using less overall training compute than standard teacher-forced training.
Visualizations suggest FCP produces a more structured representation space, potentially benefiting autoregressive world models.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can produce visually plausible videos, yet their camera ego-motion often drifts over long horizons. Camera ego-motion determines how the viewpoint changes between frames and is essential for maintaining consistent geometry and trajectories. To address this problem, we propose CausalAlign, a causal alignment framework with two components. First, we diagnose how precise ego motion is represented, used, and retained within VGMs using linear probes and causal interventions, revealing a rise-and-fall pattern during denoising. Second, we strengthen ego-motion state in VGM by aligning the representations at the identified layers to a 3D foundation model through delta-token space. This space encodes the changes between consecutive frames, allowing the alignment to focus on ego-motion dynamics rather than static scene content. With Wan2.2 fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, CausalAlign can largely improve motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness, while preserving visual quality. For example, it improves geometric consistency by more than 20% relative to the base model. Moreover, with the fine-tuned VGM, CausalAlign improves the success rate of world action models (WAMs) by 10 points on mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365 benchmark. Overall, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency in diffusion-based VGMs and yields noticeable gains in embodied models.
authors: Kai Zhu, Yintianrun Zhang, Shuwei Jiang, Ruolin Zuo, Yixin Chen, Duomin Wang, Miao Liu, Yin Li, Daquan Zhou, Yiwu Zhong
bullets: Targets ego-motion drift, which harms geometric and trajectory consistency in generated videos.
Uses linear probes and causal interventions to locate where ego-motion is represented, used, and retained during denoising.
Aligns representations at identified layers in delta-token space, emphasizing frame-to-frame motion changes over static scene content.
Fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K with Wan2.2, it improves motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness while preserving visual quality.
The improved video model also raises world action model success rates on RoboCasa365 mobile-manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of CausalAlign. Left: Existing approaches rely on external 3D caches that may propagate errors, optimize output-level preferences without directly supervising ego-motion states, or align 3D features at randomly selected layers. Middle: Our CausalAlign first identifies the targeted layers through causal diagnosis and then strengthens ego-motion states through delta-token alignment. Right: CausalAlign consistently improves camera ego-motion consistency in video generation and largely boosts downstream mobile manipulation performance.

Figure 3: Ego-motion diagnosis and retention. We compare base model Wan2.2 and our method CausalAlign through probe decodability and causal intervention effects across layers (sub-figure (a) & (b): results are averaged over timesteps) and across denoising timesteps (sub-figure (c) & (d): results are averaged over layers). Dashed vertical lines represent the selected alignment locations and shading shows the 10th–90th percentiles over the averaged dimension. Our method CausalAlign can raise both signals from rise-and-fall to rise-and-maintain pattern, indicating improved ego-motion retention.

Figure 2: Three stages of CausalAlign training. CausalAlign transfers ego-motion knowledge from a 3D teacher to the VGM through three-stage training. In Stage 1, consecutive features from a streaming 3D foundation model are encoded into a teacher delta-token space that captures inter-frame geometric transitions. In Stage 2, a projector maps VGM DiT features into the same delta-token space and is frozen after training, using a small subset of the training split. In Stage 3, with full training split, LoRA adapters are optimized only at the identified VGM layers using delta tokens, while the projector remains frozen.

Figure 5: Additional evidence for geometric state forgetting. (a) Linear and MLP probes both show a rise-and-fall pattern in ego-motion decodability. (b) Motion-only interventions produce substantially larger causal effects than norm-matched content-only controls. (c) Geometry commitment K(s) rises early and remains high, while the decodability D(s) and motion-specific causal effect C(s) reused from (a) and (b), respectively, decline during late denoising. Both probes and causal effects decline at later stages, while geometry commitment remains high, supporting the existence of geometric state forgetting.

Figure 6: Successful mobile manipulation rollouts. We visualize two policy rollouts on RoboCasa365, showing a robot placing a bowl into a refrigerator and moving a bread basket to a counter. Both examples demonstrate successful execution of mobile manipulation tasks.

Table 1: Camera ego-motion consistency. We evaluate videos generated from the DL3DV and RealEstate10K evaluation splits with the same estimators and generation settings. Methods without camera control receive the first frame and text prompt; methods that require control also receive camera trajectories and 3D caches. Bold indicates the best result for each metric. CausalAlign improves all seven metrics over Wan2.2 and leads on six of seven metrics.

Table 4: Delta-token ablations. We compare (a) semantic regions with matched-width PCA projections of equally supervised unpartitioned encoders and (b) 128D delta tokens with original 8192D/4096D LingBotMap features. Best values within each panel are bold. Delta tokens lead all six metrics in both panels.

Table 11: Effects of adapter updates and weight averaging. We evaluate different update configurations and weight averaging strategies on the 5B backbone, reporting improvements over the original model. Scaling the update at layer 22 to 0.25 achieves the highest mean gain of 0.769% among the compared configurations.

Table 3: Transfer to world action models. We report success rates (%) on the three RoboCasa365 Target100 task groups. Bold marks the best value in each column, including ties. CausalAlign improves Fast-WAM across all three groups, increasing average success from 43.5% to 54.2% and Atomic-Seen success by 19.0 percentage points.

Table 10: Effects of auxiliary motion objectives. We compare supervision using relative poses, motion dynamics, and their combination on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B under identical training settings. Relative pose supervision achieves the largest trajectory gain of 3.525%, while combining both objectives provides better geometric and temporal preservation.

Table 9: Effects of alignment placement and temporal modulation. We compare LoRA updates at different layer groups and strategies for temporal modulation on Wan2.2-14B, reporting composite gains with 95% confidence intervals. The layers selected by causal diagnosis achieve the largest gain of 3.109%, while the temporal modulation comparisons have confidence intervals that include zero.

Table 12: Effects of training objectives and configurations. We compare different objectives for motion, geometry, and appearance under various training configurations on the 5B backbone. Relative pose alignment at step 72 achieves the highest mean gain of 0.982% among the compared configurations.

Table 13: Training and evaluation settings for Fast-WAM. We summarize the training configuration and evaluation protocol for mobile manipulation on RoboCasa365 Target100. The protocol evaluates the policy on 18 Atomic-Seen tasks with 50 rollouts per task, providing the settings used to assess downstream performance.

Table 2: Visual quality preservation. We evaluate Wan2.2 and CausalAlign using VBench-I2V (quality, I2V score, and smoothness) together with FVD, CLIP, SSIM, and LPIPS. Bold indicates the best result for each metric, including ties. CausalAlign preserves visual quality comparable to Wan2.2.

Table 7: Camera trajectory accuracy under explicit conditioning. We compare CausalAlign with the native Wan2.2 camera control model and FantasyWorld using identical camera trajectories, initial frames, and text prompts. CausalAlign achieves the best results on six of seven metrics, while FantasyWorld has the lowest relative translation error.

Table 6: Ego-motion consistency in text-to-video generation. We evaluate Wan2.2-14B-T2V and CausalAlign using the same text prompts and geometric estimators. CausalAlign improves all seven metrics across motion magnitude, geometric consistency, and temporal dynamics.

Table 5: Visual quality in text-to-video generation. We compare Wan2.2-14B-T2V and CausalAlign using VBench and complementary visual metrics. CausalAlign improves quality, semantic score, FVD, and LPIPS while preserving smoothness, with slightly lower CLIP and SSIM scores.

Table 8: Specialization of delta-token regions. We evaluate the ego-motion, geometry, and visual regions using probes with a common dimension of 24 on 256 scenes across three seeds. Each region performs best on its corresponding task, demonstrating the effectiveness of semantic partitioning.

papers.abstract: Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.
authors: Marcos Junca (Senecta Inc.), Mauro Junca (Senecta Inc.)
bullets: Evaluated Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.7 Flash as deployed decision stages using one request per short thermal clip, with audio when available.
On staged laboratory data, Gemini 3.8 Flash detected 69% of held-out-subject falls and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying down and rising.
In 76 hours of occupied-home footage, it produced no false calls and detected 4 of 9 visible staged falls; the reported upper bound was 1.2 false alarms per day.
Removing a prompt warning about people leaving view substantially increased sensitivity, but caused deliberate lie-downs to be labeled as falls.
Performance fell to 34% sensitivity at 8×6 pixels; identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows, while detected falls were temporally localized accurately.

Fig. 6: Each screener as one point: laboratory falls called (held-out subjects, Wilson 95% interval) against false fall calls per 24 h of ordinary living in the home (exact Poisson 95% interval). The conventional detectors were built on the laboratory data and run at 32 × 24.

papers.abstract: How do diffusion transformers (DiTs) represent image content and learn rules for reusing it to generalize? We develop an aggregator--predictor view of DiTs as input-adaptive local denoisers, in which context aggregation and patch prediction provide functional roles for interpreting attention and MLPs. We first establish that, for Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) priors, the global Bayes denoiser can be approximated using only a subset of context patches, with error decaying exponentially in context radius. We further show that patchwise linear denoisers, often invoked to explain diffusion generalization, recover the empirical local denoiser with sufficiently informative aggregation. Within this view, AdaLN-modulated attention naturally parameterizes an input- and noise-dependent aggregator, while the MLP admits a learned key--value representation for tokenwise patch prediction. Our experiments support this view. DiTs trained on real images exhibit noise-dependent denoising contexts resembling those in the analytic GMRF setting, while attention mass exhibits a qualitatively corresponding broadening pattern. In a controlled CelebA64 study, shared-memory patch predictors used in place of DiT MLPs achieve competitive denoising and generative performance. Finally, cross-dataset component transplantation reveals compatibility patterns consistent with the proposed roles of QK in spatial weighting, VO in feature transport, and MLPs in patch prediction. Together, these results provide a component-level account of DiT denoising and motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled intervention.
authors: Gyeonghun Kang, William Xingxu Chen, Xiang Cheng
bullets: Models DiTs as local denoisers that aggregate relevant context patches and predict clean patches.
Shows that, for GMRF priors, near-optimal denoising can use a limited context whose approximation error decreases exponentially with context radius.
Interprets AdaLN-modulated attention as a noise- and input-dependent aggregator, and MLPs as learned key–value patch predictors.
Experiments on real images, CelebA64, and component transplantation support these functional roles and identify QK with spatial weighting and VO with feature transport.
The findings motivate architecture-specific fine-tuning and controlled component interventions.

papers.abstract: Understanding and modeling light transport in human-centric scenes is a longstanding challenge. While recent progress in diffusion models has boosted research in relighting, precise illumination control still lags, primarily due to the scarcity of diverse, high-quality, precisely labeled video relighting datasets. Existing end-to-end relighting approaches model light transport implicitly through neural networks, which substantially complicates controllability. In contrast, some works resort to path-traced irradiance cues as an explicit blueprint for light transport. However, such constructed irradiance cues are prone to artifacts and hinder generative quality when directly used as control signals. With the key observation that noise corruption removes high-frequency artifacts and preserves low-frequency light transport, we introduce an asynchronous joint-modeling paradigm that facilitates fine-grained illumination control. During two-stage training, we force the model to jointly denoise RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames with separate timesteps scheduling. A domain matching strategy is applied to the second stage to bridge the domain gap between irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps. At inference time, we introduce an asynchronous hijacked generation pipeline that facilitates flexible illumination control. For training data, we develop a multi-illumination high-quality synthetic video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model exhibits robust generalization to real- world scenarios and outperforms prior approaches in both lighting fidelity and generative quality. The code and dataset will be publicly released.
authors: Henglei Lv, Bailin Deng, Xiaoqiang Liu, Yichen Wang, Haoxian Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Lin Gao
bullets: Addresses limited high-quality, precisely labeled video-relighting data and poor controllability in implicit light-transport models.
Jointly denoises RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames using separate timestep schedules across two training stages.
Uses domain matching to reduce the gap between constructed irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps.
Introduces an asynchronous inference pipeline for flexible illumination control.
Trains on a synthetic multi-illumination video dataset and reportedly generalizes to real scenes, improving lighting fidelity and generative quality over prior methods.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) is a challenging task for surveillance systems due to the scarcity and diversity of anomalous events. While semi-supervised VAD approaches have advanced the field, many rely on computationally intensive optical flow networks to capture motion dynamics. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are also widely used for spatial encoding, but their effective receptive field is highly local. To address these limitations, we introduce MS2CAST, an end-to-end semi-supervised predictive VAD framework. For spatial encoding, we employ a multi-scale cross-attention encoder that fuses the hierarchical feature representations from a vision transformer (MViTv2-S) and a CNN (ConvNeXt-T) to exploit their distinct receptive fields. To model spatiotemporal dynamics without optical flow estimation, we integrate two interchangeable spatiotemporal modules in the latent space. One module (SwinLSTM) incorporates a Swin Transformer, while the other (VMRNN) integrates Vision Mamba blocks. Our objective function combines L1 loss, Gradient Difference Loss (GDL), and Multi-Scale Structural Similarity Index Measure (MS-SSIM) to ensure pixel-wise accuracy, sharpness, and structural integrity. Evaluations across the UCSD Ped2, CUHK Avenue, and ShanghaiTech datasets demonstrate frame-level Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Area Under the Curve (AUC) scores that are competitive with top-tier techniques while maintaining a peak GPU memory usage of under 1 GB.
bullets: Addresses scarce and diverse anomalies while reducing reliance on computationally intensive optical flow.
Fuses hierarchical features from MViTv2-S and ConvNeXt-T to capture complementary spatial receptive fields.
Uses either SwinLSTM or VMRNN to model latent spatiotemporal dynamics.
Combines L1, Gradient Difference, and MS-SSIM losses for accurate, sharp, and structurally consistent predictions.
Shows competitive frame-level ROC-AUC performance on UCSD Ped2, CUHK Avenue, and ShanghaiTech, with peak GPU memory below 1 GB.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative models have enabled highly realistic face forgeries, yet generalizing deepfake detectors to unseen manipulation pipelines remains a major challenge. One critical yet underexplored issue is that the learned forensic representation itself may fail to remain stable across different manipulation sources. In this paper, we provide new evidence that naively fine-tuned vision models suffer from severe \textit{forensic representation collapse}: their extracted cues are often entangled with unstable, dataset-specific artifacts, resulting in structurally fragile representations and poor cross-domain generalization. Leveraging this insight, we propose \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{S}patial \textbf{P}rototype (\textbf{HSP}) regularization, which explicitly models the forgery manifold by learning a structured prototype subspace over spatial features. We further introduce prototype orthogonality and second-order assignment balance, which jointly preserve the geometric independence of latent forgery factors and promote high-effective-rank utilization of the forensic representation, thereby reducing reliance on dataset-specific shortcuts. Empirical results demonstrate that our method substantially improves generalizability, yielding average frame-level AUC gains of 5.6\% and 5.3\% in the cross-dataset and cross-manipulation settings, respectively. Moreover, when used as a plug-in module, HSP boosts the average video-level AUC of existing state-of-the-art detectors to 95.3\% (+1.8\%). These results demonstrate the practical value of HSP as an easy-to-adopt regularization module for enhancing deepfake detectors.
authors: Chao Shuai, Shaojing Fan, Kun Pan, Jinwu Hu, Weichen Lian, Ziqi Yang, Zhongjie Ba, Zhenguang Liu
bullets: Identifies forensic representation collapse as a key cause of poor cross-domain generalization in naively fine-tuned vision models.
Learns a structured prototype subspace over spatial features to model the forgery manifold.
Uses prototype orthogonality and second-order assignment balance to preserve distinct latent forgery factors and encourage broader representation usage.
Improves average frame-level AUC by 5.6% cross-dataset and 5.3% cross-manipulation; as a plug-in, raises video-level AUC to 95.3% (+1.8%).
Designed as an easy-to-adopt regularization module for existing deepfake detectors.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the proposed Hierarchical Spatial Prototype (HSP) module for structured-manifold modeling. HSP introduces K learnable spatial prototypes to model latent forgery factors. A soft assignment matrix A decomposes each token into a combination of multiple prototypes and enables heterogeneous forgery traces to be modeled within a prototype-supported manifold. Prototype orthogonality keeps these forgery factors geometrically decoupled, while second-order assignment balance encourages diverse utilization of the prototype space and prevents the representation from collapsing into a few dominant factors.

Figure 9: Visualization of spatial prototype activation maps. We visualize the bilinearly upsampled token-to-prototype soft assignments for 8 selected prototypes (columns) across various input faces (rows). Notably, each prototype isolates distinct and consistent localized regions (e.g., eyes, mouth, or blending boundaries) regardless of the subject’s identity. This demonstrates that the HSP framework successfully disentangles forgery artifacts into diverse, independent structural patterns, mitigating over-reliance on localized shortcuts.

Figure 1: Structured-manifold modeling of forgery representations. (a) Existing methods separate real and fake samples within an entangled feature space. (b) Our approach instead organizes forgery traces into a structured manifold supported by multiple latent forgery factors. (c) The t-SNE visualization provides empirical support for this structured representation.

papers.abstract: Full 3D attention is costly in video Diffusion Transformers. Block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only selected attention blocks. However, existing methods either overlook the potential to optimize sparsity allocation or rely on heuristic rules or local metrics to guide it. In this work, we observe that sparsifying attention in different layers and at different denoising steps affects final-video fidelity to substantially different degrees. Yet the identities of the most sensitive layer-step pairs remain nearly unchanged across inputs. Building on these findings, we propose Allocating Layer-step Latency by Output Tests (ALLOT), a training-free sparsity allocation method. Treating each layer-step pair as a cell, ALLOT estimates each cell's contribution to final-video error through (i) cell probing and (ii) trajectory calibration, then jointly optimizes cell densities under a measured-latency budget. It preserves existing selection strategies and kernels, replacing only the allocation component. At equal or shorter wall-clock time, ALLOT outperforms every compared allocation strategy with XAttention, with an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo. Extensive experiments across four additional published pipelines on Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and HunyuanVideo show that ALLOT outperforms or ties the default in all nine settings.
authors: Tianze Xia, Xiaoling Zhou, Ruya Lan, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song, Shiming Xiang
bullets: Full 3D attention is expensive, and different layer–step pairs have unequal effects on final-video fidelity.
ALLOT estimates each pair’s error contribution using cell probing and trajectory calibration.
It jointly optimizes sparsity densities under a measured-latency budget while retaining existing block-selection strategies and kernels.

Across five video diffusion pipelines and nine settings, ALLOT outperforms or matches the default allocation; with XAttention, it achieves an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo at equal or lower runtime.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes ALLOT, a training-free method to optimize block-sparse attention allocation in Video Diffusion Transformers, directly addressing efficiency and video generation.
papers.title: Sparsity Should Be ALLOTted by Output: Training-Free Allocation of Block-Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: ALLOT is a training-free method that allocates block-sparse attention across layer–denoising-step pairs to improve video diffusion quality under a latency budget.

papers.abstract: Unlike question answering, where a query specifies a perceptual target, open-ended detailed captioning must determine what evidence to acquire and how to integrate it into a coherent global description. We propose Observation-Adaptive Video Captioner (OACap), a caption-centered agent that turns unsupported or missing information into targeted observation requests, uses spatiotemporal tools to acquire evidence, and iteratively verifies and revises the caption. OACap captions consistently improve performance across general video-understanding benchmarks using a fixed text-only reader. To better diagnose the information they preserve, we introduce Factual-Semantic Captioning Bench (FSCap-Bench). Its Core-Support Factuality Score (CSFS) combines claim precision with importance-aware fact coverage and responds as expected to four controlled perturbation types on 93.0-98.3% of valid caption pairs. Its Cross-Modal Semantic Round-Trip Score (CSRS) measures semantic preservation through a video-caption-video-caption round trip by matching atomic facts from source and recovered captions. Together, they connect downstream textual-memory utility with factual and semantic preservation.
authors: Hao Shi, Hong Yan, Xiaoyang Zhang, Qing Cui, Chao Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deciding what evidence to observe for open-ended, detailed video captioning.
Uses a caption-centered agent that identifies missing or unsupported information, gathers targeted spatiotemporal evidence, and revises captions iteratively.
Improves captioning performance across general video-understanding benchmarks with a fixed text-only reader.
Introduces FSCap-Bench with CSFS for importance-aware factual coverage and CSRS for cross-modal semantic preservation.
CSFS responds appropriately to four controlled perturbations in 93.0–98.3% of valid caption pairs.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces an active observation agent for detailed video captioning, relevant to video understanding and multimodal agents.
papers.title: OACap: Caption-Guided Active Observation for Detailed Video Captioning
papers.tldr: OACap actively requests and verifies visual evidence to produce more detailed, factually supported video captions, while FSCap-Bench evaluates their factual and semantic preservation.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy. Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.
authors: Junhyeok Lee, Sangyoon Lee, Jaeho Lee
bullets: Problem: Idle-time KV prefill must use restricted context, causing a mismatch because relevant query information is unavailable and irrelevant context may be included.
Method: At query time, re-prefill selected video tokens with query-relevant context and replace their cached KVs; no additional training is required.
Contribution: Enables shorter idle-time attention windows, lowering prefill computation while preserving or improving contextualization.
Results: Across three SVU frameworks and five benchmarks, accuracy improves by up to 3.9 percentage points.
Efficiency: On RVS-Ego, per-frame prefill FLOPs decrease by over 20%, while total processing time drops by 14–59% for retrieval-based frameworks.

papers.selection_reason: Selective KV recomputation for streaming video LLMs; directly combines video understanding with cache-efficiency and memory reduction.
papers.title: Cache Locally, Recompute Selectively for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FrameBlend improves streaming video understanding by selectively recomputing cached video-token representations with query-relevant context, reducing preprocessing cost while increasing accuracy.

papers.abstract: Autonomous industrial inspection requires strictly deterministic real-time inference under tight memory and computational constraints. However, existing Video Instance Segmentation (VIS) models suffer from prohibitive scaling: dense temporal memory grows with spatial resolution and sequence length, while fixed-capacity decoders fail to exploit the inherent sparsity of industrial scenes, creating a practical memory wall on resource-constrained edge platforms. We present DetM-Tracker, a streamlined VIS framework for autonomous industrial inspection, where target objects often exhibit highly similar appearance under constrained "micro" fields of view. DetM-Tracker eliminates architectural redundancy through three synergistic components: (1) Compact Scalar Memory, which condenses high-dimensional instance features into four-scalar descriptors, reducing temporal memory complexity from $O(T \cdot N \cdot R)$ to $O(T \cdot \hat{N})$. This mechanism effectively compresses frame-level representations into a bank of active instances, where $R$ denotes resolution, $N$ and $\hat{N}$ represent global and window-specific instance counts, respectively and $T$ the temporal window size; and (2) Dynamic Instance Channels, which adaptively allocate query capacity according to the actual number of visible objects; and (3) Entropy-Gated Skip Connection, which concentrates computational budget on high-uncertainty spatial regions to refine object boundaries in a single forward pass without auxiliary refinement heads. Our approach effectively bridges the gap between modern VIS models and the practical demands of industrial edge deployment, reducing inference latency by approximately 20$\times$ and VRAM consumption by 6$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art dense-feature baselines.
authors: You-Rui Lin, Jen-Chieh Wu, Tzu-Ti Wei, Jen-Jee Chen, Yu-Chee Tseng
bullets: Targets the memory and compute limits of edge platforms running autonomous industrial inspection.
Uses Compact Scalar Memory to reduce temporal memory complexity from O(T·N·R) to O(T·N̂) with four-scalar instance descriptors.
Dynamically allocates instance channels based on the number of visible objects.
Uses entropy-gated skip connections to refine uncertain object boundaries in a single forward pass.
Reports approximately 20× lower inference latency and 6× lower VRAM use than dense-feature baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the DetM-Tracker Architecture. The framework decouples VIS into persistent identity and dynamic temporal reasoning. Past states are distilled into Compact Scalar Memory s, which is processed by a memory encoder to produce resolution-invariant temporal tokens XM . These tokens provide context for Memory Attention to refine current-frame image features. The Mask Decoder then facilitates mutual refinement between image-conditioned features and Global Object Queries Pobj to generate initial masks. Finally, Entropy-Gated Skip Connection H(H(·)) selectively integrates high-resolution cues to resolve boundary ambiguities in a single forward pass.

Figure 6: Qualitative Comparison Across Environmental Complexities. While foundation models (SAM 2/3) exhibit mask bleeding and fragmentation in dense industrial arrays, DetM-Tracker maintains high topological fidelity. Especially in "Hard" scenarios with severe occlusions, our framework precisely resolves individual instance boundaries where baselines collapse into monolithic or incomplete masks.

Figure 7: Evaluation of Long-term Temporal Stability. Per-frame precision measured over a 300-frame industrial sequence. While foundation models like SAM 2.1 and LiVOS exhibit rapid precision decay and drift after initial frames, DetM-Tracker maintains near-optimal, consistent performance. Note the high-frequency fluctuations in SAM 3/3.1, indicating a lack of stable temporal memory for thin structures, whereas our framework effectively mitigates cumulative error.

Figure 5: Dataset Statistics. Our million-frame pipeline supports a three-stage curriculum: (a) Synthesis for geometric anchoring (972.9k frames), (b) Real-Unplugged for environment alignment, and (c) Real-Plugged for modeling complex occlusions and cable routing. The table (right) details the datasets statistics.

Figure 3: Compact Scalar Memory. Instance attributes [xc, yc, a, τ ] are extracted from T frames and stacked into a resolution-invariant bank S ∈ R(N̂×4). This scalar abstraction ensures O(T · N̂) memory complexity, decoupling VRAM overhead from spatial resolution.

Figure 4: Bidirectional Mask Decoder. Bidirectional Mask Decoder. Memory tokens Tmem and object queries Pobj undergo mutual refinement through symmetric decoder layers to yield imageconditioned features zmask and instance embeddings zobj . A final scaled dot-product generates the predicted masks zmask ∈ RN×N ′ . This design decouples tracking capacity from network dimensions, enabling high-cardinality segmentation in a single pass.

Figure 2: Reference Encoding. Initial identity anchoring is performed by processing geometric configuration (Conf.) and a reference image (Iref ) through parallel encoding streams to produce structural embeddings Fobj and visual features Fref . These modalities are integrated by an Object Decoder using a query-key/value mechanism to generate Global Object Queries Pobj . This initialization is executed only once per sequence, providing persistent prototypes that maintain identity across the temporal horizon while minimizing per-frame computational overhead.

Table 2: Detection Performance and Instance Robustness. Comparison against various foundation models, fine-tuned variants, and VOS baselines. DetM-Tracker achieves the highest stability and accuracy across all metrics.

Table 1: Quantitative Evaluation of Segmentation Capability. We compare our DetM-Tracker against foundation models (SAM 2/3), fine-tuned variants, and VOS baselines. Our model achieves superior segmentation fidelity while maintaining significantly lower inference latency and memory footprint.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-efficient deterministic video instance segmentation for edge deployment; fits temporal visual understanding and inference efficiency.
papers.title: DetM-Tracker: Deterministic and Memory-Efficient VIS for Autonomous Industrial Inspection
papers.tldr: DetM-Tracker enables deterministic, memory-efficient real-time video instance segmentation for industrial inspection by exploiting sparse scenes and compressing temporal instance memory.

papers.abstract: The scarcity of high-quality annotated visual data remains a critical bottleneck for autonomous-driving perception. Simulators provide training data at scale, but the limited realism of synthetic videos compromises perception performance in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose NeuralSRender, a sim-to-real video translation framework that enhances the photorealism of synthetic videos while maintaining geometric consistency with the source scenes. Built on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT), NeuralSRender uses a lightweight projector to inject geometric and material priors from G-buffers, and LoRA enables parameter-efficient adaptation. The model is trained in two stages: it first learns G-buffer conditioning from synthetic videos with accurate G-buffers, then adapts to real-world appearance using real videos with estimated G-buffers. During the second stage, an additional LoRA module is trained while the projector and first-stage LoRA remain frozen to reduce interference from estimation noise. NeuralSRender introduces only 1.45\% parameter overhead and can be trained on consumer-grade GPUs with 24 GB of memory. To support training and evaluation, we introduce GenReal, a large-scale driving video dataset comprising synthetic and real-world videos with corresponding G-buffers. Experiments demonstrate improved photorealism with competitive geometric consistency. Training perception models on our translated videos instead of raw simulator renders improves detection $\mathrm{AP}_{50}$ on nuImages from 35.1 to 40.6 and segmentation mIoU on Cityscapes from 32.4 to 40.8. Our code, data, and model weights are available at: https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/NeuralSRender.
authors: Yipeng Lu, Youqi Liao, Zhenyu Wang, Yuning Peng, Zhen Dong
bullets: Targets the realism gap between simulator-generated videos and real-world autonomous-driving imagery.
Injects geometric and material priors through a lightweight G-buffer projector and adapts a pretrained video DiT with LoRA.
Uses two-stage training: synthetic G-buffer conditioning followed by real-world appearance adaptation with an additional LoRA module.
Introduces GenReal, a driving-video dataset containing synthetic and real videos with corresponding G-buffers.
Translated videos improve nuImages detection AP50 from 35.1 to 40.6 and Cityscapes segmentation mIoU from 32.4 to 40.8; geometric consistency remains competitive.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of NeuralSRender. In Stage I, the G-buffer projector and LoRA modules are trained on synthetic videos with accurate G-buffers. In Stage II, the model is adapted to real-world videos using estimated G-buffers. In Stage II, the projector is frozen to protect the conditioning mechanism learned from synthetic data, while only the LoRA modules are optimized.

Fig. 1. Photorealistic sim-to-real synthesis with the proposed NeuralSRender. Our approach leverages video generation priors to synthesize photorealistic driving videos from G-buffers, reducing reliance on high-fidelity textures and materials while enabling text-guided changes in weather and time of day.

Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison of control signals and training strategies. Depth and edge controls produce overly smooth results with semantic, texture, color, and lighting errors. Basecolor control provides richer appearance cues but may flatten geometric structures. Two-Stage w/o Freeze degrades learned lighting and shadow patterns, while Single-Stage training may distort geometry and road markings. Our full model best preserves geometry, markings, textures, lighting, and shadows.

Fig. 3. Qualitative results on the synthetic test sets (GenReal-City and GenReal-CARLA). Unlike baselines that retain artificial simulator aesthetics, our approach leverages the explicit geometry and physical priors of G-buffers, alongside text prompts, to achieve photorealistic sim-to-real synthesis while maintaining structural integrity.
Fig. 5. Qualitative perception results with different synthetic training data.

papers.title: NeuralSRender: G-Buffer Guided Video Diffusion for Sim-to-Real Rendering
papers.tldr: NeuralSRender uses G-buffer-guided video diffusion to make synthetic driving videos more photorealistic while preserving scene geometry, improving downstream perception performance.

papers.abstract: In video action detection, modeling the temporal dependencies in continuous video streams is crucial. Previous methods based on deep neural networks can perform frame-level video recognition tasks. However, these methods struggle to model dynamic temporal patterns, facing challenges such as redundant frame information, difficulty balancing global and local features, and insufficient fusion of visual and textual features. To address these issues, we propose a video temporal attention module based on the Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention, which aggregates continuous temporal sequences into feature representations across diverse temporal scales while efficiently reducing redundancy. We also introduce a Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion module that leverages cross-attention at both latent and standard feature levels, achieving fine-grained fusion between video and textual features to enhance semantic alignment and feature interaction. Experimental results across multiple video recognition benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed methods achieve superior performance compared to existing methods, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability.
bullets: Addresses redundant frames, weak global-local temporal modeling, and limited video-text fusion in continuous video recognition.
Uses Multi-Scale Latent Temporal Compression Attention to aggregate sequences across temporal scales while reducing redundancy.
Introduces Video-Text Cross Attention Fusion at latent and standard feature levels for fine-grained semantic interaction.
Experiments on multiple video recognition benchmarks report superior performance and generalization versus existing methods.

papers.tldr: A multi-scale temporal compression and video-text cross-attention framework improves video action detection by reducing temporal redundancy and strengthening visual-semantic alignment.

papers.abstract: Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube $\{-1,1\}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.
bullets: Addresses reward-guided sampling from exponential tilts using only a diffusion model trained on base-distribution samples.
Exploits an exact identity: for discrete hypercube data, the denoiser of a linearly tilted density equals the base denoiser at a shifted and rescaled input.
Trains the denoiser with random diagonal data rescalings so it supports the required out-of-distribution evaluation points.
A single network handles binary reward tilts, class-conditional sampling, and infilling without fine-tuning or external guidance terms.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes 'internal guidance' as a sampling method for tilted diffusion models. This technique modifies the evaluation point of the denoiser, relevant to diffusion-based video generation and sampling.
papers.title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: Internal guidance samples tilted binary diffusion distributions by evaluating one base denoiser at shifted, rescaled inputs instead of modifying its output or diffusion transitions.

papers.abstract: Amodal video segmentation asks for the complete mask of an object in every frame, including the parts hidden behind other objects. The best current methods generate these masks with fine-tuned video diffusion models, which need many denoising steps and an extra depth network, and give a different answer for every sample. Self-supervised video world models of the JEPA family are trained on a closely related task: predicting the representation of masked space-time regions from the visible ones. We therefore treat occlusion as masking. The tokens that the object's visible mask does not cover are dropped, the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor fills them in, and a light head decodes the observed and predicted features into amodal masks. The resulting model, OccJEPA (Occlusion-as-masking JEPA), is deterministic and 33.5x faster than the diffusion-based state of the art, and more accurate on SAIL-VOS, on TAO-Amodal, including a held-out test split (+4.00 AP50) and visible masks tracked by SAM2, and on Kubric. Controlled experiments trace the gain to the predictor's pre-trained weights rather than to its capacity, for world models from 87M to 1.85B parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/zgp110/occjepa.
bullets: Amodal video segmentation must infer object regions hidden behind occluders in every frame.
Visible-mask tokens are retained while uncovered space-time tokens are masked and predicted by a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor.
A lightweight decoder converts observed and predicted features into complete object masks.
OccJEPA is deterministic, 33.5× faster than diffusion-based methods, and more accurate across SAIL-VOS, TAO-Amodal, and Kubric.
Controlled experiments attribute improvements to pretrained predictor weights rather than model capacity across 87M–1.85B-parameter world models.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overall framework of OccJEPA. The clip is cropped around the object’s visible mask. Tokens whose visible-mask coverage ρi is below τ are dropped; the encoder E reads the kept tokens and the pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 predictor P predicts features at the dropped positions, giving the filled features f (Eq. (4)). The same encoder also reads the full clip (z); it stays frozen except for one LoRA adapter (bow tie: a low-rank bottleneck) shared by both passes. The mask head H decodes [z; f ], together with the RGB crop and the visible mask, into amodal masks, which are pasted back into the frames; at test time, a second pass re-crops objects that leave the first crop. Real data of a SAIL-VOS validation sequence: feature maps show the first three principal components of z and f (in f , the black outline encloses the kept tokens; everything outside it is predicted); magenta: completed hidden part.

papers.abstract: Coarse-to-real (C2R) video generation converts coarse animation, simulation, or game-rendered videos into photorealistic videos while preserving scene layout, camera motion, and dynamics. Training such models requires aligned (coarse, realistic) video pairs, which are expensive to create and confine prior systems to narrow synthetic domains. We exploit a simple asymmetry: paired videos are hard to obtain, but paired real-to-coarse images are easy to construct with existing editing and 3D reconstruction tools. Using these image pairs, we train the DINO-R2C model to transfer realistic images to coarse images in DINO feature space, and apply it frame-wise to ordinary real videos to synthesize pseudo-coarse videos. The C2R# model then learns to generate each real video from its pseudo-coarse counterpart, free from needing (coarse, realistic) video pairs. At inference, the DINO-R2C model is discarded and actual coarse videos drive the C2R# model directly. Thus, our pair-free training scales with any real-video corpora rather than with paired synthetic videos. We will release the model and project webpage at https://gonzalognogales.github.io/coarse2real-sharp/.
authors: Gonzalo G\'omez-Nogales, Daohan Lu, Peiye Zhuang, Tinghui Zhou, Yi Zhou
bullets: Addresses the high cost and limited domain coverage of paired coarse–real video data.
Trains DINO-R2C in feature space to convert real-video frames into pseudo-coarse frames.
Trains C2R# to reconstruct real videos from these pseudo-coarse videos.
At inference, C2R# directly uses actual coarse videos; DINO-R2C is discarded.
The approach can leverage broad real-video corpora without paired synthetic videos.

papers.abstract: Instruction-guided video generative models offer a scalable solution for stress-testing autonomous driving systems by simulating diverse environmental conditions. However, driving scenes operate within a dense Operational Design Domain (ODD) governed by strict traffic semantics. When applied to global driving-condition edits, general-purpose instruction-guided video editors frequently corrupt these semantics, leading to structural hallucinations and ``temporal shock.'' This work distills and protects traffic semantics during video editing at three levels. First, we construct a hybrid dataset by combining temporally aligned real-world videos with synthetic edits, balancing foundational scene structure with unambiguous appearance signals. Second, during training, we adapt advantage conditioning from offline reinforcement learning to align the model using dense rewards. We extract dense, pixel-level rewards from the hybrid data to serve as a localized signal and actively steer generation toward structurally reliable pixels. Finally, our model mitigates temporal shock by introducing thinking frames, a transition mechanism that seamlessly reconciles static image conditioning with dynamic video context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method prevents the corruption of multi-actor dynamics, establishing state-of-the-art spatiotemporal consistency, yielding consistent user preference (39% relative improvement in content preservation and 12% in temporal consistency), and achieving a significant 5% gain in downstream road line segmentation and 7% gain in downstream multi-object detection.
authors: Mauricio Soroco, Yuqiu Liu, Zaid Tasneem, Francesco Pittaluga, Abhishek Aich, Wuyang Chen, Manmohan Chandraker, Ziyu Jiang
bullets: Targets structural hallucinations and “temporal shock” caused by general-purpose video editors in driving scenes.
Uses a hybrid dataset combining temporally aligned real videos with synthetic edits to preserve scene structure and clarify appearance changes.
Applies advantage conditioning with dense, pixel-level rewards to steer generation toward structurally reliable edits.
Introduces “thinking frames” to smoothly connect static image conditioning with dynamic video context.
Reports 39% relative improvement in content preservation, 12% in temporal consistency, 5% in road-line segmentation, and 7% in multi-object detection.

papers.abstract: Conventional surgical segmentation relies on closed-set categories or explicit text queries, which cannot resolve implicit queries that require reasoning about workflows, instrument functions, and temporal relationships. To address these limitations, we propose SurgReasonSeg, a complexity-aware method that brings reasoning segmentation over digital twin (DT) representations to surgical video. Specifically, SurgReasonSeg constructs DT representations from surgical foundation models and trains two low-rank adapters (LoRA) of one large language model with reinforcement learning (RL), each specialized for a different query complexity. A lightweight router, also trained with RL, selects between the two adapters to balance latency against accuracy. SurgReasonSeg also sets the temporal context with an adaptive sliding window conditioned on query complexity and workflow phase, and retrieves relevant historical cases from a surgical context memory by workflow similarity and procedural relevance. We further introduce EndoVis-ReasonSeg, a surgical reasoning segmentation benchmark with 1,460 training and 961 test samples across semantic, spatial, and temporal categories. On EndoVis-ReasonSeg, SurgReasonSeg improves J&F over the strongest baseline, ReSurgSAM2, by 0.178, 0.237, and 0.297 on semantic, spatial, and temporal queries, and it also achieves the best results on the Ref-EndoVis17 and Ref-EndoVis18 referring segmentation benchmarks. A backbone-matched attribution protocol separates the contribution of the upstream segmenter from that of the reasoning modules. Our method runs at 18.8 FPS averaged over the query distribution, enabling real-time reasoning segmentation in surgical videos.
bullets: Addresses limitations of closed-set labels and explicit text queries that cannot capture workflow, instrument-function, and temporal reasoning.
Builds digital-twin representations and uses two reinforcement-learning-trained LoRA adapters, with a learned router balancing accuracy and latency by query complexity.
Adapts temporal context windows to query complexity and workflow phase, while retrieving relevant historical cases from a workflow-aware surgical memory.
Introduces the EndoVis-ReasonSeg benchmark with 1,460 training and 961 test samples across semantic, spatial, and temporal queries.
Reports higher J&F than ReSurgSAM2 across all three query types, best results on two referring-segmentation benchmarks, and 18.8 FPS average speed.
