papers.abstract: Objects move, cameras pan, and weather drifts with the wind: much of what changes in sequential data is motion. Motion changes where things are, not what they are, and is therefore a symmetry of the data. Yet standard recurrent networks are not equivariant to it: their memory stays put while the input moves on. Flow equivariant recurrent networks first brought this symmetry into sequence models, for motions of constant velocity, or flows, by enumerating a bank of velocities. We extend this idea in three directions: from simple recurrent networks to convolutional LSTMs, from flows to motions whose velocity changes in time, and from enumerating velocities to estimating them. Treating a sequence as a field over time, we show that motion becomes a gauge symmetry: a global symmetry made local in time. Built on this view, our motion equivariant convolutional LSTM (MELSTM) uses its velocity model as the gauge field and is provably equivariant to every motion. Across future-frame prediction, classification of digits visible only through their motion, and action recognition under camera shake, MELSTM outperforms a convolutional LSTM and its flow equivariant counterpart with the same number of parameters: it is more accurate, generalizes to longer horizons and to unseen motions, and carries a fraction of the flow equivariant model's state.
authors: Vahid Hosseinzadeh, T. Anderson Keller, Michael Puthawala
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between moving inputs and stationary recurrent memory.
Extends motion-equivariant recurrence from simple RNNs to convolutional LSTMs and from constant-velocity flows to time-varying motion.
Estimates motion rather than enumerating a bank of velocities.
Demonstrates gains in future-frame prediction, motion-based digit classification, and action recognition under camera shake.
Outperforms parameter-matched convolutional LSTMs and flow-equivariant models while using substantially less state, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Hidden-state transport under RNN, Flow Equivariant RNN (FERNN), and Motion Equivariant RNN (MERNN) models. The first row shows the transformed input, ϕ ▷ Xt in the flow column and ψ ▷ Xt in the motion column. Here an MNIST digit undergoes two simultaneous changes: a geometric transformation along the group orbit (the motion, which differs across columns) and an intrinsic appearance change transverse to the group action (identical across columns). The second row shows the hidden state of an untrained leaky accumulator, ht+1 = λht + Xt (λ = 0.92), which can be viewed as a convolutional RNN, ht+1 = W⋆ht+U⋆Xt, with kernels W (x) = λδ(x) and U(x) = δ(x). The third row shows FERNN’s hidden state, which is lifted to velocity copies g ∈ {−3, . . . , 3}2 and evolves as hgt+1 = λ g ·hgt +Xt; we show the copy of maximum energy, i.e., the copy with the largest ∥hgt ∥2 2. The fourth row shows MERNN’s hidden state, ht+1 = λTvt ht + Xt, where Tvt is the transport operator and vt is the digit’s velocity at time t. Matched transport stacks evidence into a sharp digit at the true location, whereas mismatched transport leaves a decaying ghost trail along the residual motion.
Figure 4: Motion generalization sensitivity. Each model normalized by its own training error (1.0 = no degradation).

Figure 5: Motion-Only MNIST: Training efficiency and test accuracy. Right: five-seed mean ± s.d. of the best validation and the test accuracy and of the median time per epoch. Dotted lines: chance (10%).

Figure 3: Rollout stability and context-boundary sensitivity. Left: median rollout MSE. Middle: MSE at t = 16 of sequences whose last velocity change came 1–3 frames before the context boundary (boundary velocity age), relative to settled sequences (age ≥ 4). Right: the age-1 group over the rollout; the FELSTM penalty persists through mid-rollout before gradually decaying.
Figure 2: Training efficiency and test error. Right: test MSE over the trained horizon and at t = 100; mean ± s.d. over five seeds.

Figure 6: Motion generalization sensitivity in classification. Relative to their own training accuracy (far lower for LSTM), LSTM and FELSTM respond alike, except at speed 1, where LSTM improves because its 3 × 3 recurrence can move its memory with the digit.

Figure 7: KTH: training and generalization to camera shake. Left: validation accuracy under the training shake. Right: test accuracy under shakes of amplitude A and frequency f (A = 0: static camera); mean ± s.d. over three seeds.

Figure 9: The channel-handover penalty across the seven motion regimes. Top: kinematics of the seven evaluation regimes and the training baseline. The unpredictability ρ collapses the switching rate r and the jump magnitude |∆v| into a single number; net context displacement falls as ρ rises, because the trajectories become diffusive. Bottom: FELSTM’s architectural penalty (MSE normalised by the LSTM baseline) against ρ(1 − ρ). Because FELSTM allocates separate channels to discrete velocities, a velocity change forces a handover that strands accumulated temporal history; we model its cost as the product of the disruption (ρ) and the predictive value of what is stranded (1 − ρ). The penalty is negligible up to ρ(1 −ρ) ≈ 0.1, including under pure chaos (churn_max, ρ → 1), where the stranded history is worthless, and grows steeply above it. random_walk (frequent tiny jitters) and churn_half (less frequent but far larger jumps) are kinematically opposite, yet sit at nearly symmetric points of the parabola and show nearly equal penalties.

Figure 8: Length generalization beyond the trained horizon. Two held-out sequences; rows are the ground truth, LSTM, FELSTM, and MELSTM. The dashed box marks the 25 frames seen in training (15 context + 10 predicted); the rest is extrapolation, run out to t = 140, past the 85-step horizon scored in Figure 3. LSTM collapses almost immediately, FELSTM smears into high-frequency artifacts late in the rollout, and MELSTM stays sharp throughout.

Figure 12: Stochastic frame-pair velocities. In training, MELSTM uses frame-pair velocities with a probability that decays to 0 by epoch 25; validation uses slot tracking only. Losses (MSE + L1) are means over three seeds with the min–max range shaded; faint traces are recorded every 25 batches and circles once per epoch (Appendix B.1.2). Table: test MSE over the trained horizon and at t = 100; mean ± s.d.
Figure 13: Frame-pair curriculum. As Figure 12, but training uses frame-pair velocities on the first steps of the context, a window that shrinks from the whole context to none by epoch 25.

Figure 11: Velocity accuracy (one training run). The estimator is parameter-free and receives no gradient, so the rise from ≈ 66% at epoch 5 to above 99.5% by epoch 8 reflects the hidden-state template improving, not the estimator being fitted. Final values are means over the last five epochs. In the same run, the validation loss stays on a plateau near 7 × 10−2 until about epoch 6 and then falls by an order of magnitude while the accuracy climbs: the model leaves the plateau when the slots lock onto their digits. The five seeds of Figure 2 leave it at different times, which smooths their mean.

Figure 14: Hidden states on Motion-Only MNIST. Channel-averaged state of each MELSTM slot (a) and of the FELSTM copies at the velocities the digit takes during the context (b); the bottom rows show the input frames. The digit’s outline is drawn only for the reader: the frames themselves are pure noise. MELSTM’s slot s1 follows the digit and accumulates its shape, while s0 follows the background; because the digit’s velocity keeps changing, no FELSTM copy accumulates the shape for long.

Figure 10: Slot specialisation. Hidden-state evolution for a validation sequence (top) and a training sequence (bottom). Within each block the first two rows show the channel-averaged states H̄1, H̄2 of the K = 2 slots and the third the corresponding frame; column titles give t, in red once the decoder takes over. Each slot localises onto one digit and tracks it, and this is the template that Eq. (97) correlates against the incoming frame.

Figure 15: Example KTH clip with and without camera shake. All 16 frames of a handwaving clip from the test set. Top: original clip (static camera). Bottom: the same clip with the camera shaking horizontally, with A = 8 px and P = 8 frames (1.6 Hz).

papers.selection_reason: Motion-equivariant convolutional LSTM for future-frame prediction and action recognition; relevant to predictive video models and video understanding.
papers.title: Motion Equivariant Convolutional LSTM: When Motion Becomes a Gauge Symmetry
papers.tldr: MELSTM makes convolutional LSTMs equivariant to time-varying motion by estimating motion as a local gauge field, improving robustness to unseen and longer-horizon motions.

papers.abstract: Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion. Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene. For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene. Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video-motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion. Videos and additional results are available on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/par/projects/jca/.
authors: Noam Rotstein, Yoad Tewel, Chen Tessler, Haggai Maron, Gal Chechik, Or Litany, Yoni Kasten, Yuval Atzmon
bullets: Addresses the gap between realistic video generation and usable 3D animation for specific assets.
Separates an arbitrary-skeleton 3D motion model from a pretrained video model, linking them with lightweight cross-attention.
Predicts joint locations in video to recover the camera and register 3D motion in the scene.
Uses curated synthetic edits plus human and robot video to create nearly 200K training pairs.
Supports text-to-motion/video, video-to-rig motion, rig-motion-to-video, and keyframe control; evaluations report more faithful, scene-responsive animation than video-first pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview. Given a text prompt, a rig, and an optional reference image, the model jointly denoises video latents Zv and motion tokens Zm. A graph network encodes the rig into per-joint descriptors D, using the joints’ 2D locations in the reference image, and these condition the motion branch; a graph-attention layer inside each Motion DiT block propagates features along the rig edges. Zero-initialized cross-attention bridges exchange features in both directions at paired blocks, each branch querying the other’s intermediate features, so joint training begins from the two pretrained branches acting as they did in isolation. An auxiliary joint-localization head (right) attends from joint features to video patches and returns each joint’s image position as a weighted combination of patch coordinates, giving 2D–3D correspondences used to fit a camera.

Top: frames from the generated video, where the penguin moves forward and slides down the snowy slope. Middle: the raw 3D motion produced by the motion branch, rendered in the input scene before localization. The penguin’s motion is not aligned with the depicted scene geometry and, in later frames, appears beneath the snow surface. Bottom: the same generated motion after applying our joint-localization and camera-alignment scheme described in section 3.3. The estimated alignment correctly places the motion on the visible penguin and registers it with the generated video and scene.

papers.abstract: Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present SolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that SolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.
authors: Guian Fang, Shengju Qian, Dongyue Lu, Junchao Huang, Lutao Jiang, Xin Wang, Yiren Song, Li Jiang, Mike Zheng Shou
bullets: Addresses renderers that are engine-specific, slow, and trained with misaligned conditions.

Uses structure-guided distribution matching to render in four steps, reported as 12.3× faster than 50-step sampling.
A block-causal variant supports real-time 768p video streaming.
Trained on 136K frame-aligned clips; achieves state-of-the-art results on in-distribution and generalization benchmarks, including 11 unseen representations.

papers.abstract: Understanding human needs and selecting responses require distinct judgments that aggregate accuracy can obscure. We introduce PsycheMME, a video benchmark informed by psychology, with eight capabilities spanning grounding, states, needs, interaction decisions, memory, and risk. Drawing on Social Information Processing and the Perception-Action Cycle, this organization separates human understanding from response selection. We construct 1,000 questions from 630 episodes through independent answering with proposed references withheld and expert review. Our Reasoning-Verified protocol weights answer credit by the support and logical consistency of explicit rationales against annotated cues. Across 17 models, Timing has the lowest Verified scores and credit retention, with weaker support judgments for correct Timing answers. Models with similar Need scores still differ in answer completeness on open questions. Input controls and SFT/GRPO examine context dependence and adaptation. Evaluating answers alongside rationales locates where models fail across understanding, response selection, and justification.
authors: Heran Hu, Yuhang Dong, Zhucun Xue, Kaiwei Chen, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang

The benchmark helps identify failures in understanding, response selection, and justification; its scope centers on the evaluated video episodes and capabilities.

papers.abstract: Video generation and feed-forward 3D reconstruction typically use separate representations, requiring RGB decoding and visual re-encoding to recover geometry from generated latents. We propose Latent Bridge, which connects video generative latent spaces with geometric feature spaces to directly predict 3D geometry from video latents. We develop representation-specific bridges for Wan2.1 and V-RAE, enabling feed-forward prediction of cameras, depth, and 3D point clouds without the intermediate RGB pathway. Each bridge is trained on RGB videos through feature distillation, while the video encoder and geometry model remain frozen. Training requires neither ground-truth geometry nor execution of the downstream geometric aggregator or prediction heads. At inference, the same video latents support both RGB decoding and geometry prediction. The same trained bridge can be reused for image-to-video and text-to-video generation within the same video latent space, without bridge retraining. Experiments on Co3Dv2 and WildRGB-D demonstrate competitive geometric reconstruction quality, efficient end-to-end generation and reconstruction, and faster latent-to-geometry decoding, highlighting latent alignment as a practical and reusable interface between video generation and 3D reconstruction. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hustvl/Latent-Bridge.
authors: Shuai Zhang, Zhanpeng Ouyang, Zhengqing Chen, Ruohong Mei, Shaoyu Chen, Weiqiang Ren, Hui Sun, Qian Zhang, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of recovering geometry from generated video latents through an intermediate RGB pathway.
Learns representation-specific bridges for Wan2.1 and V-RAE to predict cameras, depth, and 3D point clouds.

The same bridge supports image-to-video and text-to-video generation within a latent space without retraining.
Experiments on Co3Dv2 and WildRGB-D show competitive reconstruction, efficient generation–reconstruction, and faster latent-to-geometry decoding.

papers.abstract: Smart glasses can help users understand their activities and surroundings, but small vision-language models must preserve useful evidence within limited computation. This is difficult because redundant frames consume the visual budget, while aggressive spatial compression can discard relevant details. Although gaze identifies the wearer's focus, the question may require evidence from the surrounding scene. To address these constraints, we propose GazeLens, which combines frame selection with gaze- and question-guided token reduction. First, HOG transitions and image sharpness select frames before visual encoding. For each selected frame, Gaussian pooling then forms gaze-focused and complementary summaries. Because their relevance depends on the question, a lightweight gate blends them into a primary token. Together with a global scene token, this retains both focused and contextual summaries within two tokens per frame. On StreamGaze, GazeLens achieves higher macro and micro accuracy than the evaluated full-grid and token-reduction baselines, with lower input-forward FLOPs than the shared-backbone token-reduction baselines.
authors: Trong-Thang Pham, Anh Nguyen, Hien Van Nguyen, Ngan Le
bullets: Addresses limited computation in smart-glasses VQA while preserving both gaze-focused evidence and surrounding context.
Selects frames using HOG transitions and image sharpness before visual encoding.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed focus-aware, question-conditioned token reduction framework. (1) Dynamic Frame Selection. A continuous video stream is filtered using HOG transition and sharpness cues to retain informative frames while discarding small-change and blurry frames. This filtering process produces a dynamic input sequence V . (2) Focus-Aware Gaze Aggregation. Each selected frame is encoded into spatial features and combined with gaze (xt, yt) to produce a focus token gt, an unfocus token ct, and a global token mt. (3) Question-Conditioned Semantic Gating. Question token embeddings are mean-pooled and L2-normalized to t. A two-layer MLP and sigmoid then yield a scalar gate s ∈ [0, 1]. The gate modulates gaze-focused versus contextual information as pt = s · gt + (1− s) · ct. (4) Token Assembly and Training Objective. The per-frame tokens pt and mt are linearly projected, concatenated with the question, and fed into a language model to predict the answer, optimized with a cross-entropy (CE) loss.

In the middle panel, existing VLM approaches suffer from inefficient frame selection (too dense or too sparse) and often ignore gaze or rely on computationally expensive adaptive attention mechanisms. In the right panel, our approach combines (1) Dynamic Frame Selection, (2) Focus-Aware Gaze Aggregation, and (3) Question-Conditioned Semantic Gating. Together, these modules produce two visual tokens per frame. This design reduces the visual token budget and model computation while improving performance under strict token budgets.

papers.title: GazeLens for Efficient Egocentric Video Question Answering with Simple Gaze-Driven Adaptive Token Reduction
papers.tldr: GazeLens improves egocentric video question answering efficiency by selecting informative frames and compressing each into two question- and gaze-aware visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.

papers.abstract: Vision-language trackers (VLTs) accept descriptions intended to assist tracking, but accepting text does not establish that its content changes tracking decisions, particularly as visual evidence deteriorates. We introduce DISTRACT, a matched-intervention benchmark that holds video, target, and distractor fixed while crossing four text priors with four image degradations along a controlled severity axis. We evaluate five VLTs on four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise representation probes, and activation patching. Molmo2 and JointNLT exhibit directed text use. Some effects contract under degradation, whereas others show no significant endpoint change after multiplicity correction. UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack respond only weakly to changes in text semantics, with no directed behavioral effect surviving FDR correction in the tested settings. Model-internal analyses reveal that at decision-near states, correct-versus-conflicting text is decodable in Molmo2 and JointNLT but not in the other three systems. In the responsive models, decodability peaks at late states where replacement produces little behavioral change, whereas replacing selected earlier states redirects conflict-associated trajectories toward the target. Because matched-correct donors do not significantly outperform unrelated donors, these interventions identify earlier intervention-sensitive states without establishing target-specific semantic rescue. DISTRACT thus exposes when and where text affects tracking under degraded visual evidence.
bullets: Uses matched interventions crossing four text priors with four controlled image-degradation levels while holding video, target, and distractor fixed.
Evaluates five trackers across four datasets using behavioral contrasts, layerwise probes, and activation patching.
Molmo2 and JointNLT show directed text use; UVLTrack, MMTrack, and DUTrack show no significant directed behavioral effects after FDR correction.
In responsive models, text is decodable near decisions, but earlier-state interventions more effectively redirect conflict-associated trajectories.
The benchmark identifies intervention-sensitive states, but does not establish target-specific semantic rescue because matched-correct donors did not outperform unrelated donors.

papers.abstract: Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.
authors: Zhenghan Chen, Zekai Shao, Xin Lin, Leting Cheng, Siming Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of broad evaluation for complete code-based video creation beyond specialized tasks.

Combines 12 objective metrics with five subjective MLLM-judged metrics for operational performance, quality, alignment, fidelity, instruction following, and holistic quality.
Evaluation of 15 MLLMs shows persistent difficulty producing high-quality, requirement-aligned videos, with performance declining as task complexity increases.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.
authors: Yuhang Chen, Guangyue Liu, Shilong Liu
bullets: Targets a gap in streaming benchmarks that focus mainly on timestamped question answering rather than deciding whether, when, and how to respond.
Defines six tasks across proactive intervention, continuous engagement, and coordination during overlapping or multi-party interaction.
Provides 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and temporal metadata.
Separately evaluates response quality, participation decisions, and timing using response quality, window response rate, and reaction latency.
Leading models respond in under a second on average, but window response rates reach at most 53.77%; adapting responses to new information remains difficult.

papers.abstract: As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai
bullets: Covers five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing.
Uses 300 scripted 15–300-second test cases with incremental multimodal requests, initial assets, and explicit preservation requirements.
Evaluates task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination through ten task-specific metrics.
Results from 37 models show that visual quality and identity retention do not guarantee reliable request execution or sustained consistency.
Request execution scores remain low across evaluated tasks, highlighting a key bottleneck for real-time interactive systems.

papers.abstract: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.
authors: Marc Chapus, Carlos Crispim-Junior, V\'eronique Eglin, Atilla Baskurt
bullets: Existing VideoQA benchmarks are dominated by small ground-truth counts, masking errors at rarer cardinalities.
The benchmark contains 2,600 synthetic videos with 26 balanced counts from 5 to 50, controlled camera motion, and single-class static objects.
Sixteen video-language models are evaluated zero-shot; none exceeds 27.6% exact-match accuracy.
Accuracy varies unpredictably with cardinality, including monotonic declines and peak-and-collapse patterns.
Models favor particular integers, with performance dropping sharply at neighboring counts, motivating balanced diagnostic benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic benchmark for object counting by video-language models; directly targets video understanding and multimodal LLM evaluation.
papers.title: CountVideoBench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Prediction Biases on the Object Counting task by Video-Language Models
papers.tldr: CountVideoBench reveals strong, model-specific biases in video object counting that standard, small-count-skewed benchmarks often hide.

papers.abstract: Autonomous video editing from open-world resources remains a challenging problem in multimedia content creation. Retrieval-based methods are constrained by fixed source material and lack creative flexibility, while generative models struggle with long-horizon coherence and often diverge from user intent. Both paradigms fail to replicate the structured, multi-stage reasoning that underlies professional post-production. To address these limitations, we present Auto-Director, a tool-augmented multi-agent framework that mirrors professional editorial workflows: a Planning Agent decomposes abstract topics into fact-grounded scripts via retrieval-augmented planning; a Material Agent indexes open-world footage through shot segmentation and visual tagging; an Editor Agent assembles semantically aligned clips with MLLM-driven spatial adaptation; and a Critic Agent governs an iterative Reflect-and-Revise loop that checks scene-level alignment and pacing. To rigorously evaluate this new paradigm, we introduce VEdit-Bench, a benchmark of 100 expert-curated topics with human-annotated Golden Scripts and a five-dimensional metric suite covering Narrative Logic, Factual Accuracy, Semantic Alignment, Compositional Quality, and Stylistic Cohesion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Auto-Director significantly outperforms baseline methods in both automated metrics and human evaluation, effectively bridging the gap between amateurs and professional-grade video production.
authors: Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang, Teng Zhong, Yu Zhang
bullets: Addresses limited creative flexibility in retrieval-based editing and poor long-horizon coherence or intent alignment in generative approaches.
Uses four specialized agents: Planning, Material, Editor, and Critic, coordinated through retrieval, visual tagging, semantic alignment, and iterative revision.
Introduces VEdit-Bench, a benchmark with 100 expert-curated topics, Golden Scripts, and five evaluation dimensions.
Reports better automated-metric and human-evaluation performance than baseline methods, narrowing the gap between amateur and professional video production.

papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent autonomous video editing framework and benchmark, relevant to temporally structured visual content generation and editing.
papers.title: Auto-Director: Leveraging Multi-Agent Collaboration for Autonomous Video Editing
papers.tldr: Auto-Director uses collaborating agents to plan, source, assemble, and critique videos, enabling more coherent and professionally structured autonomous editing from open-world content.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Siqi Guo, Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang, Teng Zhong, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets premature responses and other timing errors in streaming video understanding.
Uses a question-specific plan to identify observations and completion signals.
Checks draft answers at informative moments for stability, frame grounding, and event completion.
Maintains verified observations in an event ledger while the video stream unfolds.
Improves official protocols by up to 5.9 PAUC points and 6.2 accuracy points across evaluated benchmarks and backbones.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Response timing on a video stream: evidence for a question posed at t0 arrives over time. A chunk-wise baseline answers at every chunk; its first two replies are premature, and it cannot know that its third is final. PACE holds the draft until its watch plan’s completion signal fires, then answers once, correctly.
Fig. 2. PACE plans what to observe, schedules activity-triggered probes, checks each draft, and records verified events and evidence for subsequent probes.

Fig. 3. Qualitative cases from ProactiveVideoQA: a rolling web video, top, and a singletruth anomaly clip, bottom. Each case shows sampled frames with their timestamps, the ground-truth replies with their reply windows, the direct chunk-wise replies of the backbone, and the behavior of PACE.
Table 3. Module ablation of PACE on ProactiveVideoQA with the closed-source backbone GPT-4.1-mini. Each row removes one module from the full system; subscripts give the change from the full system.
Table 4. Module ablation of PACE on ProactiveVideoQA with the open-source backbone Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Each row removes one module from the full system; subscripts give the change from the full system.
Table 1. PAUC on ProactiveVideoQA [29] with ω=0.5. Published results are taken from the corresponding papers. The bottom block compares each backbone with and without PACE.
Table 2. Accuracy on OVO-Bench Forward Active Responding [20]. Published results are taken from the corresponding papers. The bottom block compares each backbone with and without PACE.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free framework for streaming video understanding and temporal response timing, directly relevant to video-language understanding.
papers.title: PACE: Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit for Training-Free Response Timing in Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: PACE is a training-free framework that helps video LLMs decide both what to answer and when to emit it by checking answer stability, evidence grounding, and event completion.

papers.abstract: Oddly Satisfying Videos (OSVs) can evoke strong viewer responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility, and ASMR-like sounds despite containing few explicit semantic emotion cues. This makes OSVs a challenging setting for Video Emotion Analysis (VEA), since most existing methods focus on semantic video content and under-model the physical sensory dynamics that shape viewer responses. To support Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis (OSVEA), we construct the Oddly Satisfying Video Dataset (OSVD), comprising 12,000 annotated 5-second clips. Each clip provides viewer-emotion labels under video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual conditions, together with explanations grounded in visual and acoustic sensory evidence. Building on OSVD, we propose PI-MLLM, a psychophysics-inspired multimodal large language model that integrates Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment (MSDA) and Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution (CAVA). MSDA uses auxiliary prediction objectives to align modality representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics. CAVA evaluates emotion scores across modality coalitions and applies Shapley attribution to identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting. Experiments show that PI-MLLM improves both viewer-side emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality, suggesting the value of physical sensory cues to video emotion analysis.
authors: Yuheng Zhang, Jie Zhang, Yuecong Min, Yunwei Zhao, Meichen Liu, Qiankun Li, Shiguang Shan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of analyzing emotions in videos with few explicit semantic cues but strong sensory effects.
Introduces OSVD, a dataset of 12,000 annotated 5-second clips with video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual emotion labels and sensory-grounded explanations.
Uses Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment to align representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics.
Uses Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution with Shapley values to identify dominant modalities and audiovisual synergy or conflict.
Experiments report improved emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overall framework of PI-MLLM. Visual and audio inputs are encoded into FV and FA to generate viewer emotion c and a sensory-grounded explanation e. MSDA aligns the visual representation with optical-flow dynamics and the audio representation with RMS loudness and onset strength. CAVA uses modality-conditioned emotion scores to estimate visual and auditory contributions and their interaction. The total objective combines generation, dynamics-alignment, coalitionclassification, and attribution losses.

Figure 1: Existing VEA methods rely on sensory-ungrounded semantic annotations and implicit multimodal fusion. Our approach addresses these limitations with psychophysics-aware sensory annotations and explicit multimodal modeling that preserves modality-specific dynamics and cross-modal relations for viewer-emotion reasoning.

Figure 2: OSVD construction and annotation pipeline. Word-cloud-derived keywords guide data collection. Then segmented clips are semantically deduplicated, filtered for resolution, and checked for audio integrity. Visual annotations are structured as scene, motion, and state change, while audio annotations are structured as sound character, temporal envelope, and spatial impression. Finally, the modality-specific reports are fused into audio-visual annotations and evaluated against human judgments.

Table 3: Comparison with SOTA methods on OSVD. ACC (%) denotes 27-class viewer-side emotion classification accuracy, and RS denotes semantic similarity between generated and reference explanations. Best per column in bold.

Table 4: Ablation study on OSVD. VMD and AED denote the visual motion dynamics and acoustic energy-onset dynamics auxiliary objectives inside MSDA, respectively. CLS, MC, and MI denote the coalition emotion classification loss, modality contribution loss, and modality interaction loss inside CAVA, respectively.

Table 1: Comparison between OSVD and representative VEA datasets. Emotion-label columns indicate whether annotations are provided under audio-only (A), video-only (V), and audio-visual (AV) viewing conditions. Emotion explanations are divided into semantic descriptions and physical sensory descriptions.
Table 5: Out-of-distribution evaluation on VCE and VE8. Both datasets are evaluated after re-annotation under the OSVD viewer-side 27-class taxonomy and sensoryexplanation protocol.
Table 2: Average human agreement with OSVD labels on 100 randomly sampled clips under three modality views.

papers.selection_reason: Psychophysics-inspired MLLM for video emotion analysis with modality dynamics alignment and audio-visual attribution.
papers.title: PI-MLLM: Psychophysics-Inspired Multimodal Large Language Model for Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis
papers.tldr: PI-MLLM models visual motion and acoustic dynamics to better predict and explain emotions elicited by oddly satisfying videos.

papers.abstract: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112ms. Single-step generation achieves 83FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.
authors: Jihai Zhang, Runjia Qian, Kaiqin Kong, Biao Jiang, Puyi Wang, Siru Chen, Tianle Li, Guanjie Chen, Junyi Wu, Chubin Chen, Yuanhang Li, Kaichen Huang, Haobo Zhang, Yangguang Li, Wei Yu, Guibin Chen, Yu Cheng, Yahui Zhou
bullets: Addresses the gap between controllable video generation and playable worlds requiring persistent state, executable rules, and low-latency interaction.

Separates game execution from visual generation: an engine manages state and mechanics, while an autoregressive video model renders detailed visuals from low-poly proxies, captions, and memory references.
A multimodal coding agent converts player ideas into game code and dynamic scene descriptions.
Demonstrates customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics.
Achieves 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on an RTX5090 with 112 ms key-press-to-display latency; code, weights, and assets are released.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Architecture of the rendering model. The noisy latent of one chunk (one latent frame, four video frames) and the low-poly proxy encoded by TAEHV are concatenated into 148 channels and patchified into 405 tokens per latent frame at 480×864. Thirty causal DiT blocks apply self-attention over a KV cache that holds spatial-memory frames, reference frames, and the latest 20 chunks, cross-attention to the cached text keys and values of the dynamic caption, and a feed-forward network, each modulated by the timestep through AdaLN. The output head predicts a velocity, one or two flow updates produce the clean latent, and TAEHV decodes four frames. The finished chunk is then re-run at t = 0 without the control input to write its keys and values into the cache.

Figure 6: Overview of the inference optimizations. (a) Per-block GPU time on an RTX 5090, broken down by kernel category. (b) Decoding is moved ahead of the clean-KV update, so frames are output earlier. (c) Instead of shifting the whole KV window at every step, the ring cache writes the new frame into the oldest slot. (d) Self-attention is split into seven window ranges whose quantized keys and values are cached; the partial outputs are combined by log-sum-exp.

Figure 2: Roadmap of Matrix-Game V4: The multimodal coding agent and the game engine form the harness for the video generation model. The player sends ideas and requests to the agent and actions to the engine (1). The agent writes the world, turning ideas into game code and scenes for the engine, and translates the world, turning the state and events reported by the engine into text descriptions. The engine maintains the world state and the rules in code (2) and sends control signals as a structural rendering of the scene (3). The video generation model renders frames in real time from the text description, its past frames, and the structural rendering (4). The generated frame returns to the player as visual feedback (5).

Figure 4: Dynamic captions follow the engine state. Top: low-poly proxy frames of one CitySample driving clip; numbered markers are the visible objects that the engine reports for this frame, each linked by its instance ID to a semantic description. Below: the caption that the rule-based template produces for the same frame, without any vision-language model. Orange text comes from object states and events, and blue text from object positions and distances. As the car moves, parked vehicles leave the description, pedestrians change from standing to approaching, and newly visible objects are announced under “Changes”.

Figure 8: Game modes written with the coding agent, rendered in real time. Top: in the thirdperson shooter, the agent adds health and ammunition control, shield durability, a faster shotgun, a game-over condition, and simple sound effects. Middle: in the driving game, the agent implements a time trial with route checkpoints and collision penalties. Bottom: the same driving game turned into a pursuit mode, in which the player must intercept a target vehicle and stay close to it for five seconds. The engine evaluates every rule; the video model renders each frame from the engine output.

Figure 7: Re-rendering over 40-second held-out rollouts. For each game, the upper row is the low-poly proxy from the engine and the lower row is the frame generated by the distilled causal model at the same time step. The generated frames follow the proxy layout, camera, and object motion throughout the rollout, while the model fills in materials, vegetation, lighting, smoke, and muzzle effects.

Figure 3: UE5 paired training data. (a) Each clip is captured twice in Unreal Engine 5 under the same camera and frame index: once as a low-poly structure render (BBox) that preserves scene layout and motion, and once as the high-fidelity RGB frame. (b) For every 81-frame clip, frame-aligned CSV records of camera pose, actions, visible objects, events, and environment are turned into a prompt: visible object IDs are looked up in a description table, spatial and temporal cues are composed, and a template produces the clip prompt.

Table 3: Latency, hardware, and openness of recent real-time interactive generation systems. Latency is the end-to-end latency, and resolution is the output resolution at which each system reports its timings. For the systems that generate in chunks, the latency is two chunk generation times. Code World Model (streaming) renders a 17-frame chunk in 5.1 s on one H200. For StreamRender-H3, the chunk time of 258 ms is the sum of the three warm-renderer stage times reported on its project page: 16.67 ms for reference encoding, 217.96 ms for the two-step render, and 23.8 ms for causal video decoding, the last measured at 720p on one GB200. AgentGarten renders a 16-frame chunk in 439 ms on one H100. For Magpie, the latency is the end-to-end time reported by its authors: 0.83 s for the engine to prepare a 20-frame chunk, about 0.1 s for transmission and encoding, and 0.62 s for rendering. Matrix-Game 4.0 latency is measured from a key press to the first frame that reflects it, with the game running at 60 FPS. Open release is checked against the GitHub and Hugging Face pages of each project on October 19, 2026.

Table 2: Inference speed and latency, applied cumulatively. Each row adds one optimization to all rows above it. FPS is the steady-state generation rate of the model; latency is the time from a key press to the first generated frame that reflects it, with the game running at 60 FPS. Speedup is the FPS ratio to the previous row. Setting: 480× 864, chunk size of one latent frame (four frames), KV window of 21 latent frames, one NVIDIA RTX 5090.

Table 1: UE5 paired training data. Each clip is a pair of pixel-aligned low-poly and high-fidelity videos at 1280 × 720. Held-out clips come from capture sessions (for air combat, whole multimachine capture batches) that contribute no training clip.

papers.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
papers.tldr: Matrix-Game 4.0 combines an executable game engine with a real-time video renderer and coding agent to create and modify playable game worlds from natural language.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation requires retaining an ever-expanding history, but conditioning on its growing token sequence is costly. Existing methods restrict or compress historical context, potentially losing information needed for future generation. This work proposes ReCam, which groups local spatiotemporal blocks of historical latents into vectors and projects them directly into the high-dimensional hidden space of a Diffusion Transformer. The model learns to use the resulting memory tokens through native self-attention, reducing token count while retaining block-level access to the full history. To mitigate temporal drift during autoregressive rollout, we further introduce dual-pointer denoising with separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames. Among the evaluated methods, ReCam achieves the highest VBench-Long overall score of 80.1 and competitive static-scene revisitation performance on R2M-Bench. It also leads on all four consistency metrics for off-screen subject reappearance, including clothing consistency of 4.09 versus 3.03 for the best baseline.
authors: Yukuo Ma, Cong Liu, Junke Wang, Junqi Liu, Haibin Huang, Zuxuan Wu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the cost and information loss of conditioning on growing video histories.
Groups local spatiotemporal latent blocks into vectors and projects them into a Diffusion Transformer’s hidden space.
Uses native self-attention for block-level access to the full history with fewer tokens.
Introduces separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames to improve autoregressive stability.
Achieves the top reported VBench-Long score (80.1) and leads all four off-screen subject reappearance consistency metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of ReCam. Historical latents are grouped into local spatiotemporal blocks and projected into memory tokens by a lightweight MLP. The first frame remains a clean visual anchor. Native self-attention connects the historical memory and current chunk, while text cross-attention is applied only to the current chunk.

Figure 1 A coarse read on fine-grained history. We compare our method with other representative methods. Keyframe-based approaches, such as CaM [Yu et al., 2025], typically employ an external rule-based selector to retrieve a subset of frames as memory. In contrast, compression-based methods [Zhang et al., 2025] encode history into a compact representation through a separate reconstruction stage. Different from these approaches, ReCam allows the video model itself to learn how to represent history and how to retrieve it via its native attention mechanism.

Figure 6 Overview of the general-purpose video corpus. (a) Percentage of videos in each duration interval. (b) Word cloud of the 60 most frequent words in the captions after filtering out template terms such as “captures” and “environment”.
Figure 4 Efficiency and optimization. (a) Peak GPU memory and forward-pass time on one H100. (b) Dual-pointer loss approaches clean-context loss and remains below single-pointer loss.
Figure 5 Anti-drifting via dual-pointer denoising. Generated frames from clean context (top) and dual-pointer denoising (bottom), with time progressing from left to right.
Figure 7 Example history-generation prompts with the subject (a) initially present and (b) initially absent. Ellipses indicate omitted text.

Figure 8 Probability densities of the training noise level. The reference uses a single shifted logit-normal sample with shift 5. Our min/max branch takes the larger of two samples with shift 2.5; the full training mixture additionally includes 10% uniform samples from [0.95, 1].
Figure 9 Context noise schedules with sm = 5. Larger sc keeps the context noisier; sc = 0 is clean and sc = 5 matches the current-chunk schedule.
Table 2 Static-scene revisitation on R2M-Bench. MemoryGain (MG, top) and Normalized Memory Ratio (NMR, bottom); higher is better for both.
Table 1 VBench-Long evaluation results. We report the VBench-Long metrics on videos generated at 480p, 30 seconds. Higher values are better for all dimensions.

Table 4 Ablation studies. (a) History block shape and MLP bottleneck dimension. (b) Context design: VBench changes between the first and last two-second windows (∆ = last− first); negative values indicate degradation. Bold marks the best result per column.

Table 3 Off-screen subject reappearance. For each consistency metric, we report the mean metric over all cases (All), the cases where the subject is visible in the first frame (Present), and the cases where it is absent from the first frame (Absent). Bold indicates the best result in each column.
Table 5 Temporal drift with sm = 5. ∆ = last 2 s − first 2 s, averaged over videos; negative values indicate degradation. Bold marks the best result per column.
Table 6 Effect of the context noise shift on VBench scores. The current-chunk shift is fixed at sm = 5. Bold marks the best result per column.

papers.selection_reason: Diffusion Transformer long-video generation with memory tokens and dual-pointer denoising.
papers.title: Recast the Past: Stable Long Video Generation with Full Context Memory
papers.tldr: ReCam enables stable long-video generation by compressing full historical context into memory tokens and using dual-pointer denoising to reduce temporal drift.

papers.abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.
authors: Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long, Fangneng Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Hongyu Liu, Hongfa Wang, Peihao Li, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Existing condition-guided methods suffer from geometric estimation errors, while motion-only transfer often loses contact dynamics and causes hand collapse.
EgoACT is a test-time framework that operates directly during video-diffusion denoising.
Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring stabilizes hand–object structure early in denoising.
Sparse Correspondence Calibration refines reliable local correspondences in later denoising stages.
EgoActionBench evaluates action preservation, visual quality, and hand–object plausibility; experiments report more coherent and physically plausible videos than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the proposed framework. Given an egocentric manipulation video, our framework uses a reference branch and an optimized generation branch for test-time action transfer. We apply Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring (VSA) in the early denoising steps to preserve hand-object structure, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration (SCC) in the mid-to-late steps to refine local correspondences and improve interaction realism.

Figure 6. The overview of EgoActionBench. EgoActionBench contains 350 reference manipulation videos and 1,400 target prompts, covering indoor/outdoor scenes, single-/two-hand interactions, and diverse manipulation categories. The benchmark evaluates whether generated videos preserve the reference action semantics while adapting to new visual contexts.

Figure 5. Gallery of proposed method. EgoACT can transfer a wide range of egocentric manipulation videos, covering diverse interaction categories, object types, and motion patterns. The generated videos preserve plausible hand-object structure, contact dynamics, and temporal coherence while adapting the reference action to new visual contexts.

Figure 16. More Comparison with Baseline. Our method consistently produces more coherent action transfer and more plausible handobject interactions than baselines, which often suffer from structural collapse, temporal inconsistency, or physically unrealistic interactions.

Figure 14. Failure case. Our method may struggle with actions involving very fast hand or object motion, which can lead to motion blur, temporal aliasing, or loss of hand-object correspondence. This limitation is primarily due to the base video diffusion model, which was not specifically trained to handle rapid egocentric dynamics and tends to produce temporally smoothed outputs when the inter-frame displacement is large.

papers.abstract: Endoscopic video contains state transitions induced by camera displacement, deformable tissue, and instrument interaction, yet existing pre-training methods treat dynamics implicitly. Inspired by action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive world models and by the observation that endoscopic optical flow contains both shared image-plane displacement and localized residual motion, we reformulate passive endoscopic video pre-training as causal motion-guided latent-state prediction. We present EndoWorld-JEPA, to our knowledge the first latent world-model pre-training framework designed for general-purpose endoscopic video representation learning. In place of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics, the model conditions prediction of the next latent state on motion observed up to the current state. Its Optical Motion-guided module separates dominant displacement from residual motion and converts the resulting evidence into an ordered temporal motion condition and spatial local-motion weights. Complementary global and motion-local predictors use these outputs: the temporal condition modulates both latent transitions, whereas the local weights define an auxiliary motion-local state that extends prediction from scene-level evolution to spatially selective dynamics. Patch-wise motion weighting emphasizes localized change while retaining anatomical context, and past-motion-window dropout randomly withholds the complete motion condition to reduce dependence on unreliable motion. This global--local formulation learns predictable visual--motion dynamics in representation space without reconstructing stochastic appearance artifacts. Evaluation shows that a common pre-trained checkpoint achieves strong transfer across four downstream benchmarks, supporting motion-guided global--local latent prediction as an effective pre-training paradigm for endoscopic video.
authors: Jie Wang, Shilong Yang, Tao Zhou, Juan Yu, Rong Qu, Jianfeng Ren, Zhicheng Zhang, Linlin Shen

Combines global and motion-local predictors, with motion-window dropout to reduce reliance on unreliable motion cues.
A shared pre-trained checkpoint transfers effectively across four downstream benchmarks, supporting the proposed paradigm.

papers.abstract: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.
authors: Chuanyang Ma, Chenye Wang, Yixuan Wang, Huiling Zhou, Xingqun Qi, Muyi Sun, Man Zhang, Caifeng Shan, Zhenan Sun
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in predicting semantically and geometrically distinct futures from similar egocentric observation histories.
Uses fixation strength and recency to modulate a vision-language model via Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation for intention inference.

Generates 6-DoF object trajectories and articulated motion for both hands using a diffusion-based model.
Introduces the phase-aware EgoAIM benchmark with fine-grained intention annotations; reports state-of-the-art intention and motion forecasting, with near-oracle performance in some phases.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
authors: Siyuan Ma, Yu Qi, Cheng Ye, Ruotian Peng, Xinyi Xu, Zitiantao Lin, Zedong Cai, Yijian Huang, Weiyang Liu, Siyuan Wang, Yandong Wen

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models have recently achieved remarkable progress in Real-world Image Super-Resolution (Real-SR). However, existing methods consistently exhibit a persistent seesaw effect: enhancing perceptual realism compromises structural fidelity. This effect, we argue, is not intrinsic to diffusion models, but largely stems from the architectural constraints of prevailing two-stage frameworks. To address this challenge, we propose PixelSR, a novel single-stage Pixel Diffusion Transformer for Real-SR that operates directly in pixel space. Specifically, PixelSR consists of two core designs: Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling. The former establishes an effective pixel-space restoration framework by integrating spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement, thereby bypassing VAE compression and enabling end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space. Complementarily, the latter decomposes the asymmetric flow target into a low-rank semantic component and a noise-free orthogonal texture component. By routing these components to specialized branches, it achieves decoupled optimization with reduced mutual interference. Benefiting from these designs, our PixelSR restores perceptually realistic details while faithfully preserving structural content. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PixelSR not only achieves competitive performance, but also effectively mitigates the fidelity--realism seesaw effect.
authors: Xiang Lv, Kai Zhao, Qiang Wang, Qiao Mo, Chao Zhou, Mingwen Shao
bullets: Targets the realism–fidelity trade-off attributed to architectural limitations in two-stage diffusion frameworks.
Uses pixel-space conditional diffusion with aligned low-resolution conditioning, semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement.
Introduces Orthogonal Flow Decoupling to separate low-rank semantic and orthogonal texture components into specialized branches.
Avoids VAE compression and enables end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show competitive performance and mitigation of the fidelity–realism seesaw effect.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PixelSR framework. PixelSR comprises Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion (PCD) and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling (OFD). Left: PCD performs end-toend RGB-space restoration using spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight pixel-level texture refinement. Right: OFD factorizes the asymmetric velocity target into a projected low-rank component and a deterministic orthogonal residual, which empirically exhibit semantic- and texture-dominant characteristics, respectively. Their predictions are assigned to specialized DiT and PiT branches and recombined into the full velocity for flow matching, enabling task-aligned optimization with reduced interference.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in diffusion models have raised concerns about privacy, harmful content, and copyright violations. Concept erasure methods aim to address these risks by removing undesirable concepts from pretrained models without full retraining. However, existing approaches often degrade non-target generation quality through heuristic strength scaling (e.g., classifier-free guidance or negative prompt scaling), leading to uncontrolled and excessive semantic drift. To address this, we propose Push-Pull Attentional Anchoring (PPAA), a mechanism in the cross-attention space that displaces target representations while anchoring the scale of erasure via bounded cosine-similarity constraints. By using a relative similarity ratio instead of an absolute difference, our adaptive threshold represents a meaningful percentage of semantic retention, facilitating a single value to be applied uniformly across layers. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple concept categories, including celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property. Our method achieves favorable trade-offs against prior approaches on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and demonstrates its applicability to modern architectures such as FLUX.
authors: Nattanat Chatthee, Tagon Sompong, Ekapol Chuangsuwanich, Supasorn Suwajanakorn
bullets: Addresses semantic drift caused by heuristic erasure-strength scaling in existing concept-erasure methods.
Operates in cross-attention space, displacing target representations while constraining their cosine similarity.
Uses a bounded relative similarity ratio to express semantic retention and apply one adaptive threshold across layers.
Evaluated on celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property concepts.
Reports favorable trade-offs on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and applicability to FLUX.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Concept erasure and preservation results on FLUX. (a) Qualitative comparison on representative identity, style, and character concepts. Our method erases target concepts, such as Barack Obama, Van Gogh, and Mickey Mouse, while preserving non-target concepts, such as Will Smith, Picasso, and Donald Duck. ESD causes substantial semantic shifts in non-target concepts, whereas UCE fails to semantically erase Mickey Mouse. (b) Quantitative results. Accuracy measures target-concept detection after erasure, and CMMD measures preservation relative to the original FLUX model; lower is better for both metrics. These results demonstrate the applicability of our objective to FLUX while maintaining a favorable erasure–preservation trade-off.

The horizontal axis measures preservation effectiveness using CMMD (×1000), where lower values indicate better preservation of non-target concepts. Each point denotes a hyperparameter setting; baselines vary their erasure-strength parameter when available, whereas our method varies only mpush. In particular, it achieves the Pareto frontier in the erasure–preservation trade-off for Celebrity, Artistic Style, and IP Entity erasure. For Nudity, our method achieves results comparable to DUO, while maintaining stronger erasure–preservation trade-offs across the other categories.

Although our method is not explicitly optimized for robustness, it remains competitive among methods without robustness-focused objectives (MACE, UCE, AC, and ESD).
