papers.selection_reason: Introduces a mechanism for concept erasure in diffusion models using attentional anchoring, relevant to video diffusion and multimodal model safety.
papers.title: Push-Pull Attentional Anchoring for Diffusion Concept Erasure
papers.tldr: PPAA erases unwanted concepts from diffusion models by pushing target representations away while anchoring semantic retention to reduce unintended quality loss.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding with multimodal LLMs is fundamentally constrained by the mismatch between video length and the model's limited visual context budget, making frame selection essential for practical reasoning. Existing query-aware methods typically rely on heuristic pipelines: they assign one-dimensional query-conditioned scores to frames and then apply sampling, ranking, or extraction rules to form the final subset. While effective in practice, such methods are generally not derived from an explicit optimization objective and struggle to capture the heterogeneous evidence required for complex reasoning. In this paper, we revisit long-video frame selection from a principled optimization perspective. We formulate it as a structured evidence-allocation problem and propose OTFS, an optimal transport framework that maps multiple evidence sources onto video frames. To reflect the asymmetry of this problem---important evidence should be preserved, whereas redundant frames need not absorb mass---we instantiate this view with a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective and an efficient solver, OTFS-Sinkhorn. Combined with an exact dynamic program for coverage-aware subset extraction, OTFS yields a practical two-stage training-free pipeline. We further show that, in the single-source case, our formulation induces a Gibbs-type distribution over frames, making Q-Frame's temperature-scaled distribution a special case of our framework while also providing a broader perspective for understanding related prior methods. Experiments on three long-video understanding benchmarks show that OTFS consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines. Codes are available at https://github.com/barry664/OTFS.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between long videos and multimodal LLM context limits, where heuristic query-aware selection may miss heterogeneous evidence.
Maps multiple evidence sources to video frames using a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective.
Uses an efficient OTFS-Sinkhorn solver followed by exact dynamic programming for coverage-aware subset extraction.
Provides a training-free two-stage pipeline and shows that Q-Frame’s temperature-scaled distribution is a special single-source case.
Outperforms strong training-free baselines across three long-video understanding benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison between prior training-free frame-selection procedures and our principled OT-based framework. Existing methods typically compute one-dimensional frame scores and then apply hand-designed sampling or extraction rules. In contrast, OTFS formulates frame selection as semi-unbalanced transport from evidence atoms to video frames, producing a soft frame-importance distribution that is converted into a coverage-aware subset by exact dynamic programming.

Figure 2: Left: Three evidence atoms over time. Middle: The optimal transport plan π∗, shown as a heatmap from evidence atoms to video frames. Different evidence sources assign mass to distinct temporal regions, highlighting their complementary roles in grounding the query. Right: The resulting frame-importance marginal w and the final subset selected by dynamic programming (red arrows indicate all selected frames, and red dots mark five representative examples).

papers.title: A Principled Optimal Transport Framework for Frame Selection in Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: OTFS formulates long-video frame selection as semi-unbalanced optimal transport to allocate diverse evidence under limited visual context.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to understand user-generated videos by integrating multiple modalities. Existing methods often treat modalities as symmetric, overlooking the fact that language provides a dominant semantic prior while nonverbal signals are complementary and noise-prone. To address this, we propose a Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing, termed TAME, that reformulates MSA as an uncertainty-guided refinement paradigm, where the language prior is calibrated and enhanced by selectively trusted nonverbal evidence. Specifically, TAME adopts an asymmetric Mixture-of-Modality-Experts framework, in which textual features act as a fixed and always-activated shared expert, while audio-textual and video-textual cross-modal branches serve as dynamically routed auxiliary experts. Furthermore, we introduce lightweight Prophet Heads to quantify the sample-level predictive uncertainty of each individual modality, and this uncertainty metric is further incorporated into the modality router to realize reliability-aware expert aggregation and fusion. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS datasets demonstrate that TAME achieves state-of-the-art performance on the majority of metrics while reducing parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2% over the mixture-of-expert baseline. %These results confirm that asymmetric expert construction with uncertainty-guided routing is an effective paradigm for MSA.
authors: Xiaohua Huang, Bingrui Lei, Xiuyan hao, Ling Zhou, Yuan Zong, Wenming Zheng, Guoying Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating text, audio, and video as equally reliable, despite language providing a stronger semantic prior.
Uses an asymmetric mixture-of-modality-experts design with an always-active text expert and dynamically routed audio-textual and video-textual experts.
Introduces lightweight Prophet Heads to estimate modality-specific, sample-level uncertainty for reliability-aware expert routing and fusion.
Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS report state-of-the-art performance on most metrics.
Compared with a mixture-of-experts baseline, reduces parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2%.

papers.selection_reason: Multimodal sentiment analysis with uncertainty-guided MoE routing; transferable to video-language understanding and efficient expert routing.
papers.title: Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.tldr: TAME improves multimodal sentiment analysis by anchoring fusion on language and routing complementary audio/video evidence according to predictive uncertainty.

papers.abstract: Few-step trajectory distillation aims to learn accurate global updates from dense local supervision along a teacher's sampling trajectory. Existing approaches construct within-step dynamics using specific trajectory parameterizations or discrete interval predictions, tying the learned update to a prescribed temporal structure. We propose \method, which directly learns a continuous trajectory primitive representing cumulative displacement along the teacher trajectory. By supervising finite differences of the primitive with local teacher velocities, \method learns the accumulated motion directly, while obtaining global updates through endpoint differences. This formulation avoids prescribing a temporal basis or fixed query grid and instead learns the temporal evolution of cumulative displacement from local supervision. We further establish a local-to-global error bound to characterize how local regression errors affect full-interval displacement accuracy, and introduce endpoint absorption to eliminate the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-network-evaluation inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that \method achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, improving both metrics over a trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, it retains comparable performance, achieving a T-FID of 20.86 and an HPSv2 score of 28.33.
bullets: Targets few-step trajectory distillation, where global updates must be learned from dense local supervision.
Learns cumulative displacement directly and obtains global motion from endpoint differences, avoiding a prescribed temporal basis or query grid.
Provides a local-to-global error bound linking local regression errors to full-interval displacement accuracy.
Endpoint absorption removes the auxiliary primitive branch while retaining one-network-evaluation inference.
On large-scale text-to-image generation, reaches T-FID 20.92 and HPSv2 28.35 at one NFE; endpoint absorption remains comparable at 20.86 and 28.33.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Training and deployment of PRIMFLOW. A single source feature supports continuous primitive queries. Local endpoint differences are matched to teacher velocities, and the learned deployment endpoint is subsequently absorbed into the native prediction head.

Figure 1: Representing within-step trajectory geometry. A prescribed temporal family or fixed interval grid constrains how the teacher trajectory is represented. PRIMFLOW directly represents interval integrals as differences of one source-anchored continuous primitive.

Table 2: Endpoint absorption. “Native head” removes the primitive branch after learning its endpoint update; “primitive retained” evaluates the trajectory-trained endpoint directly.

papers.selection_reason: Trajectory primitives for few-step distillation improve generation efficiency and dynamics modeling, relevant to video generation and efficient AI.
papers.title: PRIMFLOW: Learning Trajectory Primitives for Few-Step Distillation
papers.tldr: PRIMFLOW learns continuous cumulative trajectory primitives from local teacher velocities to enable accurate one-step diffusion distillation without a fixed temporal parameterization.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in unified visual editing have begun to consolidate image and video editing within a single model, while 3D scene editing remains largely separate and constrained by scarce paired training data. Given the rich image and video editing supervision now available and the common editing semantics shared across modalities, a natural question is whether this knowledge can be transferred to data-scarce 3D editing. We present VitronEdit, a universal framework for image, video, and 3D scene editing. VitronEdit adopts a shared sequence representation and progressive multimodal training to transfer editing knowledge across modalities. We further introduce geometry-aware post-training, which leverages a pretrained geometry reconstruction model to provide depth and camera-pose supervision. Surprisingly, applying geometric supervision only to 3D samples yields the best overall performance, while image and video editing also improve despite receiving no direct geometric supervision, suggesting that geometric regularization transfers through the shared backbone. Our analysis further shows that image and video training mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, whereas 3D supervision primarily improves multi-view consistency. The project page: https://vitron-llm.github.io/VitronEdit/.
authors: Jing Wang, Yanlin Li, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu, Shengqiong Wu, Hao Fei
bullets: Addresses the separation of 3D editing from better-supervised image and video editing.
Uses a shared sequence representation with progressive multimodal training.
Adds geometry-aware post-training using depth and camera-pose supervision from a pretrained reconstruction model.
Geometry supervision applied only to 3D samples improves overall performance, including image and video editing.
Image/video data mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, while 3D supervision improves multi-view consistency.

papers.abstract: With the rapid expansion of online video content, video temporal grounding has become essential for localizing moments based on user-specific queries, comprising two subtasks: moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD). While recent approaches adopt DETR-style decoders or temporal pyramid architectures, they rely on single-scale feature maps or uniformly downsampled representations, limiting their ability to capture semantic boundaries and variable-length events. In this paper, we present SuperClip Video Temporal Grounding (SCVTG) built on a multi-scale temporal hierarchy that better captures distinctive events at various granularities. SCVTG constructs a SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments, termed SuperClips. Further, to aggregate these SuperClips having variable duration and temporal location, we introduce a temporally adaptive kernel that aggregates SuperClips through temporally conditioned weights, enabling flexible aggregation. On top of this, we design relative saliency losses to guide the model in learning inter-clip importance, enhancing its ability to distinguish relevant events. Extensive experiments show that SCVTG achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks with promising gains.
authors: Sanghyeok Lee, Juyeon Ko, Joonmyung Choi, Jongha Kim, Dohwan Ko, Ji Soo Lee, Hyunwoo J. Kim
bullets: Targets moment retrieval and highlight detection in long, variable-length videos.
Builds a multi-scale SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments.
Uses a temporally adaptive kernel to aggregate SuperClips with location- and duration-aware weights.
Introduces relative saliency losses to learn the importance of different clips.
Achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks, with promising gains.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overall architecture of SCVTG. After multi-modal fusion, video clip features are progressively grouped and aggregated to form a SuperClip pyramid with varying temporal granularity. Given this multi-level hierarchy capturing distinctive events, task-specific heads predict both foreground moments and clip-wise saliency scores.

Figure 5. Qualitative results of SuperClip Pyramid. The interval indicated by the red arrow denotes the ground-truth moments. The SuperClip highlighted with a red hatched region perfectly aligns with the ground truth, serving as an ideal candidate for temporal grounding.

Figure 4. Illustration of SuperClip grouping and aggregation. (a) Given the input clips, a non-anchor clip is assigned to one of its adjacent anchor clips based on semantic similarity, forming coherent SuperClips. (b) Next, each clip is projected using its corresponding weight generated by the temporally adaptive kernel (TA-Kernel), followed by pooling and a linear layer. (c) Unlike fixed convolutional kernels, which cannot handle varying lengths or temporal characteristics, we generate TA-kernel weights for SuperClips, considering the temporal information (ϕ(fi)) of its constituent clips.

Figure 2. Comparison between (a) conventional temporal pyramid and (b) SuperClip pyramid. Unlike conventional temporal pyramids that segment videos at uniform intervals, our SuperClip pyramid adaptively groups adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments.

Figure 1. Performance comparison. SCVTG outperforms all baseline models, demonstrating its effectiveness in video temporal grounding. For moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD), we use R1@0.7 and mAP@Avg, respectively.

papers.abstract: Online action detection (OAD) identifies ongoing actions in streaming videos. Many existing OAD systems combine RGB appearance with optical flow, but dense-flow extraction remains a major computational bottleneck. Codec motion vectors (MVs) are available during decoding, avoiding a separate optical-flow computation. On THUMOS'14, optical flow exceeds MVs by 11.2 mAP points with motion-only inputs, whereas the gap narrows to 3.7 points after RGB fusion, with the largest reduction in action-category discrimination. We propose CodecMotion-OAD, which replaces optical flow with decoder-provided MVs while retaining existing temporal detector architectures. Its two-stage training first aligns MV features with a pretrained flow-feature interface without action labels and then trains RGB+MV detectors using ground-truth labels and soft predictions from a frozen RGB+Flow teacher. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of codec MVs to frame-level OAD. On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, CodecMotion-OAD achieves 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow, while reducing decoder-to-prediction processing time by 11.48-fold on CPU and 2.04-fold on GPU.
authors: Zepeng Sun, Naichuan Zheng, Hailun Xia, Junjie Wu
bullets: Optical-flow extraction is a major OAD bottleneck; codec motion vectors are available directly during video decoding.
The method retains existing temporal detector architectures and uses two-stage feature alignment and teacher-guided RGB+MV training.
On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, it reaches 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow.
Decoder-to-prediction processing is 11.48× faster on CPU and 2.04× faster on GPU.
Scope: evaluated on THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD; performance remains below the optical-flow counterpart.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of Interface-Preserving Motion Transfer (IPMT). (a) Stage I adapts a codec-MV encoder initialized from Flow-ResNet50 by matching its 2048-dimensional per-step features to those of a frozen Flow-ResNet50, without action labels. (b) Stage II freezes the RGB and adapted MV encoders and trains the original RGB+MV temporal detectors with ground-truth labels mixed with soft labels from a shared, frozen CMeRT RGB+Flow teacher. (c) Under the H.264 IPPP protocol, decoding supplies RGB frames and codec MVs to the student detector, without optical-flow extraction or the teacher at inference.

The columns show RGB center frames, TV-L1 optical flow, spatially coarsened Flow (16×16 block averaging, with block means tiled back to the original resolution), and codec motion vectors. papers.selection_reason: Efficient online action detection using codec motion vectors instead of optical flow.
papers.title: CodecMotion-OAD: Efficient Online Action Detection with Compressed-Domain Motion
papers.tldr: CodecMotion-OAD replaces costly optical flow with decoder-provided motion vectors for efficient online action detection, achieving near-flow accuracy with substantially faster processing.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.
authors: Haonan Zhao, Jiaxuan Chen, Qingyang Liu, Shuochen Chang, Siyu Sun, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of re-encoding or retrieving video evidence for every question.
Uses causal tracing to identify video-specific model layers for memory adaptation.
Distills the representation changes caused by visual clips into a text-only memory under compact multi-scale supervision.
Evaluated on LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, achieving data-efficient video-free QA with fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods.
Scope: memory is adapted separately for each video, so it is not a universal video memory.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MIT3. (a) A VLM constructs multi-scale descriptions, temporally grounded local QA, and global QA to cover video knowledge. (b) Delta-injection causal tracing estimates each model layer’s causal memory utility and selects top-K layers under a fixed adaptation budget. (c) Visual memory distillation optimizes LoRA modules in selected layers to reproduce normalized video-induced representation changes, transferring visual evidence into text-only memory.

For short windows (≤ 40 s), overlapping information from the high-, mid-, and low-level descriptions is fused into one coherent, redundancy-reduced training example, whereas for long windows (≥ 80 s), the descriptions are retained as three separate examples. Local QA pairs include explicit temporal grounding, while global QA pairs are timestamp-free. Ellipses denote omitted content.

NKR trains a video-specific LoRA adapter on synthesized text using a fixed all-layer configuration. MIT3 instead selects videospecific model layers through causal tracing and distills the visual-evidence-induced representation change into these memory-writing locations, enabling video-free question answering.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared reference anchor at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.
authors: Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Heeji Yoon, Seungryong Kim, Joon-Young Lee
bullets: Addresses flickering edges and discontinuous transparency caused by independently processing short video chunks.
Uses separate RGB and mask token streams with full spatio-temporal attention for adaptive conditioning.
Introduces learnable preserve and refine tokens to propagate previous mattes during sliding-window inference.
Adds a shared reference anchor to maintain global consistency and limit error accumulation without extra training.
Outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, including on long in-the-wild videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the VideoMaMa++ training and inference. (Top) During training, RGB frames are paired with either a binary mask or the ground-truth alpha matte as guide input, encoded into separate token streams by a frozen VAE encoder E , and tagged with a refine token (R) or preserve token (P). The DiT processes both modes jointly within a single clip, supervised against the ground-truth matte. (Bottom) At inference, long videos are processed in a sliding-window manner. Each chunk receives the refine token on its non-overlapping frames and the preserve token on its overlap frames, which carry the previous chunk’s predicted matte. A globally selected reference anchor frame is additionally supplied as preserve input to every chunk, providing a stable anchor that prevents error accumulation across the sequence.

Figure 3: Long-video temporal consistency. Qualitative comparison between VideoMaMa++ and other methods. MAD-T, computed only within the transition region, isolates the matting quality that actually matters and avoids the bias introduced by such annotation gaps.

papers.abstract: Adapting existing manga into coherent animation that stays faithful to the source is a valuable yet challenging task. Existing methods either access the manga mainly through text, losing its characters and art style, or feed manga pages directly into video generation models, which misinterpret the manga's structure and produce incorrect storylines. In this paper, we propose Manga2Animate, a multi-agent framework that grounds every stage of generation in the source manga. We decompose the task into two intermediate representations, an animation script and a visual storyboard. Each representation is produced by a creator agent and reviewed against the source panels by a paired reviewer agent. We tailor representation-specific selection and dual-level feedback to progressively refine both before synthesizing the final animation. Extensive experiments and a user study demonstrate that Manga2Animate produces animations more faithful to the source manga and more consistent across shots than state-of-the-art approaches. Project page: https://annchenn.github.io/Manga2Animate/
authors: Sheng-Wei Zhang, Hsi-An Chen, Yan-Ting Liou, Chih-Hsuan Chen, Shih-Chen Tseng, Yu-Lun Liu

Uses representation-specific selection and dual-level feedback to progressively refine the plan before animation synthesis.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video supports diverse applications, including robot learning, augmented reality, and human activity understanding. Recovering metric 3D hand trajectories from such video requires estimating both hand motion and camera egomotion to express the hands in a consistent reference frame. Many existing pipelines recover hand and camera motion in separate stages, combining hand detection, hand reconstruction, camera tracking, and trajectory refinement. We present V-JEPA Hand, a simple feed-forward video model that jointly reconstructs bilateral hand motion and camera motion from egocentric clips. It uses a self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to extract spatio-temporal features from full-frame video and a query-based predictor to decode these features into per-frame hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion. We use the predicted camera motion to express the hand trajectories in a common world frame. The model accepts known focal lengths or predicts them when unavailable. It reconstructs each clip in a single forward pass. We train both components end to end in a single stage on a mixture of diverse pseudo-labelled videos and high-precision 3D annotations. A single model achieves the lowest coverage-aware mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard. It also yields lower world-frame trajectory errors than the compared SLAM-based pipelines. Ablations support the benefits of video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision. V-JEPA Hand achieves a forward-pass throughput of 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000. Project page: https://qft-333.github.io/V-JEPA-Hand-Page/.
authors: Ruicheng Li, Qixiu Li, Yu Deng, Sicheng Xu, Jiaolong Yang, Baining Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating hand motion and camera egomotion together for metric, consistent 3D trajectories.
Uses a self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 video encoder and query-based predictor to estimate hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion.

Achieves the lowest coverage-aware MPJPE among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard, with lower world-frame trajectory errors than compared SLAM pipelines.
Runs at 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000; ablations indicate benefits from video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision.

papers.abstract: Recent video generation models produce visually compelling outputs, yet their physical plausibility remains poorly measured. Physical plausibility asks whether generated objects obey geometry, kinematics, dynamics, and conservation laws. Existing benchmarks rely on coarse visual-language model judgments or target embodied world models rather than video generation itself. We introduce PVBench, a physical video benchmark that quantitatively measures the plausibility of generated videos across 46 dimensions organized into seven domains, spanning: i) instruction and semantic fidelity, ii) behavioral and causal consistency, iii) perceptual and temporal quality, iv) geometric and spatial consistency, v) material properties and field states, vi) kinematic and spatiotemporal persistence, vii) and mechanical plausibility with conservation laws. PVBench comprises 600 carefully crafted prompts, of which 30% involve physical embodied agents such as robot arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and multi-agent systems. For challenging physically tractable dimensions, it pairs each with specialized vision models that derive verifiable, physically grounded measurements, such as object-level 6D pose, metric scale, surface normals, kinematics, and numerical conservation-law residuals. It thus avoids relying solely on subjective scoring, while supporting both text-to-video and image-to-video generation. Finally, we validate the agreement between automatic metrics and human judgments through human evaluation. Meanwhile, we evaluate mainstream open-source and closed-source models and present several insights. By releasing the benchmark, prompts, and calibration protocol, we aim to foster physically grounded video generation.
authors: Kaiwei Chen, Moran Li, Zhenye Gan, Yabiao Wang, Chengjie Wang, Kexin Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang

papers.abstract: We investigate how frozen pretrained visual and depth representations support dense optical flow when coupled with a supervised matching network. Building on TTSFlow, this paper studies Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) feature decoding and one coarse-to-fine refinement stage. Our method fuses features from frozen DINOv2 and Depth Anything V2 models and estimates optical flow through a trainable transformer-based matching pipeline. After optical-flow training on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings3D, it achieves 2.37 endpoint error (EPE) on the Sintel training split, Final pass, compared with 2.52 for the FlowSeek (T) configuration reported here. Our RoCo-Spring 2026 entry, RoCo-29.VSAI, obtains a robustness-balanced score of 1.1038, Spring EPE of 1.411, and RobustSpring proxy EPE of 4.739, with a lower balanced score than seven of the twelve listed reference baselines. These results characterize the complete pipeline, which reuses frozen foundation backbones and performs one refinement stage. Code is available at: \url{https://github.com/Visual-and-Spatial-AI-Lab/FFlow}

papers.abstract: Video face swapping transfers the reference identity to a target video while preserving its other attributes and motion. Despite recent progress in reference-guided flow-based methods, jointly achieving faithful identity transfer, high fidelity, and real-time generation over long video streams remains challenging. To address this challenge, we rethink the task-specific structure of reference-guided video face swapping. First, face swapping changes only identity while preserving most visual content, yet flow-matching supervision is weakly sensitive to these changes. We therefore develop Joint Rec-ID Loss, which balances explicit identity supervision and latent reconstruction according to the noise level. Second, the target video already provides non-edited attributes and temporal dynamics, enabling generation with fewer spatial tokens and shorter temporal contexts through Face-RoI Generation and Short-Context Rollout Training. By integrating these designs, we propose StreamingSwap, a reference-guided flow-matching framework for real-time streaming video face swapping. We also introduce HumanFaceVid, comprising 1,000 hours of cinematic training data and evaluation sets of 200 short and 200 long videos. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves competitive identity transfer and visual quality at 20 FPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, with stable generation over videos up to 10 minutes long. Project webpage: https://aim-uofa.github.io/StreamingSwap/
authors: Zekai Luo, Yuwei Liang, Ruiqi Ma, Haoyu Huang, Xuehao Wang, Huanyi Zheng, Mingyu Liu, Linhao Zhong, Chenchen Jing, Yuling Xi, Hao Chen

Achieves competitive identity transfer and visual quality at 20 FPS on one RTX 4090, with stable generation for videos up to 10 minutes.],

papers.abstract: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observer's motion, surrounding geometry, and hand-object interactions must fit together in a consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EgoXperience, a full-stack paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EgoX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EgoX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EgoX, trained with EgoX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in a shared world coordinate frame with a single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%.

papers.title: EgoXperience: Learning World-Grounded Egocentric Representations from Human Experience

papers.abstract: Human egocentric experience offers a rich foundation for learning how the world is organized and how it changes through interaction. Realizing this potential at scale requires turning growing volumes of recordings into learning resources that connect scene structure, object semantics, and interaction histories across viewpoints and time, while reducing dependence on costly manual annotation. We introduce HOLI-WORLD, an integrated ecosystem connecting experience capture, world representation, automated data construction, model learning, and independent evaluation. To sup- port learning at scale, HOLIWORLD-Foundry combines complementary static and dynamic perception to automatically construct world records that connect persistent scene structure and evolving object states with interaction histories and supporting observations. HOLIWORLD-Data organizes these records from approximately 100 self-collected scenes into grounded learning resources, including approximately 80K QA pairs used to train HOLIWORLD-VL-4B. Independent human annotations of heldout recordings form HOLIWORLD-Bench, supporting evaluation of both annotation quality and learned spatial and temporal understanding. Experiments on ScanNet, ScanNet++, Aria Digital Twin, and HOLIWORLD-Bench demonstrate strong performance in static perception and dynamic tracking, while training on HOLIWORLD-Data substantially improves HOLIWORLD-VL-4B's spatial and temporal reasoning on HOLI- WORLD-Bench and EgoDynamic4D. HOLIWORLD provides a practical foundation for expanding learning resources from the continuous flow of human experience and advancing machine understanding of the dynamic world.
authors: Hao Li, Xiyuan Zheng, Yuanyuan Gao, Yalun Dai, Xinhao Ji, Xuan-Li Chen, Jing Zhao, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Ziwei Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting large-scale human-egocentric experience into richly connected, low-annotation learning resources.
HOLIWORLD-Foundry combines static and dynamic perception to build records linking persistent scenes, changing object states, interactions, and observations.
HOLIWORLD-Data organizes approximately 100 self-collected scenes into resources including approximately 80K QA pairs for training HOLIWORLD-VL-4B.
HOLIWORLD-Bench uses independent annotations of held-out recordings to evaluate annotation quality and spatial-temporal understanding.
Experiments report strong static perception and dynamic tracking, with training data improving spatial and temporal reasoning on HOLIWORLD-Bench and EgoDynamic4D.

papers.abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models can produce unsafe content, while output filtering intervenes only after synthesis. We investigate whether native generation signals enable early detection of unsafe and adversarial inputs. We find that classifier-free guidance exposes strong safety signals in conditional responses, accessible through compact statistics and linear readouts. Based on this finding, we propose Conditional Semantic Trajectory Interception (CSTI), which aggregates activation contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses at early checkpoints for calibrated risk detection. CSTI fits concept-specific detectors using canonical concept and safe examples, without attack samples, intermediate image decoding, or generator modification. Across five generators, four adversarial attack collections, and two general NSFW datasets, CSTI achieves the strongest overall performance among six baselines at a matched 5% FPR. Early interception reduces generation latency by over 60% on intercepted paths. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of native conditional responses for early safety interception.
authors: Yanchun Li, Yujin Wu, Gangkai Shen, Ming Yang, Li Zeng, Xianlong Wang, Hangtao Zhang, Shujuan Tian
bullets: Addresses the limitation of output filtering, which acts only after unsafe content is synthesized.
Uses contrasts between conditional and unconditional responses at early diffusion checkpoints with compact statistics and linear readouts.
Trains concept-specific detectors from canonical concept and safe examples, without attack samples.
Across five generators, four attack collections, and two NSFW datasets, it had the strongest overall performance among six baselines at 5% FPR.
Intercepting unsafe generations early reduced latency by over 60% on intercepted paths.

papers.abstract: While VideoLLMs have made significant progress in understanding short video benchmarks, they often struggle to summarize long-form ones. This is mainly due to performance degradation caused by long-context prompts, the inherent difficulty of preserving temporal continuity and a lack of semantically rich concepts in event descriptions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces the first recursive Video Language Summarization Model (RVLSM) designed for video processing and tailored to long-form video-to-text summarization. RVLSM recursively decomposes videos into semantically coherent segments and delegates chunk-level reasoning to VideoLLM sub-models and external tools. It employs (1) Semantic Temporal Decomposition (STD), which preserves temporal coherence and continuity through a scene-aware chunking strategy that dynamically partitions videos according to semantic boundaries, and (2) Adaptive Multimodal Tool Calling (AMTC), which ensures semantic richness of the summary via a routing mechanism that selectively invokes auxiliary modules such as action recognition, optical character recognition, automatic speech recognition, and object detection. Experiments on the VideoXum and MixTyVSum benchmarks show that RVLSM consistently improves over zero-shot VideoLLM baselines across multiple model settings and performance metrics, and is competitive with a state-of-the-art fine-tuned model for video-to-text summarization. Importantly, the named entities in the RVLSM's summaries align more closely with those detected in the ground-truth summaries than those detected by baseline and state-of-the-art methods, confirming the saliency of the event descriptions it generates.
authors: Alessia Intini, Lorenzo Vaiani, Enrico Chen, Luca Cagliero
bullets: Addresses VideoLLMs’ difficulties with long contexts, temporal continuity, and sparse event descriptions.
Uses Semantic Temporal Decomposition to split videos at meaningful scene boundaries while preserving continuity.
Uses Adaptive Multimodal Tool Calling to selectively invoke action recognition, OCR, ASR, and object detection.
Outperforms zero-shot VideoLLM baselines across VideoXum and MixTyVSum settings and metrics.
Generates summaries with named entities more closely aligned to ground-truth summaries and is competitive with a fine-tuned state-of-the-art model.

papers.abstract: Bringing legacy video back to contemporary screens does not necessarily make it look contemporary. Earlier imaging pipelines often leave color casts, muted chroma, weak con- trast, and tonal imbalance, while correcting these character- istics still relies heavily on expert colorists and scales poorly to long, multi-shot videos. We formulate long video color modernization, a task that updates the chromatic and tonal appearance of legacy color footage while preserving scene content and coherence across frames and shots. We introduce a scalable, training-free framework that jointly modernizes grids of temporally adjacent keyframes using a pretrained text-guided image editing model, producing coherent con- temporary references without paired supervision. Compact shot-specific color transforms then propagate these adjust- ments throughout each shot, preserving spatial structure and temporal stability. We conduct a multidimensional evaluation on diverse legacy videos spanning five decades. We combine a human evaluation of perceived modernness with quantita- tive measures of content fidelity, temporal stability, percep- tual quality, and efficiency, and introduce Source-Weighted Inter-shot Grade Consistency (SW-IGC) to assess grade co- herence across shots. On our evaluation set, our frame- work achieves the highest perceived modernness while re- maining competitive across complementary measures, open- ing a path toward the systematic study of long video color modernization. Code is available at https://github.com/jiwoomood/ Video_Color_Modernization.git
authors: Dongyun Kim, Jiwoo Choi, Jaeseong Lee, Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Targets color casts, muted chroma, weak contrast, and tonal imbalance in legacy footage without relying on expert colorists.
Uses a pretrained text-guided image editor to modernize grids of temporally adjacent keyframes without paired training data.
Propagates keyframe adjustments through each shot with compact, shot-specific color transforms for spatial and temporal stability.
Evaluated diverse legacy videos spanning five decades using human modernness judgments and measures of fidelity, stability, quality, efficiency, and cross-shot consistency.
Achieves the highest perceived modernness while remaining competitive on complementary evaluation measures.

papers.abstract: Video-Language Models (VLMs) excel at visual recognition but struggle with causal reasoning. Current evaluations are flawed: multiple-choice QA allows shortcuts, and open-ended QA lacks robust automatic evaluation. We introduce Causal Chain Generation (CCG), a novel task where models have to generate the sequence of intermediate events connecting a cause and an effect. This structured setup demands genuine reasoning and enables reliable automatic scoring. We accompany this task with two complementary metrics: SODA-Embedding, which measures the semantic matching of a generated chain against a reference, and Causal-QA, which probes the chain's causal coherence by asking whether it contains the specific causal facts needed to reconstruct the narrative. We provide two test sets: SF20K-CC, a manually annotated diagnostic on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, a movie clip benchmark derived from audio descriptions. Our analysis reveals that state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with narrative causality understanding, frequently hallucinating or omitting key events. To address this, we fine-tune VLMs with GRPO using a composite reward that combines a format reward, SODA-Embedding, and Causal-QA accuracy, demonstrating substantial improvements over strong baselines.
authors: Ridouane Ghermi, Vicky Kalogeiton, Ivan Laptev
bullets: Existing multiple-choice and open-ended evaluations can enable shortcuts or lack reliable automatic scoring for causal reasoning.
Causal Chain Generation (CCG) requires models to produce intermediate events connecting a video’s cause and effect.
SODA-Embedding evaluates semantic similarity to reference chains, while Causal-QA tests whether generated chains contain essential causal facts.
Two benchmarks are presented: SF20K-CC, based on 20 short films, and CMD-CC, derived from movie audio descriptions.
State-of-the-art VLMs often hallucinate or omit key events; GRPO fine-tuning with a composite reward substantially improves performance over strong baselines.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses video-language causal reasoning and VLM fine-tuning, fitting video understanding and multimodal LLM interests.
papers.title: From Cause to Effect: Generating Intermediate Event Chains in Videos
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a structured task and evaluation framework for testing and improving video-language models’ ability to generate causally coherent event chains between causes and effects.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Diffusion Transformers have emerged as a powerful paradigm for long video generation. However, they are often constrained by prohibitive computational overhead and substantial memory footprints. This inefficiency arises from dense computation mechanisms that allocate uniform processing resources across all spatiotemporal regions, failing to leverage the inherent temporal redundancy of video where motion is typically confined to sparse areas. In this paper, we propose Dynamics-Aware Sparse Attention (DASA), a unified framework that shifts from dense computation to sparse, motion-driven generation to eliminate both storage and computational redundancies. Inspired by video codec principles, our approach explicitly decouples video content into dynamic and static regions. To mitigate memory bottlenecks, we selectively compress the historical KV cache by retaining only dynamic features within the generated chunk. Furthermore, to reduce computational overhead, we employ a region-level computation allocation strategy based on localized dynamics. Additionally, a dynamics-guided distillation method is introduced to enhance performance via a lightweight distillation training process. Experiments on VBench demonstrate that our approach accelerates autoregressive video generation by 2.16x, while preserving high visual fidelity.
authors: Yuanyu He, Zhuokun Chen, Yefei He, Zhiwei Tang, Jiasheng Tang, Yinghao Yu, Jianfei Cai, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and memory usage of dense autoregressive video diffusion.
Separates dynamic and static regions to exploit temporal redundancy in videos.
Compresses historical KV caches by retaining dynamic features and allocates computation according to localized motion.
Uses dynamics-guided distillation to improve performance with lightweight training.
On VBench, achieves 2.16× faster generation while maintaining high visual fidelity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of the proposed framework. We introduce a unified approach to optimize AR diffusion generation for both storage and computational efficiency. Storage Management (Left): Tokens from historical chunks are selectively cached in memory based on a layer-wise threshold σl, discarding redundant information. The final frame of the immediately preceding chunk serves as a reference frame, with all its tokens unconditionally preserved. Computation Optimization (Right): This reference frame acts as an anchor to guide token selection for the current chunkC . Redundant tokens are filtered out via a threshold γ to reduce computational overhead. AR Diffusion Generation (Middle): Finally, the retained historical tokens from memory and the active tokens from the current chunk are concatenated and processed by the AR diffusion.

Figure 1: Spatiotemporal dynamic analysis of video generation under different motion priors (left: camera panning; right: subject motion). (a) Real-world scenes. The videos are synthesized via Self Forcing, conditioned on a single text prompt provided at the initialization stage. (b) Attention distributions. Visualizations reveal the distribution of temporal attention scores, indicating that the generation process predominantly focuses on active dynamic elements alongside adjacent temporal context. (c) Cosine similarity between the currently generated frame and preceding frames. The consistently high similarity observed in static background regions demonstrates the potential for extensive feature reuse during computation.

Figure 3: Dynamics-guided Distribution Matching Distillation. To mitigate static bias, we introduce a dynamic weight mask based on temporal cosine similarity. By amplifying loss in high-motion regions, it penalizes static predictions and forces the model to learn complex dynamics.

papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.
authors: Tiange Xu, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of diffusion transformers for high-quality video generation.
Uses training-free reciprocal correction: cached dense refinement fixes sparse-attention omissions, while fresh sparse statistics monitor input changes.
Employs online error feedback to coordinate sparse attention, hierarchical caching, and correction aging without changing the reuse schedule.
Evaluated across multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention, caching, and direct-composition baselines.
On HunyuanVideo at 720p for 5-second videos, reports a 3.05× speedup and better fidelity and speed than tested direct compositions.

papers.abstract: RGBA video generation is essential for creating compositable visual assets in filmmaking, game development, and digital content production. However, generating high-quality RGB appearance alongside temporally coherent transparency remains a significant challenge. Existing text-to-RGBA video methods often entangle RGB and alpha distributions and offer limited control over the precise appearance of a target asset. In addition, incorporating image conditioning typically suffers from the emergence-disappearance effects, which fail existing first-frame or first-and-last-frame conditions due to their fully transparent boundary frames. To address these issues, we present Wan-Alpha++, a unified framework that brings controllable RGBA video generation to both text- and image-to-video diffusion backbones through a shared RGBA latent space, extending our conference version Wan-Alpha from the text-conditioned setting to image-conditioned generation with an interior reference frame. Our method first learns shiftable RGB-alpha distributions while preserving the pretrained RGB prior. Specifically, we introduce a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion objective to produce distinguishable RGBA latent representations, and a transparency-guided mean sampler that shifts the noise distribution to improve transparency generation and enable spatial controllability. Building upon this RGBA generation prior, we introduce temporal phase reparameterization for image-conditioned effect generation. By cyclically transforming a zero-positive-zero alpha pattern into a positive-zero-positive pattern, it relocates visible content to both temporal boundaries, facilitating effective appearance conditioning with limited RGBA data.
authors: Haotian Dong, Xin Wang, Wenjing Wang, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Yan Tina Luximon, Ping Li, Wanchao Su, Ke Xu, Di Lin
bullets: Targets entangled RGB–alpha generation and weak image-conditioning behavior at transparent video boundaries.
Uses a shared RGBA latent space across text-to-video and image-to-video diffusion backbones.
Introduces transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion and a transparency-guided mean sampler for improved and spatially controllable transparency.
Applies temporal phase reparameterization to convert zero-positive-zero alpha patterns into boundary-visible positive-zero-positive patterns for image conditioning.
Extends Wan-Alpha from text-conditioned generation to image-conditioned transparent effects using an interior reference frame.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion has emerged as a leading paradigm for efficient video generation, yet its practical deployment remains bottlenecked by the trade-off between generation quality and inference efficiency. We attribute this bottleneck to three error sources in AR rollouts: the base model error, the train-inference distribution mismatch, and the upstream error propagation. Building on this decomposition, we derive closed-form upper bounds on the per-step and cumulative errors, providing a principled basis for jointly optimizing generation quality and inference efficiency. Guided by this analysis, we propose TriTD, a Tri-Partite Trajectory-Distribution co-optimized distillation framework with three complementary modules. First, for ODE initialization, we adopt a Next-Node Trajectory Distillation (NTD) objective, which shortens the supervision horizon and admits a lower regression-error floor. Second, we introduce Chunk-Graded Noising (CGN), a monotonically non-decreasing per-chunk noising schedule that helps narrow the expected train-inference noise mismatch and removes redundant KV-cache updates, yielding substantial speedups at no quality cost. Third, we propose Orthogonal-Parallel DMD (OP-DMD), a distribution-matching loss that retains the original DMD supervision while introducing an additional regression constraint in the orthogonal subspace to suppress off-axis drift, improving both training stability and final generation quality. Extensive experiments show that TriTD consistently surpasses existing baselines in visual quality while reaching a real-time throughput of 26.8 FPS on a single H100 GPU, delivering a balanced quality-efficiency solution for interactive streaming video generation.
authors: Jia Li, Xurui Peng, Haowei Zhu, Tianyu Zhao, Jiexi Wang, Youwei Zheng, Yuxi Ren, Xinglong Wu, Xing Wang, Hayden Kwok-Hay So
bullets: Targets three AR rollout issues: base-model error, train–inference distribution mismatch, and upstream error propagation.
Derives closed-form bounds for per-step and cumulative errors to guide quality–efficiency optimization.
Combines Next-Node Trajectory Distillation, Chunk-Graded Noising, and Orthogonal-Parallel DMD.
Chunk-Graded Noising reduces redundant KV-cache updates without sacrificing quality, while OP-DMD improves stability and generation quality.
Experiments report consistent visual-quality gains over existing baselines and real-time throughput for interactive streaming video generation.

papers.abstract: Despite achieving high visual fidelity, video models still suffer from physical hallucinations, limiting their reliability as world simulators. Existing methods leverage model-internal or external signals to improve physical plausibility, but their roles and limitations require a unified explanation. We propose a two-dimensional physical-hallucination risk framework that defines low-density sampling risk and high-density drifting risk. The first risk captures generations assigned low likelihood by the video model, for example, a ball suddenly teleporting despite the model favoring continuous motion, while the second risk captures physical inconsistencies in high-likelihood generations, for example, a ball bouncing progressively higher without additional energy. Our analysis explains how model-internal signals steer sampling toward higher-density regions of the learned distribution to address low-density sampling risk. However, higher model likelihood does not guarantee physical plausibility, motivating external guidance to address high-density drifting risk. Based on this framework, we develop Hallucination-Aware Sampler (HA-Sampler), which applies external physical guidance within latent refinement to generate physically plausible videos, and HA-Scorer, which derives a likelihood-based signal from the generator itself for evaluating generated videos using continuous normalizing flow (CNF), with coarse ODE integration and finite-difference divergence estimates. Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy benchmarks support our theoretical analysis and demonstrate that our methods outperform the compared sampling and scoring SOTA baselines.
authors: Chenyan Zheng, Fan Wu, Ruibo Li, Jiaxing Li, Minghao Yang, Bang Zhang, Guosheng Lin

Introduces HA-Scorer, a generator-based likelihood signal using continuous normalizing flows for video evaluation.
Experiments on Physics-IQ and VideoPhy support the analysis and report better performance than compared SOTA baselines.

papers.abstract: Dense temporal audio-visual captioning is important for multimodal video understanding and generation. However, prior work is constrained by three main limitations: (1) the lack of a dataset combining high temporal resolution, longer videos, and bidirectional alignment between time and events; (2) the reliance of most existing RL methods on checklists; and (3) the lack of a benchmark that bidirectionally evaluates event semantic correctness and temporal accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose: (1) AVTime-50K, a high-quality 50K-scale dataset with temporally precise, semantically accurate captions and longer videos; (2) AVTime, a state-of-the-art model optimized with a novel Bidirectional Temporal-Semantic Alignment (BiTSA) reward that imposes explicit bidirectional constraints between time and events; and (3) AVTime-Bench, a specialized benchmark that introduces a novel bidirectional evaluation of temporal accuracy and semantic correctness. Our code, models, and datasets are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/Apryle/avtime.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has improved video reasoning in multimodal large language models. However, standard video GRPO varies only linguistic trajectories while conditioning every rollout in a group on the same sampled frames, which can produce homogeneous rewards and weaken group-relative learning when the shared visual evidence is insufficient or distracting. We propose \textbf{FrameGRPO}, a simple and effective reinforcement-learning framework that requires neither auxiliary networks nor changes to the model architecture. Specifically, FrameGRPO combines two lightweight components: (1) \textbf{Multi-Frame Rollouts}, which use only uniform temporal subsampling of a single maximal-frame decode to construct aligned views that diversify visual evidence and reasoning trajectories; and (2) \textbf{Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit}, which selectively reinforces a correct lower-ratio trajectory when all rollouts in a fixed full-ratio reference subset fail, without imposing an unconditional preference for fewer frames. Extensive experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate robust overall improvements over standard GRPO, highlighting temporal-view diversification as an effective mechanism for exploration and credit assignment in video MLLMs.
authors: Jiaxuan Sun, Biao Wang, Shuai Li
bullets: Standard video GRPO gives every rollout the same frames, which can cause homogeneous rewards and weak group-relative learning.
Multi-Frame Rollouts create aligned, temporally subsampled views from one maximal-frame decode to diversify visual evidence without architectural changes.
Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit rewards a correct lower-frame-ratio trajectory only when all full-ratio reference rollouts fail.
Experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks show robust improvements over standard GRPO.
The method uses no auxiliary networks or model-architecture modifications.

A shared policy generates {oi}Gi=1, and a verifier assigns rewards {ri}Gi=1. The outcomes of the fixed full-ratio subset jointly determine the gate for Temporal Efficiency Credit, which produces the modified advantages {Ãi}Gi=1. papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models can jointly understand video, audio, and text, yet they remain weak at temporal grounding, a capability essential for real-world audio-visual applications. To understand this limitation, we look beyond final predictions and examine the model's internal temporal evidence. We identify a temporal generation gap: the internal attention of the model localizes the target moment more accurately than the timestamps it generates. To close this gap, we propose TACG (Temporal Attention-Consistency Grounding), a post-training method that treats internal attention as a reliable temporal pivot and aligns it with both the model prediction and the ground-truth annotation through attention-consistency training. We further build a 580K-sample training dataset by reconstructing temporal QA from dense audio-visual annotations and organizing general omni-modal instruction data. Using TACG and this training dataset, we train OmniGround, a general-purpose omni-modal model with stronger temporal grounding capability, without injecting any additional temporal cues. OmniGround reaches state-of-the-art omni-modal temporal grounding, including 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while staying competitive on both general audio-visual understanding and vision-only grounding.

Achieves 37.5 mIoU on LongVALE and 35.7 mIoU on UnAV-100, while remaining competitive in broader audio-visual and vision-only tasks.

papers.abstract: Video vision-language models (VLMs) have strong semantic understanding, yet remain unreliable at precise temporal grounding. Existing gains from explicitly aligning video frames with absolute time suggest that VLMs may already encode accurate temporal locations internally but lose precision when expressing them as timestamps. Our analysis across four VLMs and two grounding datasets confirms this hypothesis: attention intervals outperform predicted intervals on approximately 66% of valid examples. We term this discrepancy the temporal generation gap. Because precise temporal annotations are expensive, this finding motivates closing the gap to improve temporal grounding using only unlabeled video-query pairs. We propose Self-Supervised Attention Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses internal temporal attention as self-supervision for Group Relative Policy Optimization and applies a ground-truth-free criterion to select high-value samples. SAPO consistently improves temporal grounding across multiple datasets and models spanning weak to strong initial grounding ability. Relative mIoU gains reach 33.7% on Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 5.4% on the strong Time-R1-7B. The improvements transfer across datasets while preserving general video understanding.

Improvements transfer across datasets while preserving general video understanding.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models primarily rely on general-purpose ODE-based numerical methods for training-free accelerated sampling, but performance degrades with coarse time discretization. In this paper, we propose optimal linear leaps (LEAP), a specialized method grounded in theoretical and empirical investigations of sampling trajectory geometry. Built upon low-dimensionality and cross-trajectory consistency, LEAP formulates a supervised least-squares optimization problem within the local trajectory subspace, achieving a precise approximation of future states without model evaluations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LEAP outperforms previous methods across diverse modalities, including text-to-image (Stable Diffusion 3.5, FLUX.1-dev) and image-to-3D (TRELLIS.2) generation. Furthermore, LEAP can be seamlessly integrated into existing solver-based methods, offering a plug-and-play enhancement for modern diffusion models. Code is available at https://github.com/zju-pi/LEAP.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot diffusion image compression based on reverse channel coding achieves high perceptual quality at low bitrates without retraining, yet its bitstream remains vulnerable to bit flips. Prior work has shown that a joint combinatorial representation can amplify a single bit flip into substitutions of multiple atoms and that indexing each atom independently confines this error propagation. However, independent indexing reduces the number of atoms that fit within the bit budget and gives the decoder no indication of which atoms are corrupted. To address these issues, we propose BitFlat, a training-free error-localizing bitstream framework with two components. Blockwise Locality Alignment (BLA) decomposes the globally coupled atom selection at each diffusion step into independent selection units, each describing one signed atom from a dedicated codebook with a fixed-width field, so that any bit error affects only the unit in which it occurs. Reliability-Aware Diffusion Control (RADC) uses the bits saved by BLA to impose structured valid-codeword constraints within each field and converts the decoding state of each field into a binary reliability gate, which turns detected corrupted atoms into erasures at known positions and excludes them from noise synthesis. BitFlat requires neither target residuals nor additional network forward passes and leaves the diffusion model unchanged. Experiments on Kodak, DIV2K, and CLIC2020 show that BitFlat outperforms conventional, learned, and diffusion-based codecs at bit error rates from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$ and, even with $26.7\%$ fewer bits, surpasses Robust Turbo-DDCM.

papers.abstract: Video generation models produce visually compelling motion but systematically fail on fluid phenomena, including smoke, fire, and explosion debris, where outputs lack coherent vortical structure and collapse to bland dynamics that violate the physics of real fluids. Classical solvers achieve high physical fidelity but require detailed 3D scenes and carefully tuned parameters, making them impractical for in-the-wild imagery and video generation. We address this gap by injecting a data-driven fluid prior into a pre-trained video model, trained on a mixture of high-fidelity Houdini simulation data with paired velocity-field ground truth and curated in-the-wild fluid video data for appearance diversity. The core of our approach is a dual stream architecture that predicts per-frame velocity fields alongside RGB, supervised by simulation ground truth. This auxiliary signal regularizes generation toward physically consistent motion and exposes an interpretable physical quantity that we further leverage as a reward for velocity-aware direct preference optimization. Our model produces substantially more realistic fluid dynamics sequences than strong video baselines and optimization-based methods. Project page: https://y-zheng18.github.io/FluidGen/

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces {\Delta}-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.
authors: Wenqing Wang, Joonghyuk Shin, Jonathan Tremblay, Chan Hee Song, Yun Fu
bullets: Addresses exposure bias and compounding errors that cause streaming video quality to collapse over time.
Learns a counterfactual velocity gap shown to be largely deterministic across noise seeds.
Trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector using closed-loop, DAgger-style rollout aggregation and drift-contraction training.
Requires no real videos when using the frozen base model’s own single-shot generations, and adds no inference cost after merging.
In 50-second generation, reduces Δ-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to −0.16 with 40 real clips, outperforming prior reported results with far less data.

papers.abstract: Language-guided video generation often captures scene content while missing the requested motion. We present ViMoLa (Video Motion Language), which predicts a motion prior from language and injects it into a frozen image-to-video backbone. A spatial vector-quantized autoencoder compresses dense trajectories into 64 tokens from a 512-entry codebook; a 28M-parameter transformer predicts the tokens from text; and zero-gated cross-attention adapters condition every frozen Wan~2.2 DiT block through forward hooks. Trained on 462K videos from Something-Something~v2 and Kinetics-400, ViMoLa raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442 (chance 0.250), with similar measured generative quality. Across-prompt shuffled codes achieve 0.283, supporting the importance of prompt-matched token content. A low-rank adapter reaches 0.428 at 1.45% additional forward-pass FLOPs, and reusing the tokenizer and language model with newly trained CogVideoX adapters raises accuracy from 0.301 to 0.398. Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound-motion gains are smaller, and the adapter does not explicitly preserve token-to-patch assignments.
bullets: Targets the common failure of videos to follow requested motion despite matching scene content.
Compresses dense trajectories into 64 discrete tokens and predicts them from language with a 28M-parameter transformer.
Uses zero-gated cross-attention adapters to condition frozen Wan 2.2 DiT blocks; a low-rank variant adds 1.45% forward-pass FLOPs.
Raises directional accuracy from 0.287 to 0.442, with similar measured generative quality; shuffled motion codes provide little benefit.
Control remains imperfect: oracle codes reach 0.531, compound motions improve less, and token-to-patch assignments are not explicitly preserved.

papers.abstract: Video Question Grounding (VideoQG) requires both accurate question answering and precise temporal localization. Existing supervised methods rely on costly temporal annotations, while existing zero-shot approaches are primarily designed for Video Question Answering (VQA) and are not optimized for temporal grounding. We propose DiffGround, an action-driven zero-shot framework built upon frozen Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Our framework first predicts an answer-relevant action cue that transforms the input question into an explicit semantic target for grounding. Action Cue converts a reasoningoriented question into an action-centric retrieval query. Guided by the action cue, a Vision-Language Model (VLM) efficiently selects informative keyframes for reasoning. Finally, we introduce Semantic Diff Refinement, a training-free temporal refinement method that exploits semantic differences between neighboring SigLIP2 embeddings to recover complete action segments from sparse predictions. Extensive experiments on NExT-GQA and STAR show that DiffGround consistently outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods, establishing a new state of the art for Video Question Grounding.
authors: Cheng-Han Lee, Amir Salimi, Hsiang-Wei Huang, Che-Chun Su, Min Sun, Cheng-Hao Kuo
bullets: Targets Video Question Grounding without costly temporal annotations.
Uses frozen multimodal models to predict answer-relevant action cues and select informative keyframes.
Applies training-free Semantic Diff Refinement to recover complete action segments from neighboring SigLIP2 embeddings.
Evaluated on NExT-GQA and STAR, where it outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods.
Scope: relies on frozen MLLMs/VLMs and is designed for action-centric temporal grounding.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed DiffGround framework. Given a video and a question, DiffGround first performs offline, question-agnostic action segment preprocessing to partition the video into semantically coherent action segments. A frozen MLLM then predicts an action cue describing the target action with a single MLLM call. Guided by the question and predicted action cue, a Vision-Language Model (VLM) ranks video frames to select the most informative keyframes for Video Question Answering (VQA). Finally, Semantic Diff Refinement expands the initial grounding prediction by leveraging SigLIP2 semantic differences to align temporal boundaries with the complete action segment, producing more accurate Video Question Grounding (VideoQG) results.

Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed DiffGround framework. DiffGround consists of three stages. First, a frozen MLLM predicts an Action Cue from the input question and uniformly sampled video frames, converting a reasoning-oriented question into an action-centric retrieval query. Second, a frozen VLM (SigLIP2) jointly matches the question and Action Cue to retrieve the Top-K most informative keyframes. Meanwhile, an offline Semantic Diff Segmentation module partitions the video into semantically coherent action segments. Finally, the retrieved keyframes are used for Video Question Answering, and the predicted timestamps are refined by the precomputed semantic segments to recover complete temporal boundaries for Video Question Grounding.
Fig. 4: Prompt Template Design. The prompt for our final VQG prediction, which is adapted from TStar [18].

Fig. 3: Visualization of the proposed Semantic Diff segmentation. By measuring semantic transitions between neighboring clips, our offline preprocessing partitions the video into semantically coherent action segments. Besides separating distinct scenes (e.g., piano playing versus woman and child), it further identifies fine-grained action boundaries, isolating the brief “touch child” interaction (38.8–40.9 s) from surrounding activities. During online inference, Semantic Diff Refinement aligns the retrieved keyframe with the corresponding action segment, producing accurate temporal grounding.
Fig. 5: Prompt Template Design for Object Cue. The prompt for generating object cues, which is adapted from TStar [18].
