papers.abstract: Real-time streaming video question answering with vision-language models must answer queries that arrive at any time with low latency while sustaining the video-processing rate required by the application. Existing systems construct key-value (KV) caches for the entire video as it arrives, although a query typically uses only a few of the preceding frames as evidence. This highlights a fundamental trade-off: performing more computation as video arrives reduces query-time computation but can increase processing lag, whereas deferring computation can increase the video-processing rate but requires additional query-time computation for retrieved content. We present StreamAhead, an algorithm-system co-design that exploits this trade-off through adaptive precomputation: dynamically controlling how much computation to complete for each video segment before a query arrives. StreamAhead encodes video segments independently and lets each remain at a different representation level, from inexpensive visual features to costly KV caches, completing KV caches only for the retrieved segments when a query arrives. StreamAhead profiles offline the cost of advancing a segment to each representation level. Its runtime uses these profiles to schedule segment computation concurrently with query execution, pipelining it across heterogeneous CPU and GPU resources while maintaining the required video-processing rate. StreamAhead achieves accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods with up to 10.4x lower time-to-first-token (TTFT), and up to 5.9x lower TTFT than state-of-the-art streaming systems. It sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT under 0.5 s, and up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT under 2 s. To our knowledge, StreamAhead is the first real-time streaming video QA system with competitive accuracy, setting a new Pareto frontier between video-processing rate and TTFT.
authors: Haoyang Fan, Dhruv Parikh, Rajgopal Kannan, Viktor Prasanna
bullets: Targets streaming video QA, where queries can arrive at any time and only a few preceding frames are typically relevant.
Encodes segments independently at varying representation levels, from inexpensive visual features to full KV caches.
Dynamically completes retrieved segments and pipelines computation across CPU and GPU resources using offline cost profiles.
Reports competitive accuracy with up to 10.4× lower time-to-first-token than prior methods and up to 5.9× lower than streaming systems.
Sustains 30 FPS with P95 TTFT below 0.5 s, or up to 57 FPS with P95 TTFT below 2 s.

papers.abstract: Video large multimodal models have improved at identifying cross-frame visual evidence and conducting open-web retrieval, as reflected in recent video deep research (VDR) benchmarks. However, existing VDR benchmarks primarily evaluate tool-use trajectories and final responses without verifying whether a model actually uses the temporal video information or the retrieved web evidence. To fill this gap, we introduce \method{}, an evidence-grounded benchmark with three features. First, it combines human review with restricted-access probing across multiple models to exclude questions answerable from parametric knowledge or a single information source. Second, each question carries structured video-to-web evidence annotations that link the relevant video segments to their supporting web evidence. Third, its evaluation protocol separately scores video grounding, web evidence grounding, and final-answer correctness. Across eight multimodal agent systems, the best reaches 76.0\% answer accuracy, yet none recovers the complete required web evidence for more than 8\% of questions. Our benchmark is publicly available at \url{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hh721/vdr_temp}.
authors: Xiyuan Liang, Yu Wang, Zuhao Yang, Ziting Wang, Duo Li, Sudong Wang, Zhongyu Yang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Targets a gap in existing VDR benchmarks, which assess trajectories and answers without verifying evidence use.
Filters questions through human review and restricted-access probing to require both video and web information.
Provides structured annotations linking relevant video segments to their supporting web evidence.
Separately evaluates video grounding, web-evidence grounding, and final-answer correctness.
Across eight multimodal agents, the best answer accuracy is 76.0%, while no system recovers complete web evidence for over 8% of questions.

papers.abstract: Recognizing fine-grained bodily behaviors, such as self-grooming, postural shifts, and backchanneling, is a useful intermediate step for computational social signal analysis. But the behaviors that matter vary across social contexts, and retraining a model for each new taxonomy is expensive. Vision-language models (VLMs) can adapt to new categories through text prompts, yet they lack sensitivity to body structure and often confuse subtle postural distinctions. We propose PRIMA (Pose Refined Inductive Motion Adapter), a lightweight module that injects a body-structure prior into frozen VLMs using human pose as a training-time supervisory signal, requiring no pose input at inference. PRIMA separates a model-specific projection head from a shared core that encodes transferable body-configuration knowledge; adapting to a new VLM requires retraining only the head. We train PRIMA on a micro-action dataset and evaluate entirely through zero-shot prompting. The adapter improves recognition on its training domain, transfers to additional VLM backbones at different scales with the core frozen, and generalizes to two unseen target datasets from social psychology and daily activity recognition. In a supporting downstream study, the improved behavior predictions also yield higher correlations with human ratings of rapport and dominance in a collaboration context. Within the scope of the tested models and indoor datasets, the results indicate that pose-guided training can produce body-structure priors that generalize across unseen behavior vocabularies and can be partially reused across VLM backbones while preserving RGB-only inference.
authors: Mingcong Ding, Babette B\"uhler, Tim F\"utterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Enkelejda Kasneci
bullets: Addresses the cost of retraining models for changing social-behavior taxonomies and VLMs’ weak sensitivity to fine-grained posture.
Uses human pose only during training to guide a lightweight adapter, while inference relies on RGB and text prompts without pose input.
Separates a shared transferable core from a VLM-specific projection head, enabling adaptation to new backbones by retraining only the head.
Reports improved recognition on the training domain, transfer across VLM backbones, and generalization to two unseen datasets.
Improved behavior predictions also correlate more strongly with human ratings of rapport and dominance; scope is limited to tested models and indoor datasets.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant scalability challenges in long-video understanding due to quadratic attention complexity and context window constraints. Existing retrieval-based approaches typically rely on supervised learning from static keyframe annotations. However, these label priors often fail to align with the actual information required by downstream MLLMs for complex reasoning, creating a misalignment between the training target and inference needs. To bridge this gap, we propose a probabilistic framework that reformulates frame selection as latent-variable inference. We first initialize a lightweight policy using supervised learning to capture general visual saliency. Then, we treat a frozen MLLM as a task environment and use its answer likelihood as dense task evidence to refine the policy via Bayesian Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Within this formulation, the negative log-likelihood (NLL) over ground-truth answer tokens provides a principled dense reward, while a prior-matching KL term preserves semantic consistency with the elicited label prior. This process transitions the selection principle from static label priors to task evidence. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that our selector achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based scorers while retaining the inference efficiency of lightweight methods. The selector is trained once with a frozen MLLM environment and transfers directly to multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining. Code is available at \url{github.com/Miraclecsc/Frame_Selection_GRPO}.
authors: Shuochen Chang, Bingjie Gao, Qingyang Liu, Qianli Ma, Yibo Miao, Haonan Zhao, Zhaohe Liao, Xiaofeng Zhang, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static keyframe-label supervision and the evidence needed for complex downstream reasoning.
Initializes a lightweight saliency policy with supervised learning, then refines it against a frozen MLLM environment.
Uses answer-token negative log-likelihood as a dense reward and a KL term to preserve consistency with the learned prior.
Achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based frame scorers while retaining lightweight inference efficiency on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench.
The selector is trained once and transfers across multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overall framework of our methods. (a) Keyframe Selector. The lightweight selector (fθ) comprises stacked Video-Text Fusion Transformers. It modulates frame features with query semantics to output importance logits, then parameterizing a Plackett-Luce distribution. (b) Stage I: Label Prior Elicitation. We utilize keyframe label annotations to construct a Label Prior. The selector is trained via pairwise ranking loss to align its predicted logits with the label logits, establishing a robust initialization. (c) Stage II:Task-Evidence Posterior Inference. We freeze the MLLM and treat it as a frozen task environment. The selector performs Group Sampling to propose discrete frame subsets (z). The MLLM evaluates these subsets to provide dense NLL rewards (R) and advantages (A). The policy is refined via Bayesian GRPO to maximize task evidence while maintaining KL-regularization towards the label prior.

papers.abstract: Turning a moving-camera perspective video into a 360{\deg} video requires more than just generating content outside the input frame: observations revealed over time must be preserved, unseen regions completed, and the resulting scene kept consistent as the camera viewpoint changes. Existing methods assign these different requirements to a single conditional video model, requiring them to be jointly learned from panoramic video data. We instead present a modular, 3D-driven framework that distributes these three responsibilities across specialized components, all connected through a shared scene representation. Input observations are reconstructed explicitly in 3D, while a pretrained panoramic image model completes unobserved content from a selected panoramic render. This generated content is lifted into the shared 3D scene, where it remains spatially anchored across camera viewpoints. Without requiring any additional panoramic-video training, our framework achieves state-of-the-art input-view fidelity, perceptual quality, and geometric consistency on a static-scene subset of the Argus evaluation set. These results support our decomposed, 3D-driven formulation as a promising alternative to direct video generation in this setting.
authors: Michael Wakeham, Mrinmoy Kumar Das, Wenqi Wang, Ayush Tewari, Boqing Gong, Deepti Ghadiyaram
bullets: Addresses the challenge of preserving observed content, completing unseen regions, and maintaining consistency as the camera moves.
Explicitly reconstructs input observations in 3D and uses a pretrained panoramic image model to generate missing content.
Lifts generated content into a shared 3D scene representation, spatially anchoring it across viewpoints.
Achieves state-of-the-art input-view fidelity, perceptual quality, and geometric consistency on the static-scene subset of the Argus evaluation set.
Does not require additional panoramic-video training; evaluation is scoped to static scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Framework Overview. A feed-forward 3D reconstruction model aggregates observations from the input perspective video into an observed-region 3DGS [16], which is rendered into incomplete panoramic frames (Sec. 3.1). To complete as much unobserved scene content as possible, we select the frame with the least observed coverage and complete missing regions using a panoramic image model (Sec. 3.2). After estimating and aligning its depth, the completed panorama is lifted into an unobserved-region 3DGS and combined with the observed-region 3DGS, allowing the completed scene to persist when rendered along the input camera trajectory. (Sec. 3.3).

Figure 3. Qualitative comparisons. (a) Given the input video (left), we show panoramic outputs at three timesteps. Colored outlines mark novel viewing directions, with the corresponding perspective views below each panorama. (b) Colored outlines mark regions explicitly projected from the corresponding input frames. We compare the consistency of the remaining panoramic content across three timesteps.

Table 3. Framework and persistence ablations, where VBench averages the three reported dimensions, while MEt3R averages the three sampling rates. Panorama-Only 3D discards the input reconstruction, keeping only the 3D-lifted panorama. Unmasked 3D Lifting lifts the full panorama and fuses it without input-observation masking, allowing generated content to overlap existing geometry. Single-Frame Cond. conditions the outpainting on a single input frame rather than the rendered full-video reconstruction. Per-Frame Completion separately completes every incomplete rendered panoramic frame without any 3D persistence.

We report PSNR and LPIPS [45] for input-view fidelity, as well as VBench [13] Imaging Quality (Imag.), Aesthetic Quality (Aes.), and Motion Smoothness (Motion) for perceptual video quality. We additionally report a post-processed variant of our method (OURS + FILL) that applies lightweight classical inpainting to low-opacity regions.

papers.tldr: A modular 3D-driven pipeline converts moving-camera perspective video into consistent 360° video by separating observation reconstruction, unseen-content generation, and viewpoint-consistent scene rendering.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.
authors: Jaehong Myung, Seunghun Oh, Unsang Park
bullets: Full-video speech-vision decisions can fail despite useful evidence being available in nearby visual windows.
Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED) is a training-free diagnostic that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation.
TED uses ASR transcripts and utterance intervals to query audio-free windows for temporal forecasting, alignment, or cross-modal binding.
Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, temporal forecasting accuracy improves from 29.3–33.7% to 79.3–82.2% with TED.
Controls indicate that the observed temporal anchor—not merely query replacement or region availability—drives recovery.

papers.abstract: Existing motion transfer methods excel at exact, rigid motion replication from reference videos to target scenes, whereas they often fail to account for the compatibility between the transferred motion and the target scene environment in accordance with physical laws. In this work, we propose MotionShift, a novel motion transfer framework that achieves high-fidelity motion transfer while ensuring physical compatibility with the target scene. In particular, we design a planner--evaluator iterative motion adaptation mechanism, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) acts as the planner to generate motion trajectories by leveraging its strong semantic reasoning capabilities, while a Vision-Language Model (VLM) serves as the evaluator to rectify the motion based on its superior visual perception and scene understanding. Through this planner--evaluator synergistic reasoning process, the motion is adapted to the target scene in a training-free manner. The adapted motion is then used as a generative condition for an image-to-video (I2V) model to render videos in the target scene. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MotionShift achieves high-fidelity and physically compatible motion transfer across diverse and complex scenes. Moreover, we show that MotionShift can be readily integrated into existing trajectory-conditioned I2V models, endowing them with realistic motion transfer capabilities.
authors: Yanchen Liu, Junyao Gao, Yanan Sun, Wensheng Chen, Guangming Lu, Wenjie Pei
bullets: Addresses the lack of physical and environmental compatibility in existing reference-video motion transfer methods.
Uses an LLM planner to generate motion trajectories and a VLM evaluator to visually assess and rectify them.
Iteratively adapts motion to the target scene without additional training.
Feeds the adapted motion as conditioning to an image-to-video model for target-scene rendering.
Experiments report realistic, physically compatible transfer across diverse complex scenes and integration with existing trajectory-conditioned I2V models.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of MotionShift. Given a reference video and a target image, we first initialize a motion trajectory for the target scene. Then, through planner–evaluator iterative adaptation, we refine the trajectory to produce an environment-compatible trajectory and a corresponding motion prompt. Finally, these are progressively rendered into the output video: a motion generation model converts the trajectory into a semantic mask sequence, and an appearance rendering model synthesizes the final video from the masks and target image.

Fig. 5. Visual comparison with baseline methods. MotionShift exhibits superior motion consistency and environmental adaptability, accurately capturing perspective variations, realistic reflections, and synchronized hand movements compared to baseline approaches.

Fig. 4. Illustration of Planner–Evaluator Iterative Adaptation. At the beginning of each iteration, we leverage the semantic reasoning capability of the planner (LLM) to infer object–environment interactions and perform detailed motion planning along the given trajectory, producing a corrected motion trajectory. We then construct a pseudo video based on the target image and the corrected trajectory, and feed it to the evaluator (VLM) to assess visual consistency and physical plausibility, which then outputs revision suggestions. These suggestions are then appended to the planner’s instruction prompt, and we iteratively refine the motion trajectory until the evaluator detects no major issues.
Fig. 9. Visual results of Go-with-the-Flow using the initial trajectory vs. the environment-compatible trajectory produced by MotionShift as a plugin.
Fig. 3. Illustration of environment-compatible motion transfer, where identical reference motions adapt naturally to different scenes, yielding contextually consistent behaviors.
Fig. 7. Ablation on planner–evaluator adaptation. We compare variants by disabling adaptation, removing the evaluator, or replacing the planner.
TABLE I QUANTITATIVE COMPARISON. OUR METHOD SIGNIFICANTLY OUTPERFORMS THE OTHER LEADING METHODS.

papers.title: MotionShift: Environment-Compatible Motion Transfer via Planner-Evaluator Synergistic Adaptation
papers.tldr: MotionShift enables high-fidelity motion transfer that adapts to target-scene constraints through training-free planner–evaluator reasoning.

papers.abstract: Synthesizing a monocular video from a new camera trajectory requires preserving the observed scene geometry and motion while completing regions that become newly visible. Feed-forward 4D reconstructors recover the structure of the observed scene, whereas video diffusion models provide a generative prior for completing unseen content. We introduce Holo4D, a video reshooting framework that uses reconstructed 3D trajectories as a holistic source-view 4D scaffold. We project these trajectories into the requested views and encode their geometry and source appearance to guide a pretrained video diffusion model. Together with the source video and target cameras, the scaffold grounds generation in reconstructed observations while leaving unsupported regions to the generative prior. Experiments demonstrate the value of trajectory-based conditioning for camera control and novel-view synthesis. The framework accommodates different 4D reconstructors without retraining the video generator, allowing it to benefit from future advances in source reconstruction. More details can be found in our project page.
authors: Yushi Lan, Zeren Jiang, Koichi Namekata, Xingang Pan, Chuanxia Zheng, Andrea Vedaldi
bullets: Addresses monocular video synthesis along new camera trajectories with newly visible content.
Builds a holistic 4D scaffold from reconstructed 3D scene trajectories and motion.
Projects scaffold geometry and source appearance into target views to condition a pretrained video diffusion model.
Uses source video and target cameras to ground generation in observations while delegating unsupported regions to the generative prior.
Experiments show trajectory-based conditioning improves camera control and novel-view synthesis; the generator requires no retraining for different reconstructors.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HOLO4D overview. Top (4D scaffold): a 4D reconstructor R recovers persistent 3D trajectories, paired with sampled source colors, which are projected into the target cameras and encoded into track features T. Bottom (video diffusion): source and noisy target latents are concatenated along width; each DiT block concatenates T with its hidden features along channels (null on the source half) and adds camera features C encoded from Plücker rays. Flames and snowflakes mark trained and frozen modules (Appendix B). Trajectory panels show a subset of the dense tracks; the top-right overlay is for visualization only. The output is obtained by iterative denoising; Figure 11 details the DiT block.

Figure 7: Submitted pipeline (reproduced from the submitted version). Static and dynamic source pixels were rendered into a hybrid target-view RGB-D cache (projected RGB, depth, and visibility), which conditioned the video diffusion model together with Plücker rays and projected 3D tracks. This version removes the rendered RGB-D branch and keeps the track branch (Figure 2).

Figure 2: HOLO4D pipeline. An off-the-shelf 4D reconstructor estimates source geometry and 3D tracks from the input video. We split source pixels into static and dynamic regions using track motion. Static regions are fused from camera-coverage keyframes, dynamic regions use time-synchronized per-frame reprojection, and valid masks indicate observed target-view support. The resulting hybrid RGB-D condition is injected together with target-camera Plücker rays and 3D tracking tokens, and the VDM synthesizes the target-view RGB video.

papers.abstract: Camera-conditioned video diffusion models often suffer from inaccurate camera control and geometric inconsisten- cies because camera constraints and estimated geometry are only weakly enforced during denoising. Existing reme- dies often require costly geometry-aware fine-tuning or ad- ditional 3D supervision. We introduce GeoART, a training- free self-refinement framework that improves camera con- trollability through geometry-aware test-time scaling. At selected denoising steps, GeoART generates multiple can- didates within the Predict-and-Perturb cycle and eval- uates them using a geometry prior, without directly modify- ing the denoising trajectory. A confidence gate suppresses unreliable geometric evidence, while rank-calibrated prob- abilistic selection combines score magnitude and relative rank to choose the next refinement state. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in camera controlla- bility, multi-view consistency, and visual quality over exist- ing sampling and self-refinement methods, without training or modifying the pretrained video diffusion model
bullets: Addresses weak enforcement of camera constraints and estimated geometry during denoising.
Generates and evaluates multiple candidates at selected denoising steps within a Predict-and-Perturb cycle.

papers.abstract: Novel view synthesis under trajectory changes is essential for autonomous driving simulation, yet existing methods struggle to generate consistent videos when extrapolating to unseen viewpoints such as lane shifts. Reconstruction-based approaches maintain geometric consistency but degrade in visual quality under large viewpoint changes, while reconstruct-then-restore methods often produce visually plausible frames yet suffer from geometric and temporal inconsistencies. We present GeoV2V, a geometry-grounded video-to-video diffusion framework that synthesizes temporally coherent driving videos along novel trajectories by integrating LiDAR and depth-derived geometric priors with full-video conditioning in the Wan 2.1 backbone. A key challenge in learning cross-lane transformations is the lack of synchronized multi-trajectory supervision in real-world datasets. To address this, we also introduce Para4D, a synthetic dataset capturing synchronized multi-lane driving videos within dynamic scenes, which provides explicit supervision for lane-shift generation and serves as a strong training prior for geometry-consistent view synthesis. Experiments on Waymo, nuScenes, and Para4D demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in visual quality, geometric consistency, and robustness to complex lighting dynamics under large trajectory shifts. Project page: https://xiyuche.github.io/GeoV2V/
authors: Yuchen Xi, Yuhan Guo, Chenwei Hou, Zixu Liu, Jin Fang, Jason Liu, Ruigang Yang
bullets: Targets novel-view synthesis for autonomous-driving simulation under large trajectory changes.

Evaluations on Waymo, nuScenes, and Para4D show strong visual quality, geometric consistency, and robustness to complex lighting dynamics.
Scope: the method addresses trajectory extrapolation, especially cross-lane transformations, where real-world synchronized supervision is limited.

papers.abstract: Controllable video generation has recently achieved impressive visual quality, yet existing control paradigms remain poorly suited to embodied navigation. Text prompts are spatially ambiguous, while camera-trajectory control relies on low-level motion specifications that are unintuitive for human users and difficult to manipulate. In this work, we introduce Map2Vid, a novel task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV-map-to-video synthesis problem, together with a large-scale benchmark for systematic evaluation. By using BEV maps, which provide a visual representation of global scene layout and intended navigation routes, Map2Vid enables human-friendly navigation video generation. To support this task, we construct a dedicated dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes, each paired with egocentric videos, BEV maps, camera trajectories and language instructions. We further develop a unified framework that integrates multiple control signals, together with a curriculum training strategy that progressively weakens non-map inputs, enabling flexible inference under both full conditioning and map-only input. Extensive experiments across multiple foundation generation models demonstrate that controllable navigation video generation via BEV map is a viable and promising direction.
authors: Yulin Dai, Yuqian Fu, Tianwen Qian, Zhen Xing, Bojia Zi, Xiaoling Wang
bullets: Reframes embodied navigation video generation as bird’s-eye-view (BEV) map-to-video synthesis.

Uses a unified multi-signal control framework with curriculum training that supports full conditioning or map-only inference.

papers.abstract: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emph{video reference gap} between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce \textbf{Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP)}, a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \url{https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/}
authors: Junwei Wen, Deshui Miao, Guangming Lu, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Xin Li, Wenjie Pei
bullets: Addresses the video reference gap between language-based reasoning and visual evidence across frames.
Builds a chronological chain of video primitives linking entity references with temporal support and spatial evidence.
Uses selected primitives to generate box prompts and temporal guidance for video mask prediction.
Trains the representation with supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning.
Shows strong performance across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones.

papers.abstract: Understanding when during a video a model makes its critical observations is essential for interpreting video-understanding systems. However, existing attribution methods often spread evidence diffusely across near-duplicate frames. We introduce Sufficient Frame Subsets: compact sets of frames in which all other frames are masked, yet each subset independently preserves the model's prediction. We evaluate our method on two complementary benchmarks, UCF101 and Something-Something v2, using both CNN- and transformer-based architectures. Our results show that the proposed algorithm identifies highly compact and effective frame subsets for explaining model decisions. We also find that models capable of relying on a greater number of sufficient frame subsets tend to perform better, possibly because they are more robust, consistent with prior research. Finally, the extracted frame subsets help us analyze model failure cases, reveal which aspects of a video the model has learned to emphasize, and identify opportunities for improving future training procedures.
bullets: Addresses diffuse attribution across near-duplicate frames in video understanding.
Masks all frames outside each candidate subset and tests whether the prediction is preserved.
Evaluated on UCF101 and Something-Something v2 with CNN- and transformer-based models.
Finds highly compact, effective subsets and links reliance on more sufficient subsets with better model performance.
Supports failure analysis, inspection of learned visual emphasis, and future training improvements.

papers.abstract: We show that a video can be represented with just a few keyframes without sacrificing a given model's belief about the video. Our method is the first of its kind that extracts these keyframes conditioned on the model's prediction, which is massively helpful for building explainable video models. We then fairly distribute the importance of the video to the model among the keyframes with game theoretically fair Shapley values. Through qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that keyframe attribution is superior to the traditional frame attribution. Further, we conduct preliminary exploration on highlighting the important changes among the frames by looking at the differences between adjacent keyframes.

papers.abstract: Video generation models synthesize visual sequences from text and image inputs. Extending video generation to long animations requires actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments to remain coordinated across scenes. Executable scene programs make these decisions available for inspection. Constructing an entire story before observing its execution can leave later scenes dependent on unrealized events. We present SpriteStage, a progressive scene programming framework that builds animation through iterative enactment and engine reorchestration. Iterative enactment generates each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, executes it on a shared spatial stage, and uses runtime and visual feedback to revise the relevant actions or story beats. The accepted outcome becomes the starting state for the next scene. Engine reorchestration maps the resulting draft to production assets and engine capabilities while retaining its events, geometry, and timing. Inspection of the assembled sequence and frozen replay carry the accepted performance into the final video. Three complete animations, ranging from approximately 9.9 to 14.3 minutes, demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in producing extended narratives through scene programming and engine execution.
authors: Zhaoqi Wang, Zijian Zhang, Jiamou Liu
bullets: Targets the coordination of actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments across long animations.

papers.abstract: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross-modal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task-specific adapters.
authors: Kien T. Pham, Yuhao Liu, Chong Hou Choi, Zhenqi He, Yanghao Wang, Chenyang Lei, Rui Liu, Qifeng Chen, Long Chen
bullets: Addresses scarce paired audio-video data by first training audio and video branches on abundant unimodal data, then using paired data for cross-modal learning.
Uses independently warped noise schedules so video can denoise longer while audio settles earlier.
Trains asymmetric workflows where one clean modality guides synthesis or editing of the other.
Supports intent-aware editing that preserves one modality while modifying the other.

papers.abstract: Comparing videos to assess their semantic similarity remains a challenging task for current Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which are primarily trained with single-video objectives. While most prior works have focused on computing global similarity, recent studies have introduced the more challenging problem of concept-based similarity, which measures how similar two videos are with respect to specific concepts (e.g., activity, location). However, no dedicated approaches have yet leveraged LMMs to explicitly address this task. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap introducing Video Caption Entailment for video similarity estimation (VICE): a dual-branch design that leverages LMMs for cross-video reasoning. Each branch jointly processes one video and the caption of the other, measuring their alignment for a specific concept via video-language entailment. The outputs from both branches are fused to produce a final similarity score, along with a textual explanation of the model reasoning. This approach leverages the model's native single-video understanding while enabling fine-grained comparative reasoning between video and text. Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show that VICE outperforms models that process both videos simultaneously, highlighting the promise of single-video reasoning for concept-based similarity estimation.
authors: Benedetta Liberatori, Lorenzo Vaquero, Elisa Ricci, Paolo Rota
bullets: Addresses the challenge of concept-based video similarity, such as comparing activity or location, which is not directly handled by most LMMs.
Uses two branches, each processing one video with a caption of the other to assess concept-specific video–language alignment.
Fuses both entailment outputs into a similarity score and an explanation of the model’s reasoning.
Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show improved performance over models that process both videos simultaneously.
The approach is scoped to leveraging single-video understanding for cross-video comparative reasoning.

papers.abstract: Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) aims to localize and segment objects referred to by natural-language expressions throughout a video. Although large vision-language models (LVLMs) implicitly encode localization cues in their attention maps, these attentions are often noisy, diffuse, and scattered across layers, heads, and modalities, limiting their direct use for segmentation. Existing methods typically rely on handcrafted attention-selection heuristics or computationally expensive attention refinement. We propose ATLAS, an attention adaptation framework that learns to transform raw LVLM attentions into object-centric localization cues. ATLAS treats attentions from all layers, heads, and modalities as structured features, combining high-resolution frame-level attentions that capture spatial information with low-resolution video-level attentions that encode temporal context. A lightweight U-Net equipped with temporal attention and FiLM-based modulation fuses these complementary representations to generate coarse segmentation heatmaps, which are propagated across the video using SAM2. Extensive experiments on challenging referring and reasoning video segmentation benchmarks show that ATLAS outperforms existing frozen-backbone methods. Code and models are available at \url{https://hamidreza-136.github.io/atlas/}.
authors: Hamidreza Dastmalchi, Ali Cheraghian, Aijun An, Abdelwahed Khamis, Lars Petersson

papers.abstract: Flow-matching models generate samples through iterative velocity predictions, but typically do not revisit these predictions using the intermediate representations that produced them. We introduce CorrFlow, a self-correcting flow-matching framework that reuses this information through a lightweight refiner. Under rectified-flow interpolation, the error of the one-step clean prediction equals the realized velocity residual scaled by the noise level. Motivated by this identity, the refiner learns to predict residual corrections from the base model's clean prediction, conditioning, noise level and hidden states from the same forward pass. The correction is added to the base velocity before each sampling update, so subsequent predictions are made from the corrected state. This requires no additional base-model evaluations and only one lightweight refiner evaluation per step. Our theoretical analyses establish conditions under which feature reuse outperforms raw-input affine predictors and refiner training achieves greater residual-risk reduction than continued base-model training under a matched training compute budget. Experiments on class-conditional image generation, text-to-video generation and image-to-video generation show consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, including gains in visual quality and physical consistency. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/corrflow-project
authors: Hangwei Zhang, Nathan Rouill\'e, Chuanxia Zheng
bullets: Targets errors in iterative flow-matching sampling, where predictions are not typically revisited using intermediate representations.
The refiner predicts residual corrections from the base clean prediction, conditioning, noise level, and same-pass hidden states.
Corrections are applied before each sampling update, enabling subsequent predictions from the corrected state at one extra lightweight evaluation per step.
Theory analyzes when feature reuse and refiner training provide greater residual-risk reduction than simpler predictors or continued base-model training under matched compute.
Experiments across class-conditional image, text-to-video, and image-to-video generation report consistent gains in visual quality and physical consistency.

papers.abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.
authors: Kerui Chen, Jinglu Wang, Yun Wang, Xinjiang Wang, Yan Lu
bullets: Addresses long-video context limits and the cost of reprocessing videos for each query.

papers.abstract: Simulation-to-real driving video diffusion models can translate photorealistic scenes, but they typically represent pedestrians and cyclists, vulnerable road users (VRUs), as generic object classes. This is insufficient for vulnerable road users whose safety-relevant appearance depends on articulated pose and identity. We present BodyBridge and Grounded Body Layers (GBL), a simulator-derived, pixel-aligned representation that combines scene geometry, canonical per-pixel body correspondence, and exact VRU masks. GBL provides explicit articulation to the video diffusion model, emphasizes VRU regions during control-branch post-training, and supports additive composition with scene-geometry control at inference. It also enables per-joint evaluation of generated VRUs and a failure taxonomy for identity errors. On CARLA-to-real translation, BodyBridge improves near-range PCK@0.5 by 22% over the released depth-conditioned baseline. Replacing normal-map body control with canonical correspondence reduces body flips by 18%, while composition reduces near-range facing flips by 27%. These results show that explicit body grounding complements scene-level control and improves pose-faithful VRU generation. All code, data, and model checkpoints will be made publicly available to support reproducible, pedestrian-aware autonomous driving research.

papers.abstract: Sign language production (SLP) aims to synthesize expressive signing motion from written text. Modeling signing motion presents two key temporal challenges. First, fine-grained hand articulations demand higher temporal resolution than relatively slower body movements. Second, signing events unfold over variable durations, calling for adaptive temporal scheduling during generation. To address these challenges, we first introduce a Multi-Rate Vector Quantizer (MRVQ), an articulation-decoupled motion tokenizer that represents the body and both hands as separate discrete streams at distinct temporal resolutions. Building on this representation, we propose BLANC (BLock-wise Adaptive diffusioN with Articulatory Clock), a gloss-free SLP framework that generates variable-duration motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block. At its core, a Latent Articulatory Clock (LAC) learns temporal structure from multi-scale motion-derived partitions to predict block durations and sequence termination during generation. We further introduce inference-time body-conditioned hand refinement to improve coordination across articulators. Extensive experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily demonstrate that BLANC achieves state-of-the-art performance in sign language production.
authors: Youngmin Kim, Seoyeong Hwang, Sujung Hong, Seong Jae Hwang
bullets: Addresses the need for fine-grained hand timing and variable-duration signing events.
Uses a Multi-Rate Vector Quantizer to encode the body and both hands as separate streams at distinct temporal resolutions.
Generates variable-length motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block.
A Latent Articulatory Clock predicts block durations and when generation should terminate.
Body-conditioned hand refinement improves coordination; experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily report state-of-the-art performance.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query-relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally-contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame-query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert-1102/FrameScout.
authors: Haonan Hu, Shuhao Chen, Weisen Jiang, Lizhao Gao, James Kwok, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets the excessive visual-token cost of videos lasting tens of minutes to hours.
Uses a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to encode frames with temporal context.
Trains frame and query embeddings with a contrastive objective to distinguish relevant from irrelevant frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs.
Scope: focuses on query-guided frame selection for long-video question answering.

papers.abstract: Sparse-frame video-language models can change their answers when only the sampling timestamps shift. Raw agreement exposes this problem, but it need not rank errors better than token confidence or identify which additional observation will repair an answer. We argue that answer risk and action value must be estimated separately. PhaseGuard+ probes a frozen VLM at controlled temporal offsets, predicts the reliability of the phase-vote answer, and predicts the example-wise correctness gain of a specific rescue action. The second score routes only examples expected to benefit from denser frames or a stronger VLM. Both predictors use lightweight models trained on public data; the VLMs remain frozen. We use 256 Perception Test videos for method development and evaluate on a disjoint 256-video test set comprising 554 Physics questions. For Qwen3-VL-8B, reliability AUROC rises from 68.0% with token softmax to 74.8% (+6.8 pp, 95% CI [2.6, 10.7] pp). Routing 30% of questions to Qwen3-VL-32B reaches 67.87% accuracy, compared with 63.66% for budget-matched random routing (+4.21 percentage points, CI [1.89, 6.40]). All four tested rescue pairs significantly outperform random routing. Temporal sensitivity becomes actionable when the system learns both whether an answer is unreliable and whether an available action is likely to fix it.
bullets: Sparse-frame video-language models can change answers when sampling timestamps shift.
The method probes a frozen VLM at controlled temporal offsets and forms a phase-vote answer.
Separate lightweight predictors estimate answer reliability and the correctness gain from denser frames or a stronger VLM.
On Qwen3-VL-8B, reliability AUROC improves from 68.0% to 74.8% over token softmax.
Routing 30% of questions to Qwen3-VL-32B achieves 67.87% accuracy versus 63.66% for random routing; all four rescue pairs outperform random routing.

papers.abstract: Recognizing micro-expressions in real-world conversations is challenging, as these facial movements are brief and faint, and their interpretations are strongly dependent on the contextual circumstances of their occurrence. Most existing methods are de-contextualized, as they analyze isolated video clips while disregarding the semantic and acoustic cues in the surrounding dialogue that help explain the emergence of an expression. Decades of psychological studies have shown that social context exerts influences on facial behavior over two key dimensions: how an expression is interpreted and how strongly it is generated to begin with. However, existing micro-expression research rarely incorporates such contextual factors into its models. As an example, provocative utterances from an interlocutor may elicit suppressed negative affective reactions, which isolated silent clips are unable to account for. We propose TriCoME, a trimodal dataset consisting of visual, audio and text data sourced from real-world conversations. In this dataset, each micro-expression is paired with its concurrent utterance and preceding context. We further annotate the context based on conversational role to denote two categories: external stimuli from an interlocutor's utterance and internal background from the subject's own utterance. On this basis, we propose the Hierarchical Focusing Fusion Network (HFFNet), which aligns acoustic and semantic streams at fine granularity, compresses long dialogue sequences, modulates attention toward conversational roles via a context-type embedding, and routes each sample between visual-only and multimodal decisions based on visual confidence to prevent noisy context from degrading recognition performance.
authors: Junbo Wang, Yan Zhao, Shigang Wang, Jian Wei, Qiming Zhang, Yu Wu
bullets: Micro-expressions are brief, subtle, and difficult to interpret without surrounding conversational context.
TriCoME pairs each expression with concurrent utterances and preceding context across visual, audio, and text modalities.
Context is annotated by conversational role, distinguishing interlocutor-generated stimuli from the subject’s own internal background.
HFFNet hierarchically fuses aligned acoustic and semantic cues, models long dialogue context, and focuses on conversational roles.
A confidence-based routing mechanism falls back to visual-only recognition when contextual signals may introduce noise.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Architecture of the proposed Hierarchical Focusing Fusion Network (HFFNet) for context-aware micro-expression recognition. The pipeline comprises three stages. (1) Multi-modal Feature Extraction: MMNet extracts visual features Fvisual from video frames; Wav2Vec 2.0 with a sliding-window strategy extracts acoustic features Saudio from raw waveforms; BERT extracts semantic features Stext from transcribed text. (2) Context-Aware Sentence Encoding: A Cross-Modal Transformer (CmT) fuses Saudio and Stext through fine-grained interaction, followed by a Sequence Compressor that condenses the fused sequence into a compact representation; a Contextual Transformer (CoT) then injects context type embeddings tc ∈ {0, 1} to distinguish interlocutor utterances (external triggers) from self-statements (internal background), yielding the sentence feature Fsentence. (3) Intelligent Gating & Adaptive Routing: Fvisual and Fsentence interact via a cross-modal fusion block and an enhanced gating network with element-wise gate vector g; an adaptive router dynamically selects between the visual-only prediction Lvis and the multimodal prediction Lmm based on visual confidence, producing the final emotion classification.

papers.abstract: Characters, locations, and actions recur throughout a movie, so many of its moments differ only in fine-grained details. Grounding such a moment in a full-length movie requires resolving that detail rather than matching the attributes it shares with other moments, yet existing temporal movie grounding benchmarks rarely test this. We introduce CoM$^2$-Bench, a benchmark of confusable query pairs, where the two queries in each pair share most attributes but differ in a single distinguishing detail within a full movie, posing a challenge for recent temporal grounding approaches. To locate where grounding breaks down, we analyze a retrieve-then-localize pipeline, in which a retriever first selects a short candidate chunk and a localizer then performs temporal grounding within it. Separating the two stages lets us attribute each failure to either retrieval or localization. We find that retrieval is the major bottleneck: state-of-the-art retrievers often select a moment's confusable counterpart, because their choices follow the content the two moments share rather than the detail that tells them apart. To address these failures, we propose a simple, training-free remedy, Agentic Window Search (AWS): an MLLM agent $\textit{Decomposes}$ the query into attribute-level sub-queries, then $\textit{Inspects}$ each candidate window against them and $\textit{Expands}$ the window when evidence is cut off at its edge. AWS works with existing retrievers and localizers without additional training, raising mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8.
authors: Dong-Hee Kim, Seonwoo Choi, Changbeen Kim, Juyeon Ko, Youngju Choi, Il Hyeon Mun, Hyunwoo J. Kim, Donghyun Kim
bullets: Introduces paired queries that share most attributes but differ in one distinguishing detail.
Evaluates retrieve-then-localize pipelines on full-length movies and separates retrieval from localization failures.
Finds retrieval is the main bottleneck: systems often select a confusable counterpart based on shared content.
Proposes training-free Agentic Window Search, which decomposes queries, inspects candidate windows, and expands truncated windows.
Improves mIoU from 18.5 to 26.8 when used with existing retrievers and localizers.

DECOMPOSE forms numbered sub-queries, and INSPECT checks each against candidate windows with a character reference, rejecting candidates that miss a sub-query, and EXPAND adjusts a window whose evidence is cut off at its edge before accepting it.

papers.abstract: AI-generated video (AIGV) detection is increasingly important for mitigating misinformation, impersonation, and other malicious uses of synthetic media, yet existing detectors often generalize poorly to unseen generators in open-world settings. To better understand this challenge, we analyze the failure modes of AIGV detectors under cross-generator out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts and observe that detector representations strongly encode generator-specific cues, which are associated with substantial ID-OOD performance drops. Further analysis shows that naively perturbing generator-sensitive tokens can even reduce OOD performance, indicating that generator-related cues and detection-relevant evidence are only partially separable. Motivated by these findings, we propose Forensic Obfuscation of geneRator-specific cues via Gradient-guided Embedding perturbation (FORGE), a token-aware adversarial training framework for open-world AIGV detection. FORGE identifies tokens that are strongly associated with generator-specific shortcuts yet less critical to real/fake discrimination, and selectively perturbs them during training to suppress generator-dependent patterns while preserving useful forensic evidence. Through synchronized adversarial training between an attacker and a detector, FORGE encourages the detector to learn more transferable generator-invariant forensic representations. Experiments on 29 held-out benchmark entries show that FORGE achieves an average F1 of 92.62, outperforming eight strong baselines by 5.31 points, while also remaining robust under four common post-processing attacks. We will release our code and datasets upon acceptance.
authors: Qi Zhou, Yuanfan Li, Huiqi Deng, Hongbin Pei, Yazhe Tang
bullets: Existing detectors often overfit to generator-specific cues, causing substantial performance drops on unseen generators.
Naively perturbing these cues can hurt detection because generator signals and real/fake evidence are only partly separable.
FORGE uses token-aware, gradient-guided adversarial embedding perturbations to reduce reliance on generator-dependent patterns.
Synchronized attacker–detector training encourages generator-invariant forensic representations.
On 29 held-out benchmark entries, FORGE reaches 92.62 average F1, surpasses eight baselines by 5.31 points, and remains robust to four post-processing attacks.

papers.abstract: Long-video agents must map hours or days of multimodal evidence into a bounded context while respecting token and latency budgets, making memory design a context-management challenge. Existing memory systems largely rely on hand-designed policies, leaving open how to jointly optimize memory design for performance and efficiency. We propose Long Video Meta-memory Harness (LVMH), an automated multi-agent framework that formulates memory-policy development as multi-objective code search around a fixed answer model. To guard against self-certification and development-set overfitting, LVMH separates implementation from independent review and enforces protected observation boundaries. Persistent meta-memory records past proposals, traces, costs, and failures to guide subsequent policy revisions. Through this harness, we discover Self-Evolving Evidence Memory (SEEM), a "text-first, vision-second" policy that answers from compact structured event memory and evidence specialists, consulting localized frames through a selective visual gate. The policy evolved on EgoLifeQA generalizes to unseen benchmarks, outperforming Meta-Harness on both Ego-R1 Bench and Video-MME (L) with GPT-5 mini. Across the three benchmarks, SEEM with GPT-5 achieves 65.7% average accuracy, surpassing the previous state of the art by 7.7 percentage points with approximately 32x lower average evaluation token use and 91x shorter average response time.
authors: Liwei Che, Benlin Liu, Dai Li, Xiangyan Li, Zijian Wu, Changjiang Li, Minghao Guo, Chengzhi Mao, Vladimir Pavlovic, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Addresses the challenge of compressing hours or days of multimodal video into bounded context under token and latency budgets.
Uses multi-objective, multi-agent code search around a fixed answer model, with independent review, protected observations, and persistent meta-memory.
Discovers SEEM, a text-first, vision-second policy that uses structured event memory and selectively retrieves localized frames.
SEEM generalizes from EgoLifeQA to unseen benchmarks, outperforming Meta-Harness on Ego-R1 Bench and Video-MME (L).
Across three benchmarks, SEEM with GPT-5 reaches 65.7% average accuracy, with approximately 32× lower token use and 91× shorter response time than prior state of the art.

papers.abstract: Generated videos often lose geometric consistency under camera motion: structures warp under viewpoint change, parallax becomes inconsistent, and smooth camera movement may collapse into shot-like transitions. We argue that this failure is largely a data problem. In web-scale video corpora, most visible motion comes from dynamic objects captured by static or weakly moving cameras, leaving only sparse supervision for viewpoint-induced appearance changes. To address this, we propose Video Geometry Corrector (VGC), a post-hoc video-to-video model trained on synthetic paired supervision. Starting from real videos with diverse camera motion and pose annotations, we construct VG-Pairs with a synthetic paired-supervision data generation pipeline. Each video clip is treated as a geometry-consistent target and paired with a distorted counterpart synthesized by a pretrained image-to-video inpainting model using trajectory-adaptive keyframes. VGC learns to map the distorted input to the geometry-consistent target without modifying the source generator, and uses optical flow as an auxiliary cue to help disentangle camera motion from object motion. Experiments on pose-conditioned and prompt-driven benchmarks show that VGC improves geometric consistency across multiple source generators, and scaling to a larger backbone further extends the framework toward more general video refinement.
authors: Weijie Lyu, Tiancheng Shen, Jason Li, Yujing Wang, Xiaoyuan Wang, Haobo Yuan, Yizhou Zhao, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Generated videos often warp structures, produce inconsistent parallax, or collapse smooth camera motion into shot-like transitions.
The paper attributes this largely to limited viewpoint-change supervision in web-scale video data.
VGC is trained on synthetic distorted/geometry-consistent video pairs created from real videos with camera-motion and pose annotations.
It refines outputs without modifying the source video generator and uses optical flow to separate camera motion from object motion.
Experiments across pose-conditioned and prompt-driven benchmarks show improved geometric consistency across multiple generators; larger backbones extend refinement capability.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of Video Geometry Corrector (VGC). Starting from a real video with diverse camera motion, we select trajectory-adaptive keyframes and use them to condition an image-to-video inpainting model, which produces a geometry-distorted video that serves as the training input. We then train VGC to map this distorted input to the geometry-consistent target video with a reconstruction loss. Optical flow is computed from the distorted video and used as an additional conditioning signal for VGC, providing motion cues that help disentangle camera motion from scene dynamics. The 3D reconstruction is shown here only for visualization and is not used in the pipeline.

Figure 2: Effect of adaptive keyframe selection. The red arrows indicate a constant 3D direction while the camera is moving. For clips with large, nonlinear camera motion, conditioning the image-to-video model only on the first and last frames often produces a shortcut trajectory that deviates substantially from the ground-truth path (top; about 45◦ rotation versus about 225◦ in the ground truth). Our adaptive keyframe selection inserts intermediate keyframes, generates shorter segments conditioned on their boundary keyframes, and stitches them together. This produces geometry-distorted videos that remain close to the target camera trajectory and are therefore suitable as paired training data (middle), compared with the ground-truth supervision video (bottom).

Figure 7: General video refinement results. VGC corrects several geometric failures produced by the baseline models. In scene 1, HunyuanVideo [3] changes the cabinet into a glass door, while VGC restores the correct scene structure and camera motion, placing the door on the right side of the cabinet. In scene 2, HunyuanVideo generates a camera trajectory that passes through the wrong side of the doorway, whereas VGC recovers a plausible path. In scenes 3 and 4, VGC restores a consistent appearance and recovers fine geometric structure, such as the wooden supports. In the dynamic scenes, VGC better preserves identity and motion continuity: in scene 5, it maintains the same man in the leather jacket across frames and recovers a plausible motion trajectory, whereas the Wan baseline fails to infer coherent human motion; in scene 6, it restores the missing cyclist produced by CogVideoX [2]. The green boxes further show that VGC enhances local detail while remaining more faithful to the source video than SeedVR2 [20] and VEnhancer [15]. Please zoom in for details.

Figure 5: Visual results on DL3DV [24]. The first two rows show image-to-video results. In the baseline CogVideoX [2] outputs, the streetlight is duplicated, while VideoGPA [16] produces a distorted and tilted streetlight (red boxes). VGC corrects these geometric errors and restores a more plausible structure. The last row shows a text-to-video example, where VGC better preserves the original appearance of the sculpture, while VideoGPA changes its structure and other scene details.

Figure 6: Comparison of model sizes. In static scenes (top), both VGC 1.3B and 14B correct geometric distortions produced by the baseline model that SeedVR2 [20] and VEnhancer [15] fail to restore (red boxes). The 14B model further improves the geometry of moving humans and objects in dynamic scenes (bottom).

Figure 4: Visual results on RealEstate10K [27]. DFoT [28] and GF + REPA [10, 29] produce inconsistent lighting across frames, while GF [10] generates an incomplete sofa structure (red box). VGC restores more consistent lighting and more coherent scene geometry.

Table 3: General video refinement results on SpatialVID [25]. We compare VGC with general video refinement and enhancement methods [20, 15] on dynamic videos generated by CogVideoX [2], HunyuanVideo [3], and Wan [4]. Although VGC is designed for geometry correction under camera motion rather than generic enhancement, it achieves competitive performance across multiple perceptual and temporal metrics, and is particularly strong in dynamic degree, imaging quality, and DOVER [32]. These results suggest that the proposed correction framework extends beyond static-scene geometry and remains effective in more general settings.

Table 2: Quantitative results on DL3DV [24]. We evaluate VGC on three CogVideoX [2] source generators in both text-to-video and image-to-video settings. VGC consistently improves PSNR, SSIM, and MSE over the corresponding baselines, and further improves VideoGPA [16] when applied as a post-hoc corrector. These results show that VGC transfers across different generation settings and can be flexibly combined with other geometry-aware refinement methods.

Table 1: Quantitative results on RealEstate10K [27]. VGC achieves the strongest PSNR, SSIM, and revisit error (RVE) among the direct baselines. When applied as a post-hoc corrector to Geometry Forcing (GF) [10] and GF + REPA [10, 29], it further improves their performance, showing that it can be flexibly combined with geometry-aware generators. Comparing VGC with and without optical flow shows that flow yields modest gains in image quality while maintaining similar longrange geometric consistency.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a post-hoc video-to-video model to correct geometric consistency in generated videos, relevant to video generation and refinement.
papers.title: Learning to Correct Geometry in Generated Videos
papers.tldr: VGC post-processes generated videos to correct geometry and improve consistency under camera motion using synthetic paired supervision and optical-flow cues.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space diffusion models have recently re-emerged as a compelling alternative to latent diffusion, avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder. JiT shows that a vanilla diffusion transformer can generate directly in pixel space by replacing the commonly used velocity prediction ($\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction) with clean image prediction ($\boldsymbol{x_0}$-prediction). In this work, we revisit this choice and introduce MFlow, an adaptive parameterization that learns to interpolate between $\boldsymbol{x_0}$- and $\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction across principal directions of the data, learned end-to-end with diffusion training. We find that the preferred parameterization varies systematically with the data representation and model capacity -- notably, increasing model capacity shifts preference toward velocity prediction. We evaluate MFlow across ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation, demonstrating competitive or improved generative performance across diverse settings. In addition, we find that vanilla pixel diffusion transformers, irrespective of parameterization, retain a persistent high-frequency deficit relative to real images. To address this, we introduce ConvRefiner, a lightweight convolutional module trained post-hoc with an adversarial loss while keeping the diffusion backbone frozen. With only a small amount of additional training, ConvRefiner restores the high-frequency statistics of generated images while preserving FID. Project webpage: https://soumik-kanad.github.io/mflow-diffusion/.
authors: Soumik Mukhopadhyay, Long Mai, Abhinav Shrivastava, Aniruddha Mahapatra
bullets: Pixel diffusion avoids the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder, but its prediction parameterization strongly affects performance.
MFlow learns the preferred interpolation between x₀- and u-prediction across data principal directions during diffusion training.
The preferred parameterization depends on data representation and model capacity; larger models favor velocity prediction more strongly.
Experiments on ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation show competitive or improved generative performance across settings.
Pixel diffusion transformers exhibit a persistent high-frequency deficit; post-hoc ConvRefiner addresses it with lightweight adversarial training while freezing the backbone and preserving FID.

We reshape the first 64 eigenvectors of the 16 × 16 × 3 patch-PCA basis into RGB patches; the value λ denotes the variance of each direction. The leading ordering interleaves patch-global or very low-frequency modes with spatially varying modes. In particular, PC0 is dominated by low-frequency patch-level tone, PC1 is an approximately uniform chromatic mode, PC2–PC3 encode spatial gradients, and PC4 returns to an approximately uniform chromatic mode. Eigenvector signs are arbitrary, so the interpretation is based on spatial structure rather than the displayed color polarity.

papers.abstract: Central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSIs) remain a major source of preventable morbidity and mortality in healthcare settings. Proper execution of the central line dressing change (CLDC) procedure is essential for infection prevention, yet current approaches to competency assessment rely primarily on manual ob- servation by clinical educators, making evaluation time-intensive, difficult to scale, and limited in consistency and granularity. These challenges highlight the need for AI-assisted skill evaluation methods that can support more objective, reproducible, and scalable assessment of clinical performance. However, progress in this area has been constrained by the lack of broad-scale, clinically grounded datasets for developing and evaluating such methods. In this work, we present the collection process of a large-scale video dataset for CLDC skill evaluation, comprising 365 recordings of registered nurses collected during the 2026 annual competency exam at Houston Methodist Hospital. Each video is paired with subtask-level temporal annotations and clinical performance assessments spanning 17 subtasks of the procedure. We describe the data collection and curation pipeline, including pilot testing of record- ing configurations, annotation protocol design, and post-collection processing. We further establish the feasibility of video-based skill assessment through benchmark experiments with spatiotemporal deep learning models. This dataset provides a foundation for future research on automated clinical skill assessment, feedback generation, and AI-assisted training in nursing education.
authors: Ummey Tanin (Pam), Shannan K. Hamlin (Pam), Hsin-Mei Chen (Pam), Peizhu (Pam), Qian

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models (VDMs) trained on internet-scale data encode a rich prior on appearance, motion, and physics that is difficult to replicate with explicit 3D rendering and costly 3D data capture. We introduce Video Diffusion Avatars (VDAs), a method that creates photo-realistic, multi-view consistent avatars from a single image by fine-tuning a VDM for precise control over camera viewpoint, facial expression, and upper-body pose. Departing from 3D morphable models (3DMMs), VDAs use a learned expression space that lifts the expressiveness ceiling of 3DMMs, e.g., for the tongue and mouth interior. However, learned expression codes exhibit heavy viewpoint bias, as our DISTRACT benchmark reveals. We show that this bias can be removed through disentanglement, enabling their use as driving signals for multi-view consistent avatars. Camera and upper-body pose are controlled jointly via proxy-mesh renderings, giving independent control over expression, pose, and viewpoint. A camera-triplet training strategy makes the approach efficient: our models train for 34 hours on a single A100 using only public multi-view data. VDAs outperform state-of-the-art single-image 3D avatars on novel-view reenactment, reducing face LPIPS by 29% and improving perceptual quality (JOD) by 66% on BecomingLit. A static 3DGS reconstruction probe further confirms that our generations are the most multi-view consistent. Built on a video prior, VDAs produce effects beyond the reach of explicit renderers, including physically plausible hair dynamics, shadows, reflections, and refractions.
authors: Simon Giebenhain, Tobias Kirschstein, Liam Schoneveld, Davide Davoli, Zhe Chen, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of reproducing video diffusion models’ rich appearance, motion, and physics priors with explicit 3D methods.
Fine-tunes a video diffusion model using disentangled learned expression codes and proxy-mesh renderings for independent control.
Uses a camera-triplet training strategy and public multi-view data to improve efficiency.
Outperforms prior single-image 3D avatars on novel-view reenactment, with lower face LPIPS and higher perceptual quality on BecomingLit.
Produces effects difficult for explicit renderers, including plausible hair dynamics, shadows, reflections, and refractions.
