papers.abstract: Audio-driven lip synchronization aims to match target speech through localized mouth and jaw articulation while preserving subject identity, head pose, and surrounding facial context. Naturally recorded videos provide synchronized reconstruction targets but rarely offer pairs that are matched in identity and pose yet differ primarily in speech-related articulation. Mask-based training enables reconstruction from these videos, but random-reference inputs differ from the aligned self-reference used at inference. We present LiveSync, an iterative self-training framework in which a single mask-based model generates pseudo pairs and is refined for deployment. The model is first trained on a curated real-video corpus augmented with externally generated clips covering under-represented visual conditions. A frozen checkpoint then uses independently sampled audio to generate mouth-edited references from real-video frames, copying pixels outside the edit mask from each source frame. After confidence filtering, these references are paired with aligned masked inputs and original real-frame targets. The retained pseudo pairs are mixed with real training data to refine the same model from its current weights, updating training supervision without adding inference stages. Although we instantiate the framework with a single-pass GAN-based model, the self-training strategy could in principle also be adapted to diffusion-based models. Experimental results show that LiveSync achieves leading synchronization performance on HDTF and competitive performance compared with the baselines on the AIGC-LipSync subset, while maintaining low inference latency.
authors: Huaishao Luo, Huan Zhang, Guanbo Bao, Yinglu Liu, Youzheng Wu, Xiaodong He
bullets: Addresses the lack of real training pairs matched in identity and pose but differing in speech articulation, and the mismatch between random-reference training and aligned self-reference inference.

First trains on curated real videos augmented with externally generated clips, then uses a frozen checkpoint to create mouth-edited pseudo references from real frames with independently sampled audio.
Confidence-filtered pseudo pairs are combined with real data to refine the same model without adding inference stages.
Achieves leading synchronization performance on HDTF and competitive performance on the AIGC-LipSync subset while maintaining low inference latency.
Demonstrated with a single-pass GAN-based model; adaptation to diffusion models is suggested but not evaluated here.

papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of pedestrian crossing intentions plays a critical role in enhancing the safety of pedestrian-vehicle interactions in autonomous driving. However, effectively capturing subtle spatiotemporal patterns in pedestrian pose sequences and integrating complementary visual and ego-vehicle motion information remain challenging. This paper proposes a spatial-temporal-channel attention-enhanced multimodal graph network (STC-MGNet) for pedestrian crossing intention prediction. STC-MGNet introduces a spatial-temporal-channel (STC) attention-enhanced pose graph encoder to learn discriminative representations from pedestrian pose sequences. Three parallel attention branches selectively emphasize informative skeletal joints, observation frames, and feature channels, with their outputs integrated through learnable fusion weights. To leverage complementary visual and ego-vehicle motion information, a multi-stage cross-modal channel modulation mechanism is introduced to adaptively refine pose representations through modality-specific channel gating at successive graph encoding stages. Experimental results demonstrate that STC-MGNet achieves accuracy rates of 70%, 87%, and 88% on the JAADbeh, JAADall, and PIE datasets, respectively, outperforming several representative baseline methods. Ablation experiments further highlight the complementary contributions of visual and ego-vehicle motion information to prediction performance.
bullets: Targets safer pedestrian–vehicle interaction by modeling subtle spatiotemporal cues in pedestrian pose sequences.
Uses parallel spatial, temporal, and channel attention to emphasize informative joints, frames, and feature channels.
Applies multi-stage cross-modal channel modulation to refine pose features using visual and ego-vehicle motion cues.
Reports accuracies of 70%, 87%, and 88% on JAADbeh, JAADall, and PIE, respectively.
Ablations indicate that visual and ego-vehicle motion information make complementary contributions.

papers.abstract: Recent diffusion models have advanced image-conditioned video generation, but their accessibility raises risks of unauthorized manipulation. Image immunization has emerged as a promising defense for Image-to-Video (I2V) protection, yet existing methods often rely on degrading visual quality or temporal coherence. In this work, we revisit I2V immunization as reducing source-content preservation, shifting the focus from output degradation to weakening source-conditioned content propagation. To this end, we propose I2V-DETACH, an image immunization method that prevents unauthorized I2V generation through source grounding detachment. I2V models preserve source content by propagating source-image cues into video latents during denoising. Accordingly, I2V-DETACH disrupts this process in two complementary ways: it suppresses source-video grounding to reduce source cue propagation, and strengthens intra-video interactions to shift denoising toward video-side dynamics with reduced reliance on the source image. To obtain informative optimization signals, we initialize auxiliary video latents with source-oriented states that remain within the source-conditioned generation regime while deviating from source-preserving trajectories. Extensive experiments across diverse diffusion architectures show that I2V-DETACH substantially reduces source-content preservation, improves over prior immunization methods, and exhibits strong black-box transferability.
authors: Chanhui Lee, Yeonghwan Song, Yewon Kang, Jeany Son
bullets: Targets source-content preservation, avoiding reliance on visual-quality or temporal-coherence degradation.
Suppresses source–video grounding to weaken propagation of image cues into video latents.
Strengthens intra-video interactions so denoising relies more on video dynamics than the source image.
Uses source-oriented auxiliary video latents to generate informative optimization signals.
Experiments across diverse diffusion architectures show reduced source preservation, improvement over prior immunization methods, and strong black-box transferability.

papers.abstract: This paper presents the overview of the runs related to the Ad-hoc Video Search (AVS) and Video Question Answering (VQA) tracks of TRECVID 2025 on behalf of the CERTH-ITI team. For the AVS track, we introduce a two-stage framework built on foundation models. In the first stage, multiple vision-language models (VLMs) encode both the input query, augmented through LLM-generated rephrasings, and the candidate video shots, producing weighted similarity scores for initial retrieval. In the second stage, we utilize a Multimodal-LLM(MLLM)-based reranking module that evaluates the semantic alignment between each shot among the top-N highest-ranked ones and the original query, generating updated relevance scores for reordering these shots. This MLLM-driven reranking significantly improves contextual matching and produces more accurate final rankings without requiring any model training. Regarding the VQA track, we fine-tune an audio-visual MLLM model on the provided TRECVID training dataset and we implement an inference-time scaling technique to enhance the multimodal understanding capabilities of the MLLM. For the open-ended Answer Generation (AG) task, we aggregate multiple model responses per question via a majority vote. The responses are generated with greedy sampling from different random frame subsets of the video and they are ranked based on the number of votes. For the Multiple-Choice (MC) task, instead of voting, we use mean pooling on the logits assigned by the fine-tuned model to each candidate response. Through the combination of fine-tuning and frame subset ensembling we achieve the highest score across 3 metrics in the VQA AG task and the second highest in the VQA MC task.

The approach achieves the highest score on three VQA answer-generation metrics and the second-highest score on the multiple-choice task.

papers.abstract: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.

bullets: Addresses fixed-shape compilation constraints across varying pipelines, prompt lengths, and denoising-time caching decisions.

Fused attention is 1.2–4.3× faster than PyTorch/XLA attention and is the only attention variant compiling at 32.8k visual tokens.
Resident serving is 1.5–3.4× faster than reloading weights for each generation on four of five models.

papers.abstract: In real-world videos, sound events are often associated with localized and fine-grained visual cues, such as object motion, object-part dynamics, contact events, and interactions between objects. Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods employ implicit conditioning based on global visual representations or explicit control derived from temporal and spatial cues. However, subtle sound-producing and sound-indicative interactions remain insufficiently captured, leaving room for more precise visual conditioning of sound-event semantics and temporal dynamics. Motivated by this observation, we refer to regions containing such sound-relevant visual evidence as Semantic-Critical Regions (SCRs) and introduce SCR-V2A, a V2A generation framework that explicitly localizes and encodes SCRs as fine-grained visual guidance for audio generation. Specifically, we first identify SCRs through sound-related visual localization. We then transform the localized regions into a control representation through adapter-based dual visual encoding, which jointly captures global visual context and fine-grained sound-relevant evidence. The representation is used to condition a downstream audio generation model. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that SCR-V2A achieves strong performance in distribution matching and audio quality while remaining competitive in cross-modal alignment and requiring few trainable parameters. These results highlight the value of prioritizing fine-grained, sound-relevant visual regions for V2A generation.

bullets: Targets subtle cues such as object motion, contact events, object-part dynamics, and inter-object interactions that global video representations may miss.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become a common backbone for high-quality text-to-image and text-to-video generation, but repeated dense self-attention remains a major inference bottleneck as token sequences grow and the same operator is invoked across many denoising steps. Our study suggests that dense attention in pretrained DiTs contains reusable layer/head-specific high-mass structure that can be identified from a small offline calibration set and reused across future generations. This leads to Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention, a train-free attention replacement that reuses static sink masks and supplements them with a lightweight pooled-KV branch, while leaving model weights and sampling schedules unchanged. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, the method attains 1.54$\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining generation quality. On Z-Image-Turbo, it attains 1.57$\times$ end-to-end speedup with competitive GenEval2 performance. These results indicate that reusable importance-aware sparse support can provide an effective train-free acceleration path for both T2V and T2I DiTs.
authors: Bingxin Xing, Yu Zhang, Jiatong Ding, Lei Lu, Ping Wang
bullets: Targets the inference cost of repeated dense self-attention in DiTs with long token sequences and many denoising steps.
Uses small offline calibration to identify reusable, layer/head-specific high-mass attention structure.
Combines static sink masks with a lightweight pooled-KV branch as a train-free attention replacement.
Achieves 1.54× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B while maintaining generation quality.
Achieves 1.57× end-to-end speedup on Z-Image-Turbo with competitive GenEval2 performance; scope covers T2V and T2I DiTs.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform well on audio-visual question answering, but correct answers do not necessarily imply that their stated reasoning is grounded in relevant perceptual evidence. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate final-answer accuracy, offering limited insight into whether model-generated rationales correctly identify visual regions, temporal intervals, and audio events supporting predictions. We introduce ANCHOR, a benchmark and evaluation framework for measuring grounded-rationale alignment in multimodal reasoning, comprising 2,319 videos and 8,272 question-answer pairs with structured reasoning traces, temporal evidence, spatial bounding boxes, and salient audio cues, including a human-refined test set of 224 videos and 975 question-answer pairs. We separately measure answer correctness, hallucination, logical divergence, and conciseness, with direct spatial and temporal grounding measurements on a focused subset. Across the full benchmark, twelve contemporary MLLMs show a substantial alignment gap: models with comparable answer performance can differ markedly in whether their explanations are supported by annotated evidence. On a matched subset of 100 videos and 446 question-answer pairs, rankings remain highly stable across human-refined, Gemini-generated, and GPT-generated references (mean Pearson r=0.99), providing evidence against model-reference circularity within this subset. Grounding-cue ablations of three MLLMs on the full human-refined test set reveal a consistent modality hierarchy: removing video reduces accuracy by 38.4-41.8 points, while removing bounding boxes (3.2-7.7 points) and audio (4.2-5.6 points) causes smaller, complementary, model-dependent drops. These findings show answer-only evaluation obscures important grounding failures and position ANCHOR as a testbed for evaluating accurate and evidence-aligned audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Joel Julin, Souraja Kundu, Liza Dahiya, George Z. Wei, Liuyue Xie, Jingru Yi, Xu Zhang, Hao Yang, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Introduces a benchmark with 2,319 videos and 8,272 question-answer pairs, including structured reasoning traces and annotated evidence.
Measures answer correctness, hallucination, logical divergence, conciseness, and direct spatial-temporal grounding.
Finds a substantial alignment gap: models with similar answer accuracy can differ greatly in evidence-supported explanations.
Reference rankings are highly stable across human- and model-generated rationales on a matched subset (mean Pearson r=0.99).
Ablations show video removal causes the largest accuracy drop, while bounding boxes and audio provide smaller, complementary benefits.

papers.abstract: Large-scale diffusion models are commonly trained with a constant learning rate (LR) and exponential moving average (EMA), despite the strong performance of LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization in training large language models. We study whether EMA is uniquely suited to diffusion training, or whether stronger alternatives have been underexplored. Our theory shows that averaging a constant-step trajectory has an inherent optimization limitation, whereas LR decay and Schedule-Free optimization admit vanishing stationarity guarantees under standard nonconvex assumptions. Empirically, LR decay and EMA provide complementary benefits: combining decay with EMA further improves the standard baseline at most tested starting points, although the gain remains sensitive to when decay begins. Schedule-Free avoids this timing requirement and consistently outperforms EMA with a constant LR across training stages, achieving both lower fixed-evaluation objectives and better generation quality. Our analysis further shows that all three strategies substantially reduce parameter variability, yet stronger stabilization is not always better: EMA with a constant LR retains comparatively higher parameter variability, while aggressive decay combined with EMA achieves the lowest checkpoint variability but also weakens continued optimization. Schedule-Free substantially reduces parameter variability while preserving more late-stage progress, providing a better balance between parameter stability and continued optimization. Finally, the benefits of Schedule-Free extend beyond pretraining to ReFL and generator-side DMD, demonstrating its transferability across distinct diffusion optimization settings. Overall, our results suggest that large diffusion models need more than parameter averaging alone: effective optimization requires balancing variance reduction with continued optimization.
authors: Chuyu Hu, Huanran Chen, Shitong Shao, Yinpeng Dong
bullets: Constant-step EMA has theoretical optimization limits, while learning-rate decay and Schedule-Free optimization support vanishing stationarity guarantees under standard nonconvex assumptions.
Learning-rate decay and EMA are complementary, but decay’s benefit depends sensitively on when it begins.
Schedule-Free consistently outperforms constant-LR EMA across training stages in both fixed-evaluation objectives and generation quality, without requiring decay timing.
Aggressive decay with EMA minimizes checkpoint variability but can hinder continued optimization; Schedule-Free reduces variability while preserving late-stage progress.
Schedule-Free also transfers to ReFL and generator-side DMD, suggesting applicability beyond diffusion pretraining.

papers.abstract: Physical reasoning about humans in videos has largely focused on everyday interactions, where contact, pressure, pose, and motion support embodied perception and contact-aware applications. Still, short and forceful properties like impact events remain relatively underexplored, despite their relevance to broader understanding of how abrupt physical events affect the human body. To fill this gap, we introduce human-centric impact localization, a new task that localizes target physical impacts temporally within a video and spatially on the human body. We further present HAPACT, a HumAn-centric imPACT dataset and benchmark built from movie clips, containing over 2.8K video-query pairs with more than 20K fine-grained human-annotated frames. We built HAPACT around viewer-grounded annotation, text-conditioned localization, and supervision at frame-level temporal and SMPL-X-based spatial granularity. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our benchmark, we conduct extensive evaluations of existing methods, employing video moment retrieval models for temporal localization and human-scene contact models for spatial localization. For the spatial task, we propose a text-conditioned baseline by reformulating localization as query-guided body-region selection. Benchmark results show that physical impact localization remains challenging for existing methods, motivating HAPACT as a dedicated benchmark to support physical impact reasoning in videos.
authors: Youngrae Kim, Yejin Jang, Eunho Kim, Youjin Sung, Kun-Woo Song, Sangpil Kim, Sang Ho Yoon
bullets: Defines human-centric impact localization as joint temporal and spatial localization of abrupt physical impacts.
Provides over 2.8K video-query pairs and more than 20K fine-grained, human-annotated frames from movie clips.
Uses viewer-grounded, text-conditioned annotations with frame-level timing and SMPL-X-based body-region supervision.
Evaluates video moment retrieval and human-scene contact models, and introduces a text-conditioned body-region selection baseline.
Results indicate that existing methods face substantial challenges in physical impact reasoning.

papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard component of conditional diffusion models, and guided generation performance has become the \textit{de facto} measure of state-of-the-art models. Recent work on latent diffusion models seeks to learn latent spaces that are easier to model with diffusion. However, under CFG, generation additionally depends on how conditions are arranged in the latent space. We study this arrangement under discrete class conditions, termed \emph{class geometry}, and investigate what class geometry allows a latent space to work well with CFG. Under a Gaussian class model, we show that shifting variance from intra- to inter-class at fixed total variance makes classes more distinguishable under noise, and derive a noisy posterior objective whose per-sample descent direction is proportional to the oracle CFG correction. Based on the analysis, we propose Prototype Regularization (PR), a lightweight surrogate for the intractable noisy posterior objective, which applies a cosine prototype classifier to spatially pooled latents. With a controlled training budget (20 epochs for VAE, 80 epochs for DiT), adding PR to an LDM baseline reduces guided gFID on ImageNet from 3.31 to 2.28, surpassing a DINOv3-aligned VA-VAE (2.44) with negligible overhead. We further demonstrate that PR generalizes to pseudo-labels derived from clustering, continuous text-embedding conditions, and video latents. Together, our findings highlight class geometry as a critical factor in guided generation and take a first step toward CFG-compatible representation learning. Our project page is available at: https://maps-research.github.io/cfg-geometry/.
authors: Haoming Liu, Junhao Zhu, Shaoyi Zheng, Yuanhe Guo, Jinnuo Liu, Shenji Wan, Hongyi Wen
bullets: Motivation: CFG performance depends not only on diffusion modeling but also on how conditions are arranged in latent space.
Analysis: Under a Gaussian class model, increasing inter-class variance relative to intra-class variance improves class distinguishability under noise.
Method: Prototype Regularization (PR) approximates a noisy-posterior objective using a cosine prototype classifier over spatially pooled latents.
Result: Adding PR reduces ImageNet guided gFID from 3.31 to 2.28 with negligible overhead under the stated training budget.
Scope: PR also works with clustering-based pseudo-labels, continuous text embeddings, and video latents.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Noisy marginals of zt at several t ∈ (0, 1) for toy Gaussian mixtures with fixed total variance but different allocations between inter-class and intra-class variance. Background colors mark the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) decision regions argmaxc qc(zt), with opacity proportional to the confidence maxc qc(zt). With larger inter-class variance, classes become separable at smaller t, i.e., at noisier levels, and the confident MAP regions align more closely with the true class supports.

Figure 5: Oracle velocity fields on toy Gaussian mixtures with fixed total variance. From top to bottom, the fraction of variance allocated to class means increases. For each space, we show the conditional velocity v⋆c (conditioned on the red class), the unconditional velocity v⋆u, and the correction g⋆c = v⋆c − v⋆u at t ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.8}. Gray contours mark the 95% density region of zt, and dots mark the class means of zt. With clearer class geometry, the conditional and correction velocities point more consistently toward the target class mean, and the correction vanishes where the posterior concentrates on the target class. Zoom in for the best view. Better view with colors.

Figure 2: (a) Energy decomposition of per-channel normalized latents into global mean ∥µ∥2, interclass variance Ec∥µc−µ∥2, and intra-class variance E∥z−µc∥2. (b) Average target-class posterior E[qc(zt)] on noised validation latents (solid) and CFG sampling trajectories (dotted), where qc(zt) is computed analytically from the empirical distribution of ImageNet training latents under Gaussian forward corruption. (c) gFID (10K samples) versus guidance scale ω; diamonds mark the minima of the displayed curves (ω⋆). PR allocates more energy to inter-class variance, makes the target class identifiable earlier and more confidently, and reaches a lower best gFID at a larger ω⋆.

Figure 1: Simulations under the Gaussian class model with K = 1000 classes and latent dimensions d = 8192 (Eq. 4). (a) Oracle CFG correction strength along time t (t = 1 is clean), for varying inter-class variance fraction α. The correction vanishes once the target-class posterior concentrates. (b) Monte Carlo average of the analytic target-class posterior under forward corruption. Larger α yields earlier posterior concentration. (c) Posterior losses (normalized by logK) versus α, on cleanonly and uniform-time corrupted latents. Both posterior losses are non-increasing in α.

Figure 3: UMAP visualization of full and spatially pooled latents from LDM, VA-VAE, and PR (ours). We encode 50K validation images and plot latents from 50 selected classes, colored by class label. Latents are normalized per dimension before UMAP. PR produces noticeably tighter and better separated class clusters. Zoom in for the best view. Better view with colors.

All alignment to CLIP-L adopts its text embeddings. CLIP denotes mean cosine similarity of CLIP embeddings calculated from text captions and generated images. All cluster labels use K = 1000. The best results are in bold.

Table 2: Center transplantation on LDM latents (z′ = z − µLDM c + µRef c ). Rescaled LDM centers match the inter-class energy of full PR centers. Random centers match the pooled PR energy. Spatially constant centers are broadcast over the spatial grid. ω⋆ denotes the best CFG scale.
Table 3: PR with different label set pairings for stage-1 regularization and stage-2 conditioning. We report guided gFID / unguided gFID below. The best result per-column is in bold.

Table 8: Ablation on prototype shape (reduced compute budget). All variants use the default PR setting (cosine prototype classifier on clean-only latents) and differ only in the output shape of spatial average pooling applied before the classifier, where 16×16 corresponds to no pooling. Overall, prototypes with lower resolutions perform best: 1×1 prototypes (i.e., global average pooling) achieve the best rFID and gFID without CFG, and 2×2 prototypes achieve the best gFID with CFG, while further increasing prototype resolution consistently degrades generation quality. This suggests that reducing the spatial resolution of prototypes benefits generation, likely because it avoids imposing class-level layout constraints on the latent space.

Table 10: Ablation on DINO pseudo-label granularity (reduced compute budget). This group of experiments uses a separate hyper-parameter setup, so the results are comparable within this table but not with other tables. Reconstruction is largely insensitive to the choice of targets. Unguided gFID degrades as K increases, while guided gFID remains comparable across K except for overly fine clusters. The nested variant (i.e., partitioning each of the 64 clusters into 16 sub-clusters) achieves the best generation among unsupervised targets (best unguided gFID and guided gFID close to GT labels), showing the feasibility of hierarchical PR.

Table 9: Ablation on the temperature of PR (reduced compute budget). τ scales the cosinesimilarity logits of the prototype classifier, where a smaller τ yields a sharper softmax. The default τ = 0.1 was fixed prior to this ablation and is used throughout the main text. All PR variants improve over LDM both with and without CFG, and the differences among τ values are small compared with the gain from adding PR, indicating that τ = 0.1 is a reasonable default. Adjusting τ (e.g., τ = 0.3 here) may bring further improvements, though the best value is likely setting-dependent.

Table 11: Composability of PR and VA-VAE. This group of experiments uses the same separate hyper-parameter setup as Tab. 10, so the results are comparable with that table but not with the others. We apply PR on top of VA-VAE, which aligns to DINOv3-L features. Combining the two yields better generation both with and without CFG, at the cost of mildly degraded reconstruction, indicating that PR is complementary to external feature alignment for generation.

Table 4: Generalization to video latents on UCF-101 (Soomro et al., 2012) using LeanVAE16 (Cheng & Yuan, 2025) and Latte-XL/2 (Ma et al., 2025). Official denotes the VAE and LatteXL/2 checkpoints provided by LeanVAE, used without further training. We report FVD and action classification accuracy with and without CFG. The best results are in bold.

Table 1: Results of class-conditional generation on ImageNet. All quality metrics are evaluated with 50K samples. Purity measures the fraction of each latent’s k = 10 nearest neighbors that share its class, averaged over 50K normalized validation latents. Best results are highlighted in bold.

Table 7: Ablation on the classifier type in PR (reduced compute budget). We vary the classifier head (cosine vs. linear) and the latent on which PR is applied (clean latents only vs. noisy latents at uniformly sampled timesteps). The cosine head on clean-only latents achieves the best rFID and gFID, both with and without CFG. Applying PR on uniform-time noisy latents over-regularizes the latent space: the top PCA component degenerates into a near-constant channel that fails to capture spatial variations (i.e., over-smoothed latents). The linear head, optimized with additional weight decay, collapses to a trivial solution that arbitrarily inflates the latent norm to enlarge the logits.

papers.selection_reason: Studies latent geometry for classifier-free guidance in diffusion models and demonstrates extension to video latents, directly relevant to video diffusion.
papers.title: Learning to Be Guided: Shaping Latent Geometry for Classifier-Free Guidance
papers.tldr: The paper shows that shaping latent class geometry improves classifier-free guidance (CFG) and proposes a lightweight prototype regularizer to make representations more CFG-compatible.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained alignment between text and video object trajectories is a core challenge in multimodal understanding. Existing embedding models excel at global retrieval, yet their single global representation entangles multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics, limiting direct object-level grounding. To address this issue, we propose VTrajEmbed, an embedding model that decomposes a video into object trajectories and aligns each trajectory embedding with text for object-level grounding through retrieval. Our main contributions: (1)Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding, a dual-branch architecture that establishes trajectory representations by densely sampling low-resolution frames for high-frequency motion cues and sparsely selecting high-resolution frames for scene context, aggregated by a shared LLM backbone; (2)Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning, a training objective built upon these representations that couples an intra-group loss and a batch-level bidirectional loss under a relation mask, excluding unverified relations and preventing confirmed matches from becoming false negatives; (3)Text2Traj-Bench, a trajectory-level text-video benchmark with model-assisted construction and human-verified query--trajectory relations. Experimental results show that VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively, and achieves 49.48% average R@1 across five global retrieval benchmarks, compared with 42.86% for Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B.
authors: Ruizhi Chen, Zining Fan, Yudi Guo, Jiang Liu, Zhiyu Lin, Zhongjiang He, Shouqian Shi, Hao Sun
bullets: Addresses global embeddings’ tendency to entangle multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics.
Uses Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding to combine dense low-resolution motion cues with sparse high-resolution scene context.
Introduces Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning with relation masking to handle verified matches and unknown relationships.
Provides Text2Traj-Bench, a human-verified trajectory-level text–video benchmark.
VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of VTrajEmbed. (a) Model architecture. The Slow-Fast trajectory encoder combines dense low-resolution object observations with sparse high-resolution scene context and maps trajectories and text into a shared embedding space for similarity-based retrieval. (b) Training objective. Mask-guided contrastive learning jointly optimizes within-video trajectory discrimination and bidirectional trajectory-text retrieval using verified query-trajectory relations while excluding uncertain pairs. (c) Data. Text2Traj-Bench uses trajectory curation, verified description, and relation construction to produce fixed per-video candidate pools and human-verified annotations, including descriptions and within- and cross-video query-trajectory relations.

papers.abstract: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
authors: Lieqi Liu, Rui gao, Jia-Chen Gu, Wenbo Hu, Zhaobin Mo, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar, Wei Wang, Nanyun Peng
bullets: Targets long-tail, safety-critical scenarios that existing perception and simple temporal benchmarks underrepresent.
Covers six task families, including spatial reasoning, temporal memory and extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness.
Combines multiple-choice judgments with free-form VQA requiring scene explanations and driving-decision justifications.
Across 12 models, the best reported average multiple-choice accuracy is 43.4%, compared with an approximately 20% random-choice baseline.
Finds that descriptive scene understanding does not guarantee accurate safety judgments, with motion reconstruction especially challenging.

papers.abstract: Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce $R^2$-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.
authors: Xiaoyan Cong, Tianyu Wang, Hyeonho Jeong, Zhifei Zhang, Yuqian Zhou, Yijun Li, Shaoteng Liu, Zhe Lin, Srinath Sridhar, Soo Ye Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of controlling video edits with variable combinations and numbers of multimodal references.
Uses a reference-bank interface, R²-RoPE for reference scalability, and a single-stream diffusion transformer with MLLM-derived context.
Builds synthetic OmniXRef-Data and applies curriculum learning to handle limited video-reference editing data and increasing task complexity.
Introduces OmniXRef-Bench for evaluating video-reference attribute transfer across camera, motion, content, style, and VFX.
Reports better performance than task-specific baselines and commercial models in comprehensive evaluations.

papers.abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.
authors: Faizan Siddiqui, Nirav Savaliya, Sahith Reddy Chada, Enna Sachdeva
bullets: Addresses the lack of stable spatial context in video MLLMs that primarily organize observations over time.
Back-projects visual patch features using depth and camera pose into shared BEV coordinates, averaging features within spatial cells.
Compresses 128 frames and roughly 100K patch features into 729 BEV tokens without architectural changes beyond tokenization.
Reduces LLM prefill time by 2.9× and peak memory by 3.6×.
Outperforms the matched frame-token control on VSI-Bench and ReVSI, with especially strong VSI-Bench gains in room-size and relative-direction reasoning.

The BEV projection (green) is introduced only in the final fine-tuning stage (stage 5, Tab. S3); the encoder, projector, and LLM are inherited from the unmodified four-stage Cambrian-S recipe, which trains on frame tokens.

Top: A conventional video MLLM represents each frame independently, producing repeated evidence for regions observed from multiple viewpoints. Repeated observations of the same spatial region are fused into common BEV cells, replacing approximately 9K frame tokens with 729 spatially indexed tokens at the LLM interface.

papers.title: Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens

papers.abstract: Answering complex spatial reasoning questions from egocentric video requires determining what evidence is needed, acquiring targeted observations, and combining them through multiple reasoning steps. Existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to perform this process reliably. Agentic systems address this challenge by querying external vision and geometry tools, but training their reasoning leaves these tools unchanged, so inaccurate observations can still lead to incorrect answers. We introduce EgoP$^{2}$C, a framework that internalizes a plan-perceive-compose process within a single VLM. To this end, we first train specialized Planner and Perception teachers using separate adapters (Dual-LoRA), then fine-tune the corresponding experts in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) student under their supervision. We subsequently train the student on trajectories generated by its current policy using a segment-level extension of multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), assigning different trajectory segments to different supervisors. The Planner teacher supervises which evidence-seeking questions to ask, when to stop gathering evidence, and how to compose the final answer. The Perception teacher supervises the video-grounded answers to those questions. At inference, the student executes this adaptive workflow end-to-end, without external spatial tools. Across three spatial reasoning benchmarks, EgoP$^{2}$C students built from Qwen3-VL-8B and SenseNova-SI-1.3-8B outperform their base models by an average of 9.2 and 7.5 percentage points, respectively. Across both backbones, EgoP$^{2}$C reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8-66.3% and achieves $1.29$-$1.49\times$ speedups over their shared Dual-LoRA teacher.
authors: Chaoyu Li, Arka Sadhu, Yuliang Li, Hyo Jin Kim, Yuning Chai, Pooyan Fazli
bullets: Addresses unreliable multi-step spatial reasoning caused by inaccurate external tool observations.
Uses Planner and Perception teachers with Dual-LoRA to supervise a mixture-of-experts student.
Applies segment-level multi-teacher on-policy distillation to train the student on its own trajectories.
The resulting workflow adaptively asks evidence-seeking questions, stops gathering evidence, and composes final answers.
Across three benchmarks, it improves base-model accuracy by 9.2 and 7.5 points, reduces inference FLOPs by 65.8–66.3%, and achieves 1.29–1.49× speedups over the teachers.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of the segment-level MOPD pipeline. Each training iteration (i) selects a training sample, (ii) generates a rollout with the MoE student model, (iii) assigns each segment to the corresponding frozen teacher, (iv) obtains teacher log probabilities for the sampled tokens, and (v) updates the student with a reverse-KL policy gradient. The example follows the PLAN path. Orange bars indicate the probabilities of the same sampled token under the student (top) and its assigned teacher (bottom).

Figure 2 Overview of EgoP2C. The framework integrates planning, perception, and composition into a single VLM. (d) At inference, the Planner expert either answers directly using the General expert (DIRECT) or iteratively requests subquestion answers from Perception before composing the final answer (PLAN).

papers.title: EgoP$^{2}$C: Internalizing Plan-Perceive-Compose for Spatial Reasoning in Egocentric Video

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation let users create high-quality videos from natural language descriptions, yet obtaining results that match user intent remains time-consuming: individual generations are computationally expensive, and underspecified prompts force repeated cycles of generation, inspection, and revision. Existing video prompt optimization methods improve generation through automatic rewriting, but cannot supply the ideas and preferences that were not in the initial description. We propose ProactGen, a video generation framework that learns proactive clarification, eliciting user intent through questions grounded in generated video drafts. Specifically, we train a vision-language model as a questioning policy with reinforcement learning: observing the initial prompt and a video draft, it learns to ask the questions most valuable to downstream generation, rewarded by the alignment between the final generated video and a target reference. We further find that effective questioning does not require drafts of final-output quality, and exploit this property by generating drafts with fewer denoising steps, keeping the added cost of clarification low. Experiments show that ProactGen improves target alignment over direct generation by at least 1.8x the gain of the strongest baselines. Moreover, a single round of ProactGen already exceeds the alignment that the strongest baseline reaches after four refinement rounds, in 29% of its time.
authors: Zhixiao Wang, Yang Chen, Yifan Xu, Chenbin Li, Yue Chang, Kai Long, Fengming Dong, Limin Wang
bullets: Addresses underspecified prompts that otherwise require costly generate–inspect–revise cycles.
Uses a vision-language model trained with reinforcement learning to ask questions based on the initial prompt and a video draft.
Questions are optimized for their value to downstream generation, using final-video alignment to a target reference as the reward.
Low-cost drafts with fewer denoising steps keep clarification overhead small.
A single round outperforms the strongest baseline’s four-round refinement alignment in 29% of the time, and achieves at least 1.8× its alignment gain over direct generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ProactGen. The questioning policy asks scoped questions conditioned on the initial prompt and a low-cost video draft; a simulated user answers from the reference video; the answers are merged into a refined prompt from which the final video is generated at full budget. During training, the alignment between the final video and the reference is the reward for updating the questioning policy; all other components are frozen.
Figure 3: Per-sample time versus target alignment (InstanceCap, DS-DTW). The horizontal axis is linear up to 50 s and logarithmic beyond.

Figure 1: A user’s initial prompt often omits preferences the user already has in mind (here, the hand gesture, the boy’s posture, the table’s material, and the framing). (a) Automatic prompt optimization rewrites the prompt from the prompt alone, so missing preferences can only be guessed. (b) Uncertainty-based clarification asks the user, but derives its questions from the prompt text without knowing what the generator will actually produce. (c) ProactGen first observes what the generator produces for the prompt through a low-cost draft, asks the user targeted questions grounded in it, and learns what to ask from the alignment of the final video.

Figure 4: Qualitative examples. Each row shows the reference video, the initial prompt, the draft, three question–answer pairs, and the final video, with the refined prompt below and answers highlighted. In both cases the questions land where the prompt was silent and the draft decided on the user’s behalf.

Table 3: Paired differences with 95% confidence intervals for the comparisons in the main text (n = 500). DreamSim-DTW and DnS are first minus second; 3D-VAE is second minus first, so positive values in all three columns favor the first method; parentheses give refinement rounds or question turns.

papers.abstract: Manual annotation of synchronized video and EEG recordings is a bottleneck in preclinical seizure research. We present an empirical study of seizure detection and behavioral severity grading using 24,131 paired clips from 601 sessions across 20 rats in a soman-induced epilepsy model. Ten video architectures and seven single-channel EEG models are evaluated independently on binary detection and three- and five-class severity tasks. In the session-exclusive reference comparison, R(2+1)D-18 and GRU achieve detection macro-F1 scores of 0.968 and 0.974, respectively; for five-class grading, the corresponding scores are 0.657 and 0.560. Subject-exclusive evaluation reduces five-class macro-F1 to 0.475 for video and 0.404 for EEG, highlighting the difficulty of grading unseen animals. Temporal-sampling experiments demonstrate the value of multiple frames, while detection performance varies relatively little across the evaluated video architectures. A separate video-only binary-detection evaluation on RodEpil achieves a mean seizure-class F1 of 0.979 after uniform re-encoding to reduce identified class-correlated encoding cues. The study characterizes existing models for behavior-defined severity labels under the evaluated protocol, motivating further investigation of expert-assisted annotation workflows. Our code and github page is available here.
authors: Alloy Das, Shreyan Ganguly, Nyzil Massey, Hung Phi Doan, Zhanhong Jiang, Thimmasettappa Thippeswamy, Soumik Sarkar
bullets: Evaluates 10 video architectures and 7 EEG models on 24,131 synchronized clips from 601 sessions involving 20 rats.
Detection is strong under session-exclusive evaluation, with best reported macro-F1 of 0.968 for video and 0.974 for EEG.
Five-class severity grading is more difficult, reaching 0.657 for video and 0.560 for EEG in session-exclusive evaluation.
Subject-exclusive testing lowers five-class macro-F1 to 0.475 for video and 0.404 for EEG, emphasizing limited generalization to unseen rats.
Multiple-frame temporal sampling helps; detection varies little across video architectures, and a re-encoded RodEpil evaluation reports seizure-class F1 of 0.979.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Grad-CAM [48] for R(2+1)D-18. Four of eight frames are shown, with input frames above activation maps. Activations concentrate on the animal in the Stage 4 example and are more diffuse in the non-seizure example. These observations do not establish causal reliance on behavior or exclude shortcuts. Full sequences appear in App. D.2, Fig. 14. Identifying tags are blurred.

Figure 3. Binary-detection macro-F1 versus video model size under the evaluated training budget. Scores range from 0.945 to 0.974. X3D-M (4M parameters) achieves 0.969, compared with 0.971 for R(2+1)D-18 (33M). This comparison concerns detection, not equivalence across severity tasks (Tables 2 and 9).

Figure 14. A full-width, extended version of Fig. 5. This layout shows all eight sample frames from the exact same pair of clips. For each sequence, the raw video frames sit on top, with the model’s attention heatmaps (seizure-class activation) directly underneath. While this sharp contrast strongly supports the idea that the model is genuinely focusing on the animal to make its predictions, it does not act as definitive proof against hidden visual shortcuts. (All clips have been completely de-identified, and any specific cage identifying bands have been redacted.)

Figure 15. Grad-CAM heatmaps for the R(2+1)D video model across different severity stages. The network’s attention consistently locks onto the animal across the illustrated Stages 2, 3, and 5, showing similar activation patterns in these selected examples. Still, we must treat these visualizations as descriptive rather than causal they show us where the model is looking, but they do not serve as absolute proof of how it makes its final decisions. (All clips have been de-identified, and any identifying cage bands have been completely redacted.)

Figure 11. A visual breakdown of the clip counts for each animal across the entire dataset, representing the stacked totals from Table 10. The distribution of seizures is incredibly lopsided: the four most heavily affected rats (R1-R4) completely overshadow the rest of the group, with individual contributions ranging drastically from just 11 clips up to 3,091. More importantly, the most violent seizures (Stage 4 in dark shading, Stage 5 in the darkest) barely register as a thin sliver on any animal’s bar graph, yielding only 193 Stage 5 clips in the whole study. This extreme rarity is exactly why teaching models to perform detailed severity grading is such a difficult challenge.

Figure 16. Row-normalized confusion matrices comparing both modalities across all three evaluation tasks (drawn from a representative seed-42 diagnostic run; displaying true-class fractions with raw counts in parentheses). On the granular 5-class task, the video model’s mistakes cluster tightly along the diagonal, meaning its errors are almost entirely limited to adjacent severity levels. In stark contrast, the EEG baseline not only misses active seizures completely, but also frequently commits erratic, non-adjacent grading errors.

Figure 4. A paired Stage 3 seizure from rat R7. Top: Four sample video frames. Bottom: The corresponding single-channel EEG trace (∼64 s), with the active seizure period highlighted. Watching these streams side-by-side provides a complete view of both the physical symptoms and the electrical brain activity. Identifying markers have been masked.

Figure 7. Macro-F1 across task granularities for the results displayed in this plot. Video decreases from 0.970 for binary detection to 0.662 for five-class classification; EEG decreases from 0.966 to 0.534. Both modalities perform less well as the label set becomes more detailed. The plotted values differ from the runaveraged values in Table 1.

Figure 8. Per-class F1 for the five-class results displayed in this plot. Video/EEG values are 0.97/0.78 for non-seizure, 0.67/0.45 for Stage 2, 0.90/0.38 for Stage 3, 0.36/0.10 for Stage 4, and 0.42/0.03 for Stage 5. Rare severe stages remain difficult for both modalities.

Figure 6. Per-fold binary-detection macro-F1 for unseen animals, as displayed in the plot: video 0.948 ± 0.016 and EEG 0.849 ± 0.055. The plotted video results have a higher mean and lower fold-to-fold variability than the plotted EEG results.

Figure 9. A visual breakdown of our basic yes/no detection task. We show four sample frames from a normal, non-seizure period (top) alongside four frames from an active seizure (bottom). Because both examples feature the same rat during the same recording session, the animal’s appearance, the camera angle, and the overall background perfectly match. This careful pairing drastically reduces the chance that the model can cheat by memorizing static visual shortcuts in the scene. (All clips have been de-identified).

Figure 10. Visual filmstrips for each seizure stage: Each row (S2-S5) shows five sequential frames taken from a typical seizure clip, with time moving from left to right. As the severity stage increases, the physical symptoms become much more obvious escalating from mild movements in Stage 2 to extreme rearing and violent convulsions in Stages 4 and 5. Crucially, these behavioral shifts are plainly visible on camera, whereas the recorded EEG signal only captures them indirectly through shifting brain waves. (All frames are pulled from de-identified clips and tightly cropped to hide any specific cage labels.)

Figure 12. Visual examples of variation across different subjects: a single frame taken from six different animals (where ’R’ simply indicates a de-identified subject). The exact cage placement, camera angle, lighting conditions (which alternate between natural daylight and infrared), and even the animal’s coat vary drastically from rat to rat. This massive visual inconsistency is exactly why forcing a model to generalize to entirely unseen animals is so much harder than simply testing it on new recording sessions from familiar ones. It also highlights exactly why the video model’s consistent stability across different subjects (Fig. 6) is such a crucial finding.

Figure 2. Recording setup: each rat is recorded in its home cage using a fixed overhead camera and implanted EEG sensors. Cage cropping reduces variation in the field of view but does not remove all differences in camera geometry. Identifying details are masked.

Figure 13. Examples of where the video model struggles the most. (a) A very mild Stage 2 seizure featuring only subtle movements, making it incredibly easy to confuse with normal, everyday behavior. (b) An animal that rarely experienced seizures (found at the bottom of Table 10, App. C), leaving the model with very few validation clips captured under poor, grainy infrared lighting. Ultimately, extremely mild symptoms and data-starved animals drive almost all of the network’s remaining errors. (All clips have been de-identified.)

Figure 17. Error diagnostics for the 5-class severity grading task. (a) Numeric label-distance histogram. Because baseline non-seizure behavior falls completely outside the standard Racine scale, this panel remains purely descriptive and should not be treated as a strict ordinal metric. (b) Per-class recall annotated with absolute support counts, distinctly highlighting the Stage 2 performance reversal. (c) Direct head-to-head outcomes across the strictly shared intersection of 2,830 test clips evaluated by both modalities.
Table 8. Representative human video-EEG systems. Animal fusion remains sparse and has concentrated almost entirely on simple yes-orno seizure detection [35, 42].

Table 11. R(2+1)D binary-detection data-size and pretraining experiments under session-exclusive evaluation. The validation set is fixed as the training-subject subset grows. Macro-F1 rises from 0.957 with ten animals to 0.970 with twenty; intermediate results are non-monotonic. Kinetics pretraining improves macro-F1 by 0.018. Table 2. We tested ten video models using the exact same data splits and a strict 12-epoch training limit. Scores show the mean± std over five test runs (SlowFast detection uses n=4). We bolded the best results and underlined the second-best.
Table 7. The research landscape for automated seizure analysis broken down by data type and subject. The clearest open gap is multi-level severity grading using paired animal video-EEG data.

Table 10. A complete, animal-by-animal breakdown of our combined video and EEG dataset across all 20 rats. For every subject, we track the number of recording sessions, total clips, the split between non-seizure and seizure clips, and the exact breakdown of seizure severity (Stages 2 through 5). As the numbers show, the frequency of seizures is drastically uneven across the cohort. Just four heavily affected animals (R1, R2, R3, and R4) provide nearly half of the entire dataset, with individual totals swinging wildly from as few as 11 to as many as 3,091 clips. Across the board, the most violent events (Stage 5) remain extremely rare, yielding only 193 clips. Finally, all true animal identities have been hidden, and the subjects are simply listed in order from highest to lowest clip count (R1 to R20).

Table 9. Video backbones evaluated in Table 2, outlining their core design paradigms and overall parameter counts. Network capacities range broadly from 4M to 121M parameters. The smallest model is marked in bold, while the second-smallest is underlined.

Table 12. Performance breakdown for all ten video models on the thoroughly sanitized RodEpil dataset [44], evaluated under strict subject-exclusive five-fold cross-validation. F1 and AUROC scores represent the average across all five folds, while MCC includes the standard deviation (mean± std). Notice how drastically the model rankings shuffle compared to our native dataset a clear reminder that a network’s success is deeply tied to the specific visual quirks of its training data. †We have explicitly flagged the SlowFast model; its perfect score warrants further investigation for residual shortcuts, without establishing their presence. The highest non-flagged score is highlighted in bold.

Table 13. Ablation experiment evaluating spatial resolution for the R(2+1)D detection model across three input image sizes (16 frames, session-exclusive split, seed 42, 10 epochs; batch sizes scaled to 16, 8, and 4, respectively). Because the native source footage is only ∼300 to 480 px, both of the higher resolution settings force the network to upsample the video. Consequently, performance drops steadily across all three metrics. In terms of AUROC, the gap between the top two settings only emerges past the third decimal place (0.9934 vs. 0.9926). Note that the 448 px run suffered an out-of-memory crash after completing 8 of its 10 epochs; we report metrics from its best saved checkpoint, meaning this row represents an optimistic upper bound for the largest resolution setting. The best score in each column is highlighted in bold.

Table 18. Direct head-to-head evaluation across the 2,830 heldout test clips shared between both modalities for 5-class severity grading. To ensure a strictly fair comparison, this analysis is restricted to the exact intersection of clips evaluated by both models. Per-class rows highlight “solo victories” instances where precisely one model correctly predicted the severity stage while the other failed. Notably, Stage 2 represents the sole category where the EEG model outperforms the video network in solo correct predictions.

Table 4. Seven EEG baselines use the same 6 s windows, 3 s stride, 125 Hz sampling, and log-mean aggregation (App. B.5). TCN performs best for detection and 3-class grading, while GRU and TCN are similar at 5 classes. Two LSTM runs failed to converge, so its 3- and 5-class results use n=4. Best results are in bold; second-best are underlined.

Table 16. AUROC scores for all ten video and seven EEG backbones, following the exact same row order as Tables 2 and 4 for easy comparison. We use binary AUROC for the basic detection task and a macro one-vs-rest approach for multi-class severity grading.

Table 17. AUROC scores for both the video frame-count sweep and the rigorously re-encoded RodEpil cross-validation folds. For the sake of clarity, we have broken out the specific RodEpil AUROC results into their own dedicated section immediately below the frame-count data.

Table 19. Recall evaluated across the low- and high-motion halves of each severity class, partitioned strictly at the class-specific median motion energy (900 clips sampled from the paired evaluation set). Table 15. AUROC scores comparing the standard sessionexclusive evaluation against the strictly segregated subjectexclusive cross-validation. We use binary AUROC for basic detection and a macro one-vs-rest approach for multi-class severity grading. All values represent the mean± std across five independent runs.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have increased the demand for reliable watermarking for copyright protection, yet the robustness of video watermarks against removal attacks remains underexplored. Most watermark-removal methods originate from the image domain: signal optimization injects imperceptible pixel-domain perturbations, whereas generative resynthesis produces a visually similar instance through diffusion synthesis. When extended to videos, the former introduces temporally varying noise that causes visible flickering, while the latter regenerates fine-grained structures inconsistently across frames, leading to structural motion inconsistency. To evaluate video watermark robustness, we propose PoseRegen, a pose-consistent reconstruction framework that removes watermarks while preserving the original content and motion. PoseRegen first applies a temporally shared viewpoint transformation to disrupt watermark-bearing spatial patterns and then jointly reconstructs the transformed sequence with a pose-conditioned video model. A frozen video DiT processes the complete sequence with its reference-video latent, and full-sequence Flow Matching supervision keeps identity and background consistent across frames. To further preserve motion structure, we introduce a lightweight Pose-Conditioned Motion Consistency Adapter that adapts the frozen backbone to temporally ordered pose guidance and constrains body-part trajectories throughout reconstruction. Experiments on eleven video watermarking schemes show that PoseRegen reduces the average bit accuracy to 0.505, near random guessing, while outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.34% on motion-related VBench metrics. These results reveal a practical vulnerability of current video watermarks and highlight the need to evaluate robustness jointly with temporal and motion quality.
authors: Yifan Liao, Zhen Sun, Zhicong Huang, Jiaming He, Zongmin Zhang, Xi Ai, Cheng Hong, Xinhu Zheng, Xinlei He
bullets: Existing image-based removal methods cause video flicker or inconsistent structure when applied frame by frame or through resynthesis.
PoseRegen uses a temporally shared viewpoint transformation followed by pose-conditioned, full-sequence reconstruction.
A frozen video DiT with Flow Matching preserves reference content, while a motion adapter constrains pose and body-part trajectories.
Across 11 watermarking schemes, watermark bit accuracy falls to 0.505—near random guessing—and motion-related VBench scores improve by 9.34% over the strongest baseline.
The work emphasizes evaluating watermark robustness together with temporal and motion quality.

papers.abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to jointly localize a target in space and time given a natural-language query. Despite continued advances, existing STVG benchmarks remain largely centered on localizing targets through instance-specific descriptions, leaving them largely decoupled from long-form reasoning increasingly emphasized in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In this paper, we introduce Event-STVG, a task that shifts STVG from locating what is described toward event-level reasoning by unifying long-form context, repeated-event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi-target grounding. To facilitate research on Event-STVG, we construct a large-scale benchmark comprising 4,016 annotated event occurrences across soccer and seven additional domains. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal substantial difficulty, with the strongest model achieving only 5.4% m-vIoU at the 10-minute horizon. Across domains, we consistently observe confusion among repeated same-type events, spatial grounding bottlenecks, and rare success in jointly grounding all required roles. Event-STVG establishes a new challenge for visual understanding in MLLMs, calling for future models that can jointly reason about complex events across space and time. Code and annotations are available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/EventSTVG

State-of-the-art MLLMs perform poorly, with the strongest model reaching 5.4% m-vIoU at a 10-minute horizon.

papers.abstract: Video models commonly use uniform grids even though visual complexity varies substantially across space and time. We introduce OctVideo, which approximates a video clip with an octree. This hierarchy recursively partitions a spatio-temporal volume into eight subvolumes, so that smooth regions remain coarse while detailed regions receive finer cells. Each leaf stores local RGB values and spatio-temporal gradients, supplemented by a lightweight learned residual. For reconstruction, a Conv1D VAE maps the serialized cells to a regular latent grid and selectively refines details during decoding. Our VAE achieves 36.12 dB PSNR with 38.2M parameters and 189.4 GFLOPs per clip on Kinetics-400 (K400). It also generalizes zero-shot to the high-resolution Densely Annotated VIdeo Segmentation (DAVIS) 2016 dataset with reconstruction quality comparable to the best evaluated models. On both datasets, it requires the fewest model FLOPs and achieves the fastest encoding and decoding among the evaluated models. OctVideo also supports video understanding, achieving competitive recognition performance with few input tokens when trained from scratch. By exploiting the redundancy already present in video signals and efficiently processing sparse structures, OctVideo provides an efficient representation for video.
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of uniform spatio-temporal grids for videos with uneven visual complexity.
Recursively partitions clips into eight-way subvolumes, storing RGB values, gradients, and learned residuals at leaves.
Uses a Conv1D VAE to serialize octree cells into a regular latent grid and selectively refine details during decoding.
Achieves 36.12 dB PSNR on Kinetics-400 and generalizes zero-shot to DAVIS 2016 with comparable reconstruction quality.
Reports the fewest model FLOPs and fastest encoding/decoding among evaluated models, while retaining competitive recognition with few input tokens.

papers.abstract: Sparse video understanding often requires selecting a small set of visual evidence under a fixed frame budget. Most sparse selectors allocate this budget globally, allowing all frames to compete with one another. For temporally localized events, this can be a poor inductive bias: useful evidence is often distributed across pre-event context, the event itself, and post-event consequences. We study fixed-budget evidence allocation for localized event videos and show that globally competitive Top-$K$ selectors can preserve recognition and grounding while producing unstable event evidence. On DoTA Video Anomaly Recognition, Global Top-$K$ obtains competitive recognition and temporal grounding, but low selector-event alignment at $K=12$ (Frame AUC $51.5 \pm 10.8$). We propose dKFD, a phase-structured differentiable selector that reserves evidence capacity across pre-event, event, and post-event phases after full-sequence temporal encoding. Under matched-budget multi-seed evaluation, dKFD improves Frame AUC by $+30.97$ over a matched Global Top-$K$ selector at $K=12$ ($p<0.01$), while yielding modest but statistically significant recognition gains and comparable temporal grounding. Mechanism ablations show that phase supervision is load-bearing: removing it reduces Frame AUC to $41.1 \pm 12.0$ even when phase-partitioned budgets are retained. Downstream diagnostics on VRU-Accident show consistent gains over learned Global Top-$K$ across VLM families, while dense captioning reveals a boundary condition where uniform sampling remains competitive. These results support phase-structured allocation as a controlled fixed-budget approach for event-centric sparse evidence selection, not as a universal video summarization strategy.
bullets: Global Top-K selection can recognize and temporally ground events while selecting unstable, poorly aligned evidence.
dKFD uses full-sequence temporal encoding and a differentiable phase-structured selector with reserved capacity for three event phases.
On DoTA at K=12, dKFD improves Frame AUC by 30.97 points over matched Global Top-K, with modest recognition gains and comparable grounding.
Removing phase supervision substantially reduces selector-event alignment, indicating it is central to the method.
Gains extend across VLM families on VRU-Accident, but uniform sampling remains competitive for dense captioning; the method is not presented as universal video summarization.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: dKFD overview. The full video is temporally encoded before phase-aware selectors allocate a fixed evidence budget across pre-event, event, and post-event frames. Fig. 3: Qualitative selector comparison at K = 12 on two DoTA test clips (left: OC, oncoming; right: VP, vulnerable road user). The cream band marks the annotated event interval; the three lanes per clip show Uniform sampling, Global TopK, and dKFD. Uniform covers th timeline bu is not task-supervised; Global Top-K concentrates frames near the event core; dKFD allocates the same budget across preevent, event, and post-event phases, covering causal setup, interaction, and aftermath.

(b) Hard-frame overlap by temporal region at K = 12: dKFD’s gain over Global Top-K comes from the preand post-event regions, not from over-selecting the event window. (c) Phase-supervision sweep: removing phase supervision (λphase = 0) collapses both Frame AUC and phase coverage, while moderate supervision recovers stable alignment — phase supervision is load-bearing.

papers.abstract: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p.github.io for more visual results.
authors: Yitong Xia, Zeren Jiang, Chuanxia Zheng
bullets: Processes clean video latents in one encoder pass, avoiding iterative denoising.
Uses on-demand spatial queries and continuous-time queries for flexible spatial and temporal prediction.
Adds a frozen video-depth LoRA as a geometry prior without introducing trainable parameters.
Performs strongly on 3D point tracking, video depth, and camera pose estimation, including complex in-the-wild motion.
Demonstrates the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception.

The cross-attention Query Decoder is queried independently for each query q(u, v, tsrc, ttgt, tcam), where the query timestamps are parameterized as continuous time embeddings. papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video generators enable streaming generation, yet they run every token through the final denoising step, regardless of how much refinement it needs. We find this uniform computation is often unnecessary: many tokens already closely match their eventual full-step outputs in the initial steps, while others require refinement until the end. We introduce Speculative Forcing, a framework that treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and predicts when individual tokens can be safely accepted early. Once accepted, a token is frozen as its final output and undergoes no further denoising, while its cached keys and values remain available as context for the remaining tokens. We explore two alternative verifier designs: a training-free one based on similarity to clean content and stability across steps, and a learned one that reads the frozen generator's intermediate features to estimate each token's remaining gap to its full-step output. Across short-video, long-video, and world generation, Speculative Forcing preserves the quality of full-step sampling while substantially reducing computation. On LongLive, it matches the four-step generator with ~1.7 denoising steps per token, running over 1.5x faster at 41.7 and 37.8 fps. On Lingbot-World 2.0, where camera motion continually changes the visible content, it maintains quality with ~2.5 denoising steps per token and runs 1.35x faster at 24.5 fps.
authors: Hyunwook Choi, Seungryong Kim, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Uniformly denoising every token to the final step wastes computation because some tokens stabilize early.
The method treats intermediate clean estimates as drafts and uses verifiers to decide when tokens can be accepted and frozen.
Frozen tokens stop denoising while their cached keys and values remain available as context for later tokens.
Two verifiers are explored: a training-free similarity-and-stability test and a learned feature-based predictor of remaining error.
It preserves full-step quality while reducing computation, achieving over 1.5× speedup on LongLive and 1.35× on Lingbot-World 2.0.
