papers.abstract: Understanding characteristics and activities of individuals in complex multi-person environments is crucial for real-world applications. However, existing datasets often simplify this problem to grounded group activity recognition, single-person activity recognition, or close-set activity recognition, thus limiting the generalizability of models trained on these datasets. In this work, we introduce the task of Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition (GHADAR), which involves describing the characteristics and activity descriptions of \textbf{every} person in a video, provided the location of the person in the video, which is more practical for real-world applications. To facilitate this, we introduce a new dataset derived from AVA-Actions by generating open-set captions for the person description and activity. In addition, we propose a novel method to effectively utilize the information contained in grounding during training by constraining the cross-attention masks during training in VLMs to improve performance for this task. Our experiments show that our method outperforms SOTA VLMs on this task. Finally, we demonstrate the limitations of existing evaluation metrics, which are overly reliant on human-annotations and exact text-text matching. As an added video-based evaluation, we propose a holistic VLM-based evaluation schema that compares concepts {\em directly} between the video and the generated predictions. Thus, in this work, we develop a complete framework for GHADAR, including a dataset, a novel method and an evaluation schema, thereby establishing a strong foundation for future research in this domain.
authors: Jay N. Paranjape, Jurijs Nazarovs, Rohan Sarkar, Yue Guo, Lipeng Ke, Sankar Venkataraman, Vishal M. Patel, Nataraj Jammalamadaka
bullets: Addresses the limitations of datasets focused on group activities, single-person actions, or closed activity sets.
Introduces GHADAR, requiring grounded, open-set descriptions of each person in a multi-person video.

Reports better performance than existing VLMs and proposes holistic video-to-text concept evaluation beyond exact text matching.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning. Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment. To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment. We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control. During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense).
authors: Jiapeng Shi, Qiuxia Hou, Jiaqi Leng, Junke Wang, Yanhao Zhang, Haonan Lu, Ziyi Ye, Zuxuan Wu

papers.abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
authors: Zhuoming Liu, Jinhong Lin, Lin Zhang, Yiwu Zhong, Yin Li
bullets: Addresses the context bottleneck caused by memory methods that retrieve or append historical video observations to current inputs.

Achieves 3.9%–11.8% higher performance than prior memory approaches on OVO-Bench’s backward split, with modest latency overhead.
Also improves action success on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%, suggesting applicability to vision-language-action models.

papers.abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.
authors: Agnese Chiatti, Matteo Matteucci, Viola Schiaffonati

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
authors: Dongjie Cheng, Ruifeng Yuan, Ran Wei, Ning Song, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Li
bullets: Addresses the limits of fixed visual-imagination pipelines, such as novel-view synthesis, for diverse reasoning tasks.
Uses tools and skills to help the VLM decide whether and how to imagine, formulate generation requests, and interpret visual evidence.
Introduces co-evolution of tools, skills, and execution code from feedback while keeping model weights fixed.
Improves over direct reasoning with the same VLM across seven spatial, temporal, causal, and perceptual benchmarks.
Reports relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA; the strongest variant outperforms five evolving baselines across five benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Surgical teams could benefit from assistants that watch the video for requested events, such as "tell me when the clip applier appears during Calot triangle dissection", and answer questions about what has already happened. We formalise this task as request-driven event detection with exact semantics and causal alert decisions, and present SurgStreamer. It separates procedure-specific perception, which maps the 1-FPS stream to a structured state over tools, actions and phases, from procedure-agnostic reasoning, which evaluates a formal monitoring condition over this state and an event memory, either with exact rules or with a small controller that addresses entities through pointers rather than names. We evaluate this monitoring core with gold conditions. On a pre-registered, sealed test set of 12 laparoscopic cholecystectomies, SurgStreamer reached a macro event-F1 of 0.598 over full procedures. On identical 75-s windows with only the window available to every method, it scored 0.677. The tested configurations of the streaming vision-language model OneStreamer-4B, including ones fine-tuned on SurgStreamer's state or on video with an adapted vision encoder, scored at most 0.540 (Holm-adjusted p <= 0.012). At three external centres, re-training only perception raised performance on held-out procedures from 0.239 to 0.470. On a new procedure, pituitary surgery, controller weights trained on cholecystectomy matched an in-domain controller on oracle state (0.947 vs 0.938). On predicted state they missed the pre-registered non-inferiority margin (-0.024 [-0.040, -0.008]) unless the alert thresholds were re-calibrated. The results support separating perception from reasoning and point to perception under distribution shift as the main limitation.
authors: Bowen Xiang, Jon S. Heiselman, Michael I. Miga
bullets: Formalizes monitoring with exact event semantics, causal alert decisions, structured state, and event memory.
Maps 1-FPS video to tools, actions, and phases, then evaluates conditions using rules or a pointer-based controller.
Achieved macro event-F1 of 0.598 on full procedures and 0.677 on identical 75-second windows.
Outperformed tested OneStreamer-4B configurations, which reached at most 0.540 under the reported evaluation.
Perception under distribution shift remains the main limitation; retraining helped across centres, while cross-procedure transfer required recalibration.

figures.caption: Figure 2: SurgStreamer overview, shown on a sealed Cholec80 test procedure. A natural-language request is compiled once into an executable monitoring condition. Procedure-specific perception (blue) turns the 1-FPS stream into a structured state over a closed vocabulary of tools, actions and phases (decoded flags as lines, probabilities shaded; four of the seven tools shown). Procedure-agnostic reasoning (orange) addresses the entities of the condition through pointers (e1, φ), never by name. Every second, the exact rule controller C-rule, the learned controller C-learn or their per-family hybrid outputs yt , and an alert is issued causally, once the event is confirmed. Here the earlier irrigator onset at 08:35 (×) falls in the clipping phase and is not admissible; the onset at 14:59 (▼) is confirmed and reported at 15:00 (dashed line), as in the reference (decisions of C-rule on the decoded state). The event memory logs episodes and phase transitions causally and answers retrospective requests; the count shown, 3, matches the reference. For a new procedure or centre only the blue components are re-trained; the rule semantics and the C-learn weights are reused unchanged, and only the alert thresholds may be re-calibrated.

The strongest state-text baseline (C-LLM) and the vision-adapted VLM (V-VA) stay silent over the whole window, as does V-LoRA (not shown). papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence have accelerated video generation technologies. However, AI-generated videos (AIGVs) remain susceptible to various distortions, highlighting the need for dedicated video quality assessment methods. Content semantics play an important role in AIGV quality assessment, with source prompts typically used as textual references. However, these prompts may not accurately reflect the generated video content, resulting in a discrepancy between the intended textual description and the generated result. To address this limitation, this paper proposes VGCap, an AIGV quality assessment framework guided by visually grounded captions that align better with generated content. Specifically, we introduce two forms of captions: a global caption obtained by minimally revising the source prompt based on multi-frame visual evidence, and prompt-independent segment captions that describe localized temporal content. Together, these captions provide complementary textual evidence for assessing spatial quality, temporal quality, and text-video alignment. Experimental results on the LGVQ and FETV datasets show that VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions. Further ablation studies on caption sources and temporal components confirm the effectiveness of visually grounded captions for each quality dimension, while highlighting the benefits of segment-level features for temporal quality prediction. The source of VGCap will be available at https://github.com/lolo123-123/VGCap.
authors: Kehao Zhou, Yixuan Li, Yuxuan Jiang, Fan Zhang
bullets: Source prompts can diverge from the actual video, limiting content-aware quality assessment.
VGCap uses a revised global caption based on multi-frame evidence and prompt-independent segment captions for localized temporal content.
These complementary captions assess spatial quality, temporal quality, and text-video alignment.
Experiments on LGVQ and FETV show VGCap outperforms representative baselines across all three dimensions.
Ablations support visually grounded captions and show segment-level features benefit temporal quality prediction.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overall framework of VGCap. The Text Feature Extractor extracts features from the source prompt, global caption, and segment captions. The Spatial Feature Extractor derives frame-level spatial features. The Temporal Feature Extractor produces whole-video and segment-level motion features. The Adaptive Global Blend Gate fuses the branch-specific video and textual features, which are mapped to their corresponding scores by three quality predictors.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction and intervention. We benchmark 12 representative open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems. Our evaluation shows that current models struggle to make well-calibrated response decisions. Finally, we construct additional proactive training data and train \textsc{P$^3$I-Assistant-4B}, achieving improvements on several tasks, though gains remain uneven across capabilities. Together, these findings show that effective proactive assistance requires not only visual understanding, but also precise response timing and appropriate restraint.
authors: Boyu Cui, Junhao Luo, Zhihao Wang, Linghan Chen, Zejun Li, Jiwen Zhang, Siyuan Wang, Zhongyu Wei
bullets: Existing video benchmarks focus mainly on interpreting observed content, not anticipating assistance needs or deciding when to respond.
The benchmark measures daily perception, risk prediction, and intervention.
It evaluates 12 open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems.
Current models struggle with well-calibrated response decisions and appropriate restraint.
Training P$^3$I-Assistant-4B with additional proactive data improves several tasks, but gains vary by capability.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have steadily demonstrated outstanding performance in high-fidelity, controllable generation across diverse scenarios, following the "pretraining-finetuning" paradigm established in LLMs. Despite these advances, conventional DMs still face critical limitations in sophisticated reasoning, autonomous exploration of generation pathways, and adaptability to complex, human-aligned objectives. Inspired by RLHF's success in LLMs, RL has recently emerged as a pivotal post-training mechanism to iteratively refine DMs through reward-driven trajectory optimization. This paper presents the first comprehensive review of RL-driven DMs and an empirical analysis of how RL reshapes the diffusion process towards experience-centric, goal-directed generation. We propose a novel technical panorama elucidating RL's multifaceted roles in diffusion-based language, multimodal, robotic, and scientific models, with a granular focus on diffusion trajectory optimization and reward engineering. Through extensive experiments on multiple task-specific benchmarks, we systematically evaluate representative methods to intuitively highlight the advantages of different RL post-training strategies. Furthermore, we reveal and dissect three crucial bottlenecks that currently hinder the real-world deployment of RL-driven DMs: reward design fragility, exploration-exploitation trade-off in high-dimensional generation spaces, and training instability under sparse rewards. Based on these perspectives, we provide a principled roadmap for the integration of RL into DMs and outline promising future research directions for robust, interpretable RL-diffusion systems. We also construct a public repository to continuously track the latest developments in this rapidly evolving field: https://github.com/MAIR-Lab-HUST/Awesome-RL-for-Diffusion-Models.
authors: Zhiyuan Ma, Jiabao Wei, Tianyu Wang, Hanqing Wang, Jiadong Pan, Haowen Xu, Liangliang Zhao, Ruixun Liu, Yuhan Wang, Yuwei Zhang, Liang Feng, Junhao Xiao, Kaiyan Zhang, Xuekai Zhu, Daizong Liu, Biqing Qi, Yihao Liu, Ganqu Cui, Ning Ding, Linfeng Zhang, Jianjun Li, Kun He, Xiang Bai, Bowen Zhou
bullets: Identifies limitations of conventional diffusion models in reasoning, autonomous exploration, and complex human-aligned objectives.
Presents a technical panorama of RL’s roles in diffusion models, emphasizing trajectory optimization and reward engineering.
Evaluates representative RL post-training strategies across multiple task-specific benchmarks.
Highlights three deployment bottlenecks: fragile reward design, exploration–exploitation challenges, and instability under sparse rewards.
Proposes a roadmap for robust, interpretable RL-driven diffusion systems and provides a public resource repository.

papers.abstract: Understanding video content requires reasoning at multiple levels of granularity, from identifying objects to interpreting their interactions and localizing when specific actions occur. This thesis studies three query-guided grounding tasks that answer where key objects are (object-level grounding), how they interact (relationship-level grounding), and when specific moments occur (moment-level grounding). For object-level grounding, we present QDETRv, a query-guided extension of the Detection Transformer for one-shot localization of unseen objects in videos, which combines query-context fusion, a memory module for temporal consistency, and unsupervised pretraining on synthetic object trajectories. We further propose the Temporal Object-Aware Vision Transformer (TOViT) for few-shot video object detection, which builds on a language-aligned open-set vision encoder and propagates high-confidence object features across frames. For relationship-level grounding, we introduce few-shot referring relationships in videos: given a (subject, predicate, object) query and a few support videos sharing the predicate, the entities are localized by optimizing a T-partite random field using a meta-learned relation network with query-conditioned translational embeddings, Global Semantic Aggregation, Local Localization Aggregation, and belief-propagation-based message passing. For moment-level grounding, we propose the Moment Alignment Transformer (MATR) for video-to-video moment retrieval, which uses dual-stage Dynamic Time Warping for pre- and post-fusion alignment, learnable queries for boundary prediction, and self-supervised pretraining with temporal augmentations; MATR also extends to text-to-video moment retrieval with performance comparable to, or better than, the state of the art. These contributions advance query-guided video understanding across spatial, relational, and temporal grounding.
bullets: Addresses where objects are, how entities interact, and when relevant moments occur in videos.
Introduces QDETRv for one-shot unseen-object localization and TOViT for few-shot video object detection.
Models few-shot referring relationships with a meta-learned relation network and T-partite random-field inference.
Proposes MATR for video-to-video moment retrieval, with an extension to text-to-video retrieval.
Reports text-to-video retrieval performance comparable to or better than state of the art; scope centers on few-shot, open-set, and query-guided settings.

Each node corresponds to a binary random variable (𝑢 𝑖 𝑗𝑘 ) that takes one of the two labels, i.e. {select (1), reject (0)}. Figure 1.1: Thesis Objectives. This work aims to advance query-guided video understanding by addressing three core questions: where objects are present, how they interact, and when specific actions occur. Consider a football match: understanding the play requires (i) identifying key entities such as the ball, goalposts, and the players (where important objects are), (ii) recognizing interactions like “player kicking the ball to a teammate" (how objects interact), and (iii) localizing key events such “goa" moment (when critical actions occur). Together, these tasks enable structured interpretation of complex, fast-paced sports scenes, moving beyond frame-level recognition toward temporally grounded, interaction-aware understanding.

Classification embeddings are compared against support embeddings via cosine similarity, while the detection head predicts bounding box coordinates. Figure 3.3: Unsupervised Video Pretraining: Each frame, along with its associated query patch and context frame, is fed into QDETRv. The model detects the patch on every frame using decoded object queries responsible for predicting the bounding box. These decoded queries are then forwarded to the next frame as object queries for the decoder. Containing the semantic information extracted from previous frames for patch objects, they facilitate the detection in subsequent frames. During this phase, an unsupervised query reconstruction loss is also applied as an extra supervisory mechanism. The model has been pre-trained on a synthetically created dataset to enhance its performance. [Best viewed in color].

Figure 4.2: Object-aware Temporal Consistency. We utilize the OWL-ViT encoder output tokens as queries but, critically, only forward the matched object tokens (𝑐𝑝 > 𝜏) as key-value pairs to the next frame’s decoder. This mechanism selectively propagates high-confidence object features across frames. This enables efficient feature progression, reducing noise accumulation. We empirically found a threshold (𝜏) and compared it with class probability (𝑐𝑝) scores for selective propagation. This selective propagation mechanism significantly reduces noise accumulation across frames and maintains focused, consistent visual representations of detected objects throughout the video sequence.

papers.abstract: Training-free object removal commonly redirects self-attention away from the target region, but on few-step distilled diffusion models this often leaves object-shaped residuals. We identify a temporal mismatch: a structured prediction forms inside the mask at the first forward, and the short trajectory offers few later chances to revise it, while attention rerouting acts mainly in later steps. Across four distilled backbones, magnitude-matched single-forward interventions show that background-directed state correction affects the final result more than attention rerouting. We therefore propose ReState, which corrects the masked clean prediction toward background evidence retrieved from the input using a noise-level-aware weight that vanishes at the final forward. ReState retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and adds no denoiser evaluations. Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, ReState achieves the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, improving PSNR by 3.17 dB on average over the strongest baseline. On OBER-Test, it also outperforms the 50-step attention-forcing reference on all three metrics at 6.7x lower latency. The same configuration transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning. Project page: https://tdrlee.github.io/ReState
authors: Donghwan Lee, Sanghyun Jo, Sihyun Kim, Ziseok Lee, Kyungsu Kim
bullets: Few-step diffusion models can preserve object-shaped artifacts because structured errors arise early, while attention rerouting acts mostly later.
ReState applies noise-level-aware state correction using background evidence from the input, with the correction fading at the final forward.
It retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and requires no additional denoiser evaluations.
Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, it reports the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, with a 3.17 dB average PSNR gain over the strongest baseline.
On OBER-Test, it surpasses a 50-step attention-forcing reference at 6.7× lower latency and transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of ReState. Features from the first generation forward retrieve background evidence B from unmasked source regions without an additional denoiser evaluation. At each step, ReState moves the masked clean prediction x̂0,t toward B with a noise-level-aware weight ωt. The weight vanishes at the final forward, while object-excluding attention remains active throughout sampling.
Figure 3. Qualitative results on GT-paired benchmarks. Previous training-free methods often leave object-shaped residuals in the mask, whereas ReState more closely reconstructs the paired background.

Figure 1. Motivation. With attention forcing applied, the multi-step model (SDXL) starts diffuse and forms the background gradually along the trajectory (top), while the few-step model (SDXL-Turbo) already fixes a structured image in the mask at the first forward, and the short trajectory does not absorb it. This committed structure is what attention forcing then fails to remove, leaving a residual (bottom); ReState instead corrects the prediction directly and removes it.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method for object removal in few-step diffusion models. Few-step diffusion is a critical efficiency technique for video generation, and the noise-level-aware state correction mechanism is a novel technical contribution applicable to this domain.
papers.title: ReState: Noise-Level-Aware State Correction for Training-Free Object Removal in Few-Step Diffusion Models

papers.abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation enables rectified-flow models with diffusion-transformer architectures to combine task-specific capabilities within a single student. However, matching model outputs does not guarantee that their internal representations are aligned, and it remains unclear where and when additional feature supervision is most useful. We analyze the teacher-student feature mismatch across Transformer blocks and denoising timesteps, and find that the mismatch is concentrated in deeper Transformer blocks during early denoising and persists after OPD distillation, indicating ineffective distillation. Motivated by this observation, we introduce FocusOPD, which augments the base OPD objective with token-wise directional feature alignment restricted to deep layers and early denoising steps. Across two rectified-flow backbones and multiple OPD objectives, FocusOPD improves capability transfer in compositional generation, text rendering, and preference-based evaluation. On the primary benchmark, it improves over DiffusionOPD from 0.953 to 0.967 on GenEval, from 23.797 to 23.944 on PickScore, and from 6.052 to 6.199 on LAION-Aesthetic. Ablations show that selective deep and early supervision is more effective and efficient than alignment over the full network and trajectory.

papers.abstract: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models' tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.
authors: Yun Dai, Yuyun Chen, Jiarui Wen, Huiping Zhuang, Cen Chen, Ziqian Zeng
bullets: Video DiTs are slowed by quadratic self-attention, while fixed-sparsity methods poorly reflect changing attention patterns during denoising.
Attention becomes increasingly concentrated over denoising steps, and early-selected blocks retain much of the later attention weight.
GSRS is training-free: it keeps more computation early, reduces it progressively, and restricts later searches to an early candidate set.
Top-p selection provides adaptive sparsity, with exact attention-weight evaluation integrated into FlashAttention at negligible overhead.
Validated on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1, GSRS delivers 1.55×–2.21× speedup while maintaining quality comparable to full attention.

papers.abstract: Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V$^3$, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51--8.35~dB over a controlled V$^3$-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883~FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.

On complex full-scene videos, improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51–8.35 dB and reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5% versus a controlled V$^3$-style baseline.

papers.abstract: Identifying individual dogs from barks in real-world videos remains challenging and largely unexplored. Solving this problem would enable long-term behavioral analysis, veterinary monitoring, and animal welfare monitoring by attributing vocalizations and behaviors to the correct individual. Real-world videos are challenging because multiple dogs may bark simultaneously, become occluded, or move in and out of view. Prior studies show that canine vocalizations and visual appearance contain discriminative identity information, but these modalities have largely been studied independently. We present a multimodal dog-fingerprinting framework combining visual identification, multiple-object tracking, and canine vocal fingerprinting to associate bark events with individual dogs while maintaining persistent profiles. The framework synchronizes bark events with tracked dogs and updates profiles using visual appearance and vocal characteristics, enabling identification despite occlusion, overlapping vocalizations, and off-screen barking. We also introduce a benchmark of 46 real-world videos containing 213 manually annotated bark events. Our framework correctly localizes the active visible dog in 61.83% of visible events at IoU $\geq 0.30$ and achieves a 91.33% F1 score for visible versus off-screen barking detection.

papers.abstract: Dementia affects millions of older adults worldwide, yet early detection remains difficult outside clinical settings. Traditional models primarily rely on text or voice-based responses, capturing only a limited view of human cognition despite the inherently multimodal nature of human expression. This work proposes a contactless, multimodal screening framework that leverages video, audio, and text signals collected during structured voice-based interactions with Amazon Alexa. By incorporating these modalities, our approach captures a more holistic representation of human behavior encompassing speech patterns, vocal characteristics, facial expressions, and linguistic structure, which may enable more accurate detection of cognitive decline. Different participants completed three conversational tasks designed to probe spontaneous speech, comprehension, and recall. We pursued three objectives: (1) evaluate which of the three Alexa tasks provides the most informative cognitive signals, (2) compare the effectiveness of unimodal models, and (3) assess the benefits of multimodal fusion models. Task-level analysis shows that the video model achieves its best performance on Command-Reading, with an accuracy of 0.65 (AUC 0.69), while the audio model performs best on Question-Answering, reaching an accuracy of 0.67 (AUC 0.73). In contrast, the multimodal model demonstrates consistently stable performance across tasks, achieving an accuracy of 0.76 (AUC 0.75) on Command-Reading and 0.76 (AUC 0.73) on Question-Answering. These findings demonstrate that multimodal behavioral cues captured through naturalistic interactions can reliably distinguish MCI from healthy aging, highlighting the limitations of traditional diagnostic paradigms and supporting the shift toward multimodal, real-world cognitive assessment frameworks.

papers.abstract: Early detection of mild cognitive impairment remains a critical bottleneck in dementia care, demanding scalable tools capable of capturing subtle behavioral decay. To capture the subtle temporal changes of cognitive decline, we introduce a behavioral dataset collected across seven unscripted multimodal interactions over an 18-month horizon. This dataset formalizes continuous, multi-session interactions into a dense 4D tensor (Batch * Session * Time * Feature) that explicitly preserves concurrent local dynamics alongside long-term changes. To effectively process these complex behavioral patterns, we propose CogDrift-4D: a novel, hierarchical 4D Transformer framework. To capture the complex trajectory of cognitive decline, CogDrift-4D implements a dual-level behavioral fatigue and drift modeling architecture. At the intra-session level, the model computes localized least-squares regression slopes to quantify the acute ``fading'' of frame-level facial action units and acoustic energy. At the inter-session level, a recursive cross-attention feedback encoder acts as a cumulative fatigue accumulator, mapping the patient's continuous behavioral drift across successive sessions. To mitigate environmental noise and track failures across sessions, a localized Quality Gate dynamically filters low-integrity features before final fusion, also an early fusion that integrates semantic insights with raw physical dynamics. Evaluated on structured verbal and linguistic interactions, our architecture successfully detects MCI with a classification accuracy of 0.733 +- 0.13 and an F1-score of 0.716 +- 0.14, outperforming advanced baselines. The framework provides a mathematically rigorous, scalable, and robust foundation for home-based, real-time dementia screening.
authors: Sankalp Vaish, Sumukh Veeramalla, Rishank Singh, Caroline Summerour, John A. Batsis, Xiaohui Liang
bullets: Introduces a behavioral dataset spanning seven unscripted multimodal interactions over 18 months.
Represents continuous sessions as a dense Batch × Session × Time × Feature 4D tensor.
Uses hierarchical modeling: intra-session regression slopes capture acute behavioral fading, while inter-session cross-attention accumulates longitudinal drift.
A localized Quality Gate filters low-integrity features and fuses semantic information with physical behavioral dynamics.
On structured verbal and linguistic interactions, achieves 0.733 ± 0.13 accuracy and 0.716 ± 0.14 F1; scope is limited to the reported interaction setting.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video models often generate the visual concepts requested in natural language prompts but fail to satisfy their intended ordering, timing, and persistence requirements. We propose representing these requirements as specifications in a formal Temporal Logic, and introduce Temporal Specification Guidance (TSG), a training-free inference-time framework that turns temporal specifications into executable objectives for guiding video generation during sampling. TSG scores traces of visual concept evidence using differentiable quantitative semantics and uses the score's gradients to construct a specification-guided denoising direction. We instantiate this framework with video-text attention traces, efficient differentiable scores for Metric Temporal Logic, and gradient-derived attention biases. This instantiation requires neither an external concept classifier nor backpropagation through the video transformer. Its attention-steered forward pass yields a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG). On a benchmark of 220 prompts spanning 11 categories of temporal constraints, including ordered object entry and state transitions, this instantiation improves specification satisfaction accuracy over CFG by 9.5-20 percentage points across five models, with minimal memory overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of temporal specifications and differentiable satisfaction objectives as a flexible interface for controlling video generation.
authors: Avishree Khare, Hideki Okamoto, Bardh Hoxha, Georgios Fainekos, Rajeev Alur
bullets: Targets failures in event ordering, timing, and persistence despite correct visual concepts.
Represents requirements in Metric Temporal Logic and scores visual concept attention traces with differentiable semantics.
Uses score gradients to create attention biases and a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance.
Evaluated on 220 prompts across 11 temporal-constraint categories and five models, improving satisfaction accuracy by 9.5–20 percentage points over CFG.
Requires no external concept classifier or backpropagation through the video transformer, with minimal memory overhead.

papers.abstract: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.
authors: Qian Yu, Zongyang Qiu, Juncheng Yan, Hongliang Li, Qi Qin, Keqi Wang, Siqi Luo, Junkui Ju, Yapeng Mi, Tiantian Lu, Tian Liu, Pengyu Xie, Chenhao Ji, Minghui Zhang, Yiang Zhao, Siyu Yan, Haiying Xu, Yanbo Wang, Jianghan Shen, Yuandong Pu, Jiayi Lei, Borui Zhang, Jinxin Shi, Bo Zhang, Yuhang Zang, Shenglong Ye, Lixin Gu, Hongjie Zhang, Linghan Liu, Xinyuan Chen, Yuewen Cao, Lihe Zhang, Xiaohong Liu, Junjun He, Qiangwei Liu, Qi Zhang, Yu Cheng, Tianfan Xue, Hui Xiong, Chang Xu, Yu Qiao, Yihao Liu, Bin Fu

papers.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
papers.tldr: Intern Lumina U2 is a diffusion language model that uses multiple discrete visual codebooks to unify text, image, video, and 3D understanding and generation in one backbone.

papers.abstract: Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler--Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget
authors: Zahra Dehghani, Pablo Piantanida, Mohammadhadi Shateri
bullets: Addresses the costly, empirical selection of numerical resolution for pretrained flow-based generators.
Uses training-free, simulation-free interpolation probes of learned dynamics to estimate normalized one-step discretization error.
Derives budget estimators for Euler and Heun ODE solvers and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama SDE sampling.
Maps a target numerical tolerance to an NFE budget using solver order and relates ODE estimates to terminal integration error.
Evaluated across SiT, FlowDCN, and Rectified Flow models and formulations.

papers.abstract: Accident anticipation aims to recognize anomalous driving cues before a crash while avoiding false alarms during normal driving. Existing approaches typically formulate this task as binary classification, focusing on whether an accident will occur rather than when it will occur. We propose PRE-ACT, a framework that models accident risk as a continuously evolving signal that increases as the crash approaches. By explicitly enforcing temporal ordering and distance-to-accident awareness, our method progressively raises risk while suppressing premature alarms, leading to significant improvements on MM-AU subsets and Nexar. We further introduce a Separation Score to evaluate the global behavior of predicted risk curves beyond local temporal windows. Code and visualizations are available at https://github.com/giddyyupp/PRE-ACT.
bullets: Accident anticipation must detect danger early without triggering false alarms during normal driving.
PRE-ACT replaces binary accident prediction with continuously evolving, distance-to-accident-aware risk estimation.
Temporal ordering constraints encourage risk scores to rise as a crash approaches.
The method reports significant improvements on MM-AU subsets and Nexar.
A Separation Score evaluates the global quality of predicted risk curves beyond local temporal windows.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview. We define the period before the fixed anticipation horizon th as the safe zone, and the interval from th to the accident time tacc as the critical zone with progressively increasing risk. During training, we extract spatio-temporal features using a video foundation model. Based on these features, the model classifies clips as safe or critical, assigns a continuous risk score, and ranks them using preference head outputs, encouraging higher scores for critical clips closer to the accident. Dashed arrows indicate components used only during training.

Figure 1: PRE-ACT: From binary accident prediction to progressive risk anticipation. Unlike the dominant paradigm of formulating accident anticipation as a binary classification of whether an accident will occur (baseline), we model risk as a temporally evolving signal that reflects when an accident is likely to occur. By explicitly enforcing temporal order and distance-to-crash awareness, our model reduces false alarms while progressively increasing risk as abnormal cues emerge. Scores are overlaid on frames as an alpha channel, with blue indicating safe and red indicating risky predictions.

Figure 4: Problem with current evaluation metrics. Standard AUC evaluates predictions only within local temporal windows: negatives are sampled around anomaly onset (tai− 0.5) and positives close to the accident (tacc − 2), illustrated by the yellow hatched regions. As a result, the cyan, magenta, and green curves achieve similarly high AUC (near 1) and identical TTA, since they rise relative to the pre-anomaly region at comparable times (orange line). However, their global behavior differs significantly. The cyan curve produces early false alarms before tai, while the magenta curve shows weak progression toward the accident. The green curve exhibits the desired behavior: low risk before tai, a clear increase after anomaly onset, and steadily rising risk as tacc (red line) approaches.
Figure 5: Separation profile on CAP. BCE inflates pre-onset scores, whereas our model provides a smoother rise and improved accuracy near the accident, as shown zoomed-in.
Figure 3: Varying α. Continuous risk curves with fast-increasing (red side) and slow-increasing (blue side) behavior obtained by varying α. The linear case is shown with a dashed line.

Table 1: Results on MM-AU. We report results on the CAP [26] (top) and DADA [39] (bottom) splits of MM-AU [12]. Our method consistently outperforms prior work across almost all metrics by substantial margins, with improvements becoming more pronounced closer to the accident.

Table 8: Varying backbone. Video models (V-JEPAv2 and VideoMAE) clearly outperform the image backbone (DINOv2), emphasizing spatio-temporal features; similar results across video encoders show backbone-agnostic behavior for our method.

Table 5: Results with varying risk functions. Fast-increasing risk functions with positive α improve longer-horizon anticipation, i.e., ≥ 1 sec, while slow-increasing functions with negative α perform better at shorter horizons, i.e., < 1 sec. α = 3 achieves the best overall performance.
Table 7: Performance across varying FPR. Despite drops at low FPR, our method maintains timely warnings, achieving 0.8 s mTTA at FPR ≤ 0.01.

Table 3: Cross-dataset generalization. We train our model on the largest subset, CAP, and evaluate it on DADA and Nexar. As indicated by the performance differences (diff.; increase and decrease) relative to models trained on each dataset’s own training set, our model generalizes well to DADA, with a slight performance drop on Nexar due to a larger domain gap.

Table 4: Ablation on progress and preference estimation. Compared to the BCE baseline, progress estimation (Prog.) significantly improves performance across all metrics. Adding preference estimation (Pref.) provides slight additional gains, achieving the best overall results.

papers.abstract: Representation-alignment methods effectively accelerate the diffusion transformer training. REPA, for example, uses a pretrained vision encoder to supervise an intermediate layer through an MLP projection head which is discarded after training. It aims to import semantics from the vision encoder to the diffusion backbone. While this objective is achieved at early layers by back-propagating the alignment loss, there is no guarantee that later layers, supervised by the velocity prediction loss alone, can well access such semantics. We propose a simple solution, representation conditioning (RECON), to improve semantics in later layers. During training, we feed the pretrained vision encoder tokens into later layers; during inference, because we no longer have the clean image, we reuse the MLP head (as a proxy to the vision encoder) and project its output tokens to the later layers. Our method adds no parameters and leads to much faster convergence: RECON is $63\times$ faster than SiT and $25\times$ faster than REPA. Code is available at https://github.com/saeidrazavi/RECON
authors: Saeed Razavi, Xingjian Leng, Liang Zheng
bullets: REPA aligns early diffusion layers with a pretrained vision encoder, but later layers may not access those semantics effectively.
RECON feeds vision-encoder tokens into later layers during training.
At inference, it reuses the discarded MLP projection head as a proxy for the vision encoder to generate conditioning tokens.
The method adds no parameters and reports convergence 63× faster than SiT and 25× faster than REPA.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.abstract: Long-form agentic video generation must turn a screenplay into shots that remain spatially and temporally consistent across nonconsecutive requests. Passing prompts or recent frames between shots does not provide a shared spatial frame for revisiting a scene or a time-indexed record for replaying an earlier event. We present Any Time, Any Space (ATAS), which compiles a screenplay into shot requests with explicit location, camera, and event-time references. Before generation, it retrieves relevant evidence from a scene memory of registered static geometry and an event memory of dynamic observations indexed by scene, event, and time. After generation, ATAS reconstructs and registers the clip. It updates memory only when review and state checks accept the observation, while film delivery remains independent of memory admission. Across four video generators, ATAS improves all reported cross-shot consistency measures and achieves the highest aggregate benchmark score for each backbone. It also outperforms the compared agents and 3D-guided methods on target-image spatial revisit, leads three event-recapture criteria, and receives the highest human ratings on all six criteria. The video results and code are available on our project page: https://lhmd.top/atas/.
authors: Weijie Wang, Haomin Zhang, Ye Li, Akide Liu, Zeyu Zhang, Haoyu Zhao, Yefei He, Donny Y. Chen, Feng Chen, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the lack of shared spatial and time-indexed state when generating nonconsecutive shots.
Compiles screenplays into shot requests with explicit location, camera, and event-time references.
Retrieves evidence from static scene memory and dynamic event memory before generation, then reconstructs and registers generated clips.
Admits new memory only after review and state checks, while keeping film delivery independent of memory updates.
Improves reported cross-shot consistency across four video generators and receives the highest human ratings on all six criteria.

Fig. 2 Workflow of ATAS. A high-level prompt is parsed into multi-shot requests and bounded shot requests. Scene memory supplies static point-cloud references for the requested scene, while event memory supplies dynamic references for the requested event. Shot validation either requests another candidate or sends the accepted observation to the state update. The generated shot remains available as film independently of whether the observation is added to persistent state.

papers.abstract: Interactive video generation commonly relies on small bidirectional chunks to reduce response latency. Yet our preliminary experiments show that larger chunks improve video quality and better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only a modest increase in sampling time. Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted future remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk sampling. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and sampling time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.
authors: Yubo Huang, Yuxuan Zhang, Jiaming Liu, Sirui Zhao, Enhong Chen
bullets: Interactive video systems use small bidirectional chunks for responsiveness, but larger chunks can improve quality and GPU utilization.
The method expands the modeling window with noise padding and reuses cached predictions when conditions remain unchanged.
Video predictions are delivered incrementally while uncommitted future content remains replaceable.
The approach removes the waiting-time lower bound caused by chunk boundaries, shifting focus to faster per-chunk sampling.
It supports serving large bidirectional models for interactive streaming without complex streaming-specific post-training.

papers.abstract: We present KinoGen, a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen conditions a pretrained video generator on calibrated renders of the target robot and object in a simulated task instance and recovers the reference by fitting the same models to the generated two-view video, so that the reference lies in the robot configuration space by construction without a human body proxy or retargeting. Body, hand, and object priors initialize the reconstruction, and direct optimization against cross-view evidence refines it. Since an edited keyframe is simply another rendered state, a user can prescribe a goal object pose, regenerate the video around the edited keyframe, and obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly. Across eight loco-manipulation tasks, KinoGen yields lower penetration and foot skating than video-based baselines and preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and its customized references satisfy every prescribed target with substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Tracking policies trained on the synthesized references are deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. Project webpage: https://kinogen-humanoid.github.io/.
authors: Qi Wu, Lulu Zhao, Sanghyun Hahn, Rishi Yennu, Emmy Yang, Dingqi Zhang, Tao Pang, Jiuguang Wang, Kuan Fang

Across eight tasks, reduces penetration and foot skating versus video-based baselines while preserving over 90% of annotated contacts.
References satisfy prescribed object poses and support deployment of tracking policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands.

papers.abstract: Low-light video processing remains an underexplored problem in computer vision, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality ground-truth data. Existing public datasets exhibit several limitations, including restricted motion diversity, limited scene coverage, weak degradations, reliance on auxiliary modalities such as event data, and misalignment between low-light inputs and ground truth. Furthermore, current datasets typically address either low-light enhancement or scene understanding, whereas these tasks should be considered jointly. We introduce \textbf{OLiVES}, a benchmark dataset for outdoor low-light videos with dynamic scenes, designed to support both low-light video enhancement (LLVE) and video object segmentation (VOS). The dataset addresses key content gaps by incorporating a diverse range of natural textures, animals, occlusions, dynamic activities, and close-up scenes. To the best of our knowledge, OLiVES is the first outdoor low-light video dataset captured using professional cinema-grade cameras. It provides over 25,000 aligned normal- and low-light frame pairs, along with over 46,000 VOS annotations. We benchmark state-of-the-art LLVE and VOS methods on OLiVES and show that training on it improves performance on both tasks. The OLiVES project page is available at: https://anonymous-OLiVES.github.io/.
authors: Yini Li, Joanne Lin, David Blackham, David Bull, Nantheera Anantrasirichai

Covers diverse dynamic content, including natural textures, animals, occlusions, activities, and close-ups.

Contains over 25,000 aligned frame pairs and over 46,000 VOS annotations captured with cinema-grade cameras.
Benchmarking shows that training on OLiVES improves performance on both tasks.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation underlies real-time, causal video synthesis and is the backbone of video world models. Today's dominant approach distills a bidirectional diffusion model into a causal few-step student, but existing pipelines make this conversion prohibitively expensive, requiring offline Probability Flow ODE} (PF-ODE) trajectories that cost tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of storage. We show it can be made dramatically more efficient. Pushing this efficiency to its extreme, we reduce trajectory supervision to a single sample, the strictest setting possible, and find that it causes severe quality collapse. We trace this to the teacher's trajectory geometry: the high-noise regime, governing semantic layout and motion, and the low-noise regime, governing fine texture exhibit fundamentally different curvature and optimization behavior, so a single monolithic student cannot jointly fit both, causing severe representation interference. Motivated by this, we propose Glance Forcing, a lightweight distillation framework that decouples the denoising trajectory into two complementary slow and fast experts, each guided by a tailored, stage-specific objective, while keeping the pretrained teacher entirely frozen. This decoupling further reveals a general mechanism underlying few-step distillation: PF-ODE distillation mainly straightens the few-step trajectory geometry, while the subsequent distribution-matching stage independently governs distributional quality. Using only one PF-ODE trajectory, Glance Forcing already surpasses the fully-trained state-of-the-art baseline, raising the VBench Total score from 84.04 to 84.22 while cutting trajectory-collection cost from thousands of GPU-hours to about one A100-GPU-hour, with markedly larger gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, and instruction-following, and consistent preference from human raters over strong baselines.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Junchao Yi, Hu Jian Guo, Linjie Li, Rui Zhao, Alex Jinpeng Wang
bullets: Existing causal distillation pipelines require tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of PF-ODE trajectory data.
The authors attribute single-sample quality collapse to different optimization geometry in high-noise semantic/motion and low-noise texture regimes.
Glance Forcing uses two frozen-teacher-guided slow and fast experts with stage-specific objectives to decouple these regimes.
With one PF-ODE trajectory, it raises VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.22 and reduces trajectory collection to about one A100-GPU-hour.
It also reports gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, instruction following, and human preference over strong baselines.

papers.abstract: In various industries, smoke and fire are two of the most important threats in the workplace. One of the common methods for detecting smoke and fire is the use of infrared thermal and smoke sensors, which cannot be used in outdoor applications. Therefore, the use of vision-based methods seems necessary. The problem of smoke and fire detection is spatiotemporal and requires spatiotemporal solutions. This paper presents a method that uses spatial features along with temporal-based features to detect smoke and fire in the scene. It consists of three main parts; the task of each part is to reduce the error of the previous part so that the final model has a robust performance. This method also uses transformer modules to increase the accuracy of the model. The results of our model show the proper performance of the proposed approach in solving the problem of smoke and fire detection and can be used to increase workplace safety.
authors: Alireza Mirrashid, Mohammad Khoshbin, Ali Atghaei, Hassan Shahbazi
bullets: Addresses the limitations of infrared thermal and smoke sensors in outdoor environments.
Models smoke and fire detection as a spatiotemporal vision problem.
Uses three sequential components, each intended to reduce errors from the preceding stage.
Incorporates transformer modules to improve detection accuracy.
Reports proper performance and potential to improve workplace safety, without specific quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Current video object removal methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction. We present StreamErase, enabling sub-second latency with up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU. Our approach first augments a text-to-video model with mask input to generate high-quality videos that erase target objects and synthesize coherent backgrounds, but does not perform inference on the fly. As such, we progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity. Several key challenges arise when generating videos over long, potentially infinite horizons: (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to long horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without increasing computational cost as the context grows. To address these challenges, we carefully designed sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks. By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos. Finally, we establish a dedicated benchmark, LongErase, for streaming long-video object removal. Our model achieves strong performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming. With StreamErase, users can input a mask and see the erasing results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Xiaobing Tu, Xiantao Zhang, Jinkui Ren, Yinggui Wang, Yue Ma, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high latency and non-causal processing of existing video object removal methods.
Transfers erasing capability from a text-to-video foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser.
Uses sliding-window causal attention, attention sinks, self-rollout, and KV-cache rolling to maintain fixed-context, constant-speed generation.
Reports sub-second latency and up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU.
Introduces the LongErase benchmark and supports interactive, infinite-length video erasing with strong real-world generalization.

papers.abstract: Distilling pretrained video diffusion models into few-step autoregressive (AR) generators typically combines student initialization with distribution matching distillation (DMD). An intermediate AR teacher can provide causally compatible targets for ODE initialization. However, causally compatible targets alone do not ensure high-quality generation under a short sampling schedule. We analyze the posterior-mean predictions favored by direct latent regression and empirically find that causal ODE initialization alleviates blur but still leaves fine detail unresolved. To address this limitation, we propose Representation Forcing, which learns few-step causal initialization through representation-space supervision rather than intermediate-teacher trajectory regression. The student is trained with teacher forcing by comparing clean predictions and training targets through normalized features of a frozen video diffusion transformer. This phase reuses the synthetic videos generated by a bidirectional model for AR teacher training and replaces both teacher training and causal ODE distillation, without generating additional causal ODE trajectories. The subsequent asymmetric DMD procedure remains unchanged. Empirical results show that, at four sampling steps, RepForcing better preserves generation quality than intermediate-teacher-based initialization before DMD. After DMD, our four-step chunk-wise model improves VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.66 (+0.62 points) and VisionReward from 6.326 to 10.074 (+59.25%) over the reported causal-ODE-based baseline.
authors: Siming Fu, Zheming Fu, Lianrui Mu, Haoyang Huang, Chaojie Gu, Ruizhe He
bullets: Causal ODE initialization reduces blur but can leave fine details unresolved under short sampling schedules.
RepForcing uses teacher forcing to match clean predictions and targets through normalized features from a frozen video diffusion transformer.
It reuses synthetic videos from bidirectional-model training and avoids additional causal ODE trajectory generation.
At four sampling steps, it better preserves quality before DMD than intermediate-teacher initialization.
After DMD, it raises VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.66 and VisionReward from 6.326 to 10.074 over the reported causal-ODE baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Representation Forcing Initialization Pipeline. Training videos are encoded into clean latent blocks by a VAE encoder. The trainable causal DiT reconstructs clean blocks from noisy inputs, conditioned on preceding clean blocks under teacher forcing. The predicted and target video latents are passed separately through the same truncated, frozen Wan2.1-14B to obtain features f̂ and f . A token-wise cosine loss compares these features, with stop-gradient (sg) on the target branch. Gradients propagate through the frozen extractor to update the causal DiT. This initialization replaces intermediate AR teacher training and causal ODE distillation.
