papers.title: RepForcing: Representation-Space Initialization for Autoregressive Video Distillation
papers.tldr: RepForcing improves few-step autoregressive video diffusion distillation by learning causal initialization in a pretrained representation space instead of regressing intermediate teacher trajectories.

papers.abstract: Video scene graph generation (VidSGG) aims to capture objects and their evolving relationships in videos. This requires accounting for both the persistence of object identities and abrupt changes in relationships. Existing methods aggregate information across frames to exploit temporal context, but an emphasis on consistency can obscure these changes. As a result, a model may retain its previous prediction even after the underlying relation has changed. We refer to this failure mode as relational semantic inertia. To address this issue, we propose Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer (RTAformer), a one-stage framework that separately models entity persistence and relation changes. It injects calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries to guide predicate updates, while cross-frame instance alignment during training helps reduce cross-frame representational drift. Experiments on Action Genome show improvements in recall and mean recall over existing methods, with ablation studies supporting the contributions of the proposed components and comparisons using matched backbones showing larger gains on relation-transition frames than on non-transition frames.
authors: Jaeyeon Heo, Geuntaek Lim, Yukyung Choi
bullets: Addresses the failure of temporal consistency methods to update predictions when video relationships change.
Uses a one-stage Transformer that separately models entity persistence and relation transitions.
Guides predicate updates with calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries.
Applies cross-frame instance alignment during training to reduce representational drift.
On Action Genome, improves recall and mean recall, with larger gains on relation-transition frames.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overall framework of RTAformer. (a) Frame-wise spatial triplet parsing produces instance-pair and relation queries for target and reference frames. (b) Disentangled Temporal Aggregation (DTA) refines the target queries with separate instance and relation streams, where TADI injects relation-transition cues. FFN heads produce the instance and relation predictions that form the output triplets. (c) Spatio-Semantic Instance Alignment (SSIA) aligns adjacent-frame instance-pair queries during training.

Fig. 5: Qualitative comparison around relation transition boundaries. The participating entities remain visible across adjacent frames, while predicates for ‘person–broom’ and ‘person–door’ change. RTAformer updates the changed predicates, e.g., ‘person– holding–broom’ and ‘person–not contacting–door’, whereas OED preserves previousframe relations such as ‘person–not contacting–broom’ and ‘person–touching–door’.

Fig. 3: Transition-Aware Delta Injection (TADI). TADI uses the adjacent-frame relation-query displacement ∆q = Qrel tar,q−Qrel prev,q as a transition cue. The displacement is decomposed into its numerically stabilized root-mean-square (RMS) magnitude rq and RMS-normalized direction ∆dir q , while the scale gate gq and foreground confidence cq modulate the injection strength.

Fig. 1: (a) Relational semantic inertia: the ‘person–cup/glass/bottle’ pair persists across frames, but its relation changes from looking at to not looking at, while the baseline [29] retains the previous predicate in the target frame. (b) Our reimplementation of the baseline exhibits an 11.6-point gap in SGDET R@10 between the non-transition and relation-transition frame subsets.

Table 1: Experimental results on Action Genome under the SGDET protocol. We report Recall@K (R@K) and mean Recall@K (mR@K) under With Constraint and No Constraint settings. ‘–’ indicates that the metric is not reported.

Table 3: Ablation on relation-stream transition injection design. Starting from the spatial+SSIA baseline, we compare temporal aggregation without transition injection and three relation-displacement injection variants. All variants use the same spatial branch and ViT-B/14 backbone.

Table 2: Module ablation. Starting from the frame-wise spatial baseline, we evaluate SSIA and DTA individually and jointly. The spatial baseline performs frame-wise triplet parsing without temporal refinement. DTA denotes the full temporal module with TADI. All variants use the ViT-B/14 backbone.

papers.selection_reason: Relation-transition-aware transformer for video scene graph generation, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: RTAformer: Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer for Video Scene Graph Generation
papers.tldr: RTAformer improves video scene graph generation by modeling persistent entities separately from changing relationships to reduce relational semantic inertia.

papers.abstract: Pairwise preference feedback has become a widely adopted supervision signal for reinforcement learning in video generation models, as pairwise comparisons provide a more reliable alternative than pointwise scalar ratings for evaluating the quality of generated videos. Specifically, we define a preference graph for each GRPO group under a pairwise evaluator, where nodes represent sampled rollouts and edges encode pairwise preferences. Auditing 6,976 on-policy comparison graphs, we find that cyclic preferences are prevalent and persist throughout training. Naive pairwise reward aggregation based on average win rates discards the underlying comparison structures and treats each rollout independently, which may introduce unreliable advantage estimates for certain rollouts and consequently affect reinforcement learning optimization. Therefore, we propose the \emph{Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk} (\ours{}), a graph-aware advantage aggregation method that strengthens the global preference signal from win rates with reliable relational evidence from cyclic preference graphs through a reliability-guided preference walk. Under matched evaluator, comparison protocol, group size, prompt schedule, and query budget, \ours{} requires no additional evaluator queries beyond the observed comparisons within each rollout group and improves over Pairwise-GRPO across controlled comparisons, transfer settings, and blind human evaluations.
authors: Xinrui Lin, Fan Li, Shumin Wang, Dehong Kong, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Pairwise preferences for video rollouts often form cycles, which persist during training.
Win-rate aggregation ignores relational structure and can yield unreliable rollout advantages.
Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk combines global win rates with reliability-guided evidence from preference graphs.
It uses only comparisons already observed within each rollout group.
The method improves over Pairwise-GRPO in controlled, transfer, and blind human evaluations, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RAP-Walk. Top: methods share the Pairwise-GRPO pipeline and differ only in advantage construction. Bottom: (a) same-prompt videos exhibit quality trade-offs; (b) pointwise rewards are normalized independently; (c) v1, v2, and v3 form a directed cycle yet have identical row-wise win rates, so win-rate aggregation assigns them identical advantages; (d) RAP-Walk uses reliable edges and multi-hop paths to correct the win-rate anchor.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison across eight prompts. Each prompt shows four frames from videos generated by Pretrained, Pairwise GRPO, and RAP-Walk. Pretrained denotes the original Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B model without LoRA post-training. All methods use matched prompts and initial noise.

Figure 2: Five-node illustration of cyclic preference propagation. (a) A cyclic preference graph with reliability-aware propagation. (b) Normalized preference credits from rowwise win-rate aggregation and RAP-Walk. Win-rate aggregation only considers direct comparison outcomes, while RAP-Walk exploits reliable multi-hop support and reduces the influence of conflicting local structures.

Table 2: Quantitative comparison on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with Qwen3-VL-30B/235B evaluators. Within each evaluator, runs share group size, prompt schedule, and budget; pairwise methods also share the bidirectional comparison protocol and query count. Best/second-best are bolded/underlined.
Table 4: Ablation study on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with Qwen3VL-235B. Win-rate Pairwise-GRPO is the reference; best/second-best values are bolded/underlined.
Table 3: Results across generator backbones with a fixed Qwen3-VL-235B evaluator. Best/second-best values are bolded/underlined per generator.
Table 1: Preference-graph structure over training. The Li ratio is the group-averaged maximum-to-mean ratio of unstandardized node inconsistency.

papers.selection_reason: Graph-aware preference aggregation for RL fine-tuning of video generation models, relevant to video diffusion training.
papers.title: When Pairwise Preferences Cycle: A Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk for Video GRPO
papers.tldr: A graph-aware preference-walk method uses cyclic pairwise-comparison structure to produce more reliable advantages for video GRPO without extra evaluator queries.

papers.abstract: MeanFlow predicts interval-average velocities, but conventional few-step sampling ties the interval queried from the model to the duration of the state update. We separate these two quantities at inference, fixing the model, update grid, and number of queries while varying the prediction horizon. Our central finding is that the horizon response depends on both query position and the states entering that query. Across seven independently trained CIFAR-10 checkpoints at classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale 2, a longer horizon worsens FID at early steps but improves it at the midpoint. To probe whether query time alone determines this response, we fix the midpoint query and current/subsequent guidance while changing only earlier CFG. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, the mean midpoint horizon benefit increases from 0.109 to 1.308 FID, indicating sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution. A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or extra queries, including gains on five checkpoints trained after rule selection. A milder rule also improves mean FID by 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, with fixed-rule FID gains on the evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints. However, matched-budget calibration favors query-start shifting in historical CIFAR tests, and the tested Horizon allocation adds no FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. Thus, prediction horizon is a distinct, position- and state-sensitive inference control, but not a universally preferred one.
authors: Tinglan Wang, Haixu Liu, Shaobo Chen, Nuo Qian, Qi Gao, Kai Wen, Yu Yao
bullets: Longer horizons worsen FID early in sampling but improve it near the midpoint across seven CIFAR-10 checkpoints at CFG 2.
Horizon effects depend on both query position and the states entering the query, not query time alone.
A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or additional queries; a milder rule improves it by 1.041 on a stronger grid.
Fixed-rule gains also appear on evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints.
Matched-budget tests favor query-start shifting in historical CIFAR experiments, while Horizon allocation adds no benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates inference dynamics in MeanFlow (video generation), specifically decoupling model queries from state updates, which is relevant to video generation and understanding.
papers.title: Rethinking Prediction Horizons: Decoupling Model Queries from State Updates in Few-Step MeanFlow
papers.tldr: Decoupling MeanFlow’s model-query horizon from the state-update duration reveals a position- and state-sensitive inference control that can improve FID without retraining or extra queries, but is not universally best.

papers.abstract: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in complex videos. Several recent methods improve SAM 2 with hand-crafted memory update rules, each targeting a specific failure mode, such as distractors, occlusions, or object motion. However, their gains transfer only partially to the stronger SAM 3 backbone. We instead present a more general, data-driven approach that frames memory control as a sequential decision-making task. SAM3RL is an extension of the SAM 3 tracker with a lightweight memory controller, trained by reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank in order to maximize tracking performance. SAM3RL sets a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks, outperforming all hand-crafted rules without any runtime overhead. The same approach applied to SAM 2 gives SAM2RL, which outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of the 12 benchmarks, showing the generality of our method across model generations.
authors: Tom\'a\v{s} \v{C}\'i\v{z}ek, Matej Straka, Illia Volkov, Mat\v{e}j Kripner, Ervin Maci\'c, Jiri Matas, Klara Janouskova, Martin Schmid
bullets: Addresses the limitations of FIFO and hand-crafted memory-update rules for handling distractors, occlusions, and object motion.
Adds a lightweight memory controller that treats memory selection as a sequential decision-making problem.
The controller is trained with reinforcement learning to maximize tracking performance.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks.
Applying the same approach to SAM 2 also outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of 12 benchmarks, indicating cross-generation generality.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Gains from hand-crafted rules vs. our learned memory control SAM3RL (left) and SAM2RL (right). Each axis is a tracking or video segmentation benchmark, spanning three categories: VOT(S) challenges (VOTS2025/2026, VOTS-RT2025, and VOT-LT2021/2022), visual object tracking (DiDi, LaSOT, LaSOText), and video object segmentation (MOSEv2, SA-Vval/test, LVOSv2). The radius shows the change in that benchmark’s standard metric relative to the corresponding baseline tracker (SAM 3 or SAM 2). The outer labels give our score on each benchmark. The compared methods modify what the tracker stores in the memory bank, and in most cases also mask selection or the number of banks. In contrast, our policy operates with the memory bank only. The compared methods are evaluated on SAM 2 as published and on SAM 3 after our porting to that backbone.

Figure 12: SAM3RL holds onto very old frames and successfully reacquires. A LaSOT test sequence of a military ceremony, in which the tracked soldier’s hat leaves the field of view for about 5 s among other soldiers wearing near-identical hats. The top row shows four selected frames (a–d) with the ground truth and the prediction of each method. The middle panel shows the per-frame tracking quality of each method in the selected time window, with the absence shaded red. The bottom panel shows the memory bank content of each method at the four selected frames, one row per selected frame and method and one tick per stored frame. The prompt frame at 0 s is on the left, and an arrow gives the number of stored frames older than the selected window. SAM 3 correctly predicts no target throughout the absence, with its bank holding the last five frames before it, and reacquires the hat on the first frame after its return. DAM4SAM3 also predicts no target at the start of the absence, but shortly after it locks onto another soldier’s hat. By (b) it has evicted all preabsence frames, and its bank holds only frames in which it tracks the wrong hat. It keeps following that hat for the rest of the sequence, also after the target returns. SAM3RL correctly predicts no target throughout the absence, but its bank barely changes. When the hat leaves the view, five of its six slots hold frames that are 20–30 s old. These stay in the bank through more than 30 s of tracking, from before (a) until after (d), and only the newest slot turns over. SAM3RL thus keeps the target’s appearance in memory throughout the gap and reacquires the hat on the first frame after its return.

Figure 13: SAM3RL holds sparse old frames and reacquires late. A VOT-LT2021 sequence capturing a longboarder from behind, who goes out of view on the left for about 3 s. The top row shows four selected frames (a–d) with the ground truth and the prediction of each method. The middle panel shows the per-frame tracking quality of each method in the selected time window, with the absence shaded red. The bottom panel shows the memory bank content of each method at the four selected frames, one row per selected frame and method and one tick per stored frame. The prompt frame at 0 s is on the left, and an arrow gives the number of stored frames older than the selected window. SAM 3 correctly reports the target absent on most frames of the gap and reacquires successfully. DAM4SAM3 keeps 3 old frames and 3 recent ones in all selected frames, although during the absence the 3 recent ones are the pre-absence ones. SAM3RL carries four frames from before the absence through the gap, which are 4–15 s old at the start of the absence and all show the rider small and near the center of the frame, while the rider comes back large and on the left side. The memory bank frames that would match that view all passed through the two newest slots and are not present in the bank of SAM3RL at the end of the absence, but are present in the banks of SAM 3 and DAM4SAM3. SAM3RL fails to reacquire for 4 s after the return, while SAM 3 and DAM4SAM3 reacquire immediately. Once the rider moves back towards the center, SAM3RL reacquires and updates its memory bank.

Figure 11: SAM3RL holds diverse pre-absence frames through a long absence. A VOT-LT2021 sequence captured from the onboard camera of a formula car, in which the car ahead leaves the field of view for about 22 s. The top row shows four selected frames (a–d) with the ground truth and the prediction of each method. The middle panel shows the per-frame tracking quality of each method in the selected time window, with the absence shaded red. The bottom panel shows the memory bank content of each method at the four selected frames, one row per selected frame and method and one tick per stored frame. The prompt frame at 0 s is on the left, and an arrow gives the number of stored frames older than the selected window. SAM 3 correctly predicts no target throughout the absence, with its bank fixed on consecutive frames just before it, in which the car is mostly out of view. It does not reacquire the car after its return. DAM4SAM3 wrongly predicts the target at several points during the absence, and by (b) its bank holds only frames from the absence. After the return, its predictions miss the car. SAM3RL also predicts no target during the absence. When the car leaves, its bank holds frames spread over the last few seconds before the absence and a few from the start of the absence, and at (b) and (c) it still holds nearly all of them. SAM3RL reacquires the car about 1 s after its return, and by (d) half of its bank holds frames from after the return, while the pre-absence frames remain.

Figure 2: Learned memory control for SAM-based trackers. The frozen tracker (top) embeds the frame xt and conditions it through memory attention on the current memory bank Bt. The decoder predicts the mask ŷt, and the memory encoder fuses it with xt into a new memory mt. The bank has capacity seven, where slot 0 is permanently reserved for the conditioning frame. Appending mt to slot 7 therefore overfills the bank, so one of the slots 1, . . . , 7 must be evicted. Our controller πθ observes the state st, which collects temporal, confidence, semantic, and geometric features of all eight slots, and picks the action at ∈ {1, . . . , 7} that removes the corresponding memory (here at = 3). The surviving slots form the updated bank Bt+1 that the tracker reads at step t+1. During training, πθ receives the reward rt, scoring ŷt against the annotation yt, and maximizes the expected discounted return Eπθ [∑ k≥0 γ krt+k+1 ] . At inference, πθ is fixed and the actions are taken greedily.

Figure 5: Admission rate of incoming frames by SAM3RL follows object change. An LVOSv2 video sequence in which a rabbit settles and hops off twice over 60 s. Object motion is the shift of the ground-truth box center between consecutive decisions, normalized by the square root of the box area. Appearance change is the DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) cosine distance between consecutive ground-truth crops. The middle panel is the admission rate in a 5 s window, one tick per admitted decision. Admissions are sparse while the rabbit stays still (gray) and dense when both curves rise.

Figure 4: Admission rate of incoming frames by SAM3RL on MOSEv2 against the frame’s predicted IoU score scaled by max(2σ(ot) − 1, 0). SAM 3 stores only frames above 0.01. Decisions are binned, counts in white, 95% CIs.

Figure 3: Frame age in memory slots for SAM3RL and SAM 3 on MOSEv2. Visible pools all decisions with the target present. Absent pools the last decisions of absent gaps of at least 16 decisions. Median with the 25th to 75th percentile.

Figure 10: Admission rate of incoming frames by SAM3RL follows object change II. A 75 s DiDi video sequence in which a car cruises steadily in one lane and then starts moving quickly, changing lanes until the end. Object motion is the shift of the ground-truth box center between consecutive decisions, normalized by the square root of the box area. Appearance change is the DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) cosine distance between consecutive ground-truth crops. The middle panel is the admission rate in a 5 s window, one tick per admitted decision. Admissions are sparse during the cruise and dense in the lane-changing interval (gray) when object motion rises.

Figure 9: Admission follows object change. Share of incoming frames SAM3RL admits per quintile of object motion and appearance change on our LaSOT validation split. Object motion is the shift of the ground-truth box center between consecutive decisions, normalized by the square root of the box area. Appearance change is the DINOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) cosine distance between consecutive ground-truth crops.

Figure 8: Action distributions. Frequency of each action at for SAM 3 and SAM3RL on our LaSOT validation split. Action at ∈ {1, . . . , 6} evicts the stored memory mτat , where at = 7 rejects the incoming frame. The SAM 3 rule uses only two actions. It evicts the most recent stored frame mτ6 (at = 6) if its effective IoU score falls below the memory threshold, and the oldest frame mτ1 (at = 1) otherwise.

Figure 7: Reward normalization. Validation score on the LaSOT validation split during training; mean over three seeds with a ±SEM band. The arms differ only in the bt normalized reward, rt = qt − bt against the raw quality rt = qt.

papers.abstract: Unsupervised temporal action localization (UTAL) aims to identify action categories and localize their temporal boundaries without annotation supervision. Existing methods typically derive supervision for both tasks solely from RGB and optical-flow representations, often resulting in noisy category assignments and inaccurate temporal boundaries. In this work, we reveal an overlooked property of video codecs: group-of-pictures quantization patterns preserve category-discriminative dynamics, while motion-vector and residual variations exhibit pronounced responses around action transitions. Based on this insight, we propose CoDy, a codec dynamics-guided framework that exploits the codec as complementary information to the visual view for UTAL. CoDy integrates a codec-enhanced view with RGB and flow through confidence-aware consensus clustering, producing reliable soft pseudo-labels. It further converts codec dynamics into a class-agnostic boundary prior, which supervises visual boundary learning and guides proposal initialization and iterative refinement. The codec branches are only used during the training stage and introduce no extra codec-side computation at inference. Extensive experiments on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet v1.3 demonstrate that CoDy consistently outperforms existing UTAL methods and achieves state-of-the-art localization performance. These results establish codec signals as effective annotation-free priors for jointly inferring which actions occur and when they occur.

papers.abstract: We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change-aware memory with query-driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively. papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce visually realistic videos that nevertheless violate the physical consequences implied by the prompt and scene. Existing benchmarks largely rely on holistic plausibility scores or broad quality dimensions, leaving it unclear which physical behavior is being tested and why a model fails. We introduce PhyMetric, a scene-level diagnostic benchmark that recasts physical plausibility evaluation as verifiable, scene-grounded question answering. PhyMetric contains 1{,}115 scenes spanning 50 physical categories across six domains, paired with 8{,}920 answer-balanced binary questions over 12 evaluation dimensions. Each scene is associated with eight targeted yes/no questions and a structured physical prior specifying the governing law, expected temporal sequence, observable signatures, and common failure modes. At evaluation time, a vision-language model (VLM) judge answers each question from question-aware sampled frames conditioned on the prior, and correctness is hierarchically aggregated into scene, dimension, physical category, and model scores. Experiments on four open-source T2V models and three VLM judges show that scene-specific binary QA is a critical component of the protocol: when each targeted question is replaced by a single generic plausibility query, evaluator accuracy drops to the chance level. Structured physical priors offer a complementary signal that improves human alignment of the resulting scores, with effects that vary across VLM judges of different capacity. These findings establish PhyMetric as a benchmark that turns physical plausibility evaluation from opaque holistic scoring into interpretable, scene-level inspection. Our project page is available at: https://mengsiwei.github.io/PhyMetric/.

papers.abstract: Crash Moment Localization aims to localize the major physical impact that interrupts controlled flight in an onboard first-person-view (FPV) video recorded by a drone, thereby providing a temporal reference for retrospective crash analysis in aerial robotics. However, existing crash-video datasets predominantly target surveillance or dash-camera footage, and their annotation schemes and task formulations are not designed for temporal localization of the major physical impact in UAV onboard FPV videos. To address this gap, we present FPV-CRASH, a dataset and fixed-protocol reference evaluation for offline Crash Moment Localization in drone FPV videos. FPV-CRASH contains 1,052 drone FPV clips (526 Crash and 526 Normal); each Crash clip has a single-frame reference annotation for the Crash Moment, and every clip is paired with four English captions automatically generated from sampled frames and the known Crash/Normal label. Normal clips carry no timestamp target and provide training-time background supervision. The captions support an auxiliary Text-to-Video Retrieval task, whereas localization inference remains video-only. We further provide a heatmap-based reference model that estimates a continuous Crash Moment timestamp from sparsely sampled frames. Under the fixed, non-source-disjoint clip-level protocol, the reference model reduces MAE from 1.12 s for the strongest fixed timing-prior baseline to 0.56 s (a 50% relative reduction) and achieves a median absolute error (MedAE) of 0.33 s; the fraction of clips localized within 0.5 s rises from 37.14% to 65.71%. The release includes annotations, available source video identifiers and URLs, clipping metadata, fixed split lists, and preprocessing code so that the reportable portion can be reconstructed without redistributing source footage. At submission time, all source-compilation URLs remained accessible.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.

papers.abstract: Recent work has explored visual reasoning through image generation, where models solve visual-reasoning problems by directly generating solution images. Intuitively, iterative samplers such as flow matching are well suited to this task, since each sampling step may resemble one reasoning step. However, in this work, from a circuit complexity perspective, we show that this intuition is misleading. We prove that as long as the model outputs satisfy certain mild regularity conditions, the trajectory of the vanilla flow-matching sampler can be simulated by a constant number of sequential rounds of parallel model evaluations. Consequently, additional sampling steps cannot increase the expressive power of a constant-depth backbone model under the standard complexity-theoretic model of transformers. We then reveal that self-conditioning, which conditions the model on the previous step's estimate of the final image, plays a previously unrecognized role in removing this bottleneck. Controlled experiments on diverse visual-reasoning tasks show that flow matching with self-conditioning achieves higher accuracy and greater reasoning depth than vanilla flow matching, and its performance improves with more sampling steps. Theoretically, we prove that with self-conditioning, a constant-depth backbone can achieve expressive power equivalent to that of space-bounded Turing machines. Our study suggests a design principle for future visual reasoning research: carry more information between sampling steps, so that additional steps translate into deeper reasoning.
authors: Zeyang Zhang, Linxiang Gao, Meiqi Gu, Xingyan Chen, Minrui Luo, Kaifeng Lyu, Tianxing He

Experiments across diverse visual-reasoning tasks show higher accuracy, greater reasoning depth, and continued improvement with more sampling steps when self-conditioning is used.
The theory shows that self-conditioned constant-depth backbones can match the expressive power of space-bounded Turing machines.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes self-conditioning in flow matching for visual reasoning, providing a transferable technical insight for deep sequential reasoning in generative models.
papers.title: Self-Conditioning Enables Deep Sequential Reasoning in Flow Matching

papers.abstract: Lipreading remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech cues and their sensitivity to head pose and video resolution. In this work, we propose FLARE, a framework for robust visual speech representation learning via cross-modal distillation and joint face-lip modeling. FLARE leverages semantically rich Whisper representations as the acoustic teacher signal, converting them into discrete distillation targets through a random-projection quantizer and pretraining the model with a masked prediction objective. To capture complementary visual information, FLARE employs a dual-stream architecture that jointly processes lip region-of-interest (ROI) and full-face inputs, where the lip stream captures finegrained articulatory motion and the face stream encodes broader facial dynamics. During pretraining, auxiliary audio input is incorporated to facilitate cross-modal alignment, and modality dropout is applied to encourage robust visual-only representations. For downstream lipreading, FLARE serves as a visual encoder coupled with either a lightweight Transformer decoder or an LLM-based decoder. Evaluated on LRS2, LRS3, and the out-of-domain WildVSR benchmark, FLARE achieves strong lipreading performance, with word error rates of 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3%, respectively. A progressive design study confirms the contribution of each major component. Further analyses demonstrate that joint face-lip modeling improves robustness under degraded video resolution and large head pose variation, while yielding more phoneme-discriminative visual representations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/jxzhanggg/FLARE.
authors: Jing-Xuan Zhang, Genshun Wan, Jianqing Gao, Jia Pan, Yumei Zhang, Lichen Zhang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in lipreading and sensitivity to head pose and video resolution.
Uses Whisper-based cross-modal distillation with random-quantized targets and masked prediction pretraining.
Combines dual-stream lip-ROI and full-face processing, with auxiliary audio and modality dropout for robust visual-only representations.
Supports Transformer or LLM-based decoders and reports 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3% WER on LRS2, LRS3, and WildVSR.
Analyses indicate improved robustness to degraded resolution and large pose variation, with more phoneme-discriminative representations.

papers.abstract: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query-based predictions as an over-complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross-Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine-grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM-based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment-level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer-grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query-based event segmentation and annotation.
authors: Rui Chen, Xingyu Chen, Pengxin Xu, Kai Chen, Junzhi Yu
bullets: Addresses inaccurate temporal localization and low-quality proposals in long, untrimmed videos, particularly with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries.
Uses complementary video representations and treats dense query predictions as an over-complete set of temporal event hypotheses.
Introduces consensus calibration, localization-quality estimation, and redundancy suppression to improve proposal ranking and candidate discrimination.
Supports both standard temporal action detection and LLM-based semantic event understanding through calibrated proposals.
Experiments on public benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and propose a staged evaluation protocol for localization, semantic understanding, and their combination.

papers.abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
authors: Zihao Lin, Haoyu Dong, Haobo Xu, Chi-Chih Chang, Xuying Ning, Yinglong Xia, Shuang Yang, Zhuokai Zhao, Xinying Song, Dongfang Liu, Lifu Huang, Yang Song, Qifan Wang
bullets: Recursive harness evolution is studied for agentic video understanding with a frozen vision-language model.
Analysis of over 4,000 candidates identifies validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap.
SRSI uses transferable, sufficient, pre-commitment evidence; content-free proposer feedback; instrumented warm-up experiments; and isolated probe-race branches.
Across four benchmarks, it raises the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to BRSI and reduces the validation-test gap by 37.9%.
The findings suggest that reliable harness evolution depends on search organization and evidence quality, not validation optimization alone.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Overview of VideoHarness-SRSI. Top: under information isolation, the harness executes on the validation videos and questions, but the proposer receives only scores and content-free traces, never the videos, question text, options, or answers. Bottom: evolution proceeds in three stages under this policy. Stage I (instrumented warm-up) adds a removal and an intensity change to the free proposals of each round, summarizes the evidence in a per-mechanism report, and selects a seed pool and a backbone H0. Stage II (isolated branch evolution) evolves each mechanism axis in its own branch from H0; every axis is probed with three candidates, the top half race on to fifteen, and at most three axes are kept. Stage III (factorial composition) distills each kept axis into a fixed modification, evaluates all combinations against H0 to measure transfer and interactions, and then jointly refines them into the final harness H⋆.

papers.abstract: We present Kandinsky S2V 1.0, an open family of speech-to-video models for controllable audio-driven human animation, comprising Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite (2B parameters) and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro (21B parameters). From a single reference image, a speech waveform, and a text prompt, the models generate long-form 25 FPS video in which lip motion, expression, pose, and gesture follow the speech. The architecture draws text and audio conditioning from one Qwen2.5-Omni model and adds a reference-aware three-scale visual memory. Training starts from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video foundation models [1] and combines mixed reference-memory layouts with an area-adaptive face loss. The training corpus contains 1.17M single-speaker clips selected by active-speaker detection, with captions generated directly in English and Russian. A side-by-side human evaluation against the strongest open-source baseline and two proprietary commercial models shows that Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro performs comparably to or better than these models on average and is also preferred for lip synchronization. On common speech to video benchmarks, Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro rank among the top performing models according to mean rank over five reported metrics. Beyond the base models, we provide {\pi}-Flow distilled variants of both Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro. The distilled Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro model generates video in 16 sampling steps without classifier-free guidance, achieving a 5.4 times end-to-end speedup over the base model, while matching or exceeding it on nearly all reported benchmark metrics. To accelerate open research and deployment in speech-to-video generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.
authors: Nikolay Semenov, Artem Riabinin, Sergey Bassenko, Anna Averchenkova, Julia Agafonova, Anastasia Aliaskina, Kirill Kozlov, Lev Novitskiy, Nikita Samsonov, Nikolai Gerasimenko, Denis Dimitrov
bullets: Generates long-form 25 FPS avatar video from one image, speech waveform, and text prompt.
Uses unified text/audio conditioning, three-scale reference-aware visual memory, and area-adaptive face loss.
Includes Lite (2B) and Pro (21B) models trained on 1.17M active-speaker clips.
Pro performs comparably to or better than evaluated open and proprietary models, with preferred lip synchronization; both rank highly on common benchmarks.
π-Flow distillation enables the Pro model to generate in 16 steps without classifier-free guidance, delivering a reported 5.4× end-to-end speedup while largely preserving quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the Kandinsky S2V 1.0 architecture. Text features from the frozen Qwen2.5-Omni Thinker and audio features from its frozen audio tower [17] feed trainable text and audio encoder stacks in the DiT, with Nt text blocks and Na audio blocks. The reference image is encoded by a frozen Hunyuan 3D VAE [2], and its latent is concatenated (denoted by C) with the noisy target latent zt and a multi-scale FramePack [14] memory of past frames to form the visual sequence consumed by the DiT. Each DiT block applies self-attention (V2V), cross-attention to the text tokens (V2T), an optional cross-attention to the audio tokens (V2A) injected periodically across the stack, and a feed-forward layer. The denoised visual latent is decoded back to pixel space by the frozen VAE decoder.

Figure 4: Frame-aligned audio cross-attention (V2A). Audio features from the frozen Qwen2.5Omni audio tower pass through the trainable audio encoder. In each V2A layer the target video tokens of latent frame i attend only to the audio tokens of the same time span, which gives a block-diagonal attention pattern. Memory and reference tokens skip this layer. The strips at the bottom left mark the visual decoder blocks that contain a V2A layer in the 2B and 21B models.

Figure 3: FramePack memory layout. The memory tokens are concatenated (C) with the reference and target tokens into one visual sequence for the DiT. papers.abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.
authors: Eren Cetin, Julius Erbach, Vukasin Bozic, Hyojun Go, Zixiang Zhao, Nikolai Kalischek, Federico Tombari, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between bounded memory and recalling observations when the camera revisits a location.
Uses a constant-size slot recurrence with writes keyed by the observing camera and reads queried by the rendering camera.
Avoids explicit 3D reconstruction and growing caches by conditioning recall on inter-view geometry.
Provides confidence estimates to a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, which balances retrieved content with its generative prior.
On Memory Maze and Minecraft trajectories, maintains high-fidelity recall beyond the training horizon with constant memory and per-step cost.

papers.abstract: Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks
authors: Georgios Angelidis, Aggelos Psiris, Maria Vakalopoulou, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos, Giorgos Sfikas, Iraklis Varlamis
bullets: A convergent meta-analysis synthesizes published aerial and remote-sensing video results across four evidence tiers.
Model parameter scaling yields limited gains: a median +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase, versus a human gap of at least 19 points.
Perception degrades in 315 of 318 within-paper contrasts when altitude, viewpoint, object size, or time horizon becomes harder.
Current benchmarks lack video-input evaluations with both task-specific human and random baselines, and competence drops sharply from answering to closed-loop navigation.
The paper proposes five falsifiable principles and the AVU-Card for reporting aerial video benchmark properties.

papers.abstract: Dense cardiac dynamics are essential for assessing cardiac function, yet in practice clinicians often observe only extremely sparse measurements. However, recovering full dynamics from such sparsity is a highly ill-posed problem due to the lack of temporal cues. While auxiliary time-series signals like ECG provide physiological guidance, effectively exploiting them is challenging due to the cross-modal representation gap and phase misalignment. In this work, we present CardioFAD, a Focus--Align--Diffuse paradigm that reformulates sparse cardiac dynamic synthesis as a recoverability--alignability anchor discovery problem. Our core insight is that resolving extreme temporal ambiguity requires a compact set of anchor states that are both sufficient to recover the visual trajectory and reliable for ECG--visual alignment. We therefore learn motion-salient keyframes under two complementary principles: trajectory sufficiency, which preserves trajectory-critical intra-modal motion content, and anchor alignment, which promotes consistent inter-modal correspondence at these anchors. We implement the Focus and Align modules optimized by the two aspects. Diffuse then performs two-stage generation by first synthesizing keyframes and subsequently interpolating the remaining frames. Extensive experiments on cardiac MRI and echocardiography videos demonstrate superior visual quality, temporal coherence, and improved functional consistency under the extreme one-shot regime.
authors: Junkai Liu, Haofan Wu, Nay Aung, Joao A. C. Lima, Steffen E. Petersen, Le Zhang
bullets: Addresses the severe temporal ambiguity of cardiac dynamic synthesis from extremely sparse observations.
Learns motion-salient keyframes that are both trajectory-sufficient and aligned with ECG signals.
Uses a Focus–Align–Diffuse pipeline: identify keyframes, align visual and physiological information, then generate keyframes and interpolate remaining frames.
Experiments on cardiac MRI and echocardiography show improved visual quality, temporal coherence, and functional consistency in the one-shot setting.

(iii) Diffuse: A video DiT performs two-stage synthesis, first generating the keyframes, then interpolating the remaining frames.

papers.selection_reason: Presents CardioFAD, a Focus-Align-Diffuse paradigm for synthesizing cardiac dynamics from sparse observations using ECG guidance. This applies video diffusion techniques to medical time-series data.
papers.title: Focus, Align, and Diffuse: Time-Series-Aware Keyframe Diffusion for Cardiac Dynamic Synthesis from Sparse Observations
papers.tldr: CardioFAD reconstructs dense cardiac motion from a single observation by selecting ECG-aligned motion keyframes and diffusing the missing frames.

papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.
authors: Shashank Sule, Xinyue Yu, Boonam Shin, Yuxuan Liu, Abolfazl Hashemi, Hayden Schaeffer
bullets: Memorization is studied both as a training-time model behavior and as an individual sample property.
Average input curvature over training and validation samples can signal when a model begins regurgitating training data.
Curvature alone does not adequately measure whether a specific sample will be memorized.
The paper defines counterfactual memorization for diffusion models and proves it is controlled by input curvature of a leave-one-out model.
Experiments validate the theoretical bounds and support input-dependent curvature as a memorization proxy.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates memorization in diffusion models using loss curvature, providing a theoretical and empirical framework for understanding generative model behavior.
papers.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: Input loss curvature, measured via the diffusion-loss Hessian, is a sampling-free proxy for detecting model-level memorization and estimating sample-level memorization under a counterfactual definition.

papers.abstract: Training-free story visualization without reference images must preserve recurring entities across frames while scaling to long narratives. Existing methods typically maintain consistency by conditioning each frame on other frames of the same story, coupling generation time, VRAM, or both to story length. We introduce ELECT, which instead settles cross-frame identity before final rendering through a language-guided scene-entity mapping and stationary anchors elected from the model's own drafts. This makes the per-frame cost of the final rendering pass independent of story length. Joint attention exceeds 96 GB of VRAM at 32 scenes, whereas ELECT remains at 8.3 s per frame and under 20 GB VRAM from 10 to 1000 scenes. On the Story50 long-story benchmark, ELECT reaches 0.833 average Character Consistency Similarity (aCCS), compared with 0.826 for ten-round refinement, at one seventh of its generation cost, with lower text alignment (0.327 vs. 0.340). At 1000 scenes, to our knowledge, the first evaluation of training-free story visualization at this length, ELECT exceeds ten-round refinement by 0.017 aCCS and the nearest flat-cost baseline by 0.091, while also surpassing refinement in text alignment at one twenty-fourth of its generation time. These results show that long-horizon consistency need not require increasingly expensive inter-frame conditioning as stories grow.

Uses language-guided scene-entity mapping and stationary anchors selected from the model’s own drafts before final rendering.
Maintains 8.3 seconds per frame and under 20 GB VRAM across 10–1000 scenes, while joint attention exceeds 96 GB at 32 scenes.

At 1000 scenes, improves aCCS over refinement by 0.017 and the nearest flat-cost baseline by 0.091, though text alignment is lower on Story50.

papers.abstract: Repetition counting requires identifying and enumerating action cycles over time. While state-of-the-art video language models describe actions fluently, they fail to reliably count how many times an action repeats. To investigate this limitation, we introduce RepProbe, a benchmark of 42K real and synthetic video clips containing exactly k in [1, 20] complete repetitions, with controls for clip position, temporal coverage, and duration. These controls allow us to study the counting failure directly and locate where in the model it arises. Counting accuracy collapses at high counts across the video language models we evaluate, and controlled experiments show this collapse is not explained by frame sampling alone. We compare model outputs with linear probes trained on the final-layer representations used to generate those outputs. We find a consistent representation-to-output dissociation: substantial count information remains linearly decodable even when models fail to report the correct count. Further analysis shows this failure arises primarily at the output stage, where answers concentrate on a small set of preferred numbers rather than the available count information. The dissociation holds on both real and synthetic videos and is not explained by clip duration, position, or scene content. These results indicate that models encode repetition structure but do not reliably report it in their outputs. Project page: https://arenaa.github.io/RepProbe-webpage/
bullets: Introduces a 42K-clip benchmark with 1–20 controlled repetitions in real and synthetic videos.
Counting accuracy collapses at high counts, and the failure is not explained by frame sampling, clip duration, position, or scene content.
Linear probes recover count information from final-layer representations even when model outputs are incorrect.
The main bottleneck occurs at the output stage, where predictions favor a small set of preferred numbers.

papers.abstract: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.

bullets: Evaluates two tracks: vision-language (OmniCompass-VL) and audio-visual (OmniCompass-AV).

Uses paired text-only and text+image target specifications to test grounding consistency.
Includes manually verified annotations spanning varied domains and video durations.
Evaluation of 50 MLLMs finds open-source models behind proprietary ones, with persistent challenges in audio-visual understanding and precise grounding.

papers.selection_reason: Holistic omni-modal video grounding and understanding benchmark for MLLMs, directly relevant to video-language understanding and temporal/spatial grounding.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time. In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged. We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation. Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (GAD), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model's attention to video attention. Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames. Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations. Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths. On Wan2.2 5B, GAD improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks. Notably, GAD achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation. Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/.
authors: Junfeng Ni, Ziyu Zhu, Fan Jiang, Yu Liu, Chiyu Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Zhaoxu Sun, Mu Xu, Siyuan Huang, Yixin Chen

Across three video backbones, GAD improves long-range scene and dynamic temporal consistency across generation lengths.
On Wan2.2 5B, it improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the baseline on both long-range benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Visual agents must turn video observations into timely decisions to track progress and choose what to do next. Building on the emerging System One paradigm, we introduce VideoJev, a family of models that cast video understanding and interaction as structured decision tasks. We adapt pretrained multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by replacing autoregressive answer decoding with a shared head that scores temporal intervals and textual options against video evidence. These scores yield event spans or answer choices, unifying temporal grounding and multiple-choice video question answering. This combines the semantic flexibility of MLLMs with efficient decisions that agents can use directly. As an interaction unfolds, new goals and intermediate results prompt further queries about the same visual history. VideoJev therefore reuses visual computation through Cached inference for queries as they arrive and Joint inference for multiple queries in a single forward pass. Across three temporal grounding benchmarks, VideoJev-4B and VideoJev-35B-A3B improve mean mIoU over their backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, respectively, with measured inference speedups of $2.8$-$3.1\times$. On four video QA benchmarks, both achieve performance comparable to their backbones in Thinking mode, with measured inference speedups exceeding $100\times$. These results offer a unified, reusable decision interface for composing structured visual judgments into complex, open-ended workflows.
authors: Yuhan Zhu, Xiangyu Zeng, Qingyi Si, Chenxu Yang, Yifei Li, Luozheng Qin, Junhao Zhou, Dingyu Yao, Jun Zhang, Chuanyu Qin, Zhiqiu Zhang, Yuandong Yang, Yuqi Xu, Tianyu Zhang, Hongcheng Guo, Jiaqi Wang, Nan Duan, Limin Wang

Improves temporal-grounding mean mIoU over backbones by 6.7 and 10.8 points, with 2.8–3.1× inference speedups.

papers.abstract: Video understanding benchmarks are the primary yardstick for measuring progress in video-language modeling, and a growing body of work relies on them to claim improvements. The reported benchmark scores in these works, however, are almost always produced by frameworks (e.g., lmms eval) used as black boxes: certain evaluation choices like frame sampling, preprocessing, and input formatting are inherited from preset defaults and seldom inspected carefully. We show these unexamined choices are a major source of variance. Even for the same model checkpoint, evaluation configuration alone can shift accuracy by up to 19.5pp. Hence, it is unclear whether reported gains reflect genuine improvements in capability or differences in evaluation setup. Moreover, many benchmark samples offer little evidence of visual capability, since they can be answered without the video, and the full suites are expensive to evaluate. We address these issues in two parts. First, we curate existing suites for discriminability and efficiency, producing Meta-Video, a balanced 1,000-question benchmark over 791 videos spanning diverse tasks and durations, which largely preserves model rankings, at 5 times inference speedup for a full-frame count sweep experiment (4-128 frames). Second, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol by sweeping the configuration space to isolate choices that measurably affect results, distill them into best practices and reporting standards, and release reproducible reference scores across five models and seven benchmarks. We hope that the proposed evaluation framework and the Meta-Video benchmark will support video understanding research by providing a reproducible and efficient foundation to measure progress in a reliable way.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in generative models has made talking-head deepfakes highly realistic and easy to create, jeopardizing public trust. However, most audio-visual deepfake detectors rely on lip-speech synchronization and are designed for static, frontal videos, limiting their reliability in dynamic, in-the-wild recordings where the speaker moves and lip cues are degraded or missing. As an alternative, we propose a physics-aware detector for dynamic speaking videos that leverages an acoustic constraint: in real recordings, speech energy varies predictably with speaker-to-camera distance, whereas deepfake generation can break this coupling. Our method combines distance estimates from video with distance-dependent acoustic measures from speech to detect deepfakes. Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show that the proposed physical cue is effective in dynamic scenarios, and that it complements lip-sync-based detectors, with a simple ensemble achieving consistent gains across datasets. Codes are available at https://byulharang.github.io/PADD/.
authors: Kyeongrae Kim, Kim Sung-Bin, Oh Hyun-Bin, Tae-Hyun Oh
bullets: Targets realistic deepfakes in dynamic, in-the-wild videos where lip-sync cues may be unreliable or missing.
Estimates speaker-to-camera distance from video and compares it with distance-dependent acoustic properties of speech.
Uses a physical consistency cue that deepfake generation may disrupt.
Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show effectiveness in dynamic scenarios.
The cue complements lip-sync detectors, with a simple ensemble providing consistent gains across datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Physics-aware deepfake detection framework. Our method extracts speaker distance and acoustic measures from video and audio streams. For speaker distance, we calculated dspk by averaging monocular depth values (MiDaS [12]) within facial landmarks (RetinaFace [13]). For acoustic measures, SNR and C50 were calculated using speech and noise separated by SAM-Audio [14] with a ’speech’ prompt. Distance-wise binning is then applied and the variance and entropy of the acoustic measures are aggregated to form statistical features v. Finally, v is fed into a lightweight MLP detector to predict whether it is an authentic or a deepfake video.

Figure 3: Qualitative examples of authentic (left) and deepfake (right) videos. We visualize the temporal trends of distance, SNR, and C50. In authentic videos, the acoustic measures increase as the speaker moves closer to the camera, following the expected physical relationship between distance and speech energy. In contrast, deepfake videos often exhibit inconsistent trends between distance and acoustic measures.

(C) reports scoreaveraging ensembles between lip-sync-based detectors and ours.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Ziyu Wan, Nanye Ma, Long Zhao, Dong Chen, Hongyu Liu, Qifeng Chen, Dongdong Chen
bullets: Uses on-policy velocity regression as the foundation for few-step distillation.

Supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation; reports outperforming strong few-step baselines and surpassing multi-step teachers on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models have emerged as a foundation for long-horizon world rollout. However, when extended far beyond their training windows, these models suffer from progressive drift: visual quality deteriorates, motion becomes inconsistent, and object identity gradually collapses as generated frames are recursively reused as context. We study a supervision-horizon gap: short-horizon distillation leaves later rollout states without direct supervision. We show that matching short-window marginals need not determine long-horizon behavior, while longer on-policy trajectories expose delayed failures to training. This motivates temporal manifold matching at scale for long-horizon world models. Building on this insight, we introduce LongForcing, a distillation approach that scales teacher supervision to long student self-rollouts. LongForcing preserves the short-horizon teacher-forcing and causal ODE-distillation stages, while replacing the realscore teacher in the final distribution-matching stage with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher. The long-horizon teacher supervises extended student self-rollouts using the standard distribution-matching formulation, without modifying the student architecture or increasing inference cost. We evaluate LongForcing on text-to-video generation and interactive action-conditioned world models, achieving a VBench Quality score of 85.52 and improving WorldRoamBench 60s action score by 23.9 points in first-person ablations. Qualitative stress tests further sample interactive rollouts up to 24 hours, far beyond the training horizon. These results suggest that scaling supervision along the temporal axis is a practical step toward long-horizon world models. The project website and code are at https://github.com/Fantasy-AMAP/LongForcing.
authors: Ziyu Zhu, Zhaoxu Sun, Fan Jiang, Mengchao Wang, Junfeng Ni, Ting-Bing Xu, Zhicheng Liu, Mu Xu
bullets: Targets progressive visual degradation, motion inconsistency, and object-identity collapse beyond the training horizon.
Identifies a supervision-horizon gap: short-window distillation does not constrain delayed rollout failures.
Extends temporal manifold matching by replacing the final-stage realscore teacher with an extended-horizon bidirectional teacher.
Preserves the student architecture and inference cost while supervising long self-rollouts.
Reports a VBench Quality score of 85.52, a 23.9-point improvement on the WorldRoamBench 60s action score in first-person ablations, and qualitative rollouts up to 24 hours.

papers.abstract: Cross-domain few-shot action recognition (CD-FSAR) aims to recognise unseen action classes in a target domain from a handful of labelled videos. Despite advances in representation learning, CD-FSAR inference still relies on prototypes estimated from extremely limited support examples. To assess this bottleneck, we perform an oracle analysis with the representation fixed. Constructing oracle prototypes and decision boundaries from ground-truth query labels improves 5-way 1-shot accuracy by 7--20 percentage points across five target datasets. This reveals a substantial estimation gap: the representation contains useful discriminative information, but prototypes and boundaries estimated from scarce supports fail to capture each episode's true class structure. Motivated by this, we propose TRACE, a training-free transductive inference framework that improves episode-level estimation without modifying the backbone. TRACE comprises two complementary stages. Confidence-Thresholded Transductive Prototype Refinement (CTPR) refines support-based prototypes using confidently predicted queries. The refined prototypes initialise a lightweight per-episode classifier, which Transductive Classifier Refinement (TCR) further adapts by encouraging confident, class-balanced predictions over all queries. Together, the two stages improve prototype and boundary estimation, enabling better use of information in the unlabelled queries. Across five target datasets (HMDB51, UCF101, SSv2, Diving48, and RareAct) in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong CD-FSAR baseline, including gains of more than six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot, while recovering much of the oracle-estimated gap. These results suggest that improving test-time estimation is a powerful, broadly applicable complement to representation learning for CD-FSAR under extreme support scarcity.
authors: Changyi Li, Zeyu Yang, Yu Xiao
bullets: An oracle analysis shows that scarce-support prototype and decision-boundary estimation is a major bottleneck, despite useful learned representations.
TRACE uses two training-free transductive stages: confidence-based prototype refinement (CTPR) and class-balanced classifier refinement (TCR).
The method leverages confidently predicted unlabelled queries to better estimate each episode’s class structure.
Across five target datasets and both 1-shot and 5-shot settings, TRACE consistently improves a strong baseline, with gains exceeding six percentage points on HMDB51 1-shot.
The approach recovers much of the oracle-estimated gap, but its scope is limited to test-time transductive settings with available unlabelled queries.

papers.title: Closing the Estimation Gap: Training-Free Transductive Inference for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Action Recognition
