papers.abstract: Modern text-to-video (T2V) models generate visually compelling videos, yet meaning-preserving changes in prompt wording can substantially alter semantic realization and overall quality. Existing prompt rewriting modifies the inference input, whereas conventional post-training constructs supervision from one prompt formulation at a time; neither explicitly optimizes reliability across equivalent forms. We introduce VARI (Verified Alignment over Representations of Intent), a group-structured framework that treats automatically verified formulations of the same visual intent as a shared supervision unit. VARI builds matched form-seed rollout pools, cross-scores each video against all forms, and applies a wording-independent structured intent audit to identify valid realizations and hard semantic failures. Group-Consistent Distillation (GCD) aligns every verified form with interchangeable valid realizations, while Form-Contrastive Flow-DPO (FC-DPO) learns group-level preferences from audited positive-negative pairs, prioritizing same-seed, different-form contrasts. On HunyuanVideo-1.5, VARI attains the highest T2V-CompBench, VBench, and StoryEval scores among the evaluated methods. On prompt-form extensions of T2V-CompBench and VBench, it improves weakest-form alignment over the strongest prompt-level baselines by 2.45 and 3.55 points and reduces cross-form drop by 30.5% and 32.2%, respectively, while preserving visual quality. Human evaluation, natural-caption controls, prompt-enhancement experiments, diversity analyses, and transfer to LTX-2.3 further support the robustness and transferability of these gains, while VARI requires no additional inference-time module.
authors: Mingxuan Zhu, Hohei Chan, Shiyuan Liu, Yuanxing Zhang, Lu Chen
bullets: Addresses inconsistent semantic realization and quality when equivalent prompt wording changes.
Builds verified groups of formulations for the same intent, using matched form-seed rollouts and cross-form scoring.
Group-Consistent Distillation aligns valid realizations, while Form-Contrastive Flow-DPO learns preferences from audited positive-negative pairs.
On HunyuanVideo-1.5, VARI achieves the best reported T2V-CompBench, VBench, and StoryEval scores among evaluated methods.
On prompt-form extensions, it improves weakest-form alignment and reduces cross-form performance drops; results also transfer to LTX-2.3.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of VARI. (A) Verified forms and shared seeds define a rollout grid. papers.abstract: Prompt optimization and generator post-training are two complementary ways to improve text-to-video (T2V) generation, and recent systems increasingly train both modules jointly. However, optimizing a prompt policy and a video generator from the same terminal reward creates two ambiguities: prompt quality is confounded with stochastic generation, and the two modules may realize overlapping local improvements. We introduce FlowCred, a two-level framework for joint T2V post-training. First, hierarchical credit assignment uses matched prompt-seed rollout grids to separate prompt-level credit from prompt-conditioned generator residuals under shared randomness. Second, functional coordination probes alternative current-policy prompts at states from actual generation trajectories, providing generator-aware evidence for prompt optimization while selectively attenuating generator updates already supported by conditioning changes. Across multiple T2V benchmarks, FlowCred consistently improves matched joint-training baselines. On LTX-2.5, FlowCred improves a strictly matched joint-training control from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval, without increasing decoded-video or reward-model-call budgets. Factorial and realized-update analyses show complementary contributions from prompt shaping and generator routing, while human evaluation and transfer across backbones and updater families provide further supporting evidence.
authors: Mingxuan Zhu, Yanwei Huang, Shiyuan Liu, Xinzhi Zhang, Shujie Li, Yuanxing Zhang, Lu Chen
bullets: Addresses two ambiguities in shared terminal-reward training: prompt quality versus stochastic generation, and overlapping improvements between modules.

Improves matched baselines on multiple T2V benchmarks; on LTX-2.5, scores rise from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval.
Analyses and human evaluation support complementary prompt shaping and generator routing, with evidence across backbones and updater families.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
authors: Xiaoxue Wu, Xinyu Gao, Fang Yu, Yu Qiao, Xinyuan Chen
bullets: Targets redundant, frame-level memory retrieval that gives all query tokens the same historical context.
Organizes historical KV-cache tokens into online semantic clusters guided by attention patterns.
Uses query-adaptive, fine-grained retrieval to broaden historical access under a fixed memory budget.
Improves long-range and inter-shot consistency, especially when earlier content is revisited, while approximating full-memory access.
Introduces VLM-assisted metrics for evaluating faithful consistency across shots; experiments support the framework’s effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of CineMem. Existing autoregressive video generation methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level, which may result in redundant retrieval, inefficient memory utilization, and overlooked heterogeneous information needs across query tokens. CineMem combines an online-clustered KV cache with query-adaptive retrieval to enable a finer-grained memory retrieval strategy. As illustrated by the attention receptive fields, CineMem provides broader (2/3 vs. 12/12) access to historical information under the same retrieval budget.

Figure 3: Our memory retrieval framework. Through multi-stage initial adaptation, we convert a bidirectional model into an autoregressive multi-shot model with memory retrieval. During inference, queries access memory from the first chunk, adjacent chunk, and retrieved candidates via token-wise and head-wise retrieval. Previous adjacent chunks are progressively integrated into retrieval candidates through online KV-cache clustering with cluster balancing. During training, resampling ground truth frames provides memory inputs to alleviate error accumulation.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results. We compare CineMem with representative causal and bidirectional baselines on 15s multi-shot video generation. Representative examples illustrate the qualitative improvements of our method.
Figure 6: Implementation of PTCS. PTCS assigns low scores when either unchanged semantic elements are not preserved or intended changes are not correctly realized.

Figure 4: Intrinsic memory-selection patterns under the full-memory setting. Memory tokens exhibit semantically meaningful clustering structures, while different query-head pairs show distinct preferences over memory tokens. Although each query-head pair selects a subset of the most relevant tokens, their union covers nearly the entire memory. See Appendix A for more details.

Figure 10: Visualization of token clustering before and after RoPE. Compared with Pre-RoPE representations, Post-RoPE similarities exhibit stronger positional dependency and weaker semantic clustering structures.

Figure 9: Comparison of memory-token coverage and selection overlap under three selection granularities: query-head-wise, query-wise with head averaging, and head-wise with query averaging. The horizontal axis denotes the fraction of memory tokens selected by each selection unit. The left panel reports the percentage of distinct memory-token positions covered by the union of all selections, while the right panel shows the percentage of selected positions with multiplicity at least two.

Figure 11: Precision (left) and recall (right) of different retrieval strategies under varying fullmemory attention thresholds. For each query-head pair, full-memory attention serves as the oracle, and retrieved tokens are considered matched if they fall within the top-x% oracle-ranked memory tokens. Online-clustered KV cache retrieves tokens from query-specific selected clusters, while Latent-group, Frame-group, and Sliding Window perform frame-level or fixed-context retrieval. All curves are averaged over attention blocks. Online-clustered KV cache achieves a better precision-recall trade-off, providing a selective approximation to full-memory access.

Figure 7: Visualization of query-wise memory selection diversity. For the selected memory frames, different queries exhibit distinct spatial preferences within the same frame, revealing heterogeneous memory selection behaviors. Each query corresponds to the first latent of the current chunk, and each memory unit is formed by grouping neighboring 3× 3 spatial tokens.

Figure 8: Visualization of head-wise memory selection diversity. For the selected memory frames, different attention heads exhibit distinct memory preferences. We visualize multiple query regions for generality. The variations among highlighted regions across rows in each heatmap illustrate the diversity of head-wise memory selection.
Figure 15: A case of qualitative result of ablation study.
Figure 16: Distribution of evaluation prompts across different content categories, shot counts, and revisit distances.

Figure 12: Practical efficiency comparison during autoregressive rollout. The left figure shows the per-chunk denoising time, and the right figure shows the peak allocated GPU memory during 42-chunk generation.
Figure 17: Cases of longer video generated by CineMem.

Figure 13: Qualitative comparison between PTCS and similarity-based inter-shot consistency metrics. The examples illustrate cases where PTCS better reflects transition correctness by jointly considering semantic preservation and prompt-specified changes.

Figure 14: Comparison between query-wise retrieval and the query-group retrieval variant. Querywise retrieval performs independent memory retrieval for each query token, while the query-group variant recursively partitions query tokens based on intra-group content diversity. Queries with similar content preferences are assigned to the same group and share the retrieved memory.

Figure 18: A failure case in complex multi-entity scenarios. Although the generated video preserves revisitation consistency across shots, inconsistencies such as character disappearance and detail changes occur during the transition from Shot 1 to Shot 2. This example highlights the difficulty of handling multi-entity reasoning and spatial relationship preservation in autoregressive video generation.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc linearization is an attractive way to accelerate pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers (Video DiTs), yet existing methods largely treat the quality loss induced by attention replacement as a recovery problem. We show that a more fundamental bottleneck lies upstream: \emph{initialization}. Random initialization discards pretrained knowledge, whereas manual weight reuse transfers it through rigid and incomplete source--target correspondences. We introduce \textbf{LinMorph}, which recasts Video DiT linearization as a learnable softmax-to-linear weight transformation problem. Instead of copying predefined counterparts, LinMorph learns a cross-parameter morphism that lets each target Gated DeltaNet (GDN) parameter draw jointly from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including for parameters with no direct softmax counterpart. A single morphism is shared across layers and learned through local teacher alignment, while producing layer-specific initializations from their respective pretrained weights. The resulting weights are then materialized as independent GDN modules for progressive distillation and joint recovery.Since the morphism operates in weight space rather than token space, it can be learned on short, low-resolution clips and directly reused at larger video scales. Across pretrained Video DiTs, LinMorph enables markedly faster recovery and better final generation quality than random initialization and heuristic weight reuse. Results show that efficient linearization depends not only on how a converted model is recovered, but critically on how pretrained knowledge is transferred before recovery. Project page: https://lonelyling.github.io/LinMorph.
authors: Lingyi Long, Congyue Zhao, Xiaoou Li, Yanmin Qian, Tao Huang
bullets: Identifies initialization—not only post-conversion recovery—as a key bottleneck in Video DiT linearization.
Learns a shared cross-parameter softmax-to-linear morphism instead of relying on random initialization or rigid weight copying.
Allows each GDN parameter to combine information from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including unmatched parameters.
Uses local teacher alignment on short, low-resolution clips, then applies layer-specific transformed weights for progressive distillation and recovery.
Reports faster recovery and better final generation quality across pretrained Video DiTs than random or heuristic initialization.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for unified text-vision synthesis, surpassing traditional U-Net architectures in generative tasks. One key innovation lies in its Multimodal Self-Attention (MM-SA) interaction, where image and text tokens are concatenated and processed via self-attention. However, this mechanism poses significant challenges for editing, rendering conventional U-Net-based attention manipulation methods ineffective. To address this limitation, we propose QK-Edit, a training-free framework that exploits the unique attention dynamics of MM-DiTs for precise text-guided image and video editing. By introducing a novel query-key manipulation strategy, our method isolates and adjusts critical attention components to achieve an optimal balance between prompt fidelity and structural consistency. This enables seamless edits across various tasks, including object addition, object removal, object replacement, changing background, changing material, changing color, and style transformation. Notably, it can be easily implemented with feature replacement in inference. QK-Edit demonstrates superior editing performance on state-of-the-art models, such as FLUX and HunyuanVideo, effectively bridging the gap between generative power and editable flexibility in MM-DiTs, and paving the way for scalable multimodal content creation.
authors: Tiancheng Shen, Zilong Huang, Xiangtai Li, Zhijie Lin, Jiyang Liu, Yitong Wang, Jiashi Feng, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Jun Hao Liew
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of applying conventional U-Net attention-editing methods to MM-DiTs with concatenated image-text tokens.
Manipulates query-key interactions to balance prompt fidelity with preservation of the original structure.
Supports object addition, removal, replacement, background and material changes, color edits, and style transformations.
Implemented through feature replacement during inference, without additional training.
Demonstrates effective editing on MM-DiT models including FLUX and HunyuanVideo.

papers.abstract: Understanding facial behaviour in video requires answering three fundamental questions: when a key facial expression occurs, where the model attends on the face at that moment, and why that evidence is necessary rather than merely correlated. Today's multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can label and describe video, but they rarely provide faithful explanations, especially for small facial movements that change over time. We present VideoFace-X-LLM, a framework for explainable facial video understanding comprising two key components. First, we introduce ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video-text corpus for facial behaviour understanding, automatically constructed from CelebV-HQ videos and validated through human evaluation and a two-model audit (at most 2.3% contradictions), demonstrating consistent gains across two backbone architectures. Second, H-TCC (Hierarchical Temporal Spatial Causal Concepts), which finds the key temporal moments (When), the facial regions (Where), and verifies its causal necessity (Why) through targeted occlusion. Fine-tuning on ExplainFace raises appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87% (+13.39), with gains of +4.38 on actions, +6.77 on temporal emotion, and +11.84 F1 on deepfake detection. We also measure the explanations pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, an Adebayo sanity check, and a necessity test rather than only showing examples. Our models, code, and corpus are available on request for research use.
authors: Anubhav Kataria, Shreya Ghosh, Jingwen Ye, Abhinav Dhall
bullets: Targets faithful explanations for small, evolving facial movements that existing MLLMs often describe without causal grounding.
Introduces ExplainFace, a weakly supervised video–text corpus built from CelebV-HQ and validated by humans and a two-model audit with at most 2.3% contradictions.
Uses H-TCC to identify key moments, relevant facial regions, and causal necessity through targeted occlusion.
Fine-tuning improves appearance Macro F1 from 19.48% to 32.87%, with additional gains for actions, temporal emotion, and deepfake detection.
Evaluates explanation quality using pointing lift, face/edge lift, stability, a sanity check, and a necessity test.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity surgical video generation is increasingly important for surgical education, simulation, and downstream AI training, as conventional simulation pipelines are limited by cost, realism, and scenario diversity. Adapting generic text-to-video diffusion models to surgical procedures remains difficult, however, due to complex anatomical structures, intricate tool-tissue interactions, the inherently hierarchical nature of surgical workflows, and the scarcity of curated training data outside a few well-studied procedures. We propose a surgical video generation framework that combines hierarchical procedural annotation with curriculum transfer learning. Surgical procedures are decomposed into three levels (phase, task, and action) and a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model is progressively adapted from coarse to fine-grained surgical context, supported by a dynamic sampling strategy that handles variable-resolution and variable-length surgical clips. We instantiate the framework on Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach robotic thyroidectomy, a procedure for which no curated benchmark currently exists. Relative to the preceding task-level model, the final action-level model reduces FVD by 20.1% and FID by 15.7%, and a matched-budget ablation indicates that these gains arise from the curriculum design rather than from additional training. A user study with six clinicians rates visual realism highly while highlighting remaining gaps in anatomical accuracy and clinical reliability. The proposed framework offers a step toward AI-driven surgical simulation in procedures where curated data are scarce.
authors: Youngbin Kong, Seungho Lee, Jae Kyung Shin, Jong-hyuk Ahn, Hyoun-Joong Kong, Kyu Eun Lee
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of generating surgical videos with complex anatomy, tool–tissue interactions, hierarchical workflows, and scarce curated data.
Decomposes procedures into phase, task, and action levels, then progressively transfers these contexts into a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model.
Uses dynamic sampling to accommodate surgical clips with varying resolutions and lengths.

On Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach robotic thyroidectomy data, the action-level model improves FVD and FID over the task-level model; matched-budget ablation attributes gains to the curriculum design.
Six clinicians rated visual realism highly but identified remaining limitations in anatomical accuracy and clinical reliability.

papers.abstract: Reliable video reasoning requires models to produce correct answers and expose supporting visual evidence. Open-o3-Video enables verifiable reasoning by embedding timestamps and object-level bounding boxes into reasoning traces, but is restricted to frames from an initial sparse sampler. We introduce Open-o3-Video-v2, which formulates video reasoning as a unified agentic evidencegrounded process. The model identifies missing information, acquires additional observations, grounds the moments and objects supporting its reasoning, and writes this evidence into the trajectory before continuing or answering. To support this behavior, we construct STGR-v2-CoT135K, including 52K multi-turn agentic grounded reasoning trajectories, and STGR-v2-RL-13K for reinforcement learning. We further propose Clue-Seek GRPO (CS-GRPO), which tracks how tool calls change accumulated evidence, rewards clue coverage and step-wise gains, and penalizes excessive, repetitive, or uninformative retrieval. On V-STaR, Open-o3-Video-v2-4B achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM, outperforming its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone by 8.5% and 12.6%, respectively. It also delivers consistent gains across general video understanding, long-video reasoning, and temporal grounding benchmarks. These results show that active evidence acquisition and verifiable object-level grounding are complementary for reliable video reasoning. The code and models are released at https://msalab-pku.github.io/projects/Open-o3-Video-v2.
authors: Jiahao Meng, Zhongyuan Bao, Yue Tan, Haiquan Wen, Renrui Zhang, Anna Wang, Jason Li, Yanwei Fu, Yunhai Tong, Ming-Hsuan Yang
bullets: Frames video reasoning as an agentic process: identify gaps, retrieve additional observations, ground relevant moments and objects, then answer.
Introduces STGR-v2-CoT135K and STGR-v2-RL-13K datasets for multi-turn grounded reasoning and reinforcement learning.
Proposes Clue-Seek GRPO, rewarding evidence coverage and useful retrieval while penalizing repetitive or uninformative tool calls.
The 4B model achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM on V-STaR, with gains over its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone and across multiple video benchmarks.
Code and models are publicly released.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of the data construction pipelines and STGR-v2 data statistics. (a) Open-o3-Video constructs single-turn spatio-temporal grounded reasoning data through initial annotation, bounding-box filtering, and selfconsistency checking. (b) Open-o3-Video-v2 extends this pipeline to agentic multi-turn reasoning through strict data filtering, spatio-temporal evidence annotation, CoT (chain-of-thought) rewriting with tool observations, and quality checking. (c) STGR-v2-CoT-135K contains 135K SFT samples across seven task groups, including 59K spatio-temporal grounded reasoning samples, while STGR-v2-RL-13K contains 13K RL samples selected through strict filtering.

Figure 3 Overview of the reinforcement learning designs in Open-o3-Video and Open-o3-Video-v2. (a) Open-o3-Video produces a single-turn spatio-temporal grounded reasoning trace and optimizes it with format, answer-accuracy, and grounded thinking rewards; the thinking reward jointly evaluates temporal proximity and spatial overlap with the target evidence. (b) Open-o3-Video-v2 extends this formulation to multi-turn agentic reasoning with CS-GRPO. The model iteratively calls crop_video to acquire denser observations, while CS-GRPO tracks how the accumulated evidence evolves across calls and assigns credit according to whether each interaction contributes useful new evidence.

Figure 1 From single-pass spatio-temporal grounded reasoning to agentic evidence seeking and grounded reasoning. Left: Open-o3-Video-v1 reasons over fixed sampled frames and grounds visible evidence, yielding verifiable spatio-temporal support on short videos. Center: Open-o3-Video-v2 performs adaptive temporal zoom-in through iterative crop_video calls, following a seek–ground–reason process to find evidence beyond the initial frames for long video understanding. Right: Comparison of five models on V-STaR and six general video understanding and reasoning benchmarks.

Figure 7 Qualitative comparisons on fine-grained visual counting. Top: For counting food pictures on the menu at 17:49, Open-o3-Video-v2 inspects the relevant 1065–1075 s interval and grounds the menu at 1069.5 s, providing a clearer view of the individual food images and enabling the correct count of 11. In contrast, Video-o3 searches an incorrect temporal interval and produces an incorrect count. Bottom: For counting the people in the car, both methods inspect the relevant 10–12 s interval, but Open-o3-Video-v2 further grounds the car and its occupants, allowing it to distinguish three individuals rather than two. In both cases, explicit instance-level grounding complements temporal evidence acquisition by resolving the individual visual entities required for accurate counting.

Figure 4 Qualitative comparison with Video-o3. Left: Video-o3 searches an incorrect segment, while Open-o3-Video-v2 inspects the relevant 1170–1340 s interval and grounds the pigs at 1310 s, providing direct evidence for answer D. Right: although the question explicitly specifies 07:48–07:50, Video-o3 queries 478–480 s and incorrectly predicts bowing. Open-o3-Video-v2 inspects the correct 468–470 s interval, grounds the three girls at 469 s, and identifies their group handshake. In both cases, the acquired observation is converted into explicit spatio-temporal evidence and used directly in the subsequent reasoning process.

Figure 8 Representative failure cases of Open-o3-Video-v2. Top: Insufficient identity knowledge leads to an incorrect answer even after a relevant face is retrieved. Middle: During a camera pan, inaccurate instance discrimination and association across changing views lead to an incorrect count of the women appearing offstage. Bottom: The model anchors its reasoning to the wrong scoring event and misidentifies the player who ends the game. These examples expose remaining limitations in world knowledge, fine-grained spatio-temporal instance reasoning, and temporal event selection, respectively.

Figure 5 Effect of initial input-frame count and maximum interaction budget on LVBench and Video-Holmes. Results are evaluated on randomly sampled 30% subsets of each benchmark using the same model and decoding configuration.

Figure 6 Qualitative comparisons on fine-grained visual reasoning. Top: For action-change perception, Open-o3-Videov2 inspects the relevant 134–143 s interval and grounds the man’s hand, sea urchin, and fish at 138.5 s. The denser observation reveals the fish’s blue body and yellow fins after the interaction, enabling the correct answer. Bottom: For fine-grained event understanding, Open-o3-Video-v2 grounds the metal ring cutter and pineapple slice and further inspects the 33–46 s interval using denser temporal sampling. The resulting observation reveals the repeated removal of the fibrous core and provides the missing evidence for answer B. In both cases, targeted temporal observation together with explicit object-level grounding exposes the decisive visual evidence and yields a human-verifiable spatio-temporal reasoning trace.

papers.abstract: Recent video super-resolution (VSR) models achieve efficient one-step generation through diffusion distillation. However, high-resolution inference remains costly, and distilled models are difficult to align with human preferences. These challenges call for improvements in both model architecture and training strategy. We present \textbf{FlashVSR+} to address both limitations. On the architecture side, we introduce hybrid attention based on the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models, while retaining sparse global interaction for long-range consistency. It achieves up to $2\times$ DiT speedup and 45\% lower peak memory, enabling spatially untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090. On the training side, we propose Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD) for preference-aligned one-step generation. Ry-DMD uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts to incorporate black-box rewards into distribution matching, without backpropagating through the reward model. We further show that Ry-DMD generalizes beyond VSR to T2I generation. Together, FlashVSR+ delivers stronger restoration quality and substantially improves high-resolution efficiency, with consistent gains in user preference. We release our code, models, and training data at \href{https://www.flashvsr.tech}{\textcolor{FlashBlue}{\textbf{www.flashvsr.tech}}}.
authors: Ruchang Yao, Shi Guo, Junhao Zhuang, Mingde Yao, Xin Cai, Jiahao Zhan, Bin Fu, Xinyuan Chen, Yu Qiao, Tianfan Xue
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of high-resolution VSR and the difficulty of aligning distilled models with human preferences.
Uses hybrid attention that emphasizes local interactions while preserving sparse global context for long-range consistency.
Introduces Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD), which uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts without backpropagating through the reward model.
Reports up to 2× DiT speedup and 45% lower peak memory, enabling untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090.
Achieves stronger restoration quality and consistent user-preference gains; Ry-DMD also generalizes to text-to-image generation.

papers.abstract: Video reward models are trained and evaluated on human preferences between videos that often differ simultaneously on properties such as prompt alignment, visual fidelity, motion, and generator identity. As a result, aggregate accuracy does not reveal which video properties a reward model can reliably distinguish. We construct preference pairs by controlled interventions that change one property of a generated video while holding the rest fixed. The resulting pairs, by construction, provide preferences for how the videos differ along a specific dimension, without requiring any human annotation. We propose IsoVRBench, a video generation reward modeling benchmark of 8,000 such pairs across eight interventions, and show that state-of-the-art models separate broad quality differences between generators but miss important features such as temporal order. The best reward model reaches only 60.8% on reordered frames against 100% for humans, and rankings on existing benchmarks do not predict this failure. Using the synthetic isolated intervation pairs as training data leads to 1) IsoVRM, a reward model outperforming its counterpart trained with a larger human labeled preference dataset by 3.8 points on VBench-2.0, 2) IsoWan, the video generator post-trained with IsoVRM, outperforming its human-data counterpart in human preferences, and 3) gains that stack when combined with human data. Because intervention pairs are automatically generated rather than collected, the benchmark and training data can be easily extended as generators evolve.
authors: Shuyue Stella Li, Jacqueline He, Jiahui Chen, Sreya Dutta Roy, Yulia Tsvetkov, Luke Zettlemoyer, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Xiaochuang Han
bullets: Existing aggregate preference accuracy can hide failures on specific video properties such as temporal order.
The benchmark contains 8,000 pairs across eight controlled interventions, changing one property while holding others fixed.
State-of-the-art models distinguish broad generator-quality differences but perform poorly on reordered frames, with the best reaching 60.8% versus 100% for humans.
Training on these synthetic pairs produces IsoVRM, which improves VBench-2.0 performance by 3.8 points over a counterpart trained on a larger human-labeled dataset.
IsoVRM also improves post-trained video generation, with gains stacking when combined with human data; the approach can be extended as generators evolve.

papers.abstract: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.
authors: Jihye Kang, Jiwon Park, Namhyuk Ahn
bullets: Open-weight deployment creates constraints beyond user-side image defenses.
Protection should balance effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance.
Long-horizon attack simulations are used to improve resistance to protection removal and re-alignment.
Experiments with one protection tool show stronger re-alignment resistance but reduced clean fidelity.
Further research is needed for practical model-side protection.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Maintaining image protection after open-weight release. Each row shows edits of the same protected image as the attack progresses, with the corresponding clean-image edit on the right. t: attack epochs.

Figure 4: The image the artist publishes, the trigger it carries, and the target that trigger activates, on two images. (a) the original artwork; (b) the protected version the artist publishes, carrying the trigger at ϵ = 2/255; (c) the difference between (a) and (b), amplified forty times so that it is visible at all; (d) the target the protective alignment is trained to produce from (b). Columns (a) and (b) are indistinguishable by design: over the 100 evaluation images the mean distortion between them is 45.1 dB PSNR, 0.990 SSIM and 0.010 LPIPS. The target in (d) is never published. It is what the deployed model produces in place of an edit, and each target renders the identifier of the image it is assigned to, which is why the two differ.

Figure 6: The re-alignment attack on three images. Each pair is one protective alignment: the upper row of the pair received no tamper-resistance training (w/o TR) and the lower row did (w/ TR). Columns are attack epochs t ∈ {0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20} under one seed, and the last column is an edit of an unprotected image under the same model. Without the training the protection is gone after a single epoch in all three cases, and the edit becomes indistinguishable from the clean-image edit beside it. With it the edit is still far from that clean-image edit at t = 20, although the pattern is no longer crisp. The last column is what a user who never asked for protection gets from the same model, while our clean-fidelity metric quantifies changes in reconstructions rather than edits.

Figure 5: Every model we trained, placed in the plane of the two costs a provider pays. The horizontal axis is the protection surviving twenty epochs of attack, and the vertical axis is clean fidelity against the original autoencoder, so a point up and to the right is better on both. Filled points are the four that nothing else beats on both axes at once. Inside the shaded band the protection has fallen to the level of a model that was never aligned, and one ablation lies below the axis at 9.2 dB.

Figure 3: Protection under the re-alignment attack. Protection LPIPS is measured at each attack epoch. The shaded region marks scores at or below the unaligned reference of 0.225, where protection is considered removed.

Figure 2: Directional agreement with the realignment attack. Cosine similarity is measured between encoder parameter displacements; both simulations use the re-alignment objective. Long-horizon simulation better tracks the direction of later attack updates.

Table 2: Every constant used to produce the models of Table 1. The first block specifies protective alignment of the original autoencoder; the second specifies tamper-resistance training starting from the aligned checkpoint. The simulated attacks used in tamper-resistance training are drawn from a pool of thirty-six configurations, one per epoch in the listed order, so a twenty-epoch run sees encoder-scope attacks first and decoder-tail attacks after.

Table 5: What each group of the tamper-resistance objective contributes. All models are trained for twenty epochs and evaluated under the same attack; ablations remove the epoch-long refresh or a loss component from Equation 2. Protection is measured by LPIPS between the edit of a protected image and the edit of its clean counterpart, reported before the attack and after twenty epochs of it. Fidelity is measured by the PSNR of an unprotected reconstruction against the original autoencoder’s, measured before the attack. Removal denotes the first attack epoch at which protection LPIPS falls to or below the unaligned reference of 0.225; > 20 indicates that the threshold was not reached within the first 20 attack epochs. The last two ablations illustrate that a delayed removal epoch can coincide with substantial loss of clean fidelity.

Table 4: Additional protection and clean-fidelity metrics for the models in Table 1. Protection is reported in LPIPS and SSIM between the edit of a protected image and the edit of its clean counterpart, so larger LPIPS and smaller SSIM both mean stronger protection. The fidelity column reports pre-attack LPIPS between an unprotected reconstruction and the original autoencoder’s, where smaller means less collateral damage to users who never asked for protection.

Table 1: Protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, and tamper resistance. Protection is measured by LPIPS before attack and after 20 epochs of encoder re-alignment. Fidelity is pre-attack reconstruction PSNR relative to the original autoencoder. Removal denotes the first attack epoch at which protection LPIPS falls to or below the unaligned reference of 0.225; > 20 means the threshold was not reached.

Table 3: How well each way of guessing the attacker’s position actually predicts it. Tamper-resistance training evaluates its objective at some approximation of where the attacker will be, and the two candidates are K differentiable inner steps from the current weights, or the offset reached by running the attack for one full epoch. Each row reports the cosine between that approximation’s parameter displacement and the displacement a real re-alignment attack has reached after t epochs, together with the ratio of their lengths at t=10. A cosine near zero means the approximation points somewhere else; a small norm ratio means it points the right way but has barely moved. The two blocks differ only in which objective the approximation descends; the ground truth is the same re-alignment attack in both.

Table 6: The trade-off along one run of tamper-resistance training, sampled every five epochs. The first row is the aligned checkpoint the run starts from, so reading down the table shows what each further five epochs of training buys and costs. Protection LPIPS, clean-fidelity PSNR, and removal epochs follow the definitions in Table 5. Protection is reported before attack and after one and twenty attack epochs, and clean fidelity is measured before attack.

papers.abstract: Memory-based long-video generation aims to combine user control with long-range visual consistency. We organize this process into three functional components: a planner, an adapter, and a generator. Representative multi-shot systems couple memory to generator-specific interfaces or use predefined agent workflows, rather than independently training a memory policy for cross-shot objectives. We introduce REEL, a general-purpose visual-memory planner. Through a unified tool interface, REEL learns to retrieve references, create missing visual evidence, and update persistent memory. Backend-specific adapters translate its evidence plans into supported conditioning inputs, allowing the same policy to guide different black-box video generators. To train REEL, we construct two high-quality datasets, REEL-SFT-4k and REEL-RL-1k, covering diverse interaction patterns and prompt types. Training proceeds in three stages: supervised fine-tuning, single-shot Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and multi-shot GRPO. Multi-shot GRPO carries policy-generated memory across consecutive shots, so later outcomes guide earlier reference selection and memory updates. REEL-Bench tests identity preservation and intended state changes under text-only requests and timed reference-image uploads. On JoyAI-Echo~1.5 and MiniMax-H3, REEL improves cross-shot consistency on ST-Bench by 15.1\% and 20.7\%, and Core-100 on our proposed REEL-Bench by 2.41 and 8.32 points, respectively, over the no-memory baseline.
authors: Hang Xu, Guohui Zhang, Xiaoxiao Ma, Hu Yu, Jie Huang, Jiayin Xiao, Lin Song, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Feng Zhao
bullets: Targets cross-shot visual consistency while preserving user control in long-video generation.
Uses a planner–adapter–generator design: the planner manages memory, while adapters translate plans for different black-box video generators.
Trains with supervised fine-tuning followed by single-shot and multi-shot GRPO, enabling later shots to inform earlier memory decisions.
Evaluated on identity preservation and intended state changes with text requests and timed reference-image uploads.
Improves cross-shot consistency over no-memory baselines on JoyAI-Echo 1.5 and MiniMax-H3, including 15.1% and 20.7% gains on ST-Bench.

papers.abstract: Video world models must generate physically plausible futures, not just realistic frames. Existing approaches typically use semantic, physical, or predictive information to guide the visual generation stream, leaving a fundamental question: where inside the generator should predictions of scene evolution live? Standard video tokens jointly encode appearance and dynamics, but provide no distinct state for learning and reading predictive dynamics. We answer this question with the Physical Registry: temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with video tokens, and receive future-representation supervision, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. In a controlled comparison of predictive-state interfaces on Physics-IQ Verified, Physical Registry improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9/8.7 points on I2V/V2V, the largest gain among the interfaces we compare. Across all Cosmos and WAN backbones, Physical Registry improves Physics-IQ Verified scores. With only 0.45% additional parameters, it enables Cosmos 3 Nano 16B to surpass the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B (43.56 vs. 42.7). On WorldModelBench, it also improves physical adherence and the total score for all four evaluated backbones. Because the registry becomes candidate-specific while remaining readable, the Physical Registry Selector (PRS) ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate registry readouts depart from the shared forecast before full denoising is complete. Across four backbones, this selection improves I2V scores by 5.6-15.9% without completed-video external scoring. Together, these results support a broader principle: dynamics prediction should live as an explicit model state that co-evolves with the video representation. Project page: https://grainsack.github.io/physical-registry/
authors: Shinseong Kim, Jaeseok Jeong, Jianlong Fu, Youngjung Uh

With 0.45% extra parameters, Cosmos 3 Nano 16B exceeds the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B.
The Physical Registry Selector ranks futures from intermediate registry readouts, improving I2V scores by 5.6–15.9% without completed-video external scoring.

papers.abstract: Agentic video reasoning systems gather and assess video evidence across stages, selecting relevant spans as visual evidence for answering questions. New candidates and observations prompt reassessment of the current span, but revisions can correct localization errors or discard useful evidence already present in the adopted span. Systems therefore need to connect evidence organization across stages with temporal state control, allowing accumulated information to jointly inform revision assessment while explicit adoption decisions govern how assessment outcomes affect downstream visual evidence. We introduce VideoSlate, a stateful commit-control framework built around shared evidence. A typed evidence blackboard links candidate spans, provenance, construction, and verifier observations, enabling an incumbent-relative certifier to assess revision support from the candidate, current span, and related proposals. Based on certification, the controller authorizes a revision or retains the current span, separating evidence accumulation from state updates and recording each decision and its evidence on the blackboard. Extensive evaluations across video grounding and grounded question-answering benchmarks show that VideoSlate can improve temporal localization through selective revision.
authors: Shuo Zheng, Yuanjie Dang, Peng Chen, Jianjun Xiang, Ronghua Liang, Mohammed Bennamoun, Qiuhong Ke
bullets: Addresses the risk that iterative evidence gathering either retains localization errors or discards useful existing evidence.
Uses a typed evidence blackboard to track candidate spans, provenance, construction, verifier observations, and related proposals.
An incumbent-relative certifier evaluates whether a proposed revision is supported by accumulated evidence.
A controller explicitly commits to revising the span or retaining it, while recording each decision and its evidence.
Evaluations on video grounding and grounded question-answering benchmarks show improved temporal localization through selective revision.

papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in joint audio--visual generation. However, audio--visual synchronization remains a challenge, as generated speech and sound often temporally misalign with visual events. A key bottleneck is the lack of human-annotated data, reliable evaluation benchmarks, and synchronization-aware evaluation models for generated audio--visual outputs. To address these limitations, we conduct a comprehensive study spanning data, benchmarking, and reward modeling. We first introduce SyncReward-Data-80K, a dataset containing 80K professional synchronization ratings for clips from eight audio--visual generators. A taxonomy-guided construction pipeline covers four sound-event families: Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient. We further construct \textbf{SyncReward-Bench}, a held-out benchmark of 1K clips, each independently rated by multiple professionals. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate specialized synchronization metrics and omni-modal models, revealing their substantial misalignment with human judgments. Finally, we develop SyncReward, a reward model that combines semantic--temporal contrastive pretraining on real clips with human supervision on generated clips. As an evaluation metric, SyncReward achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among the evaluated methods. As a reward, it improves synchronization through inference-time best-of-$N$ selection and reinforcement learning based post-training. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and code at https://github.com/WeChatCV/SyncReward.
authors: Kaisi Guan, Ying Ba, Wenjing Wang, Xihua Wang, Chen Li, Jing Lyu, Ruihau Song
bullets: Addresses the lack of human-aligned data and reliable synchronization evaluation for audio–visual generation.
Releases SyncReward-Data-80K with professional ratings spanning Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient sound events.
Introduces SyncReward-Bench, a 1K-clip held-out benchmark with multiple independent professional ratings.
Finds that existing synchronization metrics and omni-modal models often misalign with human judgments.

Combines semantic–temporal contrastive pretraining with human supervision; it achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among evaluated methods and improves synchronization via best-of-N selection and reinforcement-learning post-training.

papers.abstract: Training-free language-based video anomaly detection (VAD) uses frozen vision--language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) to localize abnormal events without task-specific model-weight optimization. Existing approaches increasingly exploit broader temporal and semantic context, yet generic context does not necessarily foreground abnormal events or specify how video-level semantics should modify local anomaly scores. We introduce a training-free semantic feedback framework that uses VAD-guided active observation for video anomaly understanding (VAU) and returns the resulting anomaly-focused description to refine temporal detection. Starting from an upstream anomaly-score curve, we adapt reasoning-based iterative frame selection: high-score regions seed the observations, and anomaly scores together with VLM relevance assessments guide subsequent temporal exploration. A frozen video-language model generates a single open-ended anomaly description from the selected frames. The description is returned through two complementary feedback levels: video-level feedback determines whether the score distribution should be suppressed, preserved, or sharpened, with selective visual rechecking, while local feedback retrieves event-related windows and promotes scores only after target-local visual verification. All model weights remain frozen, and feedback is applied once without regenerating the description. On the HIVAU video-summary evaluations of UCF-Crime and XD-Violence, VAD-guided observation improves GPT-rated reasonability, detail, and consistency over the matched CLIP-guided variant. For VAD, semantic feedback improves the re-evaluated upstream detector from 84.36% to 86.25% AUC on UCF-Crime and from 68.07% to 72.58% AP on XD-Violence, where the final AUC is 91.74%.

papers.abstract: Test-time agentic computation can improve multimodal large language models (MLLMs) through planning, tool use, iterative perception, and reflection, but indiscriminate computation may duplicate resolved work, introduce noisy evidence, and perturb correct predictions. We propose that such computation should be residual: allocate additional computation only to requirements unresolved by the base model and, after a localized failure, recompute only the affected states. We instantiate this formulation in ReTAC, a training-free multiagent framework for video spatial reasoning. ReTAC organizes supplementary computation around unresolved requirements. It plans ordered steps to acquire missing spatial evidence and combines the observations with compatible native evidence for reasoning. In addition, it uses stage-aligned verification to localize failures to planning, perception, or reasoning. Dependency-based recovery recomputes only affected states while reusing unaffected ones. Extensive experiments show that ReTAC achieves the highest overall score among the compared methods across three mainstream MLLMs and two widely adopted benchmarks. Further analyses show that gains from additional computation depend not only on how much is used, but also on where it is allocated and which valid intermediate states are preserved.
authors: Yike Wu, Keyan Chen, Qixiong Wang, Xi Xiang, Maofei Que, Xiaolong Jiang, Xiaoqin Zhang, Ling Shao, Shijian Lu
bullets: Addresses redundant, noisy, or disruptive computation in MLLMs during video spatial reasoning.
Uses a training-free multiagent framework that plans steps to gather missing spatial evidence and combines it with native evidence.
Applies stage-aligned verification to identify whether failures arise from planning, perception, or reasoning.
Uses dependency-based recovery to recompute affected states while preserving valid intermediate results.
Achieves the highest overall score among compared methods across three MLLMs and two benchmarks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly understanding (VAU) aims to generate language-level interpretations of anomalous events in long videos, requiring visual evidence that supports explanation beyond anomaly detection alone. Existing VAU pipelines commonly rely on anomaly-centric or predefined temporal sampling strategies, which efficiently emphasize suspicious moments but overlook contextual cues, object interactions, and temporally distributed evidence needed for reasoning. Motivated by recent progress in learnable temporal selection for long-video question answering, we revisit VAU temporal sampling as a downstream-aligned evidence selection problem. We introduce the semantic-conditioned Temporal Sampling Q-Former that learns to select temporal visual evidence through the VAU generation objective. Since generic VAU prompts provide weak video-specific guidance, we condition the sampler on CLIP-embedded object tags automatically extracted from the input video. These tags are used only for temporal evidence selection and are not appended to the LLM generation prompt, separating sampler conditioning from prompt augmentation. The proposed sampler operates in visual-token space, computes soft temporal selection weights from frame-level representations, and merges duplicated selections before response generation. Experiments on HIVAU-70K show that our model achieves the best performance among the compared fine-tuned models, while ablations demonstrate that learnable temporal sampling improves over fixed anomaly-focused sampling and that CLIP-embedded object-tag conditioning further improves over generic-prompt conditioning. Our results suggest that temporal sampling in VAU should be aligned with explanation-oriented evidence utility rather than anomaly saliency alone.
authors: Hangil Park, Seungheon Kim, Tae-Kyun Kim
bullets: Targets video anomaly understanding, where explanations require contextual cues, object interactions, and evidence spread across long videos.
Introduces a Temporal Sampling Q-Former that learns soft temporal evidence selection from the VAU generation objective.
Conditions selection on automatically extracted CLIP-embedded object tags without adding them to the LLM prompt.
Operates in visual-token space and merges duplicate selections before response generation.
On HIVAU-70K, it performs best among compared fine-tuned models; ablations show gains over fixed anomaly-focused and generic-prompt sampling.

papers.abstract: Autoencoders are the core component of latent video generative models, compressing high-dimensional videos into compact latent spaces for downstream generation. However, existing video autoencoders are primarily optimized for pixel-level reconstruction, providing limited supervision for learning structured latent representations. We argue that videos should not be treated merely as signals to be reconstructed, but rather as 2D projections of dynamic 3D worlds that exhibit explicit and well-structured geometric properties. Building on this insight, we propose \textbf{V}ideo \textbf{G}eometry \textbf{G}rounded \textbf{A}utoencoder (\textbf{VGGA}), a geometry-aware video autoencoder that explicitly incorporates geometric constraints into the reconstruction process. Specifically, VGGA grounds the learned representations along three complementary geometric dimensions: \emph{Structural Depth}, \emph{Motion Correspondence}, and \emph{Projective Warping}. These objectives are unified within a Video Geometry Decoder, which employs a shared spatio-temporal upsampling trunk to jointly optimize geometric learning and RGB reconstruction. Through these geometry-grounded objectives, VGGA encourages the latent representations to capture the underlying 3D structure and motion of dynamic scenes. VGGA consistently improves video generation across both geometry-centric and human-motion domains, reducing gFVD by 28.1\% on RealEstate10K and 37.7\% on Taichi-HD. Notably, these substantial generation improvements are achieved while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality, demonstrating that geometry-grounded representation learning yields a more effective latent space for video generation.
authors: Chaofan Gan, Yian Zhao, Shijie Li, Tieyuan Chen, Zicheng Zhao, Mehrtash Harandi, Weiyao Lin
bullets: Motivation: Pixel-reconstruction objectives provide limited supervision for learning structured video latents.
Method: Incorporates Structural Depth, Motion Correspondence, and Projective Warping constraints through a shared Video Geometry Decoder.

Results: Reduces gFVD by 28.1% on RealEstate10K and 37.7% on Taichi-HD across geometry-centric and human-motion domains.
Scope: Gains are reported while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong results on video question answering, yet often fail to recover the temporal structure that makes a video coherent. They may merge neighboring events, miss single-event progression, or infer implausible relations across events. We study structured temporal understanding as the ability to recover event structure from visual evidence, including event boundaries, single-event progression, and multi-event relations. We argue that this gap arises from a mismatch between current post-training objectives and temporal reasoning, where caption-style supervision allows models to rely on language shortcuts rather than visual temporal grounding. To address this, we propose EventLens, a vision-centric reinforcement learning framework that learns video understanding through event-structure recovery. Instead of reconstructing captions, EventLens trains models to recover temporal structure under controlled perturbations, such as altered temporal granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order. We instantiate this framework with a three-level temporal ontology and derive three verifiable task families: event segmentation, progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning. These tasks admit deterministic rewards, enabling task-specialized GRPO training without human preference labels or learned reward models. We further introduce multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MT-OPD) to consolidate specialized policies into a unified model. Experiments on Qwen3-VL backbones show consistent improvements on temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning benchmarks, while preserving general video-QA performance. Learning curves further demonstrate that EventLens achieves comparable downstream transfer with significantly reduced training cost compared to direct mixed RL optimization.
authors: Guowen Zhang, Boshen Xu, Zihao Yue, Ziheng Wang, Xiaokun Liu, Xin Tao, Wenyu Qin, Pengfei Wan, Qin Jin
bullets: Targets temporal-structure failures such as merged events, missed progression, and implausible cross-event relations.
Uses vision-centric reinforcement learning with controlled temporal perturbations, including altered granularity, reversed progression, and shuffled event order.
Trains three task families: event segmentation, progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning, with deterministic rewards and task-specialized GRPO.
Uses multi-teacher on-policy distillation to combine specialized policies into one unified model.
Reports improved temporal grounding and event-sensitive reasoning while preserving general video-QA performance and reducing training cost versus direct mixed RL.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EventLens. EventLens adopts a two-stage training pipeline for event-structure reinforcement learning. In Stage I, deterministic rewards train task-specialized GRPO teachers for event-boundary localization, single-event progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning. In Stage II, MT-OPD routes each student trajectory to the corresponding teacher and distills dense token-level teacher logits into one deployable student. The teacher is selected by recovery family, so each student trajectory is supervised by the teacher trained with the matching verifier.

Figure 1: Motivation and task view of unified event-structure recovery. Existing video MLLMs often suffer from boundary ambiguity, progression ambiguity, and relation ambiguity when they must recover explicit temporal structure. We address these bottlenecks with three event-structure recovery tasks: event-boundary recovery, single-event progression discrimination, and multi-event relation reasoning through next-event prediction, fill-in, and narrative reordering.

papers.abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.
authors: Shuo Gao, Chenhao Zheng, Zhongzheng Ren
bullets: Addresses the linear memory and latency growth caused by encoding every video frame as visual tokens.
Uses a training-free, inference-only strategy that ranks frames by prompt relevance and diversity, then packs them at varying resolutions.

Experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME report consistent improvements over full-resolution, token-reduction, and keyframe-selection baselines.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, gains are 12.9%, 10.6%, and 9.7% on the three benchmarks, respectively.

papers.abstract: Detailed video captioning has become an essential semantic interface for multi-modal understanding and generation. While existing methods mainly target short videos, extending them to long videos remains challenging, primarily due to limited context windows of current video understanding models. A naive solution is to adopt segment-wise captioning followed by concatenation, yet this paradigm often suffers from inconsistent subject references and fragmented long-range narratives. To mitigate these issues, we introduce PIGEONS, an incremental long-video captioning model built upon a Persistent Identity Gallery and an Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary. Before caption generation, PIGEONS scans the entire video to construct an identity gallery that captures key subjects along with their visual references, thereby providing a stable referential anchor. The model then performs clip-by-clip captioning conditioned on the persistent gallery and an evolving overarching narrative summary, which compactly maintains and updates essential long-range contextual information after each captioning step. To enable these capabilities, we develop a three-stage training strategy that integrates supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PIGEONS markedly improves long-video captioning performance, achieving superior accuracy, completeness, and subject referential consistency over existing methods, while maintaining competitive performance on short-video captioning.
authors: Xinlong Chen, Weihong Lin, Yuanxing Zhang, Xinyu Liu, Yue Ding, Bozhou Li, Bohan Zeng, Yang Shi, Qiang Liu, Pengfei Wan, Liang Wang, Tieniu Tan
bullets: Addresses fragmented narratives and inconsistent subject references caused by segment-wise captioning and limited context windows.
Builds a Persistent Identity Gallery from the full video to maintain stable visual references for key subjects.
Generates captions clip by clip while updating an Evolving Overarching Narrative Summary for long-range context.
Uses a three-stage training strategy combining supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Experiments report improved long-video captioning accuracy, completeness, and referential consistency, with competitive short-video performance.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Inference pipeline of PIGEONS. The model first scans all video clips to construct a global identity gallery. Stage 2 further optimizes gallery construction via RL, improving both accuracy (Racc) and efficiency (Reff). Stage 3 performs caption SFT, enabling detailed caption generation conditioned on multiple contexts while evolving the overarching narrative summary. papers.abstract: Not every moment in a video is equally useful for recognizing an action. A few decisive moments often carry the evidence: the instant an object moves, the peak of a dive, or one object placed on another. Existing video datasets rarely provide large-scale, action-conditioned labels for which short segments carry that evidence. This work asks whether vision-language models can identify meaningful moments at scale and whether those labels improve action recognition.We introduce Meaningful Moments (MM), a corpus of about 4.58 million VLM-generated per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 class-labeled videos spanning Something-Something v2 (SSv2), Kinetics-400 (K400), and Diving-48 across 622 action classes. We freeze the action classifier and vary only temporal sampling. An alpha-parameterized comparison of importance-led selection against an importance-inverted control separates gains from the VLM signal from gains caused by variable-density sampling alone. Across all three datasets, VLM-derived importance is informative: at the hard-cut endpoint, keeping VLM-important segments outperforms keeping VLM-designated filler. Usefulness depends on class structure. On Diving-48, importance-led fast-forwarding preserves full-video recognition while the inverted control collapses by roughly 30 percentage points. On K400, hard-cut selection beats uniform sampling by 1.45 percentage points, rising to 2.05 under threshold selection. On SSv2, the labels carry signal but do not recover full-video performance. Direct scoring matches greedy removal within its noise floor at roughly 25 times fewer oracle calls, and a four-VLM cross-oracle study shows consistent downstream trends. We release the importance labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0; SSv2 class strings remain under CC-BY-NC-4.0.
bullets: Introduces about 4.58 million per-segment importance scores for nearly 500,000 videos across SSv2, Kinetics-400, and Diving-48, covering 622 action classes.
Uses frozen action classifiers and controlled temporal sampling, including importance-inverted selection, to distinguish VLM signal from variable-density sampling effects.
VLM-important segments preserve full-video performance on Diving-48, improve Kinetics-400 accuracy over uniform sampling, and provide signal but not full recovery on SSv2.
Direct scoring achieves results comparable to greedy removal with roughly 25× fewer oracle calls; trends are consistent across four VLMs.
Releases the labels and evaluation protocol under CC-BY-4.0, with SSv2 class strings separately licensed under CC-BY-NC-4.0.

papers.abstract: Recent trackers built on foundation models such as the Segment Anything Model (SAM) achieve strong performance by propagating object masks through memory. However, this strength is also a key source of failure: under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors, an incorrect prediction can enter the tracking loop and be propagated over time, resulting in persistent identity drift. Existing approaches seek to prevent such failures through improved memory and temporal modeling, but once a failure occurs, the tracker has no explicit mechanism to recognize or correct it. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. We address this gap with Dual-Agent, a failure-aware tracking framework that complements propagation with explicit verification and recovery. A vision-language verification agent first reasons over spatio-temporal context to determine whether the tracker is still following the target. When a failure is detected, a correction agent uses temporal context to recover the target before tracking continues. The correction agent is trained on real SAM3 failures, augmented with targeted identity-switch and distractor perturbations that expose it to challenging ambiguities during recovery. On LVOS-v2 and SecVOS, Dual-Agent improves SAM3 by 1.2 and 2.7 $J\&F$, respectively. Importantly, the proposed framework transfers without retraining to SAM2.1, SeC, and Cutie, as well as to long-term video object tracking benchmarks including LaSOT-ext, TNL2K, and VOT-LT2022. Our results show that explicitly reasoning about when tracking fails and how to recover provides a complementary path to robust tracking beyond improving propagation alone. Project page: valaybundele.github.io/Dual-Agent.
authors: Valay Bundele, Susmit Agrawal, Mehran Hosseinzadeh, The Nam Nguyen, Hendrik P. A. Lensch
bullets: Targets persistent identity drift caused by incorrect masks being propagated through tracker memory under occlusion, reappearance, or distractors.
Uses a verification agent to reason over spatio-temporal context and identify whether tracking has failed.
Uses a correction agent trained on real SAM3 failures plus identity-switch and distractor perturbations to recover the target.
Improves SAM3 by 1.2 J&F on LVOS-v2 and 2.7 J&F on SecVOS.
Transfers without retraining to multiple trackers and long-term video tracking benchmarks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video generation enables long-horizon synthesis but requires repeated forward passes through large diffusion transformers. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing intermediate computation, yet existing controllers often couple two decisions: when to synchronize the cache exactly and how much computation to repair between synchronizations. We introduce Frequency-Step Cache (FSC), which separates these roles. FSC schedules exact full-computation anchors on a dense-to-sparse trajectory, while a lightweight latent-space risk based on frequency-resolved drift and token age controls inter-anchor repair through whole-step replay, selective token recomputation, or full repair. On SkyReels-V2, whole-step reuse provides most of the acceleration, while selective token computation is most effective as fidelity repair. A controlled ablation shows that using one reactive signal for both synchronization and repair reduces fidelity at matched latency, with the same separation advantage observed on FramePack and Matrix-Game. Across multiple autoregressive video backbones, FSC improves speed-quality trade-offs. On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed reaches 2.36x speedup versus MotionCache's 2.275x while improving SSIM by 0.019 and PSNR by 0.5 dB. At MotionCache-matched speed, FSC-Quality improves SSIM by 0.031 and PSNR by 1.0 dB and lowers LPIPS by 0.024. Without retuning, FSC-Quality transfers to SkyReels-V2 14B at 2.12x speedup versus 1.79x for MotionCache.
authors: Kerry Xu, Param Misra, Zachary Stenglein, Athri Karunamurthy, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
bullets: Targets the high cost of repeated diffusion-transformer passes in long-horizon autoregressive video generation.
Uses dense-to-sparse exact-computation anchors for synchronization and frequency-resolved drift plus token age to select repair intensity.
Supports whole-step reuse, selective token recomputation, or full repair; whole-step reuse drives most speedup, while selective computation mainly restores fidelity.
On SkyReels-V2, FSC-Speed achieves 2.36× speedup with +0.019 SSIM and +0.5 dB PSNR over MotionCache; FSC-Quality improves matched-speed quality, including +0.031 SSIM and +1.0 dB PSNR.
Transfers without retuning to SkyReels-V2 14B and shows benefits on FramePack and Matrix-Game.

papers.title: Frequency-Step Cache: Separating Synchronization and Repair for Efficient Autoregressive Video Diffusion
papers.tldr: Frequency-Step Cache accelerates autoregressive video diffusion by independently scheduling exact cache synchronization and adaptive latent-space repair, improving speed–quality trade-offs across multiple backbones.

papers.abstract: We present Gen Through the Lens, a camera-controllable image-to-video generation framework that synthesizes videos from a given reference image while enabling realistic and physically consistent camera operations. Unlike previous models that treat camera motion as abstract conditioning or rely on a single coordinate system, our approach explicitly decomposes and fuses control signals across three coordinate spaces: the camera coordinate (modeled by intrinsic parameters), the world coordinate (represented by spatial geometry hints), and the object coordinate (described by 3D bounding boxes of target subjects). Through cross-coordinate conditioning fusion, these heterogeneous cues are unified to guide the generative process, enabling precise control of camera motion, focus, and framing while preserving temporal and spatial coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces controllable and visually consistent results across diverse camera operations, outperforming existing approaches in both realism and editability.
authors: Shuai Li, Jinxu Xiang, Xinyuan Li, Hanlei Guo, Xiyang Tan, Alan Zhao, Xiaotong Zhao, Ran Zhang
bullets: Addresses limitations of methods using abstract camera conditioning or a single coordinate system.
Decomposes control signals into camera intrinsics, spatial geometry hints, and 3D bounding boxes for target subjects.
Fuses these heterogeneous cues to control camera motion, focus, and framing while maintaining temporal and spatial coherence.
Experiments show visually consistent, controllable results across diverse camera operations, with improved realism and editability over existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Predictive video representations do not by themselves specify how a multimodal system should handle missing sensors. We transfer frozen V-JEPA2 features to a set of heterogeneous sensors comprised by RGB video, depth video, and radar time series. A shared fusion model uses modality queries, fixed sensor slots, and explicit availability to classify breathing activity and pose from all seven non-empty sensor subsets. The contribution is a controlled evaluation of subset supervision, pooling capacity, and representation transfer on 39 OMuSense-23 subjects with five subject-group folds and three seeds. With matched downstream parameter counts, the final model reaches recording-level activity macro-F1 of $75.23%\pm0.60$ averaged across seven subsets. Supervising all subsets in each batch improves the matched query-pooling control by 1.923 percentage points (conditional 95% subject-bootstrap interval [0.647, 3.209]), while query pooling shows no clear advantage over matched mean pooling under balanced supervision. Radar probes support transfer beyond pooled wavelet pixels, 64-token inference approximately preserves mean activity performance, and the tested Consensus-JEPA loss adds no measured benefit against its exact control.

papers.abstract: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models have emerged as powerful generative priors across domains ranging from molecular design to high-resolution image synthesis. However, standard diffusion sampling is inherently biased toward high-likelihood regions, often limiting the diversity of outputs. In many domains, a single, high-likelihood sample is insufficient. Instead, diverse portfolios of high-performing solutions are required, motivating methods that uncover a model's full expressive range. Here we show that integrating Quality-Diversity (QD) optimisation with diffusion models enables the discovery of diverse, high-performing outputs. We first propose Quality-Diversity Diffusion, a framework that adapts QD to diffusion models by directly optimising the model's latent noise and conditioning embeddings and leveraging embedding models to quantify diversity. Second, we introduce a novel h-space Spectral Mutation operator, which guides search along directions of maximal semantic sensitivity by analysing principal singular vectors of the model's input-to-activation Jacobian. We evaluate our combined approach, Spectral-Guided Quality-Diversity Diffusion, on text-to-image generation. Against 12 baselines, our method consistently achieves the lowest FID score, demonstrating an excellent balance of image quality and diversity.
authors: Hannah Janmohamed, Joao Correia, Penousal Machado, Antoine Cully
