papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are good at video understanding and code generation, but it remains unclear whether they can recover the physical laws underlying videos, a capability essential for converting videos into executable simulations and for providing structured physical supervision in robotics. Captioning motion video does not imply that a model has inferred its governing dynamics, estimated quantitative parameters, or can regenerate the observed scene from code. Existing video-physics benchmarks evaluate plausibility, property estimation, or future-state prediction, but offer limited insight into whether models can translate visual dynamics into runnable simulation code. We introduce PhySimCode, a benchmark for physics video-to-code generation: given only a raw video, a model must infer the relevant physics, recover parameter values, and generate runnable Python that reproduces the input video. The dataset contains 160.6K procedurally generated samples spanning 162 physics phenomena across analytic SciPy simulations and PyBullet-rendered rigid-body, articulated, fluid, and contact-rich scenes; each sample bundles the simulation code, physical parameters, rendered video, and a structured chain-of-thought covering observations, laws, ODEs, numerical methods, and validation checks. We evaluate ten state-of-the-art closed- and open-source MLLMs along physical-law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery. Models reliably state physics laws (4.27-4.93/5) yet score only 1.51-2.47/5 on inferring them from video, and the best system (Claude Sonnet 4.6) recovers just 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within $\pm 20\%$, exposing a substantial video-to-simulation gap. The 2,430-video evaluation set is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SourajaKundu123/PhySimCode and the evaluation code at https://github.com/SourajaKundu/PhySimCode
authors: Souraja Kundu, Aditya Gupta, Joel Julin, Yizhou Zhao, Liuyue Xie, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Targets video-to-code generation requiring physical-law inference, parameter recovery, and runnable simulation reproduction.
Includes 160.6K procedurally generated samples covering 162 phenomena across analytic and PyBullet-based simulations.
Evaluates law correctness, simulation equivalence, code executability, and parameter recovery across 10 MLLMs.
Models state physics laws well (4.27–4.93/5) but infer them from video poorly (1.51–2.47/5).
The best system recovers only 7.7% of ground-truth parameters within ±20%, highlighting the benchmark’s challenging scope.

papers.abstract: The explosive growth of short videos has presented significant challenges to content governance. Traditional manual labeling is inefficient, slow to iterate, and costly. Therefore, we explore and develop a multi-stage autopilot labeling framework aimed at progressively increasing the level of automation in short video content annotation. To move beyond the heavy reliance on human expert labeling at the initial L0 stage, we first introduce a discriminative MLLM labeler at the L1 stage, which is fine-tuned with supervised data to directly predict labels for short videos. Advancing to the L2 stage, we shift to a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data and use it for zero-shot labeling, enabling flexible generalization without task-specific supervision. In the L3 stage, we propose an agentic annotation workflow, and equip the agent with several key tools, which empower the agent to handle complex, unfamiliar, or vaguely defined cases, significantly reducing the need for human intervention. We conduct extensive experiments across various content issues, and results demonstrate that each stage of the autopilot labeling framework progressively improves labeling accuracy, and has significantly reduced manual labor costs in real-world applications by up to 85%.
authors: Junwen Chen, Hongwei Wang, Zixuan Wang, Jingbing Wang, Gorden Liu, Sheng Siong Ong, Xiaojiao Zang, JuChin Chao, Ze Jin, Kaiwen Men, Yin Li, Jeremy Li, Zhuolin Hao, Hongyu Xiong, Yang Song

L1 uses a supervised fine-tuned discriminative multimodal large language model (MLLM) for direct label prediction.
L2 applies a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short-video data for zero-shot, flexible labeling.
L3 introduces an agentic workflow with tools to address complex, unfamiliar, or ambiguous cases.
Experiments across content issues show progressive accuracy gains and substantial real-world reductions in manual effort.

papers.abstract: Coherent multi-shot audio-visual video generation requires maintaining consistent identities while depicting evolving states and coordinating sounds across shot boundaries. Although dense captions describe individual shots in detail, they rarely specify which entities persist, how their states change, or which entities and actions produce sounds. To address this limitation, we propose Structured Stateful Relational Scripts (SSRS), a textual supervision representation that separates persistent entity and voice identities from shot-specific visual and auditory states. SSRS explicitly encodes sound-source bindings and temporal relations, while a global audio-visual event sequence connects local actions and sounds, including events that continue across shot boundaries. We further introduce MSAV-Script-100K, a large-scale dataset of curated multi-shot audio-visual videos paired with detailed SSRS annotations, enabling models to learn identity persistence, state transitions, and event continuity from structured supervision. Experiments demonstrate improvements in cross-shot consistency, adherence to specified state changes, and audio-visual alignment, highlighting the effectiveness of our SSRS and MSAV-Script-100K for coherent multi-shot audio-visual generation. Our proposed dataset is available at \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/shenlehan/MSAV-Script-100K}{MSAV-Script-100K}.
authors: Chen Zhao, Lehan Shen, Qilong Huang, Hongyu Li, Zhuoliang Kang, Xiaoming Wei, Jian Yang, Ying Tai
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of maintaining entity identity, state changes, and sound coordination across shot boundaries.

Introduces MSAV-Script-100K, a curated dataset of multi-shot audio-visual videos with SSRS annotations.
Experiments show improved cross-shot consistency, state-change adherence, and audio-visual alignment.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly used to generate videos with targeted emotional expressions, yet existing evaluation methods mainly rely on holistic video-text alignment and provide limited insight into whether failures arise from target-emotion expression, intensity control, or specific affective cues. We introduce EmoTrace-Bench, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark that controls emotion intensity and selected affective cues in prompts and evaluates generated videos at multiple levels. EmoTrace-Bench contains 448 controlled prompts covering eight emotions, two intensity levels, and diverse cue conditions. Using 12 T2V models, we generate 5,376 videos and evaluate target-emotion presence, perceived intensity, and ten audiovisual dimensions of emotional expression with an automated evaluator calibrated and validated against human annotations on a subset of the data. Results reveal substantial differences across models and prompt designs. Prompts that explicitly describe a character's emotional reaction are followed more reliably than prompts that describe only events or scenes, whereas adding more affective cues or using more explicit cinematic audiovisual language does not consistently improve emotional generation. These results illustrate how aggregate alignment scores may overlook localized differences in target-emotion expression, intensity control, and cue realization. EmoTrace-Bench provides a traceable and interpretable framework for diagnosing emotional video generation without modifying existing generation pipelines, and we release the prompts and the automated evaluation rules.
authors: Yeheng Wang, Liudan Shi, Yi Zheng, Jingke Li, Shiyuan Liu, Xin Tao, Yuanxing Zhang, Guoyu Sun
bullets: Addresses the limitations of holistic video-text alignment metrics for analyzing emotional-generation failures.

Explicit descriptions of characters’ emotional reactions are more reliably followed than event- or scene-only descriptions; extra cues and cinematic language do not consistently help.
Releases prompts and evaluation rules for traceable diagnosis without changing existing generation pipelines.

papers.abstract: Video understanding agents rely on a harness to acquire evidence, use tools, and reason, but improving it requires substantial effort. Recent self evolution methods seek to optimize harnesses through execution feedback to reduce human intervention. However, existing methods often rely on annotated video questions and answers or focus on updating model parameters, leaving harness evolution from unlabeled videos underexplored. VideoEvoHarness jointly evolves a Questioner and a Solver harness from unlabeled videos with frozen model parameters. The Questioner constructs questions and computes reference answers directly from video memory records. Question quality assessments and Solver execution trajectories guide question generation policy revisions. The Solver supports evolving skills, strategies, hyperparameters, and tools using execution feedback. Executable strategies define workflows in code, reducing repeated interpretation of natural language instructions. Each round, candidate harnesses are compared on identical validation questions, with validated improvements retained for later use. Experiments on benchmarks and a dedicated benchmark question set, using videos disjoint from evolution videos, show higher overall accuracy than initially and transfer gains across backbones. Overall accuracy on this set also improves progressively across rounds. This supports our foundational framework for harness evolution from unlabeled videos, opening a promising direction for self evolving video agents. Code is available at https://github.com/Wei-Xin-Xu/VideoEvoHarness.
authors: Weixin Xu, Yifan Liu, Yi Wang, Mingfei Rong, Zhenyu Yang, Zhisheng Zhong, Shengsheng Qian, Changsheng Xu

papers.abstract: Sexual harassment represents a pervasive societal challenge, with a substantial proportion of incidents remaining unreported due to insufficient evidence and delayed intervention mechanisms. Smart surveillance systems capable of detecting such incidents in real-time could assist law enforcement and serve as a deterrent. However, video-based harassment detection poses significant challenges, including variations in clothing, illumina- tion, partial occlusions, low resolution, and diverse camera view- points. Despite its social importance, this problem has received limited research attention, primarily due to the scarcity of large- scale annotated video datasets. To address this gap, we extend the Sexual Harassment Video (SHV) dataset to 600 short video clips sourced from YouTube and annotated into harassment and non-harassment categories using consistent labeling guidelines. We fine-tune three state-of-the-art video transformer models, VideoMAE, ViViT, and TimeSformer, pretrained on Kinetics- 400, for binary harassment classification. Experimental results show that all three models achieve competitive classification performance, with TimeSformer attaining the highest test accu- racy of 92.27%, outperforming VideoMAE 91.71% and ViViT 91.16% on the extended SHV test set. Our analysis reveals that performance is notably influenced by dataset size, video quality, frame sampling strategy, and model architecture. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of modern video transformers for this sensitive real-world task.

papers.abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models are highly sensitive to prompt specificity, while iterative prompt optimization typically improves generation quality only through repeated video generation and vision-language model evaluation at inference time. We propose TIDE, a framework that distills this costly search process into an interpretable and reusable prompt-rewriting Skill. TIDE formulates prompt rewriting as a set of source-conditioned rule modules, each targeting a distinct semantic dimension. Once distilled, the frozen Skill activates the relevant rules and generates both positive and negative prompts in a single LLM call, followed by only one T2V generation, without test-time visual search or backbone fine-tuning. Evolved using only 100 prompts over 14 hours, TIDE achieves prompt-optimization performance comparable to computationally expensive search-based methods. Moreover, when transferred to previously unseen video-generation models, TIDE outperforms existing approaches specifically designed or trained for those models. Code is available at https://github.com/xiningin/TIDE_T2V.
authors: Chengxing Zhou, Yuliang Huang, Jingwei Song
bullets: Targets the high sensitivity of text-to-video quality to prompt specificity and the cost of test-time visual search.
Uses source-conditioned rule modules for distinct semantic dimensions, producing positive and negative prompts together.

Transfers to unseen video-generation models and outperforms approaches designed or trained for those models.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Pipeline of the proposed TIDE framework. (1) Prompt Rewriting: Given a raw prompt—typically a short user query—the rewriter activates relevant Skill rules to produce an enhanced prompt. (2) Trajectory Generation: The generated video is critiqued, suggestions guide revised prompt candidates, and tournament selection chooses the next-round incumbent; this loop repeats to iteratively improve generation quality. (3) Experience Distillation: Prompt-optimization trajectories yield reusable, dimension-specific patches for the corresponding rule pools. Once full, a pool’s patches update the associated rule and synchronize it with the Skill for subsequent rewriting.

papers.abstract: Reliable individual monitoring is essential for dairy cattle welfare and early heat stress detection in Precision Livestock Farming (PLF). However, translating raw multi-camera videos into automated diagnostics remains challenging due to disconnected tracking and recognition pipelines and complex physical environments. Dense mutual occlusions and cross-camera viewpoint variations fragment identities, while environmental noise, including camera vibrations, and limited agricultural data obscure subtle heat stress cues such as rapid breathing and flank undulations. To bridge low-level visual features and high-level behavioral diagnostics, we propose CowCare, a unified framework combining viewpoint-robust tracking with spatiotemporal heat stress recognition. Its tracking module, CowTrack, maintains cross-camera identity consistency through a View-Decoupled Aggregation Network (VDA-Net). Instead of relying on static global representations, VDA-Net aggregates localized textures under heavy occlusion and uses a Viewpoint Decoupling Transformer (VDT) to suppress transient viewpoint variations. CowTrack further incorporates a causal online self-supervision mechanism for continuous adaptation to dynamic farm scenes. The resulting tracklets are subsequently processed by TSDF-Net, a fine-grained video understanding network. Its Temporal Stabilization and Aggregation Module (TSAM) suppresses high-frequency jitter, while a Diffusion Semantic Prior (DSP) uses frozen pre-trained diffusion semantics to enhance subtle behavioral signals and mitigate overfitting. Extensive evaluations on two real-world farm benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness: CowTrack achieves 83.48% HOTA and 87.72% IDF1 for global multi-object tracking on MVCow, and TSDF-Net achieves 87.72% Top-1 accuracy on HSCow. These results establish CowCare as a robust end-to-end framework for automated livestock health monitoring.

On two real-world farm benchmarks, CowTrack reports 83.48% HOTA and 87.72% IDF1 on MVCow, while TSDF-Net reaches 87.72% Top-1 accuracy on HSCow.
The framework targets robust automated monitoring in dynamic agricultural environments, though its scope is limited to the evaluated farm benchmarks and visual cues.

papers.abstract: Recent video generative models have shown strong capability in synthesizing high-quality and temporally coherent videos. Yet, adapting them for controllable portrait animation remains nontrivial, as existing methods typically rely on architectural changes or extra conditioning modules, increasing complexity and reducing compatibility with pretrained models. We present CatPortrait, a simple and effective framework that enables controllable portrait animation via 3D face guidance as in-context conditioning. CatPortrait preserves the original video generation backbone and injects structured 3D facial guidance into the input space through spatial concatenation, allowing pretrained image-to-video models to animate portraits without sacrificing their pretrained priors. CatPortrait supports both video-driven and audio-driven portrait animation within a unified framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CatPortrait achieves competitive or superior results across both settings.

papers.abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. ACROSSVAM2.0 combines a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad that removes only the auxiliary component opposing the primary flow-matching gradient on shared LoRA parameters. The design preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects its primary update during adaptation. In a four-way ablation trained for 1,000 steps with three independent seeds, the full method lowers KLT forward-backward cycle error in all three seeds relative to a matched flow-only continuation (mean seed-level difference -0.00711, SD 0.00505), while robust sharpness remains positive in all three. An expanded 24-prompt evaluation (216 videos) yields 9.7% lower aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error than the matched control and near-matched performance on six VBench dimensions; however, the seed-level tracking effect is heterogeneous and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022. These results support a bounded claim: conflict-aware adaptation improves correspondence consistency without broad perceptual degradation, but does not uniformly improve video quality. We release equations, pseudocode, matched outputs, source tables, and artifact provenance.
bullets: Addresses the tension between explicit surface-motion supervision and preserving a pretrained video generator’s appearance prior.
Combines confidence-weighted track/visibility prediction, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad on shared LoRA parameters.
Preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects the primary flow-matching update during adaptation.
Improves aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error by 9.7% versus a matched control, with near-matched performance across six VBench dimensions.
Tracking improvements are heterogeneous across seeds, and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022; video quality is not uniformly improved.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.
authors: Hanxin Zhu, Jianqi Ma, Cong Wang, Zhihao Hu, Junyao Gao, Tianyu He, Junyan Lin, Jiayin Xiao, Jiateng Shou, Sen Liang, Weidong Zhang, Zhibo Chen, Jun Zhang

Combines appearance diffusion, memory-consistent depth completion, dual-stream warping, and geometry-aware refinement.
Supports coherent spatiotemporal reconstruction across dense multi-view camera trajectories.
Handles large-parallax motion, including 180° rotations without input-view overlap.
Produces geometry-faithful videos that can be optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts.

papers.abstract: Sign Language Recognition (SLR) presents complex challenges due to variable signing speeds and spatial intricacies. Specifically, Indian Sign Language (ISL) requires precise modeling of its inherently bimanual nature and is bottlenecked by the scarcity of large-vocabulary benchmarks and the inability of standard models to handle irregular signing velocities. To address this, a structurally-aware hybrid framework for efficient, gloss ISL recognition is proposed. To minimize computational redundancy, an entropy-driven SVD sampler that dynamically extracts informative keyframes is used. Because this subsampling creates irregular physical time gaps, the proposed architecture employs a Continuous Dual Positional Encoding paired with a distance-aware Elastic Transformer to preserve natural signing rhythm. Spatially, a Kinematically-Conditioned Adaptive GCN explicitly models bimanual geometry using unified bone-joint features. To validate our framework, a 120-class, 9,453-video native ISL dataset is created. Augmented by Physical Node Dropout and ArcFace optimization to mitigate subject-specific memorization, our framework achieves a competitive 89.8% accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for complex sign language modeling.

Introduces a 9,453-video, 120-class native ISL dataset and reports 89.8% accuracy, with scope focused on gloss recognition.

papers.abstract: We introduce HumanPhys, a human-centric benchmark for real-world physical perception, and a training corpus emitted by the same pipeline. Each question targets a physically grounded quantity related to people, including depth, inter-person distance, gaze angle, displacement, velocity, heading-step trajectory, blink count, and contact-deformation strength. The rendered probes additionally test illumination inference from body and face cues and camera ego-motion, both with and without a person in the frame. All labels are derived programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state, rather than written by annotators or produced by estimators on the benchmark frames. HumanPhys systematically probes six dimensions of human-centric physical perception: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose. To the best of our knowledge, no existing MLLM benchmark-and-training corpus jointly supervises this set of human-centered physical quantities under direct metadata- or renderer-derived labels. The six dimensions appear only partially dissociable across the tested MLLMs. We benchmark a range of open- and closed-source MLLMs on HumanPhys and find that all six capability dimensions remain challenging for current models. We hope HumanPhys will support future research on multimodal systems that perceive and reason about people in the physical world.
authors: Yiming Zhang, Enzhi Zhou, Junan Lin, Dulan Zhou, Weiqiang Wang, Yuge Huang, Jian Liu
bullets: Covers six dimensions: spatial state, kinematics, blink events, deformation, illumination, and camera pose.

Labels are generated programmatically from sensor calibration, source metadata, or renderer state rather than human annotation or model estimation.
The benchmark includes a training corpus produced by the same pipeline and evaluates both open- and closed-source MLLMs.
Results indicate that all six dimensions remain challenging and are only partially dissociable for current MLLMs.

papers.abstract: We present CAST-ASD (Causal Attention over Speakers and Time), a causal joint model for active speaker detection (ASD). Recent ASD models improve performance by jointly processing all faces in a scene, but operate offline, with the full clip available before any frame is labelled. Low-latency causal detectors instead process each face independently. CAST-ASD combines joint face reasoning with fully causal inference. It applies scene-level attention across faces within the current frame and causal temporal attention over each face's history, enabling information sharing across speakers with zero lookahead. Its parameter count does not grow with the number of faces. On MSDWild, where most negative face-frames contain a visible competing speaker, CAST-ASD reduces competing-speaker false alarms by 32% relative to the causal per-face detector it extends, with larger gains as scene occupancy increases. It outperforms all causal baselines on both validation splits while using only one-tenth the inter-speaker parameters of a three-block fixed-roster convolution. Code and models are available at https://github.com/prathamg007/CAST-ASD.
authors: Pratham Gupta, Haotian Qi, Tushar Sandhan, Gabriel Skantze
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between offline joint models and causal per-face detectors.
Uses scene-level attention across faces in the current frame and causal temporal attention for each face.
Keeps parameter count independent of the number of faces.
On MSDWild, reduces competing-speaker false alarms by 32% versus its causal per-face baseline, with larger gains in more crowded scenes.
Outperforms causal baselines on both validation splits while using one-tenth the inter-speaker parameters of a fixed-roster convolution model.

papers.abstract: Training-free sparse attention is a practical route to efficient video diffusion transformer inference, yet existing methods typically fix the competition domain at each query row for every attention head. Prior work primarily addresses how to estimate token-level importance within this fixed domain; whether the domain itself should adapt to head heterogeneity remains under-specified. We introduce EG-Sparse, a training-free framework that routes low-entropy heads to a grouped cross-head pool while retaining per-row local selection for high-entropy heads, using only scores already materialized by the sparse pipeline. A controlled diagnostic fixes the ranking score and varies only the competition rule: grouped cross-head selection reduces low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, whereas forcing high-entropy heads into an all-head global pool increases it by 7.9%. Across four configurations, EG-Sparse achieves higher video quality while reducing attention density and GPU denoising latency compared with strong training-free sparse-attention baselines. Mechanism ablations further show that selective domain adaptation outperforms uniform, random, and fixed domain-assignment policies. These results support competition-domain adaptation as a distinct design axis within centroid-guided training-free sparse attention.
authors: Tiantian Liu, Meng Wan, Zhiqiang Liang, Jue Wang, Ningming Nie, Yangang Wang
bullets: Existing methods use a fixed competition domain for every attention head, despite head heterogeneity.
EG-Sparse routes low-entropy heads to grouped cross-head selection while keeping high-entropy heads on per-row local selection.
A controlled diagnostic found grouped selection reduced low-entropy-head reconstruction error by 9.8%, while global pooling increased high-entropy-head error by 7.9%.
Across four configurations, the method improved video quality while lowering attention density and GPU denoising latency versus strong training-free baselines.
Ablations favored selective domain adaptation over uniform, random, and fixed assignment policies.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EG-Sparse. A fixed row-wise domain constrains low-entropy heads because the budget cannot flow across rows to where it is most needed, whereas indiscriminate all-head global competition penalizes high-entropy heads. EG-Sparse resolves both: entropy routes low-entropy heads to a grouped cross-head pool, retains per-row local selection for the remaining heads, and merges both masks for execution by the sparse attention kernel.

(b–c) Two representative heads from the same layer show distinct dense centroid-attention patterns: a low-entropy head concentrates its mass on a small set of query–key cluster pairs, whereas a high-entropy head distributes attention broadly across keys. This heterogeneity motivates head-adaptive competition domains.

Figure 3: Competition-Domain Mismatch under a Fixed Ranking Score. Bars report the relative reconstructionerror change from the per-row local baseline for low- and high-entropy heads; error bars show mean ± 95% CI over 200 HunyuanVideo-T2V-13B prompts at 480P. The overlaid curves report the retained-budget ratio relative to the perrow local baseline. Low-entropy heads benefit increasingly from domain expansion, whereas high-entropy heads incur a +7.9% error increase under all-head global selection, where low-entropy heads capture a disproportionate share of the pooled budget.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires answering questions from the observed video, with evidence drawn from recent observations or earlier events. Historical context can improve recall but may interfere with judgments based on recent frames. Its usefulness depends on both when it is introduced and which clips are selected, while relevance alone does not guarantee sufficient evidence for an answer. We propose SPARE, a framework that combines adaptive historical retrieval with visual encoder sharing. A lightweight gate predicts whether recent observations provide sufficient evidence to answer the question. When additional evidence is predicted to be necessary, a multimodal embedding model retrieves relevant historical clips to supplement the current context. LoRA instruction tuning trains the understanding model to use recent observations and retrieved history jointly and abstain when the evidence remains insufficient. To reduce redundant visual parameters, the understanding and retrieval branches share a visual encoder while retaining separate language backbones. Four linear adapters align the shared features with the retrieval model through distillation at the visual token and final retrieval embedding levels. With visual-only inputs, SPARE achieves 77.78% on the evaluated Real-time and Backward task groups of OVO-Bench and 73.31% on StreamingBench. Compared with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluated at 2 fps, SPARE improves accuracy by 20.68 percentage points on OVO-Bench and 14.15 percentage points on StreamingBench.
authors: Senbin Xu, Zijun Zhang, Xinhua Wu, Li He, Jubo Feng, Li Qiao, Zhen Gao, Yan Zhang, Jixiang Luo, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses the challenge of balancing recent observations with potentially useful—but distracting—historical context.
Uses a lightweight gate to determine whether additional evidence is needed, then retrieves relevant past clips with a multimodal embedding model.
Trains the model to jointly use current and retrieved evidence and abstain when evidence remains insufficient.
Shares a visual encoder across understanding and retrieval branches, with separate language backbones and distillation-based adapters.
With visual-only inputs, reaches 77.78% on evaluated OVO-Bench tasks and 73.31% on StreamingBench; the abstract reports gains over Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct at 2 fps.

papers.abstract: Can autoregressive video diffusion be accelerated further when only four denoising steps remain? Existing feature caching approaches struggle in this regime, as large feature changes between denoising timesteps undermine both direct reuse and lightweight predictors. We observe that features across video chunks remain strongly correlated at matching denoising timesteps, offering a complementary source of guidance. Building on this insight, we introduce TGuide, a framework that accelerates autoregressive video diffusion through a lightweight Anchor-Transport-Correct (ATC) predictor guided by historical sampling trajectories. Our ATC combines two complementary references: the current chunk's preceding-step features preserve its spatial structure, while the previous chunk's same-timestep features provide information at the target denoising stage. By integrating these references through spatial retrieval and adaptive correction, ATC improves velocity prediction accuracy despite the large gaps between denoising steps. To mitigate error accumulation across both denoising steps and video chunks, we train the predictor on its own autoregressive rollouts, allowing it to adapt to states shaped by its own earlier predictions. An optional confidence-aware scheduler further adjusts the quality-efficiency trade-off. Experiments on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay show that TGuide preserves generation quality while achieving denoising speedups of up to $1.89\times$ over the original 4-step generators. On Self Forcing, TGuide generalizes from 81-frame training videos to 333-frame generation, approximately four times the training length, while exceeding the original model's VBench score.
authors: Zhuo Chen, Bin Zou, Fanyue Wei, Lixin Duan, Angela Yao, Wen Li
bullets: Addresses feature-caching failures caused by large changes between the few remaining denoising steps.
Uses an Anchor-Transport-Correct predictor combining the current chunk’s preceding-step features with the previous chunk’s same-timestep features.
Applies spatial retrieval and adaptive correction to improve velocity prediction across large denoising gaps.
Trains on its own autoregressive rollouts to reduce error accumulation across denoising steps and video chunks.
Evaluated on Self Forcing, Causal Forcing, and HY-WorldPlay; on Self Forcing, it generates 333-frame videos from 81-frame training videos while exceeding the original model’s VBench score.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generators synthesize long videos through chunk-wise rollouts, yet they are typically trained to predict only the immediate future. This limited prediction horizon makes it challenging to maintain video quality over extended rollouts. To address this problem, we introduce Prospective Forcing, a multi-head prediction framework that injects long-range predictive signals into autoregressive video representations. Built on a rolling-window generator, Prospective Forcing attaches lightweight, offset-specific heads that share the same conditioning information and independently predict chunks at different future temporal offsets. By extending supervision beyond the next chunk, these heads encourage the shared history representation to retain information useful for longer-horizon prediction, supporting temporally consistent generation. At inference time, we accelerate sampling by using accepted future-chunk predictions to skip full-window backbone executions. We equip the head with learnable embeddings to generate multiple candidates for the next chunk, and a learned verifier either selects a candidate or rejects all and falls back to standard autoregressive generation.
authors: Yifan Shen, Yewei Xia, Gongxu Luo, Peiyuan Zhu, Boyang Sun, Zhenhao Chen, Guangyi Liu, Guangyi Chen, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses quality degradation in long video rollouts caused by training only on the immediate next chunk.
Uses lightweight, offset-specific prediction heads sharing the rolling-window generator’s conditioning information.
Extends supervision to multiple future offsets so representations retain longer-range predictive information.
Accelerates inference by accepting verified future predictions, while falling back to standard generation when candidates are rejected.
Supports multiple next-chunk candidates via learnable embeddings and a learned verifier.

papers.abstract: In autoregressive video generation, retaining all historical key-value (KV) states increases memory usage and per-step attention costs as videos grow longer. A fixed cache budget bounds these costs but raises the challenge of preserving historical content that supports consistent, high-quality generation. Existing methods control cache size through history selection or consolidation, yet deciding what to retain and how to limit the loss of useful content remains a shared challenge. Our analysis shows that spatial queries depend on different historical content and that higher current attention coverage does not necessarily yield better long-video quality. We introduce FrameFold, a training-free KV cache consolidation method that compares the content retrieved by the same recent historical queries before and after merging to guide both representative construction and merge selection. Exploiting temporal redundancy between adjacent historical entries, FrameFold merges their KV states into shared representatives while retaining complete spatial grids. It fits value-merging coefficients in closed form by matching conditional attention responses, then selects the merge with the lowest remaining response distortion. Under matched KV cache budgets, experiments on Self Forcing and Causal Forcing at 30 and 60 seconds and on LongLive at 120 seconds demonstrate improved consistency and visual quality. Continuous eight-minute Self Forcing rollouts further show less quality degradation than the baselines.
authors: Muyu Liu, Mingming Liu, Hong Gu, Yuyao Zhang, Qin Lu
bullets: Fixed-size KV caches reduce memory and attention costs but risk discarding content needed for temporal consistency.
FrameFold uses recent historical queries to compare attention responses before and after candidate merges.
It merges temporally redundant adjacent KV entries into shared representatives while preserving complete spatial grids.
Value-merging coefficients are solved in closed form, and merges are selected to minimize response distortion.
Experiments across 30-second to eight-minute rollouts show better consistency, visual quality, and slower degradation than baselines under matched cache budgets.

papers.tldr: FrameFold is a training-free method that consolidates historical KV caches for long video generation while preserving attention responses and improving long-horizon quality under fixed memory budgets.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive video generation models generate videos sequentially, with each new block conditioned on previously generated blocks. By training on the model's own rollouts, Self Forcing and its follow-up methods substantially mitigate exposure bias caused by the mismatch between training- and inference-time history distributions. However, these models still suffer from error accumulation during long-horizon generation. We identify a key underlying limitation: the model remains highly sensitive to errors in its generated history, allowing small deviations to be amplified through subsequent generations. We refer to this underexplored problem as the local history robustness gap. To address this gap, we introduce Adversarial Gradient Forcing (AGF), a framework designed to improve the robustness of few-step autoregressive video models to perturbations and accumulated errors in their own generated histories. AGF uses distribution matching gradients from future block predictions to select adversarial perturbations of self-generated histories. It then jointly trains the generator on the original and perturbed histories to improve the robustness of future generation. Extensive experiments show that AGF achieves the highest VBench Total score on 60-second video generation and the best visual quality on four-minute video generation. Notably, AGF achieves such long-horizon robustness while requiring only 5-second rollouts for training.
authors: Chenxi Xia, Yixuan Xu, Shan Liu, Jiapeng Wang, Maohua Li, Hanlin Tang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan, Weiyi Lu, Xinggao Liu
bullets: Targets the local history robustness gap: small errors in prior video blocks can be amplified over subsequent generations.
Uses future-prediction distribution-matching gradients to select adversarial perturbations of self-generated histories.
Jointly trains the generator on original and perturbed histories to strengthen few-step generation robustness.
Reports the highest VBench Total score for 60-second generation and best visual quality for four-minute generation.
Achieves long-horizon robustness while training with only 5-second rollouts.

papers.abstract: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.
bullets: Treats explainer videos as auditable programs—scripts, storyboards, and animation code—rendered deterministically into frames.
Logs revision diffs, converts recurring lessons into unit-tested rules, and applies new rules retroactively to prior reels.
Uses bounded, benchmark-gated playbook rewrites, retaining changes only after held-out human preference judgments.
Across 111 reels, learned rules caught earlier latent defects and substantially reduced violations for a weaker director, while lessons shortened revision loops without improving judge scores.
Identifies preference-signal failure modes, including position bias, and documents corresponding checks and fixes; code and data are public.

papers.title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos

papers.abstract: In film production, chroma keying composites an approved foreground performance into a new environment, but conventional workflows require coordinated background plates and dedicated harmonization. Recent generative methods often require pre-aligned backgrounds, focus on background-conditioned foreground relighting, or represent the environment only through an edited first frame. These restrictions limit background selection, scene composition, and camera motion while adding preparation or editing effort. We present FreeCHROMA, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion model in a parameter-efficient manner for generative video compositing from one to three unaligned background references. The model integrates the foreground into the referenced environment, preserving foreground identity, motion, and fine visual details while generating a spatiotemporally coherent background. Foreground-background harmonization occurs within the same generation process, without a separate relighting stage. Optional text instructions help disambiguate complex spatial relationships and camera behavior. To train the model, we construct pseudo-paired data from readily available real monocular videos through foreground-background separation and augmentation with existing foundation models. The original videos serve as training targets, while automated processing and quality verification enable scalable data construction. Across reference fidelity, foreground preservation, scene integration, harmonization, and overall video quality, FreeCHROMA consistently outperforms recent compositing and conditional video-generation baselines, with particularly clear gains under camera motion. FreeCHROMA relaxes the constraints of existing tools to enable end-to-end generative chroma keying from unaligned inputs, with exploratory experiments demonstrating its potential in robotics.
authors: Jiayi Wu, Tianfu Wang, Rui Zhao, Florian Schiffers, Zhimin Chen, Cornelia Fermuller, Yezhou Yang, Christopher Metzler, Yiannis Aloimonos
bullets: Addresses the need for coordinated background plates, manual harmonization, and restricted camera motion in conventional and recent generative compositing workflows.
Parameter-efficiently adapts a pretrained video diffusion model to integrate foregrounds into referenced environments and jointly perform background generation and harmonization.
Uses pseudo-paired training data built from real monocular videos via foreground–background separation, foundation-model augmentation, and automated quality verification.
Optional text instructions help resolve complex spatial relationships and camera behavior.
Reportedly outperforms recent compositing and conditional video-generation baselines across fidelity, preservation, integration, harmonization, and video quality, especially with camera motion.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Parameter-efficient FreeCHROMA architecture. During training, a frozen VAE encodes the target and foreground streams. The noisy target latent, foreground latent, and aligned mask condition are concatenated channel-wise and enter through the expanded patchify projector in eq. (5); background reference tokens are produced by a trainable convolution and prepended to the video sequence; optional text uses the pretrained cross-attention path. Flow-matching supervision updates the added foreground and mask input weights, the background-reference convolution, and DiT LoRA adapters. At inference, the same conditioned denoiser transforms noise into a complete video, which the frozen VAE decodes. Scene synthesis, spatiotemporal composition, and foreground harmonization occur in one denoising process, without an auxiliary relighting or frame-wise harmonization network.

Figure 5: Qualitative ablation of the two training-time augmentations. For each sample we show the environment reference (Target BG), the masked foreground control (Input FG), and two frames of the videos generated by the two ablated models and by the full model (Ours, orange). Without the foreground illumination perturbation, the model tends to copy the illumination of the input foreground instead of re-lighting it for the target environment. Without the background viewpoint augmentation, the model is trained only on pixel-aligned background plates; given an unaligned reference at test time, it tends to force the reference’s viewpoint into the output and composites a scene that is inconsistent with the foreground. The full model re-lights the foreground to match the target environment and uses the reference as an unaligned appearance cue, producing a consistent scene. See the project page for more video examples.

Figure 1: FreeCHROMA and the production constraints it relaxes. Top left: Layer composition requires pre-aligned videos and primarily relights the foreground against a fixed background. First/key-frame editing adds an image-editing step and constrains the environment only in selected views. Top center and right: FreeCHROMA preserves the foreground performance while using one or more unaligned background reference images throughout generation, jointly inferring composition, interactions, camera-aware background evolution, and harmonization, with optional text guidance. Bottom: Masked inputs retain all foreground elements for environment augmentation, the robot and interacting objects for sim-to-real transfer, or only the robot body for visual world modeling.

Figure 2: Automatic pseudo-pair construction from natural videos. Clip curation: A shot detector, conventional image-quality tests, and a vision–language model (VLM) retain clips with a visible foreground and informative background. Foreground augmentation: The VLM enumerates the foreground entities; SAM 3.1 tracks their masks M ; and a temporally coherent photometric and normal-guided illumination transform produces (F̃ ,M). Background reference construction: A motion proxy selects one to three keyframes, a frozen image editor removes all selected entities, a frozen novel-view model changes viewpoint and crop, and a VLM quality gate retains sceneconsistent references R̃. The conditions map to the untouched source video V , yielding scalable supervision without green-screen capture, manual compositing, or 3D annotation. Tool roles and selected models are labeled in the figure; further implementation details are provided in Appendix D. Visuals are schematic.

Figure 7: Qualitative robotics applications. Rendered RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2026) (top) and masked DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) (bottom) arms; green/red panels show successful/failed interactions. See the project page for more video examples.

Top: the simulated source video and the rendered robot-object interaction used as foreground control (the arm together with the manipulated objects). Below: the videos generated by FreeCHROMA from eight different environment reference images, shown at the same frames. The same simulated action is re-rendered into every environment while the arm motion and the object interaction are preserved. See the project page for more video examples.

papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) need to understand how entities move and interact as a scene develops. This requires following the same entities over time and relating their observed motion to subsequent changes. We formulate Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU), a task for predicting and interpreting this change. Given observed video, a model estimates entity histories and predicts one scene continuation through future trajectories and Events, accompanied by Visual Evidence from observed motion and a scene description. We construct SceneForesee, a benchmark for evaluating entity continuity and scene evolution reasoning through paired observed and future scenes with shared entity identities. It contains 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K Events paired with observed evidence. We propose a spatiotemporal reasoning framework, EvoSee, that learns future geometry and Event semantics through shared candidate states and joint assignment. It selects one continuation per entity from observation and uses the selected changes for entity refinement, retention, and scene representation. On SceneForesee, EvoSee outperforms Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1. On the 4D reasoning benchmark Dyn-Bench, it improves question answering accuracy and grounding J&F by 4.8 and 3.58 points over their respective base systems. These results support scene evolution as both a prediction target and a dynamic representation that brings predicted entity changes into spatiotemporal reasoning.The project is available at https://github.com/mikubaka88/SceneForesee-Spatiotemporal-Reasoning.
authors: Chaoyue Li, Shoudong Han, Haoyang Wu, Boxue Yang, Sijia Chen, Yufan Chen, Ruping Zhang
bullets: Defines Scene Evolution Understanding (SEU): tracking entity continuity, forecasting future trajectories and events, and grounding predictions in observed visual evidence.
SceneForesee provides paired observed/future scenes with shared identities, including 144.57K temporal pairs, 1.05M entity correspondences, and 272.49K evidence-linked events.
EvoSee jointly reasons over future geometry and event semantics using shared candidate states and entity assignment.
EvoSee improves over Qwen3.5-9B by 10.45 points in Combined Point-F1 and 17.24 points in Event Global F1.
It also improves Dyn-Bench question answering and grounding, supporting predicted entity changes as dynamic representations for spatiotemporal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models increasingly serve as priors for 4D generation, but the generated videos often lack geometric consistency. Recent approaches address this through post-training by designing geometric rewards, yet this can degrade texture and fine detail, requiring auxiliary appearance rewards and careful reward balancing. To address this challenge, we propose GeoFix, a unified framework that improves geometric consistency and visual quality with a single geometric reward, applicable to both training and inference-time reward alignment. Our reward measures cross-view depth consistency in static scene regions, targeting structural inconsistencies without directly constraining appearance or penalizing valid object motion. Crucially, depth agreement increases with camera field-of-view overlap even in real videos and 4D datasets, allowing a smaller camera movement to be mistaken for better geometry. We account for this effect by calibrating the reward against the overlap-dependent trend. GeoFix achieves a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.
authors: Yeobin Hong, Hyojun Go, Dohun Lee, Jeongjae Lee, Sunghwan Hong, Federico Tombari, Zhaochong An, Jong Chul Ye, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses geometric inconsistency in video-diffusion-based 4D generation.
Uses one reward for both training-time and inference-time alignment, avoiding appearance-reward balancing.
Measures depth agreement in static scene regions while preserving valid object motion and appearance.
Calibrates for camera field-of-view overlap, which can otherwise make smaller camera movements appear geometrically better.
Reports a 39% improvement in WorldScore 3D consistency and a 4% increase in VBench Quality Score.

papers.abstract: Understanding and tracking a dynamic world are fundamental to visual intelligence. Existing video benchmarks provide limited insight into whether models can maintain a coherent understanding of evolving world state. Building such a benchmark from real-world videos is challenging because the underlying world state is partially observable, making annotations hard to obtain. To close this gap, we introduce Video-Arena, a benchmark that turns competitive games into scalable, verifiable tests of how well models understand evolving world states from videos. Specifically, inspired by how humans understand dynamic events, we evaluate spatiotemporal world state understanding and tracking through three task categories: perceiving critical events, interpreting state updates, and tracking the resulting states. Our pipeline can generate videos and aligned reference labels from game records at scale. To keep evaluation affordable and reproducible, we curate a golden set of 180 tasks across 9 games and run evaluations under two protocols: native visual understanding and tool-assisted agentic analysis. The best-performing systems achieve F1 scores of and under the two protocols, respectively. The result highlights that native models struggle to perceive events reliably, while tool-assisted systems improve event recovery but still struggle to interpret state updates and track the resulting states consistently over time. Our project page is in https://videoarena-bench.github.io
authors: Kuan Zhang, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yue Su, Xiangnan Wu, Zirong Chen, Run Luo, Tao Tan, Yinhe Zheng, Yiming Li
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating coherent understanding of partially observable, dynamic world states in real-world videos.
Generates videos and aligned reference labels from competitive game records at scale.
Covers three capabilities: critical-event perception, state-update interpretation, and resulting-state tracking.
Includes 180 tasks across 9 games under native visual-understanding and tool-assisted agentic protocols.
Finds that tools improve event recovery, but systems still struggle with state interpretation and consistent temporal tracking; the abstract omits the reported F1 values.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Video-Arena. papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) typically applies a shared scale to all latent tokens, although their velocity predictions evolve differently during sampling. We introduce Trajectory-Adaptive Classifier-Free Guidance (TrajCFG), a training-free method for flow-matching models that adapts token-wise guidance using historical changes in guided velocity direction. TrajCFG maps this feedback to bounded scales, assigning stronger guidance to larger directional changes and weaker guidance to more consistent directions. It combines adjacent-step and interval-normalized longer-span feedback, reusing standard CFG predictions without additional model evaluations. Controlled diagnostics and ablations examine the roles of directional feedback, token-wise allocation, and history-span fusion. Experiments on text-to-video, image-to-video, text-to-audio-video, text-to-image, and image-to-3D generation show improvements over base samplers across multiple backbones. For text-to-video generation, TrajCFG improves VBench Total scores by 0.30-0.75 points over the strongest evaluated baseline on each of three backbones. These results support historical directional feedback as a broadly applicable signal for fine-grained guidance allocation. The project page is available at https://jyliu-98.github.io/trajcfg-project-page/.
authors: Jingyu Liu, Hao Jiang, Yikang Ding, Huafeng Shi, Xu Yang, Xiaoqiang Liu, Guoxin Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Kun Gai
bullets: Addresses the limitation of using one shared CFG scale despite different token-wise sampling dynamics.
Uses adjacent-step and longer-span trajectory feedback to assign stronger guidance to larger directional changes and weaker guidance to consistent directions.
Is training-free and reuses standard CFG predictions, requiring no additional model evaluations.
Evaluated across text-to-video, image-to-video, text-to-audio-video, text-to-image, and image-to-3D generation.
Improves text-to-video VBench Total scores by 0.30–0.75 points over the strongest evaluated baseline across three backbones.

papers.abstract: Accurate artery extraction from X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) is essential for coronary artery disease diagnosis and intervention. However, low vessel visibility, respiratory and cardiac motion, and limited annotations challenge existing methods. Moreover, most deep learning approaches produce binary vessel masks without preserving clinically relevant intra-arterial contrast information. We propose a Temporal Diffusion Bridge Model (TDBM) that formulates vessel extraction as image translation and learns from physics-informed synthetic data without manual vessel annotations. A physics-based XCA synthesis engine generates diverse, perfectly aligned pairs of contrast-enhanced and contrast-free images. Using these pairs, TDBM learns cross-domain mappings to recover high-fidelity vessel information. Temporal conditioning incorporates adjacent frames to improve consistency, while a vessel-aware contrastive loss exploits background-invariant synthetic pairs to enhance vascular discrimination. We evaluate TDBM on two XCA vessel segmentation datasets and conduct a reader study using two real-patient XCA sequence datasets. Zero-shot segmentation is further assessed on retinal imaging and fluorescence microscopy datasets. Results demonstrate that TDBM consistently outperforms existing methods and generalizes effectively across imaging modalities. Code and trained weights will be available at: https://github.com/Advanced-AI-in-Medicine-and-Physics-Lab/TDBM
authors: Jinkui Hao, Donald R. Cantrell, Ramez Abdalla, Sameer A. Ansari, Bo Zhou
bullets: Addresses poor vessel visibility, cardiac and respiratory motion, and limited annotated XCA data.
Generates aligned contrast-enhanced/contrast-free image pairs with a physics-based synthesis engine.
Uses temporal conditioning and vessel-aware contrastive learning to improve consistency and vascular discrimination.
Evaluated on XCA segmentation, real-patient sequence reader studies, and zero-shot retinal and fluorescence microscopy tasks.
Reports consistent improvements over existing methods and effective cross-modality generalization, without specifying numeric results.

papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.

Introduces 204 tasks spanning 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations.
Evaluates 8 frontier image-to-video models from an initial workspace image and natural-language instruction.
Shows a substantial gap between visually realistic videos and procedurally accurate experimental guidance.

papers.abstract: Video segmentation models recognize and track objects over time, but they do not indicate whether each segmented region moves independently of the observing camera. This dynamicity attribute cannot be inferred from semantics alone and is confounded by camera ego-motion. We introduce \method, an online framework that augments query-based video segmentation with region-level dynamicity prediction. It jointly produces the original segmentation outputs and a dynamic or static state for each predicted region. At inference, DynEoMT uses only the current frame and propagated queries, without optical flow, depth, camera pose, previous RGB frames, or feature maps. Because established video segmentation benchmarks do not annotate this attribute, we also introduce a class-agnostic offline supervision pipeline using camera-compensated optical flow and confidence-aware temporal filtering. Across VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, DynEoMT achieves balanced accuracies of 84.3, 68.0, 68.6, and 87.6, respectively, while largely preserving segmentation performance. These results show that segmentation-region dynamicity can be learned from propagated queries, enabling its online prediction without a dedicated motion-processing pipeline at inference. The complete code will be released as open source to enable full reproduction of the method and experiments.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of distinguishing independently moving objects from camera-induced motion, which semantics alone cannot resolve.
Jointly predicts segmentation masks and region-level dynamicity without optical flow, depth, camera pose, previous RGB frames, or feature maps at inference.
Introduces an offline supervision pipeline based on camera-compensated optical flow and confidence-aware temporal filtering.
Evaluated on VIPSeg, OVIS, YouTube-VIS 2022, and VSPW, achieving balanced accuracies of 84.3, 68.0, 68.6, and 87.6 while largely preserving segmentation performance.

figures.caption: Figure 3. DynEoMT architecture. Current image patches and object queries propagated from the preceding frame are jointly processed by the ViT encoder. The resulting queries feed the original classification and mask heads together with the proposed query-level dynamicity head, and are then propagated to the next frame. The propagated queries constitute the only temporal context available at inference. The dynamicity branch is the sole architectural addition to VidEoMT; no previous or future RGB frames, optical flow, depth, or camera pose are required.

Figure 1. Overview of DynEoMT. The current image and the queries propagated from the previous frame are jointly processed by a ViT. The resulting current queries feed the original segmentation heads and the added dynamicity head, producing segmentation outputs and dynamic/static predictions.

Figure 2. Offline dynamicity pseudo-label construction. MemFlow supplies bidirectional optical flow between paired frames. Forward– backward consistency filtering removes unreliable correspondences. A camera-induced flow model is then robustly selected, and its predicted flow is subtracted from the observed flow. Residual-motion evidence is aggregated within each annotated mask. Confidence-aware temporal filtering assigns a dynamic, static, or uncertain target. The procedure is class-agnostic and is used only to construct training supervision.

papers.abstract: We present HorizonNav, a video diffusion-based framework for anticipatory robot navigation that transforms a single RGB image and a text prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding 3D space. Given the initial observation and a textual description of the reconstruction objective, a vision-language model, guided by designed instructions, interprets the scene and constructs structured prompts for a video diffusion model. The resulting video sequence provides plausible future observations of the environment, which are subsequently processed using monocular ORB-SLAM3 for camera pose estimation and Video Depth Anything for dense depth prediction. Our central contribution is a geometry-guided depth alignment stage that combines the estimated camera poses with triangulated visual landmarks to constrain dense depth predictions across multiple views. This alignment improves the geometric consistency of the reconstructed 3D environment, addressing inconsistencies that temporal coherence of the generated video alone cannot resolve. The experimental evaluation of navigation in imagined 3D environment shows that across a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes increase from 13/19 at P20 to 15/19 at P81, while successful RRT trials increase from 62/90 to 75/90. In a separate corridor study, 6 of 25 evaluable generated-camera trajectories violate the reconstructed collision constraints; RRT planner recovers feasible alternatives in 5 of those 6 cases. A larger archive contains 58 usable reconstructions from 67 attempted cases, of which 36 support a downstream plan and 22 do not, exposing reconstruction and free-space failure modes rather than hiding them without lidar. Across 15 corridor reconstructions, the mean reconstruction error is approximately 0.30 m at matched structural landmarks.
authors: Hajira Amjad, Valerii Serpiva, Viacheslav Liubimov, Didar Seyidov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Generates plausible future views from one RGB observation plus a textual reconstruction objective.
Uses a vision-language model to guide prompts for video diffusion, then applies ORB-SLAM3 and Video Depth Anything.
Aligns dense depth with camera poses and triangulated landmarks to improve multi-view geometric consistency.
In a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes rose from 13/19 to 15/19, and successful RRT trials from 62/90 to 75/90.
The approach remains subject to reconstruction and free-space failures; matched-landmark error was approximately 0.30 m across 15 corridor reconstructions.

Exploratory video generation: Wan 2.2 synthesizes plausible future observations along multiple virtual camera trajectories. Geometry-guided 3D reconstruction: ORB-SLAM3 estimates camera poses and sparse landmarks, while Video Depth Anything predicts dense depth maps. Landmark-guided depth alignment, multi-view registration, and point-cloud fusion produce a geometrically consistent imagined 3D map for subsequent robot navigation and path planning.

Left: representative exploration branches showing generated RGB, dense-depth diagnostic, ORB-SLAM3 sparse structure, and corresponding real-view references. papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard technique for improving conditional generation in diffusion models, yet its activation schedule is usually selected heuristically. In practice, most existing CFG-based methods rely on a pre-defined activation policy throughout inference, while recent dynamic variants often depend on hand-designed schedules without a principled theoretical explanation of when conditional information is most useful. In order to understand how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves over the course of generation, we explore when guidance should be activated from an information-theoretic perspective. In this work, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout sampling, but becomes significantly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition. Motivated by this insight, we propose a training-free dynamic CFG strategy for inference. Rather than prescribing a fixed schedule in advance, our method constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and activates guidance when the estimated guidance gain crosses a prescribed threshold. This yields an adaptive activation rule that aligns condition injection with the underlying generation dynamics, while also recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks, demonstrate that our method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable. Beyond empirical improvements, our framework provides an interpretation of dynamic guidance methods and a principled foundation for inference-time control in conditional diffusion models.
authors: Jiayang Gao, Tianyi Zheng, Jiayang Zou, Fengxiang Yang, Luyao Fan, Lv Tang, Bo Li, Jia Wang
bullets: CFG activation schedules are typically heuristic and fixed or hand-designed.
The diffusion trajectory is modeled as a time-dependent information bottleneck.
Conditional information becomes substantially more useful after a critical stage identified by a Fisher-information balance condition.
A training-free method activates CFG when estimated guidance gain exceeds a threshold, using conditional and unconditional score statistics.
Experiments across architectures and tasks show the approach is effective, robust, and broadly applicable; interval-based guidance emerges as a special case.

papers.abstract: Video generation supports digital content creation, with applications in virtual avatars, AI-driven filmmaking, interactive game engines, and world models. State-of-the-art systems achieve controllability primarily through image-to-video (I2V) generation, in which an injected anchor image determines the identity, composition, and style of the resulting video. In modern pipelines, this anchor is synthesized by a text-to-image (T2I) generator. This raises a largely overlooked question: Are images obtained directly from the T2I model truly suitable for current video models? Our analysis shows that anchor aesthetic and quality scores are weakly correlated with downstream video quality. The structure-and-texture score is negatively correlated with I2V video quality in both the visual and motion dimensions. Fine-tuning the T2I model on an image reward accordingly yields anchors with visibly denser structural and character detail: they score higher on image metrics, yet lower the video reward on every I2V model we test and change downstream motion unpredictably. We therefore introduce Golden Anchor Learning (GAL), to our knowledge the first framework for learning golden anchors by optimizing a T2I generator with downstream video feedback. GAL evaluates candidate anchors through the videos they induce under a frozen I2V model and converts video rewards into image-level preferences for DPO fine-tuning of the T2I generator. On all four I2V models, GAL raises the VBench average by $2.97\%$--$8.46\%$ over the untuned generator. The rendered clips also score higher under VideoReward-Overall, and their extracted frames under HPSv3 and UniPercept. GAL yields consistent motion gains across all four I2V models, as measured by a $5.62\%$--$38.24\%$ increase in VBench dynamic degree. Although GAL is trained only on HunyuanVideo-1.5 renders, these gains extend to the other three I2V models.
authors: Jinyuan Xu, Shitong Shao, Lichen Bai, Zikai Zhou, Guoxi Huang, Nantheera Anantrasirichai, Zeke Xie
bullets: Image aesthetic and quality scores poorly predict the quality of videos generated from an anchor image.
Fine-tuning the image generator solely on image rewards can worsen video quality and produce unpredictable motion.
GAL evaluates candidate anchors through videos from a frozen I2V model, then uses video-derived preferences for DPO fine-tuning.
Across four I2V models, GAL improves VBench average by 2.97%–8.46% and dynamic degree by 5.62%–38.24%.
Although trained with HunyuanVideo-1.5 renders, GAL’s gains transfer to three other I2V models.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of GAL. Training (top): For each prompt, we sample K = 4 anchor images from the T2I generator, render each into a video with a frozen I2V model, and score the videos with a frozen video-reward model. We use these scores to construct image-level preference pairs and fine-tune only the upstream T2I generator with cross-modal DPO. Video rendering, scoring, and pair construction are performed offline. Inference (bottom): The fine-tuned T2I generator produces anchor images that improve video quality, while the downstream I2V model remains unchanged.

Figure 1: In the shown examples, the GAL anchor induces more in-scene motion in every one-second interval across all four I2V models. Top: within each I2V-model block, rows are clips rendered from Base (the anchor produced by the untuned image model), GAL-Image (trained based on image rewards), and our GAL anchor (trained based video rewards), under the same prompt and renderer; four frames span each clip. Bottom: line plots of per-interval motion for the same clips, measured as the mean residual optical-flow magnitude inside each one-second interval (Appendix G).

Pearson correlation between UniPercept scores of the anchor (IAA: aesthetics; IQA: quality; ISTA: structure and texture) and VideoReward scores of its HunyuanVideo-1.5 render (VQ: visual quality; MQ: motion quality; TA: text alignment) over 49,416 (prompt–anchor–video) records. Aesthetics and quality are nearly uncorrelated with every video axis, and structure/texture is anti-correlated with visual and motion quality.

Table 4: Reward-signal ablation within GAL, evaluated by video and frame rewards on HunyuanVideo-1.5. Among the compared variants, GAL-VideoReward alone improves all three scores over Base on HunyuanVideo-1.5 and all three transfer models (Table 8 in Appendix H). We therefore use it as the default variant. Metrics and parentheses follow Table 2.

Table 2: Main reward-model comparison across four I2V models. GAL (ours) improves all three reward scores over Base on every model. VideoReward-Overall scores rendered clips; HPSv3 and UniPercept score their extracted frames. Parentheses give absolute changes from Base.

Table 5: DPO pair count as a function of the absolute reward margin threshold m on the GAL-VideoReward pair manifest. All reward variants use the same operating point, m = 0.05, on their own reward-specific pair manifests (GAL-VideoReward: 52,084 pairs), each landing near a ≈ 5×104-pair budget. A controlled pair-count sweep that holds data volume fixed across margins is listed as future work.

Table 7: Anchor-seed sensitivity of the binary VBench dynamic-degree readout. For each of the 72 official VBench dynamic-degree prompts, we sample 12 seed-conditioned sibling anchors from the same T2I generator and render them with each frozen I2V model under a fixed downstream setting. VBench returns a binary label d ∈ {0, 1} for each rendered clip. We report the overall dynamic fraction and the prompt-averaged within-prompt variance across the 12 seeds. Low variance means that changing the seed-conditioned anchor rarely changes the binary dynamic/static decision for the same prompt. WAN has the highest dynamic fraction and the lowest within-prompt variance, indicating a near-saturated and low-sensitivity dynamic-degree readout.
